EDITORIAL

I am sure every one of our members who has read this magazine in the past three years would like to join me in saying an outsize thankyou to Eleanor for all the work she has put in, making it possible for us to following closely all that goes on in our happy circle, of what my small son calls "boat crazy" friends.

As she points out in the November issue, this would not have been possible without the "professional" help of all the typing by Avril. I must certainly try to keep up the high standard - but perhaps you will allow me a few mistakes to begin with.

On top of this, of course, I have now to learn how to "crew" our own boat (or is the correct term dinghy). I expect I shall get Ron and myself into quite a few muddles in the season ahead, before I begin to understand all the rules. At least I now know there is not much port left in the bottle, so with any luck we shall start the race in the right direction!

Mary Greygoose

LADY ANNE'S SUMMER CRUISE 1969

I. G. Tate

Continued from last month

Monday 21st July

0020. We cleared the harbour and headed for Dungeness, having spent three hours of a fair tide in a fruitless but necessary operation.

0135. We were back where we had to break off, and once again on looking astern for traffic I spotted flares in the same position. However, this time they were three green flares and meant that the coastguards were standing by ready to assist anyone coming ashore at that position.

0400. Found us just off Dungeness Point as dawn was making the eastern horizon visible.

0415. Clear of Dungeness, moderate swell, good visibility, wind SW 2-3. Set 255 deg. on the grid compass for Beachy Head.

0500. Frances and the dog turned in after coffee and biscuits. Full daylight, visibility 10 miles, but signs of fog to the south of us.

Started using the Seafix D.F. radio, and was delighted to hear the light programme giving reports of the American moon landing.

Soon we were in dense fog and had to shut down to three knots for safety, anxious about collisions, despite having edged well inshore of the direct line between headlands.

0530. Came into a clear patch and got a bearing of a Headland with cliffs. Hastings or Fairlight. The D.R. position was marked up every hour.

0900. Still patchy, occasional clearances showed cliffs and coastline about 4 miles N of us. Set sail, filled petrol tank and headed 330 deg. to close the coast. I was not keen to cross the Royal Sovereign shoals. Had a delicious fried breakfast.

0930. Obtained a good fix at 4 miles S. of Bexhill.

1030. I turned in leaving Frances and the children to tack westwards in fair visibility and with sure knowledge of our position.

1145. Frances called me on deck again as we were approaching more fog. Fortunately it did not really clamp down as it had earlier on.

1220. We were almost stopped by strong tide, so the engine was started and motor sailed round Beachy Head, which we cleared at 1430, stopped the engine once clear of the tide. The stretch from Beachy Head to Newhaven was made on the port tack with the old boat striding over the long swell and going like a train.

1600. Entered the outer harbour and dropped sail. Quite literally! The stopper at the base of the main track had turned and as I freed the halliard the sail ran down and out of the track, all over the decks. Replacing the sail and stowing allowed time for the "Falaise" to enter, then we got clearance and in we went.

1720. Alongside the fuel pontoon we paid 7s. 0d. harbour dues and took on 12 gallons of Petrol and six gallons of water. I took the children and dog for a walk on dry land, the latter being delighted at finding grass, the last was at Stansgate! We walked round the marina and up to the coast guard cottages where I gave full details of our incident.

- 4 -

2030. We were moored on the eastern pier just astern of Walter Standing's "Jonelle". Frances really did us proud with steak and vegetables.

2100. The children and I were in our bunks, and a long trip was over.

Tuesday 22nd July

Unanimously declared a day of rest and recreation.

Wednesday 23rd July

1400. Forecast gave variables 1-2, thundery showers, moderate to good with fog patches. We decided to make for the Beaulieu River, sailing through the night to keep the children out of the way whilst we were at sea.

1445. Started engine and left Newhaven. The harbour dues were for 48 hours stay so we didn't have to pay further.

1500. Set heading of 258 deg. for the Owers light vessel. Plotted position until we lost sight of land at 1600. Ground speed 4.3 knots. E.T.A. Owers 21.30 hrs. I kept a close check on the echosounder and we moved steadily along the 15 fathom line.

1720. A fishing boat crossed our track at right angles and we guessed he was going to Shoreham. This agreed with our D.R. position.

1800. A depth of 18 fathoms indicated that the tide had set us to the S. of our course by 1½ miles. Altered Hdg. to 264 deg. to compensate. The depth contours agreed O.K. with D.R. position until 2030 when a sudden hole of 5 fathoms showed up. A check on the chart indicated we were again ½ mile to S. of our course, but as we were now only about 4 miles from the Lightvessel we decided to hold our heading.

2015. Sighted Owers on the port bow, bearing 230 deg.M. This was unexpected, as it put us 1¾ miles N. of our course.

2040. Alongside Owers Lightvessel. A careful check of chart, tide tables, time and echosounder indicated that our echosounder was over-reading by 3 fathoms in 15. Thus we had not been set to the S. and if I had maintained our original heading I think we would only have been ½ mile off the Owers as we passed it. Anyhow, it was a relief to find the Owers, and I relaxed considerably. The run from the Owers to the Nab was complicated by a strong cross tide, but back bearings on the Owers confirmed our correction was O.K. E.T.A. Nab 2230.

2232. Alongside Nab. Set heading for Nab End buoy, visibility much improved.

From now onwards I was largely occupied in identifying bouys seen by Frances. Her visual acuity is better than mine, and she stayed on watch until we were well into Spithead, by the No Man's Land Fort. From here on the bouys were close together and I carried on alone in the cockpit. There was still not enough wind to make sail, but it was a pleasantly warm night.

Thursday 24th July

Dawn found us steaming around waiting for enough light to enter Newtown Creek on the Isle of Wight, where we dropped anchor in 2 fathoms at 0530.

The children were up and about as we came in, so a hearty breakfast was eaten and we all went back to our bunks till 1030. Bless them, Fiona and Nigel played quietly in the foc'sle whilst we slept.

Our arrival at our holiday cruising area called for celebration, so lunch was Spaghetti Bolognaise with the best part of a litre of Rose.

In the afternoon we sailed Puffin up to the delightful stone quay at the head of Shalfleet creek, and walked the mile to the village of Shalfleet. We bought provisions, cards and ices at the only shop in the village, and had a beer at the only inn!

- 5 -

We phoned my brother in Weymouth to confirm that we would meet him here sometime after Sunday.

Anchored near us was a boat that had been with Lady Anne in Christchurch many years ago, in fact as my father had admired her varnished topsides she was really the reason that Lady Anne is varnished now. She was now in new hands and apart from a really good fit out below, she remains much as she always was.

On Saturday morning the Solent became alive with craft and soon aircraft and helicopters appeared. Lots of large motor boats were dashing down the Solent and slowly it dawned on me that we were watching the start of the 'Round Britain' powerboat race. I mentally put my money on the Navy to win, as a friend in the Service says that on the bridge of H.M.S. Brave Borderer is a polished plaque engraved: 'Winner of Daily Express Offshore Power Boat Race 1959-1960-1961-1962-etc!'

Sunday 27th July

Fiona's fourth birthday and she delighted us by joining in a pre-breakfast swim off Lady Anne. She climbed down the bumpkin stays and sat on the rudder before summoning courage to float off in her lifejacket. The only other time she had floated off was off the beach at Stansgate. As she had learnt to row a fortnight earlier you may guess Frances and I felt ten feet tall.

In the evening we went ashore to Hampstead Farm for provisions (mostly ice cream of course) and imagine our pleasure at seeing Freedom entering the creek. We shouted and waved greetings from the dinghy and just had time to get aboard Lady Anne and put fenders out.

The arrival of Freedom was really the start of the 'holiday' part of our cruise. We sailed in company and spent nights on trots or on our anchor with Freedom always alongside.

We visited Yarmouth, Beaulieu, Cowes for the start of Cowes week, ending up in Bembridge harbour at the end of our second week. At Bembridge we had Freedom and Lady Anne ashore on the beach just inside the harbour. We had legs for Lady Anne, and as high water was about 7 o'clock we were able to spend 2 or 3 days of pure sand and sun with the children. Puffin was sailed a lot, on one occasion towing a tired young swimmer ashore.

to be continued...

G.P. PATTER. JAN. 1970.

As most of you will know by now the Hon. Sec. of the G.P. 14 Association, Mr. Howard Davis, has resigned his office. All correspondence to the Association should now be addressed to the Acting Sec. Mr. George Mainwaring, Park Wood, [redacted], Baldwins Gate, Newcastle, Staffs.

Mr. D. Baker of the Leigh-on-Sea S.C. has been appointed Trade Liason Officer, his function will be to keep in touch with manufacturers and suppliers with special interest in those firms which produce hulls and equipment under licence from the Association. If you should have any problems concerning poor design or bad workmanship and have not been able to obtain satisfaction yourself, then Mr. Baker will take up the cudgell on your behalf.

Taking over Mr. Baker's previous job as S.E. Area Representative will be Gordon Parr (7531) of the Stone S.C.

The development of the G.P. 14 Class continues, and by the beginning of the season we shall have new rulings on mainsheet sheeting and Genoa luff tensioning. It is almost certain that the new ruling will permit centre main sheeting complete with full width horse and traveller; so if you know where to lay your hands on some 1" diameter stainless steel tube, do so with all speed.

On the competitive side of the sport it looks as though we shall have a very full season. Apart from our own club points series and handicap events, I have arranged team events against three local clubs, viz: Osea, Stone, and Maldon. These will be Saturday events. There are also a number of open events in the localty including the Area Championships at Leigh-on-Sea on the 6-7 June. Leigh will also be the venue of the 1971 G.P. 14 World Championships.

EDITORIAL

Ladies! Are you ready - on top form? The season is quickly creeping up on us, and this year we have five races instead of one for our own cup. Lets show the men what we are made of. When I say 'we' I mean 'you', of course. I could no more helm a boat than fly an aeroplane. Anyway, I shall be there to cheer you on.

Talking of aeroplanes - for those of you who did'nt see the Maldon and Burnham Standard of January 15th - Osea Island has been purchased by two Cambridge brothers who plan to build an airstrip on the Island. This way they can travel from home to Osea in 20 minutes, a journey they hope to make at weekends whenever possible. You will also be pleased to hear that they plan to keep the Island in its present state, not disturbing the heronry, as they are both keen bird-watchers. They are also very keen sailors so we need have no fear of them upsetting us. There was an aerial view of the Island in the paper which I will pin to the notice board at Stansgate.

As you will see, Ian Tate concludes his log this month. I am sure you would all like to join me in saying thankyou for this and also for the most enjoyable talk with slides last Friday, the 6th Feb. This was attended by a great number of members. The whole evening went down very well with the expert showing (by Norman Palmer) of three films of great interest to all sailors. Lets hope we can have a lot more of them.

LADY ANNE'S SUMMER CRUISE

Thursday 7th August

'Freedom' left on her homeward voyage, taking with her memories of a very happy time spent in lots of "old familiar places" under the finest continuous spell of sunny weather I can remember.

We spent a lazy day on the beach, but the spell was broken. The return part of the voyage was now imminent and I was itching to get going whilst the weather held fair. Bembridge is a very shallow harbour and the entrance channel all but dried out, consequently we should have to leave within two hours of high water.

Friday 8th August

The forecast was NE-E 4, good; fair. The morning breeze seemed firmer than of late, and if it followed the same pattern of freshening during the day we were in for a rough ride.

0800. All was stowed, the dinghy lashed on deck, kedge retrieved from the beach, a good meal inside us and we were homeward bound.

We left under engine, but on getting outside, where it was blowing about 5 by the number of white horses, I decided to stay under engine and plug away to the Owers Lightvessel and then close reach to Newhaven. It was very rough and wet, just keeping one's balance was a major effort. The steep seas were short enough to badly hamper Lady Anne and progress was pretty slow.

1000. Alongside the Nab Tower, at this rate ETA Owers was 1300, and it seemed that we would not be able to lay Newhaven from there. The children, despite their medicine, were showing signs of distress and I was not keen to plug away to windward for the whole leg singlehanded.

1030. Decided to turn back, set headsail, stopped engine and ran back to Spithead. By this time Bembridge entrance was too shoal.

We decided to have a day out and sail to Cowes. On the way we passed the Malcolm Millar beating out of Spithead, the SS 'United States' passed us about 300 yards off, and then we passed 'Queen Elizabeth 2' at about a quarter of a mile. These big ships made very little wash and no noise and present a grand spectacle on a sunny day. The children also found the large number of hovercraft ferries absorbing, although to my ear the noise level was appaling. May we long keep them out of the Blackwater! In the evening we had a grandstand view of the traditional Cowes fireworks much to Fiona's delight.

Saturday

Funny wet stuff fell out of a grey sky on and off all day, the coachroof leaked, (too much sun), we had the dinghy on deck and the children could not go ashore. It was blowing hard most of the day, but did moderate in the evening. The forecast for Sunday was SE3-6, thundery showers, poor, fog patches, Not so good.

Sunday 10th August

One week left. We missed the early forecast, but the weather seemed to have settled fair again. The midday forecast gave us variable 3 fair, with moderate visibility.

- 4 -

1345. We were under way again bound for Newhaven. The breeze was fitful and we did not make sail until we were well past Ryde.

1500. I turned in below and managed to doze off for nearly two hours.

1700. Frances was at the helm, taking us fairly close to the Nab when suddenly it let out a VERY LARGE HOOT. There was a slight haze, and a liner about 3 miles off was changing course.

Frances took this hoot as a personal criticism by this concrete behemoth, and felt there was injustice in the world of seafarers. Why had it done it? What did it mean? The skipper was roused and mumbled somtething technical about fog in the western approaches, but really it was not foggy. Once started these things catch on, and soon we could hear the moan of the Owers Lightvessel off ahead of us.

1930. We had to motor the last mile to the Owers as the wind had died completely, leaving the sea like a great heaving mirror. The wind did not pick up again that night, and shortly after sunset I handed the sails.

Monday.

0200. Entered Newhaven, paid our dues, moored up to yachts on E.quay, and had fried fresh mackrell as an early breakfast. We had caught the mackrell on spinners whilst under way. Monday was a rest day, Tuesday brought a poor forecast, E4-5, and that night we had a severe thunderstorm.

Wednesday.

A lot less breezy, but we could see the entrance from the quay and there was a big sea running outside. During the evening the wind dropped almost to nothing, and the forecast for Thursday was quite good but with other sea areas having rain and wind.

Thursday.

In the morning the entrance locked O.K. and we decided to make for Dover or Ramsgate.

By departing Newhaven at the correct time one can carry the flood up to near Hastings, where the tidal streams change direction, then the ebb will also carry you to the east. Hence by planning to be at Hastings or Rye about an hour after H.W. Dover a fair tide of ten hours can be achieved.

0830. Departed Newhaven bound for Ramsgate. Wind var.2, long swell but not uncomfortably steep.

0950. BeachyHead, out of the lee of the Seven Sisters, we found the true wind to be E2-3. ETA Dungeness 1430.

1200. Dungeness and Beachy Head both faintly visible. Nigel and I managed to get two hours sleep.

1500. Dungeness abeam. A bit rough as we passed the point. It had now clouded over and shortly after it started to rain in earnest. Wind E3-4. ETA Dover 1830. ETA Ramsgate 2230. visibility had now decreased considerably in the heavy rain and a very anxious lookout for steamers was kept. Three times we had to turn well off course to avoid Dover harbour traffic, and as the tide was now hard against us it seemed to take an age to get clear of the harbour area. High water was at 0100 and as darkness descended we headed up the lighted Gull Stream rather than the unlit Ramsgate Channel.

- 5 -

At one stage when Frances was at the helm, while I plotted a fix out of the rain, she called for advice on a strange group of lights surmounted by a 'Qk. Fl. Or'. This phenomena was moving fast and turned out to be a hovercraft bound for Pegwell Bay.

2430. We finally locked into the inner harbour, wet and tired but feeling glad to be hearer home.

Friday.

Another day of torrential rain, I rigged sails and covers over our leaky hatch and coachroof. The local fuel merchant supplied a small bag of coke and despite the weather we got all clothing bone dry.

Saturday.

We locked out at high water.

1330. Alongside fuel pontoon and took on 11 gallons.

1400. Departed Ramsgate bound for Stansgate. Forecast N-NW 2-3 fiar, moderate.

We had to motor in a very steep short sea, which only moderated near Tongue Sand Tower. Our track took us up the S. Edinburgh channel, Mid Barrow we waited for the tide before setting off for 'home'. We picked up our mooring at 0200 Sunday morning, 12 hours out from Ramsgate with a light headwind and a spring ebb all across the Thames estuary.

CONCLUSIONS

We had achieved the object of our cruise, by getting to and from the Solent, and in successfully meeting up with Freedom.

The engine was used far more than we expected, although to be fair we had headwinds for all but our first mornings sail. It was quite uncanny how the Easterly wind swung round to the N.East when we could at last use an easterly for our last leg homeward.

The catering had panned out very well, 2 crates (36 pints) of Long Life milk had been consumed, 7lbs. of tinned butter and 1 gallon of orange squash. Occasional fresh meat, fruit, eggs and veg. supplemented our stores, the only regular demand being for fresh bread.

After a few days we had all settled down to live in the confines of a boat, and I was surprised how readily we fell into the new routine.

We lost the boathook overboard, and one warp disappeared. Extra fenders and one more long warp would have been handy. Also I feel that the seven gallon fuel tank is not sufficient, as we often had to refuel from cans.

Now we are laying up, but already we are planning to take Lady Many to Holland for next summer's cruise. She did us proud this year, and we thank her.

Ian G. Tate

G.P. PATTER

March draws nigh, and it is almost time to nail down the last fitting, check the buoyancy retaining string, shake the cat (and the kittens) out of the sailbag, and trail bravely down to Stansgate for the first race of the year. Once there, the sight of all that grey water, which is unquestionably cool at this time of the year, will drive steely resolve from our stout seafaring hearts, and we shall all retire to the clubhouse to drink tea - until the bar opens, that is.

For those of you who have not yet nailed on the last fitting, here are a few ideas, not my own, which may be of interest. Instantaneous increase in speed is not guaranteed.

Spinnaker Halliard

Try fitting a large diameter steel ring so that it is free to slide up and down the forestay, thread the business end of the halliard from the sheeve down the forestay through the steel ring and thence along the foredeck to the cockpit. On pulling on the halliard downhaul the spinnaker will move forward as well as upwards. Advantage - helps the crew to work the spinnaker around to the right side of the boat when setting. If the ring is heavy enough it will also help when striking the sail. In order to use this idea it is necessary to lop off the forestay hanks from the luff of the foresail.

Spinnaker Downhaul

It is an advantage to be able to vary the vertical angle of the spinnaker boom when under way. This is quite easily controlled by using a similar set-up as is usual i.e. a piece of shockcord attached at one end to an eye near the hounds, the other end being secured to a piece of cord which is attached to another eye at decklevel. With the improved version of downhaul the cord is passed through the deck and led aft to a cleat. The helmsman is then able to easily adjust the spinnaker boom angle by pulling on the cord. Please do not go drilling holes all over the foredeck for this modification, the position, size, and the very character of the hole are all subject to measurement rules - consult your handbook first.

Another device which is very useful when striking the spinnaker is a simple wire loop attached to the stemhead fitting, its function being to prevent the spinnaker sheet from falling under the boat - thus lessening the likelihood of being "done" for trawling without a licence.

Centre Main Sheeting

Although this has not yet been given the official blessing of the Association, it is only a matter of time before it is. A number of people have asked me various questions on how and where to fit the mainsheet horse, and what the advantages of the system are. Taking the last part first, the whole advantage of the system is that it gives the helmsman greater control over the mainsail. The position of the horse in the boat will probably be governed, but it certainly needs to be as high in the boat and as wide as possible in order to give maximum control over the greatest angle of sail setting. (See Elvestrom's book - Expert Dinghy and Keelboat Racing, two photographs of the Flying Dutchman illustrate this point).

THIS AND THAT

The other evening I was talking to some of my colleagues, and upon being asked if I had anything for 'Navigans', replied, "Yes"! "Commodores Comments or should I say Laments". This remark I hastily withdrew realising that although it had been uttered just for a harmless giggle amongst friends it was not what was intended to be said, or indeed was required to be said. In circumstances such as this so often the remark passed in humour ends in complete misunderstanding, which all the humour in the world cannot rectify. Fortunately, in this instance I was not misunderstood, neither do I hope to be, in the notes which follow.

As good Club members perhaps you will consider the points which I am about to make and realise that they are made for the Club's benefit which ultimately is your benefit. YOU ARE the Club. Many hours of work and discussion are involved in the business of running your Club by the Officers and Committee whom you appoint besides the great amount of additional work which they also do as ordinary (or associate) members on all the normal chores, in which they are assisted to a degree by those of you who have already appreciated the volume of work necessary to run the Club.

At the A.G.M. I stated that a lot of people were required each to do a little work. Please bear this in mind when considering any request made to YOU through these pages, by your Class Captains or anyone else who may seek your help. With a busy and exciting season ahead perhaps at this time of year you may have time to consider your real potential as a member, thinking of the small ways in which you may contribute to the Clubs success and your fulfilment as a real live member.

BRING OUT YOUR DIARY'S

Club Open Events

This year as last we are holding the Marconi Regatta over the Spring Bank Holiday (May 23/25). This event is of considerable value to the Club gaining us much respect, appreciation and indeed gratitude from a wide range of people, and provides competition which is necessary to the improvement of racing and sailing within our Club, and enjoyment to all that compete.

This event enables us to dispose of our regular "open events" into one large meeting which assists those responsible for the organisation, and allows our sailing members to perhaps do a little more sailing than they would otherwise do. There are several of us of course, who can't remember when they last had an uncommitted Spring Bank Holiday - and believe you me - the preparatory work followed by 3 days hard graft leaves one in no doubt as to the necessity of a holiday afterwards.

The second Open Meeting to which the Club is committed this year is one dear to the hearts of many who have now won the opportunity of organising the Enterprise East Coast Area Championships on July 4/5 - at Stansgate. This represents an honour and rightly recognizes our abilities as a leading Club in the area, therefore WE MUST DO WELL.

The third open event is the Blackwater Clubs Cruiser Championships which become our responsibility to organise from our lines this year. Our own Cruiser Cup will be competed for within this event on September 13th.

to be continued/

Although the resources of the Club will not be stretched from the administration or service angle, this event needs to be run expertly and efficiently due to the "eyes of the remainder of Blackwater Clubs" being upon us.

To service the foregoing events we shall need to apply the "lots and little technique" and the appeals which are being made through the Classes and from your Officers and Committee will be for:-

Sailing Services - Rescue Boat Coxswains and Assistants. Beach Marshalls.

KEEP RIGHT ON THINKING.

As I have stated previously your Officers and Committee do recognise and appreciate the noble efforts which have and are being made by some of our membership and we look forward to receiving all the help needed to accomplish successfully the full calendar of events this season.

NOW PLEASE DECIDE HOW YOU CAN HELP.

Our position at Stansgate

We must not be too despondent regarding our position at Stansgate which seems to totter from year to year, indeed uncertainty of tenure in a past tense disappears and is overwhelmed by the success of the past whilst our immediate future is filled with the thoughts of those pleasant busy days of this year which are assured.

Do not doubt that those of us responsible for such matters continue relentlessly to pursue whatever opportunity arises to assure the continuing presence of the M.S.C. at Stansgate. It is probable that decisions may have to be taken this year by our Landlord which may affect our future. Let us but hope that such decisions may include for us the possibilities of a long, long lease or the opportunity to purchase the ground which is needed for our Site.

Before moving from this subject I would remind you of the debt which we owe to Mr. & Mrs. Sparrow for the many kindnesses shown to our Club and its members, which rise above the level of "business".

to be continued/

- 4 -

The Galley

Margaret Cottam has agreed to "take on" galley services for us again, and will, I am sure do a wonderful job. However, considering the provision she is likely to make against the basic essential service which the Club asks her to provide, will give no-one cause for grumble when on an "after party" morning the coffee is not available at 10.30 a.m.

Bar Services

On this subject I must definitely say "HELP". Dave Polley has overall responsibility for this area whilst my old comrade in pint pulling and fellow Grandad Jack Reeve has agreed to take on where he more or less left off (or did he) last year as Chief Steward.

Now he needs about a half dozen Assistant Chief Stewards without shaky hands. These peculiar creatures must be reliable and must leave at least half of each, keg, barrel or firkin for sale. Providing these conditions are met plus the money for the whole keg being put into the till I would consider any club crazy, beer drinking sailing addict who has had his bottom wet and is capable of adding up, a likely and welcome candidate. Any lady that can meet these conditions without a wet bottom is also welcome behind the Bar.

Seriously my friends - won't you help Jack - so that he can do a bit of sailing sometimes, because he dearly loves to get his bottom wet too. Its a satisfying job, does'nt demand much time but is essential to our Club so with it must go reliability.

General Services.

We have been very fortunate with our choice of Caretakers. Claude Emerson is probably unknown to the majority of you due to the circumstances of his more regular work, he attends our Club Site at differing times. During the winter his efforts have been responsible for a great deal of the boat preparation and painting, and his efforts in the Club House will by Easter provide a completely spring cleaned and redecorated unit. Ron Greygoose, our Bosun, will I am sure join me in singing Claude's praises.

Returning to the subject of the Club House I will repeat, this has been decorated throughout and some of our ladies are in the process of making new curtains. We are unable, without extension, to improve the facilities except by introducing whatever comforts are available. This year you will find some additional comfortable chairs and recognise (I hope) the need to keep wet bottoms off them, and also children from - "doing the usual things (these days's) which they did'nt ought to do and never did in my day" - spoiling them. Perhaps we can all do a little more by getting rid of our own rubbish and generally leaving the place as we would wish to find it, thereby relieving the grumbles and making the whole Club areas much easier to keep clean. A task in which many of you may want to share is to paint and creosote the Clubhouse exterior, perhaps you will come along and join the Working Party next Sunday, the 22nd March.

Dinghy Park & Winter Cruiser Park

Here again your Officers have endeavoured to make improvements, and where Dennis Byatt left off "Jimmy" James has promised to follow.
Dinghy Owners. Please do not place your boat in the class rows until you have been allocated a "space". This won't be until after you have paid your dues and sent in your Boat Register Card.

To those of you who have left dinghy's in the park all winter - you will probably find them in some other place - unless you have made arrangements for their stay. If we have to move a boat which has been left without permission, or some attempt by the Owner to notify the Club about his or her intentions you will find us pretty bad tempered about it, as those who do care and do take trouble do not like being ridden rough shod by those who obviously don't care. This remake is made due to the

to be continued/

- 5 -

chronic state of some fine boats in our park. It might be said that this is the fault and responsibility of the owners - but I would pose the question - where does the Club's responsibility end? Should this be a matter of convenience to the member or ex-member?

To my Cruiser friends who are "winter stored" in the park I would ask that you launch your boats as soon as possible at commencement of season or confine your activities to the very bottom end in order that we may use the area below dinghy's for organised car parking, which has its problems at Stansgate, these problems could be made easier by the plans to use our areas more efficiently.

Membership

This subject is probably the most important because a Club is its members. We at Marconis are very fortunate in having a balance of most things which make for active enjoyment. We have a club which is friendly and easy - it matches all others on the Blackwater without the cost or complication. We sail, we race, we work, we watch, we fall in, but I hope we never fall out. A lot is owed to the Company for whom we work, but moreover we owe so much to the founder members of our Club and the Officers of the past. No names need mention but for these inspiration, patience and understanding I feel extremely grateful - so should we all.

In cultivating this feeling of "clubmanship" I would refer to news which I am able to give and which will quell any fears of those Ordinary Members who may be transferred to posts outside Chelmsford but within the G.E.C.-MARCONI ELECTRONICS Group of Companies. This means that any member of the aforesaid group may continue or take up a type of Ordinary Membership of the M.A.S.C. entitling them to join the Marconi Sailing Club, subscriptions to both M.A.S.C. and M.S.C. being as are now paid by present Ordinary Members.

Your attention is now drawn to our good friends who are referred to as "Associates". These remarks are not directed to those whom we hold dear as thoroughly good Club men and women who have helped us build our Club and continue to support us in every possible way, but to the "new associate", and in particular those ordinary members who leave our Company with the expectation of retaining membership of our Club as Associate Members.

No special privileges can be offered to these "ex ordinary members", they must be as prepared to leave our Club as they are to leave our Company and to take with them their boats, and belongings including all rights to dinghy park spaces or moorings.

We must, by whatever democratic means are available, choose whom may become associates of our Club in accordance with the generous numbers allowed for such membership by our governing body - The Marconi Athletic and Social Club - to who we are indebted.

To identify the value which is felt of such an Association, I will disclose the remarks passed by a person to who I was able to communicate verbally, the result of a properly presented application for Associate Membership. Upon being informed that the application was successful I was told "thank you, I feel honoured and privileged".

I DO TOO !

"This and That" is an attempt to bring us altogether thinking about the happy days ahead, to give information, to share problems and to help us help ourselves.

I can promise you that I won't do this often and am glad you have read it, although you may be bored, because it means that someone else must read it who perhaps won't be bored, and that might even mean someone who

might be "a club crazy, beer drinking sailing addict", who mught become a wet bottomed acting unpaid assistant "bar steward". What a carry on !

Here's hoping.

Stan Allerton - Commodore.

THIS MONTHS SAILING AT STANSGATE

Sailing this year starts early, as Easter is early. The first race being a tuning up race on Easter Sunday, March 29th at 2.30 p.m. This is an all in dinghy handicap race for straightening out the creases in the sails. On Monday March 30th at 2.30 p.m. is a pennant race. This is a charity event where the winner receives a pennant from an organisation like the Royal National Life Boat Institution or the Royal National Mission to Deep Sea Fishermen. Normally the entry fees would go to the charity, but as we have no separate race fees the Club makes a donation proportional to the entry.

Saturday April 4th at 2.30 p.m. sees the first of the Saturday points series. There will be 8 in all spread over the season. Each is a dinghy handicap race.

The Spring Points series start on April 5th. As last year there will be a total of 6 races for each class spread over 4 weekends up to the weekend before the Spring Bank Holiday. The exception is the Hornet class whose series spreads over the whole season as their invitation series with Stone Sailing Club is sailed concurrently with the other class series. This year in order to give the few handicap class racers a better chance for a race, as well as providing some activity for unoccupied helmsmen in the class which is providing the race officials, any class boat may enter the handicap class points races but if the boat is eligible for another class series the helmsman will receive no prizes. This will mean that on April 5th, Hornets may join the Handicap class race at 1200. Additionally if the Mirrors do not muster enough entries for their race at 1150 hours those who have entered may sail in the handicap race.

In handicap dinghy racing generally we intend more often to send the faster classes round for an extra lap, making the appropriate adjustments to the corrected times. This would mean that the slower classes would tend to be on the water for the same time as the faster ones instead of an hour or more longer.

April 11th at 3.00 p.m. is the first single handed race for any sailing dinghy. There will be 4 in all through the season.

Helmsman of the year races start on April 12th at 1130 and 1430 hours. These are a series of dinghy handicap races for the Costain Cup, a large silver race bowl presented to the club by the late Richard Costain the builder of the M.A.S.C. Clubhouse. There will be a total of 8 races in 4 Sundays spread over the whole season.

N.F. Tovey.

SAILING SEASON 1970 - SOME CHANGES WE'VE MADE

As the sailing season approaches it was decided that we ought to spotlight the major changes that we've made on the sailing side of things, although with the snow lying deep and crisp and even, at the moment, sailing seems somewhat remote!

The Ladies Cup has been extended to a five race points series - races being held throughout the year and we've re-introduced single-handeds which for some unknown reason were left out of last year's programme. There are three of these which, together with four pursuit races, make up the fun races.

Pat (GP) Black last month gave you the lowdown on two proposals that were bandied around at the time and these have since been accepted as he described them. The two proposals were the Crews Points series and the revised eligibility for Handicap Points Series. One grave error was made though: K.H.T.'s should of course purchase a Stansgate O.D.: a recent enterprise that bringing a hornets' nest about its ears, mirrors a general purpose quality (ouch!).

The "round the ends" rule has been incorporated in the Recalls Section of the Sailing Instructions. This is the rule that states if, in the minute before the new start after a general recall, a boat is over the start line, it must sail round one of the extremities of the line to re-approach the line from the correct side and not merely execute a quick about turn.

The sailing programme proper has retained its last year's form: the only addition being that Race Organisers will be asked to provide assistant coxswains as well as Race Officers. The idea is to get as many people as possible familiar with the club launches so that (a) the safety of the Club is improved as more people become competent to act in an emergency, (b) less maintenance will be required on the launches through fewer mishandlings and (c) the main point - it will help out our overworked coxswain, Bill Mortimer, and do much to keep us in coxswains when horseless carriages go off their feeds.

The sailing by-law referring to speed boats has been tightened up. Members are asked to remind any prospective member who enquires about motor boats that we are a sailing club under the terms of our lease, and, although we would obviously welcome the person, we would have reservations about the boat.

This year the hiring charge for Brazil has been dropped, and the notes

We'd like to see a lot more use made of Brazil - who knows - you could win a points series with it!

Many of you will recognise features outlined above that were put forward by members. This is a sign of a healthy club, and we would welcome any suggestions anyone may have on any aspect of the club, so that we can continue to improve the facilities we enjoy. Good sailing!

FOR ENTHUSIASTIC DINGHY SAILORS

Are you still looking for the pacemaker amongst dinghies?. Well now you've found it, the HORNET! This is the modern fast racing dinghy that achieves its enviable performance from sheer efficiency, not by brute force.

The option of sliding seat or trapeze permitted to the Hornet Class only, enables even lightweights or girls to compete on even terms with good chances of success.

The Hornet is a boat for the individualist too, unlike many other classes, the Hornet has freedom for the development of original ideas, within a basic one - design concept of hull shape and sail plan. This means that one can design a deck layout to suit your own ideas for efficiency and comfort, and also try new arrangements for sail control etc.... without the fear of breaking class rules.

One of the most recent developments is the introduction of spinnaker chutes which provide a nearer foolproof system of spinnaker handling. The Chute houses the spinnaker when not in use and allows hoisting and lowering without the crew having to go on a foredeck excursion, the latter has been known to end in involuntary bathing!

So be an individualist and enjoy your Sailing by joining the Hornet Class.

By an Enthusiast.

THIS MONTH'S SAILING AT STANSGATE

April 18th and 19th sees the continuation of the Saturday Points, and the Spring Points races as outlined last month.

On Saturday, April 25th is the first Pursuit Race. In this event everyone starts from the shore at staggered intervals, the slower classes first. The staggered start times are calculated so that, theoretically, everyone should cross the finishing line together at a certain time. The Race Officer ends the race as near to this time as possible, at the mark which the leading boat is about to round. The final positions are then the finishing order of the boats participating. This race can be quite exciting as you know your position as you approach the finishing line, and can manoeuvre to defend or improve it.

On the following morning, the 26th, is the first of the Ladies Points races. This year, for the first time, there will be a series of 5 races for the Ladies Cup. (Ladies must helm but not necessarily crew). If all the races are sailed points from three will count.

The trophy is an elegant little silver cup presented to the Club by Queenie Hallum, our Vice-President's wife. In the afternoon the first of the six Cadet Points races will be sailed. This series is for any type of dinghy, and any crew, the helmsman only must be a cadet member of the Club (over 10 and under 18 years on the 1st January).

The Cup for this series was presented to the Club by Eric Payne, another of our Vice-Presidents.

We are visited by a team from the Ariel Sailing Club on May 2nd. This is the sailing section of the B.B.C's. Sports and Social Club. The home event will be sailed in Enterprises. This is our longest standing team fixture in which we compete for the Twin Flags Trophy - a little silver mast flying both Club burgees.

For those not familiar with team racing, each Club usually enters three boats, and the team scores by their boats final positions. There is often a lot of tactical movement to slow down the opponents, and allow one's own team mates to sail through. Each Club is given a match point for each race won, that is, two races at home and two away, only in the event of a tie do overall boat points, for each Club, get taken into account.

The Spring Points series continues on May 3rd. On May 9th is another single-handed dinghy Handicap Race, while the Cruisers meet on the River Roach. The following day, May 10th, sees the second Cadet points race in the morning and the Ladies Points in the afternoon.

The season has got off to a good start, in spite of some brisk weather; and as you see from the above summary, there is plenty of opportunity for many more of you to join in the fun.

Good Sailing!

Nick Tovey.

EASTER HORNET

It has finally dawned on the Hornet Fleet, that, although they rarely miss a weekend's sailing between March and October (or January), the rest of the Club might like to know what's happening to them, when they sail away from Stansgate at the numerous open meetings.

The result of sailing away from home so much is that the Marconi Sailing Club now has the reputation of having some of the best Hornets in the country (or in the world, for that matter).

The Easter Egg, sailed from the Royal Corinthian Y.C. at Burnham, was the first open meeting of the season for Hornets in our area. This year there were 23 boats sailing from some of the biggest Hornets nests such as Sussex, Hayling Island, Stone, Brightlingsea, Burnham, etc., including such names as 'Airy 'Ippo, Dry Bones, Swashbuckler, and of course Mojo, twice National and World Champion, plus two boats sailing with members of the Marconi Hornet Fleet. These were Simon Darney and his crew, Magnus, in "O-To-San", and John Heslop crewing in Spartacus, a Sussex boat.

It was interesting from the spectators point of view (especially those building new boats) in that they had a chance to view the new deck layouts, spinnaker chutes and other ideas of which there were many.

On Freezing Friday John capsized, but I don't suppose for one minute that he got wet - it's amazing how the cold quickens ones reactions. Saturday did'nt bring any better luck, for they broke their rudder when in 3rd position. Simon and Magnus did not sail on Friday, and came fourth on Saturday. On Sunday, a relatively un-windy day, Simon, after leading the fleet most of the way round, broke his main sheet jammer, and did the tango with a Soling to lose first position to John Heslop's boat. 'Airy 'Ippo finished second, and Simon, in his usual tradition of fighting to the last, was third.

Sunday evening was rounded off with a film show (in the Corinthian lounge) of the Sydney-Hobart race and the 1964 Olympics, followed by a discotheque in the Sub Bar, which freaked out around 2.30 a.m. On Monday morning, one imagines, the Bleary-Eyed were secretly just a weeny bit thankful for the gale warnings which cancelled racing for that day. The meeting was won by Swashbuckler (1466), with Simon (1470) in equal second position, together with 'Airy 'Ippo and Tangerine. John Heslop's boat, in spite of their win in one race, finished fifteenth, as one of the retirements had to be counted.

As for the rest of our Hornet fleet, Nick Turner, Bruce Long and John Smith are still slaving over hot benches, trying to finish their three new boats. Baptisms are expected to be in the next week or so. John and Bruce did however take to the water on Easter Sunday by manning the rescue launch at Stansgate for the Handicap race.

Geoff White, our admirable Fleet Captain, has organised two fleet meetings (in the Committee Room at the M.A.S.C.) during the winter months, where the serious business of beer drinking was interspersed with discussions of against whom we should team race this year, the race officer rota etc. It was decided that the invitation points with Stone should be continued if they can withstand the thrashing they always get (although at one time it was the Marconi fleet who used to get thrashed by Stone).

All in all the Hornets are looking forward to a pretty eventful year and, through Navigans, are going to make sure you hear about it.

1. Wallet, N.E. Gunfleet, Sunk Light Vessel, Galloper Light Vessel, West Hinder, Ostend. 107 miles.

2. Swin Spitway, Sunk Head, Galloper, West Hinder, Ostend. 102 miles.

3. Swin Spitway, Sunk Swatch, across the Longsand mouth of Fishermans Gat, South Knock, West Hinder, Ostend. 92 miles.

4. Swin Spitway Barrow Light vessel, Knock John, N. Edinburgh Channel Tongue Light Vessel and then either into Ramsgate for the night or outside N. Goodwins - Sandettie Light Vessel, West Hinder, Ostend. 125 miles approximately.

There were of course some minor variations possible to some of these.

Of the four the shortest and most direct was (3) via the Sunk Swatch near the beacon. The recent buoyage of the Black Deep has made the navigation much easier nowadays and providing the wind was not S.E. was the most attractive route. However, we laid off probable courses on the chart for all four. The time of starting would also be important because the tidal flow would influence the choice of course when crossing the Thames Estuary.

We believe, that on passage work, maintaining a constant average speed makes dead-reckoning and position-finding easier, so we were prepared to use the engines to keep up the average. (We had a good object lesson during the trip on the wisdom of maintaining this).

On the shortest course an average of 4 knots would take 23 hours and at 5 knots 18 hours.

The weather during the ten days or so before the start of the cruise was diabolical. Successive depressions brought gale force winds and rain day after day and our spirits dropped lower than the barometer. The spell culminated in a deep low over Scotland with a wave depression on the trailing frontal system deepening and running up Channel to the North Sea and forming a complex system which proceeded to dumbbell about for a few days. The Met. Office in London was most depressing. On the Friday afternoon as we arrived at Stansgate, the wind was still blowing S.W. force 6 with the short steep seas breaking all the way across to Goldhanger Spit.

From log: Friday 20th June

"17.25 Dropped mooring, close reefed main and staysail only - no jib or mizzen.

17.57 Hove-to off Bradwell to listen to the weather forecast ...
"Thames West force 5, Dover 6 to gale 7. Westerly"
Most gloomy."

Stansgate to Bradwell in 37 minutes, a record I should think for SIRIUS.

From log:

"18.10. let fly and tacked into Bradwell for the night: picked up mooring Girl STELLA 24 tons (she sank off the Azores last month)."

After tea we rigged the radar reflector assisted by John Barber who was anchored with "GOSLING" in the creek. By dusk the wind had dropped to nothing and the clouds rolled away to the East.

- 8 -

From log:

"Shipping Forecast:- East Coast ...
S.W. Mod./Fresh becoming S.W./W. fresh/strong"

Well it was a bit more encouraging!

Next morning at 02.00 hrs. we rose and after hot tea and biscuits began to come alive.

From log: Saturday 21st June

"02.45 Dropped mooring, morning clear and cloudless but quite dark. Motored out of Bradwell Creek. Course from Sales Point to N.W. Knoll 120° magnetic. H.W. Sheerness 05.18 tide still flooding".

04.24 Bench Head abeam
04.40 Bar buoy abeam sailing thru' Knoll Swatch. Clear bright morning Wind force 1 W."

It was a clear bright morning with a faint rosy flush in the East. Under motor and sail we plugged on over the failing tide.

"05.40 Swin Spitway abeam - 11 miles 3 hours - average 3¾ knots."

So we went on through the Spitway to the Heaps and on to the Sunk Beacon, standing like a huge gaunt gallows in the midst of apparently endless sea. But we knew better; under that smooth, almost glassy surface (for the wind had dropped to nothing by now) lurked a sand which has claimed hundreds, nay, thousands of vessels over the centuries. From the long sharp Viking galley, the bluff old cogsof the Middle Ages, the pinks and snows of the proud English sea-nation of Napoleonic times, up to the modern diesel motor ship; there they lie, what is left of them. It is not called the Sunk Sand for nothing.

Across the Black Deep, now happily for the little ship man, well buoyed; through that wide if shallow swatch in the Longsand three miles north of the Fishermans Gat and on to the South Knock Buoy.

From log:

"09.30 South Knock Buoy 28 miles average 4 knots. Wind South by East force 3-4. Switched off engine".

Now we were really sailing. Full and by, Main, Mizzen, Staysail and jib, and pulling splendidly. Course to W. Hinder with tidal allowance 110° magnetic.

And so we sailed, but alas the bright promise of the morning faded with the wind and by midday we were almost becalmed. Constant course changes to allow for the greater effect of the tide on our slower forward speed were by now probably having no effect as we soaked towards the south on the flood.

From log:

"14.00 Crossing South bound shipping lane. Wind gone entirely, becalmed. Engine on. By dead reckoning we must be well south of our course - 5 miles at least. We will continue on our course for another hour and then if SANDETTIE light Vessel not sighted we will assume a southerly drift of 4 miles and alter to new course for W. Hinder Light Vessel."

Apart from the certainty that we were not quite where we ought to be the day was most pleasant. Warm sunshine always makes sailing happier, and now that the faithful Stuart 4 was popping away, the slatting on the oily seas had lessened.

From log:

"15.30 Saw L.V. to S. 2 miles approximately.
Alter course to S. for 1 mile to check.

"SANDETTIE"

- 9 -

"New course to COST DYCK 90° mag.
16.50 Wreck buoy Green Can with topmark
3 miles from FAIRY BANK
17.35 FAIRY BANK to port ½ mile
19.25 WEST HINDER L.V. Course for EAST DYCK 118° mag - 135° mag. to allow for tide.
20.20 EAST DYCK buoy to port".

We had changed course a couple of times towards the N.E. so as to identify buoys. A cardinal rule of pilotage is not to assume that because you see a buoy where it should be that it is the right one. So we always check! The evening was drawing on and as we set the course for Ostend (118° mag. - 135° mag. to allow for tide), we had a feeling we had been lucky with our weather. The prophets were once again wrong.

As we were approaching the coast, now only 22 miles away, the effect of the sea breeze began to be felt, drawing round towards the West. This, caused by the thermal effect of the sun on the large land mass is most noticeable along the Continental coast. In fine weather it is so reliable that one could almost set a watch by it. We knew this would continue until the land cooled after midnight and the land breezeset in. And so it was; on we sailed the wind building up to force 3 steady.

From log:

"21.30 OOSTENDE Light (Gp. fl. (3) ev. 10 secs.) seen - 118° mag - dead on course.
21.55 NIEUPORT Light (Gp. fl. (2) Red ev. 14 secs.)
MIDDELKERKE BANK buoy (R. Can Fl. Red, ev. 1½ secs.)
22.20 Still cannot see MIDDELKERKE BANK
OOSTENDE BANK (Gp. fl. (2) ev. 10 secs.) Sighted bearing 144° mag."

We never did see the Middelkerke Bank but continued happily along our position line on Ostend checking every now and again on the Nieuport Light. It was grand sailing and all our tiredness vanished as we approached the shore. Our course would take us clear of all dangerous bank into the Direct Pass N.E. of the STROOMBANK. It was indeed so very direct that the BINNEN STROOMBANK (Fl. ev. 2 secs.) suddenly appeared over our bowsprit and only swift work with the tiller avoided a collision. How ironic that would have been! The trouble was that as we approached the shore the multiplicity of lights in the background made the spotting and identification of sea lights extremely difficult. I was reminded of that night years ago when I mistook a Belisha Beacon for the light on the end of Broadstairs Pier, but that is another story.

Past the starboard side it went. A tall lattice structure looking for all the world like a thing from outer space, silhouetted against the now very bright background of the port. These pillar buoys are quite unmistakable, being so dissimilar to the Trinity House conical and can buoys to which we are accustomed.

At thirty minutes past midnight we sailed between the piers of Ostend harbour. An easy entrance without the sort of tidal stream problem met at, for example, Ramsgate with its strong set across the entrance. At the root of the starboard hand pier is the North Sea Yacht Club and at the end of this building the opening to Montgomery Dock. A smart turn to starboard and one is in the dock, and yet again on the starboard hand the yacht harbour with its high stone walls on three sides and overlooked by the Yacht Club. A snug berth indeed. Bows to pontoon and stern lines to one of the row of mooring buoys and we had arrived. 21¾ hours for 90 miles, an average of 4 knots.

to be continued next month...

VISIT TO STANSGATE OF A SAILING EXPERT

On the 21st June (p.m.) Mr. D. Forbes from Musto and Hyde, Sailmakers, has offered to come down to Stansgate and have an informal discussion with our members.

We had hoped to have Keith Musto, himself, but as you will appreciate he has a very crowded fixture list and has recommended Donald Forbes. Mr. Forbes has a vast experience in racing dinghies, and crews a lot for Keith Musto.

REGATTA '70

This is the fifth year that the M.S.C. have held a Regatta at this time of the year, and is is now well established and one of the most successful events in the area. There is no reason why this year's should not be as successful as before.

Last year the entries topped 140 and the M.S.C. members entering also increased significantly. This event provides the unique opportunity for members of Fleets to sail with other helmsmen in home waters where skills can be matched and performance measured. I have no doubt that Fleet Captains will be encouraging members to enter, and I look forward to seeing strong Marconi Representation on the water.

For the sailors, the formula is much as before, with as much sailing as possible being included in the programme of a Pennant race on Saturday, and 4 Points races per class spread over Sunday and Monday, and all for 20/-. Elsewhere in this issue Fleet Captains have provided more details for the Fleets, and entry forms can be obtained from them, from Stansgate, or from me.

The Social arrangements for the weekend include a Party on Saturday evening, with bar, galley and a raffle.

The prime purpose for running the event is to provide an opportunity for members to sail with others, but there will inevitably be members who do not want to sail in the meeting, but who may want and be willing to help with some of the many activities which are necessary to stage an event of this nature. These activities include "Manning Rescue Launches", "Spotting from the Race Box", and "Signing in, and Beach Duties", not to mention providing a welcome and general information for our visitors. I shall therefore be only too pleased to hear from anyone who is willing to help with the Regatta.

Last, but by no means least, so that our visitors may see the Club at its best, and also so that all will be ready on time, there will be a Working Party on Wednesday, May 20th from 1800 hrs. to make the final preparations. The Committee and I look for as much support as possible on this occasion from the Members, but in particular from those who are going to benefit most from the actual event, namely the Fleet members.

RESCUE LAUNCHES

At a time when we are anxious to recruit and train people to man the rescue launches, prospective helpers may find it useful to read the R.Y.A. 'Suggestions and Advice to Skippers and Crews of Rescue Launches', in the Publication YR3/69, as follows:-

The first responsibility of the rescue launches is the safety of the helmsmen and crews, and they should not return to harbour until all competitors have finished, but if the crew of a capsized boat is not distressed, points to be born in mind are as follows:-

(a) The boats will not sink and there is no hurry. Avoidance of damage to hull and mast is an important consideration.

(b) The crew should lower sails, right the boat and collect floating gear before boarding the rescue launch.

(c) Once the boat is righted, the stem should be lifted as high as possible to empty water.

(d) Crew can then get into the boat, finish bailing, and, as a general rule, sail home under reefed sail or foresail only.

(e) Once one boat has been emptied, her crew can manage while another is assisted.

(f) Buckets and spare bailers should be carried in the rescue launches.

(g) In rough or cold water it may not be possible for the crew of the boat to lower sails. In this case, the crew should be taken on board the rescue launch. The crew of the rescue launch should then get hold of the mast head of the boat, unshackle the head of the mainsail, then work down the mast and unshackle the head of the jib; then work down the forestay while righting the boat, so ending up with the boat upright and held by the bow. The boat should not be towed on her side.

Coxswain

THIS MONTHS SAILING AT STANSGATE

Sunday, May 10th sees the last of the Spring Points series.

The Major event of this month is the Regatta, which contains many of our open trophies.

The Hornet Hallam Trophy presented by Vice President Terry Hallam, the GP.14 Commodore Cup presented by Vice President Jack Bigden. The Graduate Gem Trophy presented by the Commodore of Stone Sailing Club, George Miles, and the Triple K Cup for Enterprises.

I know most about the latter as Brian Partridge and myself presented it to the Club while we were at Heybridge. It was first used for an Open Enterprise Series for B.J.R.C. Clubs, spread out over the season. The first two winners were Brian in Keel Kat, and myself in Kiora (hence Triple K). Since then it has never been in the Club. I hope we do better this year.

On Wednesday evenings, 27th May, we start the mid-week races. There are seven in all during the long evenings. These are usually even less formal than our other racing and prove an excellent relaxing handicap race after work.

On Saturday, 30th May, we have two team races at home. Hornets v Saltcote S.C. and Enterprises v Thames Estuary Y.C. (Note:- the latter is on the 30th May not 31st May as falsely (or erroneously) indicated in the programme).

Sunday, 31st May, sees the start of the main class points series, 9 races for each class spread over 6 weekends. Enterprises will be competing for the Knight Cup, presented by Ernest Knight and first used by the M.A.S.C. for chrysanthemums. Hornets for the Stansgate Cup, presented by the Club and first used for a Cadet open meeting. The GP's for the Edwards Cup presented by Mr. Edwards on his retirement from the Company.

The Mirrors will be competing for the Presidents Cup, an excellent piece of Welsh Silver presented by our President, Dr. Eastwood, initially for a Fleetwind class points. Fleetwinds were the original class in the Club, and it is a great shame that this trophy has not been competed for in the past few years.

Nick Tovey.

CRUISER MEETING

On Thursday, April 16th, members were given a really magnificent evening at the M.A.S.C., when John Todds, despite his recent activities in the U.S.A., still managed to find time to organise a very full programme of matters relating to cruising, for a large and appreciative audience.

Firstly, Dr. Woods told us about his cruise to Friesland in his Snapdragon cruiser, showing us some delightful colour slides taken in the Dutch canals, and of his family life on board. Then our old friend, Rod Baxter, who has been with us from the early days of the barge MAMGU, told us, with the help of diagrams and the blackboard, about a cruiser he was building, which he hoped would incorporate many of the good features he had gleaned during his not inconsiderable experience of sailing. We had some difficulty in stopping him, and I am sure he would have continued until midnight, but we were anxious to have an interval for refreshments, during which John had thoughtfully laid on some tasty sandwiches.

Although it was now well after 10 pm, Walter Standing then told us about his cruise to Cherbourg, and the Channel Islands, in his magnificent steel cruiser JONELLE. In spite of the hazards of his navigation between the rocks into the harbours (which would have made some of us with less substantial hulls shudder) he still had the temerity to enter for a race during his stay at Guernsey!

/continued over.

RES:

The evening concluded with the showing of a film of the 1968 single- handed Atlantic race, with close shots of the various competitors and their yachts. Vic Tait, who has also been a member of the Club since the very early days (some will remember his famous cruiser AARK) was our most efficient projectionist for the evening.

A vote of thanks to John Todds and all who had contributed to giving us such an enjoyable and instructive evening, was given by Eric Payne.

"SIRIUS" GOES FOREIGN 1969

(T. W. Hallam)

Continued from last month.

Sunday 22nd June

After breakfast we moved to a new position beam on to the pontoons under the walls of the Club House. This is the usual position for small visiting yachts and is very convenient. The inimitable Albert the bosun, who wears his immaculate white topped peaked cap when the sun shines and offers his shining bald bare head to the skies when it rains, moored us to his liking and ashore we went to make that telephone call.

How different from an English Sunday; the main post office was open for business, although obviously at a reduced tempo. An official at a special switchboard obtained the call to England and then politely indicated the telephone booth I was to use.

Back to the Club for a pre-lunch drink. But first the immigration officer accompanied by a heavily armed policeman. Passports? Yes. Ships papers? Ah, there was a difficulty. The R.Y.A. Certificate of Identity and Ownership so proudly produced meant absolutely nothing to the official. Nor, may I add, did it at any time in any of the three countries we visited on the cruise. However, all was well at last and we were quite patently not listed in the large volume of presumably unwanted visitors carried by the official. Mind you, he looked first!

In the afternoon Geof flew back home and Queenie flew out so by tea-time we were settled in.

The next few days, encouraged by a force 5-6 N. to N.W. wind, we sampled the delights of Ostend and chatted and drank with all our friends and acquaintances from the Maldon River. It seemed that half the boats on the Blackwater were visiting the Continent at the same time as us. There was only one evening during the whole fortnight when we did not run into a local boat, and in most cases we knew the owner well.

By Wednesday afternoon we felt we had seen enough of Ostend and as the wind had moderated to force 3 N.W. we cast off and put to sea. Only for a few miles mind you. To Blankenburgh in fact, where we tied up to a pontoon and wandered ashore. A delightful little watering place, everyone friendly and, in spite of the warnings in Delmar-Morgan's "North Sea Pilotage and Harbour" quite an easy entrance.

From log:

"Thursday, June 26th
H.W. Flushing 10.40
H.W. Zeebrugge 10.00
H.W. Dover 08.29

Tide sets towards the coast and then NE 1 hour before H.W. Dover
Tide sets strongly out of the W. Scheldt 4 hours after H.W. Dover

Leave at 07.30 to arrive at Flushing 12.00".

This is the sort of simple but essential calculation to be done whilst cruising in these waters. The tides up and down the coast are associated with the main North Sea stream which meet the Channel stream off Dover. High Water at the North Sea ports is seldom therefore coincident with a change of direction of tidal flow. Even the fierce tides of the E. and W. Schelde continue to flow well after H.W. at the main estuary ports. This of course is quite unlike our own Thames Estuary tidal pattern and takes a little getting used to. For Holland the tidal chart or Stroomkaart for the area being cruised is essential. This has a movable inner card which shows the tidal deviation for each hour through little windows at a number of points on each of the chartlets. They cost about 3½ Florins each. Not cheap, but worth the money.

- 11 -

A light Northerly meant a beat out to clear the mole at Zeebrugge. The book said clear by at least a mile. We only passed half a mile outside and paid for it by being thrown about on a nasty sea which came from all directions. This in only a force 2. In a strong breeze it would have been most uncomfortable. As we passed the end of the mole "Theodora" the ocean Youth Club boat from Brightlingsea came out.

The wind came more free as we approached the W. Schelde and we ran up to Flushing in fine style. The entrance to the lock is at the far end of the town beside the Breskens ferry terminal. Locking in was quick and efficient and by 11.30 we were in the canal, having cleared Customs whilst still in the lock. It was here that we really noticed for the first time the simple and efficient way the Dutch have with mooring warps. None of the business of long continuous warps festooned from one end of the vessel to the other. Short orange courlene warps, each with a large loose eye at one end and each no longer than twenty feet or thereabouts. The loose eye is dropped or flung over the bollards with which most locks are well provided and the other end made fast. To cast off after the water in the lock has dropped the rope is given a flick and off flies the eye to drop neatly on deck. Even the tiny children can do it! Four of these warps and four large fat expensive inflated fenders in bright orange plastic, and your worries about locking in and out are over.

The main road bridge over the Kanaal Van Walcheren was closed and we tied up to a dolphin for half an hour. It was warm and drowsy and the quick light lunch we had, with a bottle of wine made us disinclined to hurry so we were not too impatient with the bridgemaster.

A loud hoot woke us from our reverie. Up went the bridge and through came an enormous petrol barge. And through we went in the opposite direction. The next bridge, a small by-road opened without our asking, but at Middleburg, a main road bridge, we tied up once again to the dolphins to wait, in company with two West Mersea boats, the owners of both of which we knew.

No more bridges now, just the lock at Veere where we went through in about five minutes. Out into the Veerse Meer, a sharp turn to port and into the Stadthaven, one of the most picturesque and delightful harbours imaginable. The town is delightful as are the inhabitants, some of the more elderly of whom still wear the traditional dress. Not as a tourist attraction, or as a special Sunday costume, but unconsciously, every day. Veere has not fossilized since the Veerse meer was dammed and the fishing ended. It is a lively little town whose job it is to give pleasure to the pleasure seekers. Not by the provision of dance halls and juke boxes, but by being peaceful and pleasant and just good to look at As always in Holland the Havenmeester was courteous and obliging and the Yacht Club which runs the Stadthaven, a pleasant and nice place to have a drink ... which we did, several.

Friday 27th June

We left Veere after lunch and sailed down the length of the Veersemeer, now fast becoming a giant sailing pond for full size yachts, with a number of marinas either built or building. It seemed queer to have no tide for which to make allowances. Tame somehow, which was probably why we went aground. It was late afternoon and we were fortunate that a motor cruiser came along and spotting us out of the channel came over and pulled us off. With no wind to speak of and only a 4 H.P. Stuart with a clamshell propeller we were not having much success by ourselves.

At the East Scheldt end of the there is an enormous new sea lock which shot us through and out into the Zandkreek in record time. We had decided to try and make Goes that night and although it was late, we motored the three miles to the sea lock at Sas van Goes, where the little canal meets the tidal estuary. Once through we motored the three miles to the main road bridge at Goes. Here however, we were unlucky, in spite of a telephone call made by the lock keeper at the sea lock when we entered. So we tied up to a large barge and went to bed. About five in the morning, we were awakened by a thump on the cabin top and as we cast off the barge was away. It was a good job the skipper noticed us. After all, we were so small and his vessel seemed to us to be enormous.

- 12 -

Saturday 28th June

The bridge opened at 07.00 and through we went. A sharp turn to port about twenty yards from the bridge and we found ourselves in the most delightful yacht haven we have ever been in It almost defies description. Two little pools with a peninsula separating them surrounded by grassy banks and flowering shrubs; about forty yachts only are moored there. The butterflies flitted among the flowers and as we sat drinking a beer in the sun outside the most delightful little club house one felt that this was a place inhabited by the Little People and we humans had no right to be amongst such beauty. They keep the beer under a trapdoor in the floor and you help yourself and pop the money into a little box. We felt we could stay forever. However, go we must and that afternoon we passed under the bridge and away to sea. A fresh, force 5 N.E. wind gave us a wet beat down the E. Scheldt past the entrance to the Zandkreek and under the 2½ mile long Zeeland Bridge which spans the estuary until we reached up the mile and a half long entrance channel to the harbour of Zieriksee where we tied up alongside a Dutch yacht. The town is pleasant but not so much so as Veere, nor so pretty as Goes. The only decent restaurant we could find, on the quay, was crowded with young vigorous Dutch lads and lassies drinking and shaking away to the sound of a juke-box which was turned up to just below the threshold of pain. In the end it beat us and we ended up about midnight eating sausages and chips in a little cafe in a side street.

Sunday 29th June

Next day of course the wind was now S.W. as we beat back to the Zandkreek, for it was time to be thinking of the return to England.

A pleasant uneventful day found us at Veere once again where we met yet more friends.

Monday 30th June

SIRIUS seemed reluctant to leave. First the engine refused to start, and then the dynomotor stopped charging. The plug oiled up and the spare which should have been to hand of course was missing. However, about midday after we gave her a new plug, she decided to leave after all and away we went through the lock down the canal and out through the lock at Flushing. By this time, however, the ebb was far advanced and as we wished to make Breskens we had to drop down below the Plaat van Breskens sand which dries 13ft. above L.W. in places only to fight the tide for about a mile and a half to the harbour. Those Scheldt tides! It took us an hour with the motor flat out and all sails drawing to a force 2-3 breeze to make that last mile; and this mind you was at low water. Still we got in and tied up, went ashore and had a magnificent meal at a sort of Dutch/Italian restaurant near the Yacht Club. Four courses, a bottle of wine, personal attention from the head waiter, coffee and brandy and a chat with the family, all for under five pounds - tomorrow we are back to sea again!

to be continued next month...

MOORINGS AT STANSGATE

This year already three vessels have gone adrift from the moorings. That is three too many. We have been very lucky that in each case so far no other vessel has been damaged, and no boat has had a full salvage claim made against her. A successful salvage award may be as high as a third of the value of the boat, and knowing a little of marine insurance, it is quite possible that the owner would be liable. Several hundred pounds is not an easy sum to find.

What can we as owners do about preventing this?

Firstly by selecting tackle that is adequate for the boat.

Secondly by regular inspection of the tackle.

Thirdly by replacing any item that is below standard AT ONCE.

Stan Campbell and I have each had a look at most of the moorings from B row inshore and we are agreed that the general state is very poor. Chain is often badly worn, swivels are worn and seized up, and where the gear is in good order the shackles are often unwired and too small for the job.

There is a further hazard for the moorings on B row outwards, namely severe pitting of the chain. Last year one boat went adrift due to the chain having parted. The reason was that although the chain was only a year old, it had been scraped across the bottom by wind and tide. The abrasive action of the shingle exposes fresh metal and the result is very severe local pitting and corrosion.

Bearing this in mind I inspected the lower end of my own A row mooring at the end of May this year. I had been confident that with new chain at Easter 1969 my tackle would be in excellent condition, particularly as I had used chain 50% thicker than the club moorings sheet recommends.

- 5 -

I was most disturbed to find that it was nowhere near as good as I expected, and that it will have to be discarded at the end of this summer. The damaged area is the lower end of the scope, and the centre portion of the bridle. My swivel is not seized nor is the pin worn, but there are signs of pitting on the body where it has touched the bottom. I have been warned, you have been warned!

Another place where trouble can occur is on the connection between a large buoy and the chain. Some buoys have the lower ring swivelling, and the swivel is held by a welded nut which is not always as strong as it should be. The answer here is to follow our cruiser captain's example and secure your boat, by chain, to the top of the scope chain. Do not rely on a single rope from deck to the top of the buoy, a short length of new galvanised chain will not stain the decks and will outlast any form of rope.

A valuable boat needs careful maintenance and the mooring is part of her equipment. Take a pride in the whole outfit for all our sakes.

Ian Tate (Moorings Secretary and cruiser owner)
