"SIRIUS" GOES FOREIGN 1969

(T. W. Hallam)

* "SIRIUS"
3½ ton Aux. Burd Yawl
Built: Cardnells circa 1936. O/A 23.0 18.0 WL. 7.0 beam 3.5 draught.

(Continued from May issue)

Tuesday 1st July

From log:

"H.W. Flushing 02.40
H.W. Dover 00.31 to 12.58
Tide turn N.E. off Ostend 12.00
Cast off 07.00 Wind light southerly
07.30 off NIEUWE SLUIS Light"

Three miles in thirty minutes with a light, force 1-2 wind, some tide!

Later the land breeze dies away and after a half hour or so of calm and fitful catspaws the breeze settled down in the West about force 2. A wide berth was given to Zeebrugge and we reached Ostend at midday. The next two days, Wednesday and Thursday were spent in similar fashion tide-hopping from port to port during the mornings. Dunkirk, then Calais, - each day was a little more hazy with a little less wind. Contrary to expectation we found Dunkirk yacht haven a pleasant little place although the town is rather mean and dirty. At least around the dock area.

At Calais we picked up a mooring in the Event Porte, until high water, when the lock gates and road bridge open to allow passage to the very quiet and clean Bassin de l'Ouest, where on the northern side the new and very pleasant club-house of the Yacht Club is situated. The club harbour-master speaks excellent English and the charges are not too unreasonable.

A warning however - the water is suspect. We emptied, cleaned and refilled our containers from the club stand pipe only to find after two days a growth of green slime around the neck of the bottles. We emptied them in Ramsgate harbour! Others, we found when discussing it, have had the same experience.

Two days were spent lazing on the beach, sampling the excellent mussels and watching dinghy racing near the shore.

Saturday 5th July

From log:

"H.W. Dover 04.06 - 16.24
Lock gates open 0.300 hours".

- 10 -

It was not much use going straight out across the Channel at high water because the tides on the English side would be wrong. So we laid to anchor in the Event Porte and tried to sleep. The rolling was abominable; a force 4 westerly sent a swell up the harbour which was reflected off the walls, amplified from time to time by the wash of craft entering and leaving the cross-channel packet berths. No, Calais is not a nice place to be unless within the enclosed basins.

We left thankfully just about 09.30 with a smart westerly breeze. All plain sail, course N.W. by N. (326° mag.) A fine sunny day with the big channel seas, still unbroken, shining green as they passed abeam. SIRIUS felt alive and vibrant after the light contrary wind of the past week. At 12.00 hours we sighted the cliffs of Dover and at 13.00 hours altered course to run up the Downs. Three and a half hours to cross the channel. We will probably never do it as quickly again. We were now well ahead of our tide which was still running hard to the west. As we approached the land the high cliffs tended to blanket the wind even a mile out. Slowly we crept past the S. Foreland, Walmer and Deal. A thunderstorm off Sandwich killed the wind, but by now the tide had turned in our favour. The wind came out of the North East light, then moderate as we drove on, hard on the wind, to Ramsgate. It was a race now against the clock with high water twenty minutes after H.W. Dover. A quick tack just outside the harbour entrance and we were through. On engine, down sails and we shot through the lock gates with minutes to spare. Alongside the wall, a quick scramble ashore to ask a belated permission from the lock-master to enter the basin, (readily given I must say although they can be difficult at Ramsgate) and then Customs clearance - twenty- two shillings duty on a six bob bottle of brandy. I presented it gracefully to the Queen!

We just sat back and looked at Ramsgate. A noisy, sleezy, friendly town with the twentieth Century veneer sitting very lightly on its victorian buildings, like an East End Yiddisher Momma in a mini-skirt. Indeed we saw some of those too - and we loved them.

There is not much to add now, a false start next morning, returning from the N. Foreland where the weather forecast promised gales. The glass and sky confirmed it too. So we left SIRIUS in the very able care of the Bosun of the Royal Temple Yacht Club and collected her the following week. The prophets were right this time - Force 8 - 9!

The trip back across the Estuary the following week was memorable for only two things. One almost a complete lack of wind with poor visibility, turning the trip into a motor cruise. The other, a view of the River Blackwater from above the Bench Head at seven o'clock in the evening.

With the sun low in the west the whole estuary was bathed in a golden glow that was breathtaking. Smooth water, hazy blue hills over Tiptree Heath, Mersea Island like a green jewel set in liquid gold, and far, far away the trees of Osea lifted above the horizon in a mirage - a South Sea Island in Essex.

Surely the most beautiful river in the whole wide world.

APPENDIX

Finally a word about navigation. We used Imray's bluebacks and although we had Admiralty charts they were several years old so we did not trust them. We would not use Imray's again. They are difficult to read, with too much detail in places and not enough in others. The Admiralty charts were very clear indeed. The best of all were the Dutch Yachtsman's charts. These are beautifully printed in booklets, very clear indeed and are automatically re-issued in April of each year.

Delmar-Morgan's book is informative, but as it excludes all the inland ports and most of those enclosed by the Delta Plan its use is limited. I bought the official guide to the Dutch waterways - Almanac voor Watertoerisme, Deal II. Although in Dutch I found it useful and remarkably understandable. For tidal information the charts published by the Netherlands Hydrographic Department and mentioned earlier are invaluable, as is the Admiralty Pocket Tidal Stream Atlas North Sea, Southern Portion. All backed up of course by the current year's Reed's.

TERENCE W. HALLAM

EDITORIAL

If it had'nt been for my ever patient husband you would have a very short Navigans this month. Did'nt any of you have a diary for Christmas? My calendar tells me that today is the 14th July, exactly a fortnight after my so called "deadline". If I had kept to my word and typed on the 2nd there would have been no need to have struggled downstairs with my typewriter, I could have stood in the cupboard and done it.

As I told you in the May issue there will be no August issue due to our holiday, but I shall be pleased to accept anything for the September Navigans anytime up to the 14th August. We are returning on the 8th September so I shall be typing that issue on Friday 11th September, without fail.

As you read on you will see that two features in this issue are concerned with safety - something we cannot afford to be complacent about!

See you at the Barbecue - don't forget the family.

Mary Greygoose.

ACCIDENTS

We have been asked by the Chief Executive of the M.A.S.C. to inform all members that in the event of a member of the M.A.S.C. being involved in an accident on Club premises or when taking part in an official activity elsewhere, and which results in an injury through whatever cause, the accident must be recorded in the Accident Report Book provided immediately.

This book is kept in the M.A.S.C. Office during working hours, but in the evenings and at weekends it will be kept at the Reception Desk.

GET WELL SOON

Freddie Harrison, a popular member of the Enterprise Fleet, unfortunately met with an accident on Chelmsford Station, when he was hit by a train door being thrown open as the train pulled into the station.

We are pleased to report that he is now home from hospital, but the Committee and members all wish him a speedy recovery, and look forward to seeing him back at Stansgate sailing again.

CRUISING PARTIES.

The following letter has been received from Mr. J.W. Green, of [redacted], South Woodham Ferrers. Phone Woodham Ferrers [redacted]. Anyone interested should contact Jim direct.

"I am writing to see if any of your members would be interested in going foreign for a week on the 33' Bermudan cutter "Tarika"? She is a fast, comfortable cruising boat, built in 1964, with a 16 hp. diesel auxiliary, and is completely equipped and fitted in all respects.

Normally we go abroad, weather permitting, to France, Belgium or Holland, and the charge for the week is £21 inclusive, except for any meals eaten ashore. "Tarika" is 5 berth, so I can take parties of 4. Your party works the boat and I have a watching brief. Comprehensive insurance is carried".

Yours sincerely,

Jim Green.

ENTERNATIONAL ENTERPRISE EAST COAST AREA CHAMPIONSHIPS

The Championships are over. As always the weekend seemed to rush by - but it rushed by smoothly without any major catastrophies (except Nick Tovey's tragic Gate Start, of course, which we were very sorry about).

From reports received, it appears that everyone had a thoroughly enjoyable weekend's sailing. The only disappointment was that the sun must have forgotten that we had booked it for the weekend, but even this did not seem to dampen anyone's spirit.

Out of the 42 entries we were very pleased to see twelve Marconi boats, our five best overall results being 2nd, 9th, 12th, 18th and 22nd. A special mention should be made of Ron Greygoose and Dennis Byatt who came 26th and 39th respectively. Well done Ron and Dennis in your first season's sailing.

The Burnham boats again made their dynamic presence felt, and congratulations go yet again to Roger Hance who was the overall winner. It is interesting to note, however, that his habitual pattern of winning every race was rather spoilt by Mike Taylor of Burnham and Julian who both won a race each.

Jill.

I would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who helped to make the Enterprise Championship the success it was.

It has generally been felt that the prestige of the Marconi S.C. has benefitted greatly from this event following reports in the Times (6-7-70), Essex Weekly, Newsman Herald, Essex Chronicle, Marconi News, Yachts and Yachting, and Yachting and Boating.

Thanks to Bernard Tillotson who carried out the difficult task of Race Officer very well with his willing assistant John Tillotson.

Assisting in the launches were Bryan Urry, Geoff White and the Hornet Boys plus Peter Crick (just for good measure!). Perhaps the Enterprise Fleet will be able to assist with a Hornet meeting in the future.

Our very great appreciation to Walter Standing for the use of his yacht "Jonelle" and his general assistance. HORNETS AWAY AT THE SUSSEX SLIDE - 20th and 21st June 1970

Friday night, rush home from work, packed the boat up on Thursday, thank goodness. Hitch it onto the car and away we go to the Sussex Yacht Club at Shoreham-on-Sea.

Thank goodness we have arrived, dropped the boat at the Club, pitched the tents in Mr. Payne's garden. Mr. Payne(Tony) sails a Hornet, and for the last three slides has entertained a fair proportion of the Marconi Fleet.

We watched the semi-final of the World Cup on their television over delicious coffee, after which we retired outside to bed.

Out come the mattresses, cushions and foam rubber (none of this sleeping rough - not good for your)

In the morning we made friends with Fred the tortoise, Tiger the Cat, and Lee the dog, the normal habitants of Tony's back garden. Down we go to the Club to find virtually all the Fleet there, most camped or dossed, or did it in style and had B & B.

The first race was at 1.00 pm. Lots of time to get the boat rigged, chat, boast, watch the wind gather strength - Force 5 strength.

/continued

- 4 -

We sail out of the harbour to the start line, heave to until the 10 min. to preserve energy. Waves enormous. Bruce Long and John Heslop do not start as peculiar weather, helm and lee helm, develops. There we all are about 35 of us hanging aroundand, B A N G, off we go... bit bumpy on the beat, fantastic on the reach - spinnakers not in evidence much today. Colin and Kevin virtually sink and retire; Mick's mast breaks, tears the sails and splits the foredeck, cracked the centre board and he retires.

Geoff's crew did usual swimming act, but they finished - 10th. Simon finished 4th. Peter Woods gets blown onto the shore, and leaves Dick to look after it while he goes back to the Club for the trailer to tow it back to the Club.

Race over, now it's time to sail back up the dock. Absolute AGONY, high sides, gusty wind and fast running tide (against us, of course) and at the end of it Geoff's and Jane's rudder falls to bits, and then - MUD of the black variety.

Back at the tent Heather White has cooked the most welcome stew of all times. Then back for usual jig about to a group in their most super Clubhouse. What a fantastic day's sailing, everyone is saying - except Mick and Brian, and Geoff, who is trying to fit Mick's rudder.

Next morning first race is at 11.00 am, no wind to speak of, everyone is on the water at 10.00, trying to sail out that damned dock. Eventually we cotton on to a gallant rescue launch, who tows about 20 of us out. Of course, there has to be this German timber boat wanting to go out at the same time. Harbour Master uses megaphone to his best ability:- 'Keep clear of the channel'. Where does he expect us to go'. Once out of the harbour entrance we gently sail out to the start line, arriving there about 11.30 am. Race starts about ¾ hr. late. Mick and Brian are on the Committee Boat, as they obviously cannot sail their own boat, and afterwards we find they had quite an interesting time. The owner of this boat which has every instrument under the sun (including a fan in the loo, which switches itself on when you enter and turns itself off 1½ mins. after you leave) is the inventor of the automatic pilot system in aeroplanes, and incidentally had a lot to do with Marconis' around the time of the first broadcasts.

Anyway, back to the race, none of the Marconi team seemed very inspired by the force 1 wind, and large rolling waves, but Simon and Mike finished 4th, Geoff and Jane were 7th, and the rest were in the teens and over. After the race we slopped around, and ate our packed lunch, as there was no time to go back to the Club, besides which one's patience would'nt allow four journeys up and down that dock in one day.

Second race, and there is even less wind. The guns for the finish of a handicap race go, and Geoff and Jane think the Hornets are finishing, so after crossing the line Jane takes the helm and they sail towards the dock entrance, which also is the direction of the next mark. What are they doing coming back from the mark, hav'nt we finished? Let's retire. At least there's not so much mud to climb over at the end of the sail back. Stupid dock...

Dinner waiting again, boats packed up, journey back, super weekend, Sunday evening...

SAMANTHA.

SAIL SETTING

At about lunch time on a very warm Sunday, a group gathered at one end of the hard, around Mr. Donald Forbes of Musto and Hyde, Sailmakers.

His talk opened with a statement of priorities: Sails are the equivalent of an engine, the mast and rigging merely support the sails, and the hull is to keep your feet dry!

Ustng an Enterprise as a demonstration model, Mr. Forbes showed us various jib settings for various weathers, tight leach, loose foot for light winds (cone effect), and loose leach and tight foot for heavy winds. The latter setting is required so that the leach goes away at the top and does'nt backwind the main. On the Enterprise used, the sliding track needed to be fixed diagonally across the side decks a few inches aft of the shrouds, set about 3-4 inches further back on the outside, end than the inner end.

The mainsail settings were also clearly described, including the order
of
setting. .

1. Pull mainsail up to black band.
2e Pull out foot of sail by means of the clew outhaul until the sail is
a nice full’ shape - further in than you think.
Se Pull dow kicking strap when afloat and close hauled.
4, Adjust Cunningham hole setting until the creases going up and back from the mast disappear.
5. Setting of track width at the stern depends on wind - in light wind it
may be central. This keeps the leach tight as the sail is pulled down, A wider setting allows the main to be held down,- but the leach can go- away at the top to reduce heeling in heavy a

The general rules were:~ Strong wind flat sea, everything tight. — Strong tee wind lumpy sea, baggy sails and don't try sailing too close to the wind. Keep . ‘sailing fast. In a light wind keep everything baggy and full. seek

Another general. rule was that at any time during 2 race you are pulling - in the. mainsheet and stretching the leach, you-should also pull down the Cunningham to stretch the luff as well. In this way there are no peculiar stresses in the sail. Each time you let out the mainsheet, the Cunningham
should also be lct out. 7 |

HEADS ABOVE WATER

A recent experience whilst assisting in a rescue launch brought home the absolute need for adequate and effective bouyancy in dinghies.

About thirty boats took part in the meeting, the majority of which were usually sailed on inland water, and under quite different circumstances to those which we experience at Stansgate. On this occasion there was a strong tide running with the wind gusting 4 to 6, and even before the first race started, there were many capsizes. Conditions remained very much the same throughout the day, and with dwindling entries for each of the three races, until only about five boats were in condition to sail the last one.

Several of the boats were relatively easy to assist to the shore whilst the difficult ones were really only fit to sail on wet grass.

Two small damaged side bouyancy bags and a few unsecured pieces of plastic foam in the bows will not keep a popular 14' dinghy in an easily salvaged position. Even after the boat has been forced upright it remains waterlogged, and the wind catching mast, rigging and remaining sails (jammed) often turns it over again. After a struggle the boat may be secured alongside. Bailing is almost impossible, even providing there is a bailer or it has not been lost through insecure fitting etc. Seas break over the awashed decks, water forces up through the centre-board housing, (this can be stuffed with rag or towel). Towing a waterlogged boat is both difficult and time consuming. An extended individual rescue operation seriously jeopodises the service, and someone may be in greater trouble due to injuries etc.

Adequate and securely fitted bouyancy and bailers are essential for the safety of both yourself and others. Observe the M.S.C. and Class Associations' Rules and Recommendations. Fit extra bouyancy in the bows where it greatly assists both alongside and astern towing.

Check that securing straps and fittings are adequate and in good condition and remember the rule never to swim away from the boat, not even to try and salvage those expensive bits floating away.

Capsizing is not quite the horror some like to think. Being unprepared and unfamiliar with the event is the main cause for concern. Some people capsize quite regularly, some even intentionally. This experience enables you to get familiar with the procedures to assist oneself, to check both boat and personal bouyancy, to give confidence and help eliminate the fear of an unexpected ducking.

/continued.

- 7 -

Try a few voluntary capsizes near the Club, choose a day when there are plenty of people about and the rescue boats not occupied with racing, and let the O.O.D. or Coxswain know your intentions.

Recommended procedures and detailed capsize drill are beyond the scope of this article. Study the many sailing books and publications, and ask the experienced helmsman and crews - then practice. Planing into a capsize is a most stimulating experience, particularly when the helmsman has already involuntarilyleft the boat!

LIFE SAVING CLASSES

It may be of interest to Club Members, particularly those associated with rescue boat operation, to know that classes for the Royal Life Saving Society Awards are held at Chelmsford swimming baths on Tuesday evenings by the Chelmsford Swimming Club.

Normally these classes concentrate on the Bronze Medallion award since this is a recognised minimum qualification for those directly concerned with water safety (eg. baths attendants),and anyone of average swimming ability should be able to attain this standard. In addition there are also awards by the Amateur Swimming Association for personal survival which involve such skills as swimming in clothes, treading water, removing clothes in the water, and swimming a set distance without clothes (but with swimming costume!). The tests are in 3 grades with increasing distances and timed tests and so form a good basis for later life saving awards if required. The classes are very informal and include all aspects of water safety. There is no age limit for the A.S.A. awards, but for the R.L.S.S. Bronze Medallion the minimum age is 13, for youngsters under this age there is an Intermediate award.

I should also add that Chelmsford Swimming Club run classes to teach children and adults to swim, In the case of children there is a long waiting list unfortunately, but there is no harm in adding your children's names to the list. For adults I am not sure what the situation is, but can easily find out.

The need for the right sort of knowledge was highlighted by a recent newspaper report of the drowning of a small boy in a canal - the person who finally did something positive was too late; his comment was that when he arrived on the scene there were enough people there to start a football match. Also one of those earlier on the scene was a boat-owner.

If anyone is interested in any of the above classes, or has any queries at all please contact me either at work at Baddow - Room 259, B Block, Phone Int. 395, Ext. 353, or at home at 18, [redacted], Maldon, Phone Maldon [redacted].

MOONSHINE IN FRIESLAND

by

Barbara and Donald Woods and Richard Brown

North Holland is a little far to reach and return without hurried travelling in three weeks. We had twice visited the southern Dutch waters in other people's boats; this year in our own Snapdragon 26 the aim should be to take the family of children 13, 12, and 9 to Friesland and back.

The plan was for Richard Brown (R.G.B.) to make the Harwich-Hook trip with a volunteer crew and then carry on up the canals to Amsterdam, which with stops for beer should take nearly a week. Barbara and Donald Woods (B.W. and D.W.) with children would then take over and visit the Ijsselmeer and Friesland returning via the canals to Flushing. Then a coast hopping trip, joined at some point by R.G.B., to return home probably Ostend-Ramsgate.

Here's what actually happened.

By. R.G.B.

There were to be five members of the crew - Bob and Freddie, Donald Craig, Ernest and myself. A good number - two per watch and a spare in case of mal-de-mer. The previous weekend the boat had been loaded with extra petrol, and food to last a single-hander for three months. (A similar Snapdragon moored alongside had an extra inch of freeboard). That weekend we discovered the heads were leaking. A pressure test later showed there was a small crack in the foul pipe. The spare part arrived the day before sailing.

July 11 22.30 The first three crew members were delivered to Stansgate by D.W. after farewells and a reminder from D.W. to write up the log, we rowed the 12ft. Avon out to Moonshine.

23.00 As a final salute, we turned on all the ship's lights just to cheer D.W. up and make him envious. After a quick beer - bed.

July 12 06.40 An ideal weather forecast - winds light N.W. Breakfast, and then down to Bradwell to pick up Donald Craig and Freddie. A minor disaster struck as we were dragging the Avon on deck - a ventilator was broken, leaving a gaping hole in the deck. With acute dislike of holessin the deck and memories of a previous very rough crossing, a spare ventilator was tracked down at Burnham, collected and fitted.

11.40 Barometer 1036. At last under way, and it seemed a good deal longer than this narrative! Whilst Don and Freddie were on watch, I found the heads were again leaking For the next twelve hours whilst we sailed at a gentle 3 - 4 knots up the Wallet to the Sunk L.V., that loo was dismantled, reassembled - taken to bits, put togetheragain, until finally to the urgent relief of the entire crew the blankety-blank thing was at last declared open! (I absolved myself from the cooking for the remainder of the crossing).

14.00 We got a fix off Clacton and also handed the Genoa. The wind was now definitely N.E. This was a disappointment as the forecast was N.W. Only the week before we had bought a spinnaker and everyone had hoped for a light tail wind to try out our new toy.

16.30 The Sunk L.V. two miles away and set course for the Hook.

19.10 The echosounder and log showed that we were on the Inner Gabbard shoal.

22.20 With the log reading 43.4 we sighted the Galloper L.V. A short while after this, while I had the electrics of the hand bearing compass scattered all over the floor, the helmsman called out that 'there was a great big thing awful close' - when I heard its engines I dropped the bits and arrived on deck ... we changed course.

22.58 We obtained a fix on the Galloper light dipped (range 9¾ miles) on a bearing 255 magnetic; almost immediately the Noord Hinder light appeared. At this time we were helping the wind with the engine to maintain a speed of four knots.

- 11 -

July 13 Log 55.1 Course changed to 78 M but not for long. The wind veered and at 0.500 back to 90 M. Speed was stepped up to 5 knots - thoughts of Dutch beer.

08.33 A radio position line from the Goeree L.V. dictated a course change to 78 M. Visibility was not more than 3 miles and we never did see that L.V. However at 11.05 the colour of the water changed dramatically from dark blue to muddy brown with all sorts of litter. We assumed this to be the Maas.

11.35 Log 100.1
Land-ho and an hour later a positive fix was obtained on the S.G. Buoy. Soon after this both Freddie, (who had spent some years in the R.N.) and Bob decided to check our position with an astro-fix. A great deal of discussion followed and our position was finally jubilantly declared to be exactly seven miles from our known position. There followed the usual excuses, but of course in fact it was a very good fix.

15.12 Entered the Hook and tied up alongside a large tug in Berghaven. The log read 115 sea miles which meant we had gained about 10 miles from the tide. During the passage we had run the engine for 20 hours and used only 4½ gallons of Petrol.

The Berghaven is not a yacht haven but a tug/pilot boat harbour. It is only possible to stay one night. Stores can be got from the Hook. The following day the intended early start never materialised, partly because of the previous night's celebration, but mainly because of the tide. (The party had been a farewell for Bob and Freddie who were returning to England, and curiously enough found themselves on the wrong ship after two hours at sea!)

July 14 We eventually surfaced to a beautiful day. A nearby Belgian yacht told us they had fouled their propeller with polythene sheeting no less than three times on their journey down the Nieuwe Maas. They now carried a pair of oars on deck in case it was necessary to get out of the way in a hurry!

11 45 Took the beginning of the flood to Rotterdam. A fascinating trip through the docks and centre of the town.

15.45 Arrived at Konigshaven and waited an hour for the double bridge to open.

19.10 Turned into the Hollandsche Ijssel. A further wait at the lock bridge, the Krimpen aan de Ijssel. Gouda was our destination for the night and we moored adjacent to the lock at the head of the Gouwe which is in the centre of Gouda.

July 15 All Tuesday morning we explored the town's pottery works, museum, town hall and Cathedral. It is a fascinating town and it would be easy to spend several days there. However at 16.10 we pushed the starter and motored down the canal to the first bridge, which opened as we arrived.

19.30 We entered the Brassemermeer, a magnificent piece of water, which we drifted across at 2 knots, arriving at the Kaclof Arendsveer yacht haven at 20.00 hours.

July 16 Wednesday was yet another beautiful day and very hot. We stopped twice en route for the Kager Plassen, once for beer and once for petrol. Then on again, giving a tow to a boat-load of sea scouts from the Marco-Polo troup. Their boat was so large it nearly stopped us! However for the first time that week there was a faint breeze and with the help of a lot of sail we toured the islands of the Kager Plassen. The day finished with a run under spinnaker at 2 knots to the yacht haven at Kudelstart. The entrance is to port just in case you visit it!

The boat then received a service prior to the last lap into Amsterdam. As the rail bridge into Amsterdam harbour only opens at 01.00 hours, we decided to lower the mast, as none of us fancied Amsterdam harbour in the dark. The operation took about 40 minutes using improvised sheerlegs made from the spinnaker boom guyed to the anchor plates.

18.00 As we were passing the Central Station in Amsterdam.I noticed masts to port. This was the Sixhaven, not clearly marked on our charts, but remarkably central and convenient. The next day Donald Craig left for England and after sight-seeing in Amsterdam, Ernest and I and Moonshine left for

- 12 -

Durgedam entering the Ijsslermeer at 19.00 hours. It took only 30 minutes to reach the little village, and yacht club. The latter was very busy, and boasts a marvellous collection of 1900 Yachting Monthly magazines.

09.30 17 July We were under way in a freshening wind on a dead run for Volendam. With the boat going like a bomb at 6½ knots, I removed the whisker pole prior to shortening sail in the increasing wind. The only difference was that she steered less well. Eventually we sailed with four reefs in the main and the working jib. The speed was still over six knots. We tied up in Volendam at 12.30 and after a quick lunch went and explored the village. All the shopkeepers were wearing Dutch national dress. We left for Amsterdam at 14.00 - a dead beat. It seemed odd to have no tide to help or hinder. Four and a half hours later we were again at the bridge leading to the harbour. The sailes were stowed and the engine started. A couple of minutes later it stopped dead. This came as a complete surprise as it had previously given no trouble. There were five minutes to the bridge opening and an on shore wind. A quick check showed clean filters but dirt in the carburettor. I think this was the products of evaporation and now we always run the carburettor dry when finished with engines. We passed through the bridge into the lock followed by a 1,000 ton barge. It passed within 12 inches of us with a woman at the helm. It seemed a sight too close!

21.00 Moored again opposite the Central Station.

During the week we had covered about 220 miles. The weather had been beautiful with the barometer never below 1028 M.B. A marvellous week finished when we climbed into the train for Rotterdam and England.

EDITORIAL

To those of you who were able to get away from it all I hope you had as good a time as we did. It dose'nt take long to get back into a routine again, does it? Never mind, it's only twelve months to your next one!

PLEASE can we all in future be more careful with our belongings. Last Sunday week shoes and sunglasses were taken from the changing rooms. Also bouyancy bags and sails were stolen from one of the dinghies in the dinghy park. Please remember that this area can in no way be protected against thieves during the week. Surely you can find just a few square inches to stuff your sailing gear into your car each week, and make sure that your cover is well tied down on your boat. A few strong knots will soon put a would be thief off, even if you do have to get to Stansgate a bit sooner to undo them yourself.

Also there are still many items unclaimed (some from last season) including keys, sunglasses, towels and clothing. Please see the O.O.D. if you feel you might be a "lost" owner.

Most of you must already know that Julian Bigden came 6th overall in the International Enterprise World Championships at Weymouth last week. Congratulations Julian! You certainly did the Club proud.

Mary Greygoose.

SOCIAL NEWS

What a Barbecue! With a near perfect evening, warm and still air, the crowds flocked to Stansgate for our Annual Barbecue.

The tent was erected on the concrete hard and the bar facilities moved in, the barbecue range gave off the smell of onions and sausages and the disc jockey played his records at near full blast. It has been suggested that next year we put the D.J. on Osea Island, then the volume would be just right for Stansgate, but nevertheless he did do a grand job.

/continued.

- 2 -

As the evening wore on the hard was full of dancers, and all seemed to be having a good time, even the young children were still running about at midnight, helping in their own way to clear-up.

As you will appreciate a lot of work in preparing for a Barbecue like this is involved, and I thank very much indeed all who came forward on the Friday evening, all day Saturday and Sunday (to clear-up) for their help. It was very much appreciated.

The Commodore has kindly agreed to the Club giving a Childrens party to all members children (or grandchildren) the age limit being 4 to 12 years old.

I hope parents will be able to leave their children and go off shopping for a few hours, so if anyone would like to give me a hand in entertaining these youngsters I would be pleased to hear from them. Also perhaps you could let me know who will be coming along to give me some idea for catering purposes (sausages on sticks, ice-cream, lemonade etc.)...

Avril Stevens.

THREE MIRORS TO MALDON

H.W. at 14.24 wind westerly 3 - 4. A 12.00 start from Stansgate would give us about 2½ hrs. to see how far up river towards Maldon we would get. At least we would have a fair wind and tide to bring us back.

Initially there were two boats, Frank's crewed by his 7 year old son Mark, and my own. Then Alf joined us and so there were three.

It was a beat for most of the way and we seemed a long time just reaching the Doctor. After this the surroundings became less familiar and I did not notice the time at all. There were two disconcerting moments early on, the first was when I did not have my feet firmly enough under the oars (toe straps!) and nearly fell out; the second was more serious. Whilst settling on the port tack to beat up to Mill Beach and contemplating the sea, sky and the perfection of Mirror dinghies, a cry of starboard from the other side of a wall of red sail forced me to tack rather hastily. From then on a sharp lookout was kept - the river is very crowded on a Sunday afternoon.

The stretch between the Blackwater Sailing Club and Heybridge Basin was very busy and interesting. There was a barge tacking up, they are magnificant, however I did not have the nerve to shout starboard and claim right of way. There was a lot of activity around the lock itself with boats locking out of the canal.

Another tack and Maldon came into view. Several more short tacks, with the water peaceful and calm, and we were able to "go ashore" by the swimming pool and enjoy our lunch. Maldon is a busy place especially at H.W. There were barges being towed up, timber ships, and pleasure craft of all shapes and sizes. It was interesting to speculate on what the scene would have looked like in the age of sail when the barges were used commercially. We had time to sit and watch, perhaps feeling more a part of the scene having arrived by boat. The tide continued to come in for a little while. It covered a piece of rusty chain then uncovered it again.

The run back to Stansgate proved uneventful as the wind had dropped slightly. I could not catch the other two up - but put that down mainly to a bad start. It had been a very interesting and enjoyable adventure.

Geoff. Farnie.

Team Race - Marconi versus Stone - 20th June.

Draper, James and Black were responsible for not winning this event. Stone proving difficult to hold on the long beat from Breezy point to 'A' mark. Lessons on short tack tactics were learned.

During the practice race it was noticable that one boat was extremely fast on the run, equally noticable was that her spinnaker was rather large. It was in fact a 'Fireball spinnaker and after a few words in the right place it was seen no more. I have it on good authority however that this sail was used during the Rum Tub and Bung race - rather naughty - someone should have protested.

Nick Beavins, after having represented his school in the Essex Schools Regatta at Brightlingsea early in July, went on as a member of the ten-man Essex entry to the National Schools Sailing Association's Regatta held at Felixstowe Ferry Y.C. from 20-24th July.

G.P. PATTER

Firstly I must offer some sort of excuse for the non-appearance of G.P. Patter in the last issue of Navigans; some of my readers were saddened and downcast about it and even went to the lengths of writing terrible poems to express their disappointment.

The reason was not, as one wag suggested, that I had not got any lead in my pencil - it was simply that I lost my pen.

The pen was recovered some weeks later when a special branch squad raided a Mexican restaurant on the Isle of Dogs, where it was being used by an African Bushman dressed in plastic dicky and spats to dot the eyes in Chilli Sauce - so help me.

G.P. 14 fleets in our area are very active; the South East Area Championships at Leigh attracted a fleet of 73, while our local open events on the Blackwater usually manage a turnout of 20 to 30 boats. I am happy to report that a small proportion of the Marconi fleet has been attending open meetings this year.

The results of our efforts have been varied, at times giving rise to jubilation and at others to abysmal depression.

G.P. 14's at Leigh-on-Sea - Cockleshell Trophy - May 9th-10th.

This was the first open we attended and results-wise was not very impressive. Thirty boats (approx.) participated in four races in rather light airs over a triangular course. Triangular courses and committee boat starts are usual at Leigh.

Leigh is a pleasant place to sail from, it is surprisingly quiet, there is plenty of car park space and the travelling time is about the same as from Chelmsford to Stansgate. On the occasions that we have been there launching has been very easy, although I imagine that things become rather more exciting with a strong on-shore breeze.

South East Area Championship - Leigh-on-Sea - June 6th-7th.

Seventy-three G.P's. took part in this event. Conditions varied from light to force 5 and back to light again, gate starts were used.

I am not sure of the overall result but our best individual race position was 26th. The winner was Ian Willis from Hamble River Sailing Club with his boat Turmoil.

Your actual Bill Morris was there with 'Frantic'. We gave his boat a swift scrut and were pleased to note that the layout was similar to ours with the exception that she had an elastic powered roller to collect the spinnaker halliard fall and that centre main sheeting was fitted.

There were very few boats with centre main sheeting at this meeting. 'Musto & Hyde' sails seem to be popular with the front runners.

/continued.

- 5 -

Race No. 2 between Stone S.C. and Thorpe Bay was a bit of a mess with one TBYC boat being disqualified through being over the line at the start, and one S.S.C. boat retiring. Thorpe Bay still managed to win, taking 1st and 2nd place.

Race No. 3 between Marconi and Thorpe Bay was a hard fought battle with T.B.Y.C. finally gaining 1st, 3rd, and 6th place to give them a win. Although Thorpe Bay managed to beat both us and Stone S.C. they did not manage to gain sufficient points to win the series.

Result - 1st M.S.C. 2nd. T.B.Y.C. and 3rd. S.S.C.

Somewhere between races there was the Barbecue, a most enjoyable affair. Many 'hosannas' to Avril for doing away with the "Three old men and a dog Toby" type dance band. How about a Discotheque type thing for the 'laying-up Supper'?

Our team races against the Osea Club have not happened. Osea could not make it for the first leg at Stansgate, and we could not supply a reasonable team for the return match at Osea. I have given Mr. Weston of the Osea Club a number of dates when team races will be possible. I am still waiting for a reply.

The South East Area Championships will be held at Stone S.C. next year.

There are two measuring sessions for G.P.14's this month - see the notice board for details.

Pat Black.

LETTER TO THE EDITOR.

"I would like to support Ian Tate in his plea for more adequate moorings and in particular for regular inspection. Last year my own boat went adrift inspite of having a riding scope of ⅜ chain only 9 months old. I was appalled at the condition when I inspected it after lifting it at the end of last year. A great number of us tend to use black chain which is only too frequently lift chain. This seems to explain the peculiarity that the surface of the links breaks up into irregular lumps. I have never known this happen with galvanised chain and can only assume that this is because the material from which lift chain is made is a harder steel, more prone to corrosion. Similarly, shackles used for lifting gear seem to corrode more than galvanised shackles used for rigging.

Finally, may I offer my congratulations to the Commodore and those responsible for what was a most successful regatta. I was unfortunately unable to be there as I was cruising by the coast, but from the result sheets and what I have heard, it was quite an affair. I know from experience the amount of sheer hard work that goes into these events!

Terry Hallam.

ENTERPRISE WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS 1970

It has been left to me to do a write-up on the Enterprise World Championships which this year were held at Weymouth in Dorset. Three Marconi boats entered - Chris Cooper with Peter Crick as crew, Terry Roper, and also Julian with Charles Hewlett as crew. Tim Bigden and Peter James also took part in the racing as they offered their services as crew. The total entry this year was 203.

After a slow but jolly drive down through heavy traffic and boiling hot sun on the Saturday, Sunday morning saw a great bustle of activity in the dinghy park. I have never seen so many bottoms being lovingly cared for as one boat tried to outshine the next. There were last minute adjustments to be made, toe straps to be lengthened, jib fairleads moved, kicking straps tightened, compasses positioned and burgees raised, yes and believe it or not, even jib sticks given a last minute polish!

Well, at last they were all off on Sunday afternoon for the practice race. The wind was fairly light but the day was fine and everyone was set for an enjoyable week's racing. Little did they know what was in store. Julian and Chris came 39th and 92nd respectively.

Monday awoke to a considerably stiffer breeze, and discounting several capsizes the race passed off without a hitch with P. Martin of Looe S.C. taking 1st place, Julian 7th, and Chris 93rd.

By Tuesday the wind force had increased to force 6-7 and the race was cancelled before the start. Wednesday saw a full gale with similar conditions Thursday.

However, by Friday the wind had decreased to force 4-5 and the race Committee ran two races. Roger Hance from Burnham won the first race on Friday with Julian 13th and Chris 76th. This result put Roger Hance ¼ point behind 'Hell's Bell's', an Irish boat. To win the Championship he had to beat 'Hell's Bell's' and come better than 4th.

Results of the last race were 1st. S. Storrar from Tynemouth with Roger Hance 2nd, Julian 8th and Chris 57th.

/continued.

- 8 -

This gives Roger the World Championship for 1970. Congratulations Roger, with Julian 6th overall and Chris probably between 30th and 50th overall. The full results are not available yet.

In spite of the disappointment at the loss of racing for three days, morales remained high with the beach becoming one large football ground.

It appears already that there will be five Marconi entries for next year's World Champs. which are being held at Harwich. Maybe we can get even more. It is certainly a very enjoyable and thorcughly worth while week.

Jill Bigden.

MOONSHINE IN FRIESLAND

by Barbara & Donald Woods and Richard Brown

By D.P.W.

24.7.69 The Family Woods, B.W., D.W., Katie (13) Richard (12) and Deborah (9) joined ship in the Sixhaven, Amsterdam after a pleasant steamer and rail trip. This old yacht club harbour is magnificently placed. It is going to be extended and improved in the near future for the service of visiting yachtsmen. Do not use the temporary harbour in the shadow of the Harbour Masters building; it is incredibly uncomfortable from a constant swell.

Amsterdam is a charming city and worth more than the three days we spent there. We squeezed in a visit to the Rijkmuseum and the Royal Dutch Touring Club also on the Museumplein where all charts are available. We ate out several times: excellent food, moderately expensive but vast helpings; four orders between five seemed quite adequate.

27.7.69 11.00hrs. Left for Ijssellmeer: not a good day to choose being Sunday when bridges are often only partially manned. However we passed our first locks - the Orangesluis at noon, seeing the bridge open and shut ahead of us so lunched until it opened again at 1400 hours. Into the Ijssellmeer and up spinnaker for the first short leg. Great thrill at being here at last. The three tourist villages of Marken, Volendam and Monnikendam are within easy half-day sail. Within the next four years they will be reached only by a canal as the last polder of the old Zuider Zee is completed. This will confine the open water to an area north of Enkhuizen and Urk. We chose Monnikendam and were perhaps fortunate in finding it on a Monday morning, quite free of tourists and a pleasant place to stay.

The routine in Holland is for very relaxed sailing: no tides so no clock to watch. One rises late, shops and sightsees; then in the afternoon just before or after lunch sails for the next port which should be reached in time for an evening meal. In Monnikendam, in a bank overlooking a canal with fountain and aviary of exotic birds, we found an unusual procedure. Customers wait in a room, then are summoned by a bell to interviews with a cashier in an individual cell with a closed door and grille between customer and chashier. It was more reminiscent of visiting hours in an American penitentiary than cashing a cheque.

28.7.69 Sailed before lunch for Hoorn where we arrived mid-afternoon. Lunch incidentally was eelburgers - they are delicious. Once upon a time Hoorn gave its name to Cape Horn: these ports were the head-quarters of the Dutch East Indiamen and one of the first things seen entering the vast outer harbour are the warehouses dating from the great 17th-century Dutch maritime successes. We swam in the outer harbour, then moved into one of the new marinas. Two years ago when we were last in Holland I was told they were going to make new berths for 6 - 8,000 yachts, to turn the country into Europe's centre of sailing. This is happening: almost every port has its old traditional harbour and moorings plus a brand new marina opened this year. Hoorn is an attractive town of which we saw too little. We did see two teenage girls hosing and scrubbing the outside of a 17th-century dockside house. This could explain why Dutch houses look so spotless after 300 years.

29.7.69 Sailed before lunch for Enkuizen. Unsuccessful battle with spinnaker followed by sail reduction and reefing as wind increased. Decided not to cross Ijssellmeer to a lee shore in worsening weather so beat back to Enkhuizen. There we met our first English yacht

- 10 -

another SD 26, No. 45, sailed by a West Country family working in Holland. Clearly the Ijssellmeer must be given its due respect, they told us, as a fishing boat had been overwhelmed and lost only three weeks before off its harbour of Urk.

30.7.69 In view of weather laid over in Enkhuizen and visited the West Friesland Museum (a branch of the Rijksmuseum). This is a must being a marvellous display of boats and gear, costumes and paintings of the old fishing port, all beautifully displayed. The town is pleasant but has little else to offer, but one can eat out well on the usual principle of 5 into 4 will be enough.

31.7.69 Beautiful gentle sail, though hard on the wind, to Lemmer. This tideless crossing seemed ideal to assess leeway, which seems to be 7-10° in this weight of wind. Into Friesland via the lock at Lemmer to find the town totally full of boats, so had to motor out a mile or so to moor to the canal bank. Memo: Mond anchors are desirable although usually there is a post or ring for at least one warp: we used the kedge anchor on the other.

1.8.69 Friesland is like an enlarged Norfolk Broads and very much less populated. However the canal twisted, the wind remained astern so we had a magical sunny slow sail to Sneek. This is the main town of Friesland and each year on the Sneekmeer some 3 miles east of the town there is a big regatta. This was due to begin the next day and when we arrived in the afternoon the meer approaches were incredibly crowded. It is a marvellous lake, triangular with about 2 mile sides with several large islands. People come from all over by car and boat with caravan, tent or cruiser and live for the week's racing. It was blowing about 3 from the North, so after sailing round the lake we found a berth for the night in the lee of the island with the starting box on it. More and more boats arrived: as night fell an impressive electrical storm with heavy horizontal rain and hail blew up. It was in the cockpit enjoying a semi-voluntary fresh water shower when a lightening flash revealed a late arrival - a single handed International Finn under full sail who scooted into the lake and drove his bow into the first available weather shore gap.

2.8.69 Dawned as usual sunny and increasingly hot. Racing began at 10.00 the there must have been 2-3,000 boats on the lake. There were a number of modern classes such as Finns, Flying Juniors, O.K.s and Vauriens, and many classes derived from the Dutch school with gaff type sails, the most popular, of considerably varying ages, rather resembling a Burnham One-Design. Races were starting continuously every 15 minutes and one could see at any time five races in progress round the circuit. A great informality reigned as the start of one class of, say, 25 yachts would be accompanied by practice starts from some of the succeeding classes, plus odd cruisers going over the line about their own business and a small child happily sailing a lugsail dinghy in the middle of it all. Fortunately the 1,000 ton commercial barges' route led them round the margins of the meer so caused no interference. Although we should like to have stayed, especially to watch the race of the unengined steel sailing talk type barges (which are raced representatively, for districts, and very hard, up and down Holland at various regattas), our time-table caused us to leave about teatime. We had a leisurely motor sail, trailing children astern on warps and stocked up for supper in Heeg, a very lovely village with a difficult mooring problem. Then down the Heegermeer some ten miles in the lightest of evening breezes with the Sunlog recording nil with genoa and two knots with spinnaker. About 2100 we reached a narrow part, and attempted to moor in the lee beyond. So gentle was the evening, we lay head to zephyr with main up, and genoa and spinnaker in heaps on the deck as we hilariously tried to come alongside the grassy bank. However our bilge keels prevented this, so we recovered Katie, who was ashore, just in time to notice a weather change. We doused the main about 30 seconds before the wind arrived and then had a maniac half hour. The wind was a good 6-7, and within 2 minutes waves were

- 11 -

breaking over the shore and the boat was taking the wavetops aboard. There was no risk as we were bumping on firm muddy shore with no tidal problems, but it was uncomfortable none the less - lee shores are deeply ingrained in tidal sailors' nightmares. However with poling from ahead, and engine full astern we came off, and round into the narrow canal which now gave a lee. The storm blew itself out after an hour or so and after a quiet night, another sunny day dawned.

ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING

The Annual General Meeting of the Marconi Sailing Club will take place on Friday, November 20th, 1970 at 8.00 pm in the M.A.S.C. Hall, Beehive Lane.

This is the occasion of the year when members have the chance to discuss the running of the Club with the retiring Committee and to make suggestions for changes and improvements for the new Committee to consider.

The new Committee and Officers are of course elected at this meeting and to do this volunteers for Committee are required. To this end a nomination form is attached to the back of this issue of Navigans, and we would like to see many of these returned to the Secretary with suggestions for potential Committee members.

If you feel you would like to serve on the Committee and nobody has suggested it, don't be put off, just fill in the appropriate bits and wave the form in the air, and the other formalities will soon be completed. Or more seriously, return it to the Secretary as an indication of your willingness and he will do the rest.

We do ask all members to consider the Committee seriously and even if you don't feel you can serve on the Main Committee perhaps you would indicate if you are interested in serving on a Sub-Committee as there are many many things that have to be organised each season. Just a few of the Sub-Committees that participate in the running of your Club are:-

Social - Clubhouse and precincts - sailing - bar etc.

Please don't delay - nominate today.

CRUISER WINTER STORAGE

Cruiser owners are advised that before putting their boats into the Dinghy park, they must apply either to John Todds at Baddow or Jimmy James at Witham for a storage place to be allocated.

In view of our existing tenancy arrangements at Stansgate, it would be advisable for the very minimum of boats to be left their during the winter. Great difficulty may be experienced should they have to be moved when the ground becomes waterlogged.

Despite numerous requests, there are still several unidentified boats in the area. Some may be abandoned as they do not appear to have been used or moved during this and previous seasons. It could be that their owners are no longer readers of Navigans, so that the message has not reached them. If anyone recognises any of these boats or knows their owners, please assist by either informing them or myself so that arrangements for the boats removal or disposal can be made.

Should your boat not comply with the Club ruling regarding identification please see that a label of some sort is fitted during the next few weeks, otherwise it may be treated as abandoned.

G.P. PATTER

October, month of mists and mellow fruityness, brings to a close the 1970 summer sailing season.

One of the duties I regarded with dread forboding at the beginning of the season was that of nominating race officers and rescue boat crews - visions of mass absenteeism and eleventh hour cancellations. I need not have worried, everyone turned out to do his or her duty and I would like to thank you all for making what could have been an awkward task an easy one. On behalf of the G.P. fleet I would also like to thank the members of the Enterprise, Hornet and Mirror fleets for officiating during our events.

Team racing events against the up river clubs have been a complete failure this year. Both races against the Maldon Y.C. have been cancelled, and as far as I can determine the situation will not improve for the 1971 season.

The Mulberry Trophy attracted 49 boats to Thorpe Bay Y.C. over the weekend 19-20th September.

Conditions were very light, the last race on Sunday being cancelled because of the lack of wind. The only Marconi boat present was 7532, and she finished 31st, 11th, and 7th, to gain 10th position overall. The winning boat sailed by P. Connolly came from Chase S.C.

Limited swing spreaders were noted on some of the boats in attendance.

Leigh-on-Sea S.C. are running a winter series consisting of 9 races commencing on the 31st October, and finishing with the Brass Monkey race on the 27th December. They usually manage to muster about a dozen G.P.14's for this series. Tony and I will enter 7532 and subject to a rapid and successful paint job Dave Draper will enter Gunga Din (possibly renamed Eskimo Nell).

Future. G.P. 14 fleet meeting - date to be arranged.
Winter Jugs series - first event probably towards the end of November.

Pat Black.

1970 HORNET NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS

Thorpe Bay Yacht Club were chosen as the Host Club to run the 15th Hornet National Championships, "confirming the Club as one of the premier Clubs on the East Coast, and confirming the Hornet as a thoroughbred class with a phenominal rate of development" (" Yachts and Yachting Sept. 70 issue).

The total entry was seventy boats, this was up on last years entry, and we were represented by no less than five Marconi boats.

Thorpe Bay is a fine place to sail from, and the Club facilities were excellent, but unfortunately the Championship was dogged by the most varied of weather conditions.

SUNDAY:- The practice race was cancelled due to gale force winds, although two boats ventured out to give the press photographers something to put in the papers.

MONDAY: Race was postponed and taken forward to Tuesday due to gale force winds.

TUESDAY: Morning 1st race, very little wind, first beat leg, the leaders 2 mins. ahead at the windward mark only to experience an 180° shift and have the rest of the fleet catch up by running under spinnies up the beat leg of the course, whilst they beat down the reach leg. Following this the leaders sail into a big hole and the fleet gleefully sails right round them.

These conditions were to become typical for the whole week, but spirits were not dampened. The Social organisation was well up to Hornet standards, and Southend gave us a fine Civic Reception, with free eats, drinks, and mod music, in their new super Civic Suite, Other items in the Social programme were as follows:- free Bar-B-Que, free Barrel of beer! to the chap who could bring it back from the Mulberry harbour wreck at low tide, 10 Pin Bowling Champs. etc....

The final results were as follows:-

First overall 'Hot Rod' - M. Martin, Brightlingsea S.C.
Second " 'Dry Bones' - A. Reynolds, R.C.Y.C.
Third " 'O-to-San' - Simon Darney, Marconi S.C.

The next Marconi boat was Bruce Long in 17th position. Well done Simon and Bruce.

A remark overheard during the week which sums up the Championships was, that a typical Thorpe Bay course had a beat on every leg!

Congratulations to Bruce and Jane on their marriage - October 3rd, 1970, from all the Hornet fleet.

Geoff White.

THREE MIRRORS UP THE CREEK

The day dawned bright and clear,
The weather man said, 'Be of good cheer,
Too much wind there will not be,
There may be enough - just wait and see'.

The boats prepared, we were ready to go,
Up Mayland creek, a trip nice and slow,
In line astern we made our way,
The Marconi Flag was on display.

We rounded the point, and ran up the creek,
This was the place we had come to seek.
The natives proved friendly, so much so indeed,
That tea was provided in our hour of need.

Out of that tortuous creek we beat,
No stick in the muds, the Mirror Fleet.
Occasional incidents serve to remind
That to sail on wet mud - boats are'nt inclined.

MOONSHINE IN FRIESLAND

by B. & D. Woods & R. Brown

(continued)

3.8.69 Again a Sunday with bridge delays, and for the first time we got lost in canals not shown on the charts. We passed through towns on unmarked waterways, and arrived at Staveren in time for the 1400 hrs. lock opening. One must lock both in and out of Friesland. In attempting to come alongside the quay the R.C.A. Dolphin failed to reverse, a thing never before known. It persisted in running ahead with the result that we hit the quay a resounding crack and bounced off, damaging the outboard of the boat ahead. Fortunately damage all round wasn't great: marks only on our gel coat and £4 damage to the motor (mostly labour costs) to replace a small broken bracket.

This stopped the 1400 hrs. exit: whilst preparing to delve into the electrical mysteries of the engine, a click was heard from the reversing solenoid and reverse could again be obtained. I cleaned the solenoid points but wondered whether the real trouble was excessive heat because of poor ventilation and climatic conditions: it was really hot that day.

So at 1800 hrs. out into the Ijsselmeer. After our two previous experiences with very hot days followed by electrical storms we were a little apprehensive and hurried down wind, motorsailing at 4½ knots to make Enkhuizen by 9 p.m. Again experiencedreversing troubles entering harbour, but forewarned is forearmed; we didn't hit anything!

4.8.69 Still very hot: routineshopping: the consumption of fluids being fantastic - I know why Dutch lager is so popular! Removed some insulation, drilled more holes in the electrics cover and again cleaned points of solenoid. After this we had no further trouble. After lunch sailed for Hoorn and had an uneventful passage.

5.8.69 On to Amsterdam, a wonderful hot downhill motorsail spoiled only by the noise of the motor, and myriads of minute flies, fortunately non-biting variety. Through the bridge and locks into the Sixhaven to find some five English yachts, varying from a 40' Fifer with 6' draft to a TH 90. Reverting to Eleanor Witter's Editorial in August Navigans, one yacht from Grimsby had a family with three girls on board, the youngest aged 3. They had arrived safely, tied up to the usual staging and a very brief while later the 3 year old was found, minus lifejacket, face down in the water. Fortunately she survived but spent the holiday in hospital. The other two children were now firmly wedded to their jackets.

The routes out of Amsterdam going South are three:

(i) The Rhine canal - big, traffic-ridden, with fixed bridges down to the Lek (nee Rhine) where it becomes beautiful and the bridges lift.

(ii) The Amstel river, the usual route involving passing the railways bridgein Amsterdam at 0100 hrs. unless the mast is lowered.

The Nord Zee Canal turning off at Zijkcanaal C and going south by the Haarlemmer polder. The railway bridge over the Nord Zee canal opens frequently and those at Haarlem and Gouda are not bad for delays. The block on this route comes at Sassenheim motorway bridge which opens only 0600-0700 hrs.

- 11 -

The Dutch of course lower masts at the drop of a clog because they have the gear for it. We didn't want to do this so set out on foot to study this awkwardly timed bridge in Amsterdam. However on stopping to ask the way we accidentally spoke to one of the senior officials of the Amsterdam Harbour Masters Office who most courteously told us we couldn't use the Amstel route because of a bridge permanently closed for that week. He then took us back to the office and showed us the route we could use via Zijkanaal C.

6.8.69 Motored 0600 and after half an hour found engine seriously overheating due to no water cooling. Fault for this entirely mine having failed, owing to distraction by pretty girl to reopen sea cock I had shut the previous evening. Anchored for an hour whilst engine cooled to working temperature, then praise be, all seemed still sound and motored again with cool rusty water flowing! N.B. Should check every time to see it is.

After short wait passed through swing railway bridge preceded by a car ferry and followed by a Goliath crane on tow. Couldn't quite clear the closed bridge with out mast; we need 10 metres for a margin of safety. A steady plot, then left hand down into Canal C to begin a typical canal journey to Haarlem where we arrived about noon. We had 20 minutes wait in company with three Dutch yachts for the railway bridge. The next bridge did not respond to the usual 3 toots on the horn - it had a temporary fault soon rectified by the bridgekeeper. The next bridge showed no signs of life and in the keeper's lodge I could see with binoculars a notice which looked as though it said the bridge was closed 1200 - 1400. We tied up and prepared to shop - then a barge appeared the other way and suddenly men appeared and opened the bridge. A hasty dash through and we tied up at the next inactive bridge and prepared to go shopping. We had a foot off the boat when a pleasure steamer appeared and the bridge opened. So back on board and on to a brand new twin bridge which opened on demand, and thosewere the Haarlem bridges passed in 1½ hours! The town looked as attractive as most Dutch towns and the waterside residential quarters were magnificent. Incidentally the bridges of the Haarlem area have toll of 15 cents each dropped in the shoe the keeper swings out to you.

We tied to a bank perforce for lunch because of sudden loss of power due to a plastic bag round the propellor. This is fairly easily cleared by fishing (whilst suspended in a bowline) with the toes, whilst someone turns the propellor in reverse by hand. Off again on a pleasant motor until arriving at the Sassenheim roadbridge just at the north end of the Kagerplassen at about 1600. The Dutch yachts, about 18ft. long arrived a little later and in half an hour had lowered masts, passed the bridge, re-erected and were sailing again. We decided to wait in company with a vast barge on our side, and a large Belgian school ship on the other.

7.8.69 0545hrs. A lovely morning with heavy mist banks over fields and canals, being soaked up by a fast rising sun. At 0600on the dot the bridge opened and we were through, watching with interest the barge following with only a foot to spare each side. At a steady 4 knots past the Kagerplassen and the Brassemer-meer, both beautiful sailing areas with reeded islands to spend the nights or days idling, fishing, sailing, bird-watching or whatever other shipboard pastime might be available! The birds were almost always worth watching! Some 30 minutes holdup at Alphen railway bridge, but otherwise no problem.

Finally we came to the enormous structure of the lock and storm gate at Krimpen aan de Ijssel. This is very strange to look at: there is a vast but ordinary lock to starboard. To port the river runs without impediment between two pairs of enormous towers, the first of which are in reserve and carry no gear. The second pair of towers carries a roadbridge, clearance 8m, and a colossal storm water barrage gate which can be raised

- 12 -

or lowered to dam the river completely. An incredible structure. The operator waved us under the bridge but as the tide gauge showed 8m I indicated 10 to him and without more ado the huge lock functioned just for us: in fact the change of water level is negligible of course since the river is flowing unobstructed under the bridge.

Here begins the journey on tidal and very commercial waters. This for the uninitiated is at first alarming in view of the size, quantity and speed of the barges. However traffic discipline is excellent, the main hazard being towed barges: a tug and a barge is obvious, but one barge towing another, or as in one instance a large motor vessel towing simultaneously three two-thousand ton barges is not so obvious in the flood of traffic, and covers a lot of distance. An attempt unwittingly to cross such a tow would result in disaster, so a careful eye should be kept for the white on red square flag indicating a tow. We plodded down in the constantly disturbed water and turned left and southward in the Nieuwe Maas: where that becomes the Lek (or lower Rhine) we branched right into the Noord. Just before the large Sydney Harbour type bridge (clearance 12m with lifting span) we wormed our way into a tiny yacht harbour hidden between shipyards at Alblasserdam.

Here, because I disregarded the cardinal rule of one hand for yourself, the family voyage came to an abrupt stop, as I fell whilst stepping on to the pontoon. This caused facial and rib fractures which made surgery necessary. We all flew homeon 8.8.69.

By B.W.

Donald was fortunate to have his accident in such a convenient and friendly place as Alblasserdam. We had always been delighted by the kindness of the Dutch, but here they excelled themselves. The local doctor was with us in five minutes. (We discovered later that it was his boat we had unknowingly moored alongside). Within half an hour Don had been X-rayed and tucked up in bed in a clinic only a quarter of a mile from the yacht harbour.

Ten days later I returned to Alblasserdam to collect Moonshine and along with R.G.B. and two other friends (John and another Bob) sailed her back to England. R.G.B. was in charge - I was cook.

We left London Airport on Friday evening, August 15th after a day of many telephone calls and indecisions. The weather seemed kind with a light N.W. at present - but was there a chance of it turning S.W. and increasing? It would be such a waste of time and money to fly out and have to fly back. It wqs getting towards the end of August and therefore the possibility of equinoctial gales were not far away. Also we were keen to have the boat to sail in England. We went.

After eating and drinking in Rotterdam, we reached Moonshine at 02.00 for four hours sleep ( too little) before catching the tide to the Hook.

16.8.70 06.00 We left the yacht harbour and turned starboard into the Lec for Rotterdam. Although we had six hours of tide in our favour, the wind was dead against us so it was engine only for some time.

08.00 We tied up at the double bridge in Rotterdam, replenished the beer and petrol, and then noticed a familiar boat approaching. It was Bill Clark-Lewis in his yacht Minuet from the Blackwater. There was just time for a quick chat before going through the bridge together. They then turned to starboard into the Royal Maas Yacht Club for a crew change. It rained, and rained, and still rained as we plugged our way down the Nieuwe Maas. I prepared soup, sandwiches and coffee ready for whatever the night might bring.

- 13 -

12.00 We were able to put up the main and genoa and thankfully turn off the engine. The N.W. wind was increasing, and the seas were building up as we left the Hook doing six knots, with Bob and John doing the first watch. We intended passing two miles north of the Goeree L.V. but by 14.00 found we were heading to the south of it. The course was adjusted to allow for this leeway.

16.00 Log reading 36.6. We were pounding uncomfortably into heavy seas and were obviously over-canvassed. All except John felt ill. A change to reefed main and working jib was an improvement. We also inflated the rear compartment of the Avon dinghy at this point. The boat was going marvellously, and despite feeling ill, it was an exhilarating sail.

17.00 Log 41. We were overtaken by a Nicholson 32 under full sail. A fine sight as she emerged from the troughs.

23.15 Near the Noord Hinder. Log 70. The wind moderated and we shook out our reefs. Altered course to 283M.

02.30 Sighted the Galloper light which we continued to see for far too long as the wind moderated more andmore. Still it was a lovely night. I would not have changed places with anyone during my two hours alone at the helm. The others were sleeping below and I was safely strapped in my safety harness steering on a convenient star. There were plenty of ships to keep an eye on, but none came too close. This wonderful two hours certainly made up for any previous miseries.

09.00 Started the engine after trouble with water in the petrol. We were again too far south and there was very little wind at all. We identified the wreck in the Black Deep, and set a course for the Sunk.

12.40 Sighted the Roughs Towers.

13.45 The Cork L.V. loomed out of the mist.

15.00 Landguard Point and as it was a dead beat into Harwich we dropped the sails.

15.30 Moored opposite the Customs House. After a meal and clearing Customs we put up our spinnaker and chased a Cutlass up to Pinmill. He had no spinnaker and it was agreed that we would have overtaken him given time!

We left Moonshine at Pinmill until the following weekend when R.G.B. and friends sailed her back to Stansgate.

Apart from Donald's accident it had been a very successful holiday. We had all learnt a lot about coping with bridges and locks and tying up alongside.

One of the children summed up the holiday by remarking that it had been 'Happy sailing in the sun!'

FOREWORD TO THE ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING

Your Officers and Committee have given considerable time to evaluation and discussion of the problems reported to them by me, which have arisen out of recent demands from and negotiations with our Landlord and his Agent.

Following the Report to be given by me at the Annual General Meeting, approval will be sought to the recommendation by your Committee to the payment of Rent at the rate of £1,000 per annum for our Sailing Site at Stansgate, commencing December 1st, 1970. Obviously this recommendation comes to you coupled with the conviction that our interests are best served by meeting this demand.

A second recommendation is also tabled by your Committee wherein the raising of subscriptions and alterations to methods of subscribing - equitable to the use of facilities - is made, in order to recover the additional expenditure.

Opinions may differ as to how this may be done but the bleak answer is, irrespective of whatever system may be applied, if applied fairly, can only result in a family man boat owner paying roughly double the present low rates for facilities similar to those enjoyed in the past, subscriptions to the M.A.S.C. being precluded, as always, from such calculations.

Your tolerance and understanding is especially sought at this difficult period in the Club's history so please come along to the A.G.M. - all of you - and help those that toil - your presence will be their reward.

SOCIAL NEWS

Our last social get together for this year is our Christmas Party. This year it is at M.A.S.C. Beehive Lane, on Friday December 4th. The tickets are 12/- each, which includes the buffet. We have booked an excellent band, so I hope as many members as possible will come along and bring their friends. During the evening there will be some form of entertainment. Tickets will be on sale from the usual sources.

As mentioned in my last note, I said we were trying to obtain the film "Sail to Win" for dinghy sailors. Well I'm now pleased to say that we have this film and it will be included in our first winter get-together in January. More news about the programme for this evening in the December issue of Navigans.

Sixty excited children turned out for their Party at the M.A.S.C. They all seemed to enjoy themselves thoroughly, and not only did the children go home tired, so did the organisers. My thanks go out to all those who turned up to help with the preparation of food, particularly to Stan Campbell and Ian Tate who organised the children's games. When they went off to help the magician to bring his gear in, I took over musical chairs - chaos reigned, everything was out of control - so you can see we really did need Stan and Ian.

Avril Stevens,

LAYING-UP BOATS

After another grand seasons sailing, the time has come to lay-up our boats, and I expect that as in previous years, quite a number will be wintering (at your own risk) at Stansgate.

Do remove and take home all those sets of sails, lifejackets, clothing and loose fittings, in fact anything which might prove a temptation to those unwelcome visitors. Outboard motors, Calor Gas bottles, anchors etc. can disappear, a few screws and lashings are not always adequate protection against theft.

Now to the actual laying-up :-

Cruisers. Please contact either John Todds at Baddow Labs. (Extn. 670) or myself at Witham (Extn. 467 or evenings Chelmsford [redacted]) if you wish to leave your boat in the Dinghy/Car Park. If unable to contact us, please berth

/continued overleaf

- 3 -

your boat as close to the Race Box as possible and in the lines already started. Leave about three feet only between it and the next one.

The areas between the boat shed and the first dinghy row, and that just beyond the last dinghy row must be kept clear for other activities.

Remove or lower your mast and make sure that the boat is adequately propped up and secured, so that the wind cannot blow it over. Also put extra lashings over any covering.

Dinghies The first essential is to remove your mast - despite requests to do this, last winter several dinghies were blown over because their mast was left rigged. Please do not leave mast projecting into gangways between rows. I would suggest taking them home. If they cannot be stowed under cover, either prop up and secure vertically to a leeside drainpipe or secure horizontally alongside a garden fence and support with cord at several points.

If possible turn the dinghy upside down, support on a few old tyres and last down a cover of some sort, trollies can be lashed down on top.

If the dinghy is left on the trolley either last securely to trolley or to some stakes alongside. Use a piece of timber to lift overboom covers up to normal position. Extra lashings over the cover will help prevent wind getting underneath and tearing it.

Remember - delamination and other damage can be caused by frost on damp plywood, so try to protect against it.

I am still trying to find the owners of several abandoned boats including a Mirror (?) HILO (L.S.C.), a Solo and a Sprite. It would be a shame if these and other apparently seaworthy boats were to form the basis of next years Barbeque Bonfire.
