Minutes of the Sailing Section Annual General Meeting held at 8.00 p.m. on Friday, 20th November 1970 at the M.A.S.C. Beehive Lane.

Chairman - Mr.S.R.Allerton (Commodore)
Number Present - 95

1. APOLOGIES FOR ABSENCE Mr.J.Bigden and Mr.C.Cooper apologised for their unavoidable absence.

2. MINUTES OF THE LAST A.G.M. Copies were provided to members at the meeting. Adoption of the minutes was proposed by F.Partlett, seconded by R.Sims and carried unanimously.

3. MATTERS ARISING FROM THE MINUTES Nil.

4. THE COMMODORE'S REPORT The Commodore presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans", December 1970). A vote of thanks to the Commodore for his service and his report was delivered by E.Payne.

5. THE SECRETARY'S REPORT The Secretary presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans", December 1970). The adoption of the report was proposed by G.Golding seconded by A.Adam and carried unanimously.

6. THE TREASURER'S REPORT The Treasurer provided copies of estimated accounts to members at the meeting, and explained the various items, and answered questions on small matters of detail. The report showed an estimated surplus of income over expenditure for the year of approximately £560.

The report adoption was proposed by G.Charlton, seconded by R.Greygoose and unanimously adopted.

7. SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT The Sailing Secretary presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans", December 1970).

Adoption of the report was proposed by G.White, who also offered a vote of thanks to Peter Crick, who was retiring as Sailing Secretary, for his services in 1970. The adoption was seconded by J.Witter and carried unanimously.

8. COMMITTEE PROPOSALS Before putting the proposals to the vote, the Commodore asked for questions relevant to the proposals.

(1) A.Adam - "Is a development proposal outstanding for Stansgate"

Commodore - "Yes - there is still a proposed development likely to come up"

(2) B.Tillotson "Who is our landlord"

Commodore - "We are a sub-tenant of Mr.Sparrow"

(3) J.Hooper - "Is there outline planning for the site"

Commodore - "Yes"

T.Hallam - The latest proposal was for a Marina complex including a Marconi Club, according to the planning map. Marconi's have prior planning permission, originally for three years, and extended by a further five years. This is due to be terminated in the Spring of 1972"

(4) Mrs.Mendoza "Might we not find we are to be asked for a £2,000 p.a. rent next year?"

Commodore - "This is unlikely. When Gonvill & Caius bought the land, they had 3 years to develop the site, after which it could revert to the original owner"

- 2 -

(5) J.Hooper - "Should we not ask for a further extension of our planning permission?"

Commodore - "Yes. We are continuously surveying the situation. Also we have always been assured that we shall be included in any other development plans"

J.Hooper - "Should we not submit plans for extension now?"

Commodore - "Yes - this is under consideration"

(6) A.Adam - "We must make sure that professional advice is maintained in these transactions. I would like to point out that it is the hard work of past and present committees that have made the club strong enough to meet this demand. It certainly could not have been contemplated when the club started at Stansgate"

T.Hallam - "The original rent asked was £250. This was reduced to £150 for the first year, and £200 thereafter, but we have never paid more than £150."

(7) D.Bolwell - "Did our landlord fix the rent or does this go to the colleges?"

Commodore - "It is to our landlord"

(8) Mrs.L.Golding "Should we not have Company Property experts to talk to us and explain the situation"

Commodore - "They can tell you no more than I"

J.Witter - "They are in fact helping the Commodore at all times"

(9) R.Waller - "Why are the negotiations discussed in such guarded terms"

Commodore - As sub-tenants of a tenant of a developer we are more confused than guarded.

(10) J.Hooper - "Are we not sitting tenants?"

T.Hallam - "No, we have an annual lease"

Commodore - "We are not sitting tenants, but we do have planning permission for the Clubhouse".

Mr.A.S.Bigden pointed out that the Committee had presented all the facts they had available and the option was pay up or get out and proposed that Committee Proposal 1 be adopted. This was seconded by T.Hallam and carried unanimously.

Committee Proposal 2 was read out, and the following questions answered.

(1) K.Beavins - "What is the additional M.A.S.C. subscription for Associates"

Commodore - £3.

(2) K.Monger - "Do the new subscriptions include the dinghy park"

Commodore - "There are no other fees or charges to pay"

J.Witter - "The dinghy park fee was previously a bye law, but now and in future all fees will be rules and brought before members for ratification.

F.Harrison "Do we pay two hard fees for two boats"

J.Witter - "Yes, if used regularly"

(4) A.Adam - "Does the hard fee refer to moorings in the case of cruisers, as some members who frequent the club moor elsewhere? I would be prepared to make some payment"

Commodore - "No payment is necessary if there is no regular mooring, but donations are always welcome"

- 3 -

(5) B.Partridge - "How about occasional visits of dingies normally sailed say at Southend"

Commodore - "There will be some discretion. It is the blatant offender we would object to"

R.Sims - proposed acceptance of Committee Proposal 2, which was seconded by J.James and carried unanimously.

C.Allerton said that he knew the Committee had worked hard on this problem for the club and would like to thank them for making a good job of the problem.

9. ELECTION OF OFFICERS AND COMMITTEE

The election of officers and committee as per agenda (by Rule 10g) Mr.E.Payne took the chair and suggested that the Officers be accepted en bloc. This was proposed by G.Charlton and seconded by L.Mendoza and carried unanimously. The Commodore then reintroduced the officers, proposed support for the Associate and new Committee members. This was also accepted unanimously.

10. ANY OTHER BUSINESS

(1) G.White - "Will we be able to accept more Associate Members?"

Commodore - "The Associate membership is an M.A.S.C. rule, but we will look into this further with our new committee.

(2) B.Urey - "Are Associates re-elected each year?"

Secretary - "No, this would be rather hard on them. However, partly in order to speed up entrance of new Associates, we have reduced the dead line for subscriptions to the end of February"

(3) A question was asked regarding improved car parking. The Secretary said it was hoped that parking labels would help deter interlopers and improve parking.

The Commidore noted that over 300 non-member cars had been turned away in 1970.

(4) A.Adam - "Could we have more single handed events?"

P.Crick - "Four were scheduled for last year, but only one held due to lack of support"

(5) The question of dangerous speedy driving in the club premises was raised. The Commodore said this was a constant source of worry to the Committee, and asked everyone to do their best by example to improve this.

Meeting closed 9.40 p.m.

D.W.G.Byatt.
Hon.Sec.

Members of the Marconi Sailing Club. On this occasion a year ago you elected me to be the Commodore of your Club and today I am called to make = a reporte

On that same evening were elected your other Officers and Committee Members to which further names and appointments were added throughout the yar. as the needs arose.

I am very happy to -report that these good people carried out their duties to the best of their ability and obtained results (with some help from the weather) which gave us all a very successful season of Sailing and social fellowship. oe

T have no intention therefore of interfering with the duties of my friends who are also called to report tonight, as having been charged with competency by their appointments will, I am quite sure, report to you the
business
of the Club in a way which is understandable to both you and myself--

At your Laying Up Supper I passed my sincere thanks on your behalf
to all of th®se people who in any small or large way have laboured for the Club
during the past season and tonight I would repeat these thanks with the hops that they received satisfaction from the results which have been obtained.

/continued.

- 3 -

"Commodore's Report"

My appreciation of their efforts is again added together with a thank you for the compliment which has been paid by the retiring Officers and Committee in offering themselves for re-election almost without exception.

Before I advance to the more serious subjects of the evening I will take the Commodores privilege to digress a little from a report to well meriting comment.

In recent weeks I have had occasion to meet officials from many clubs in the course of both social and business duties, and I can assure you that as your No. 1 representative, I am also your No. 1 supporter, whether it be for the best in Sailing, women, boats, beer or babies - the Marconi Club has them all. Ladies and Gentlemen it is my happy lot to tell you that over exuberance on my part in supporting the qualities of our Club has not been necessary - we are accepted, liked and welcomed as a Club wherever we go on the Blackwater, Crouch, Colne and in so many other places - but - and more important still - our opinions are requested and our reasoning and advice is considered.

Having reached this stage of competency I salute the efforts of our Fleet Captains and members in going out for the competition but at the same time appreciating always that which is always at home. Last season saw a wonderful improvement in the organisation of our racing fleets as far as manning and officering were concerned an appreciation not fully shown before of such necessities from a Fleet angle - Bless you all - keep it up!

Whilst on the subjects of sailing and racing I hope you will permit me to point out that we must first be introduced into and go through the wet and sometimes painful lessons connected with learning before we can sail, afterwards comes the even more wet and painful job of learning the arts of racing, to which some of us may never aspire, but - and this is the point which was put to me - you must first sail before you race and the objects of our Club as our rules so positively point out are "the promotion of Sailing and the encouragement of Social fellowship amongst all who are interested in the Sea".

Following this I would ask - do we really try to assist our shy potterers or cruising members into racing when we so meticulously fight to the last protest fee over episodes which happen around the sticks and yet blatantly impose adult crews on cadet helmsmen, another sex into Ladies Races and much below forties into the over forties race, whilst in the best Mud Race for years some of us grumble about the mud. Please do not misunderstand me as these comments are not made to offend but rather to make us think. Let us have a lot of fun together and occasionally stretch the rules, but otherwise, let us keep all the rules, including the unwritten ones - next year.

And now my friends for several years a shadow has darkened the thoughts of those privileged to be the policy makers and responsible for the future of our Club due to our inability to control events outside of our jurisdiction. I refer of course to security of tenure in relation to our Club Site. This year, my friends the shadow has become a cloud due to the demands by our Landlord for a rent increase to £1,000 per annum.

Such matters have caused me great anxiety for our immediate future and although the last word tonight is yours, your Officers and Committee unanimously approve the action so far taken on your behalf and propose to you that you - the Club - should pay the rent now requested.

We still have no security of tenure beyond the one year which acceptance of proposal and payment of rent would ensure and due to the involved sub-tenant problems and plans to push ahead with the Marina Scheme which we are assured do not exclude us as the Sailing Club on the Site, we cannot at the moment get far with any negotiations. I have been assured that our interests have been and will continue to be considered and I have no reason to disbelieve this statement except to add - at a price. Let us hope that we can contain that price and eventually break through the years of

/continued.

- 4 -

"Commodore's Report"

uncertainty ( which is not unfamiliar to several clubs on the river) to time when the position may offer us an opportunity to purchase or lease for a long time.

The acceptance by you of this situation tonight will of course mean that our Landlord and his Agent will be informed and negotiations will re-commence.

To save the question - could'nt we have got this cheaper than £1,000 - the answer is No! - and to argue might have cost us much more than we would want to face.

I believe you all want the Marconi Club to exist and flourish at Stansgate and that my friends is the object of my endeavours and those of your Officers and Committee.

Later, under item 8 of the proceedings you will be asked to support the proposals of your retiring Committee, if you support the need to stay at Stansgate you must similarly support the need to find the money required by payment of additional subscriptions.

It is your Club and your decision.

I shall be only too pleased to answer to the best of my ability any relevant questions.

Thank you for listening to me.

SECRETARY'S REPORT

Our rule book states that the "object of the Club shall be the promotion of amature sailing, the encouragement of social fellowship among all those interested in the sea, and the provision of all possible facilities to this end".

The rules also state that - "At least one Committee Meeting shall be held in each calendar month".

The object of these meetings, although not exactly stated, must be to carry out the sentiments expressed in the object of the Club. Committee meetings have been held regularly every month this year, usually on the first Monday in the month, and Committee members attendance has been very high, ranging from 17 to 11, the highest figure relating to the Extraordinary Meeting called to discuss the action required to meet the rent increase.

The Sub-Committees functioned effectively again this year, and the Dinghy Park secretary appointment was continued and he has carried out still more improvements.

Although we seem to say the same every year, this year really has been, I'm sure, a very successful one, helped by the weather of course, and participation in sailing has been very high, both in racing and sailing generally.

However, Membership is down a little on last year, the Club now has the following membership:-

Marconi Members:- - 178 Family
94 Single Adult
63 Junior and Cadet

Associate Members:- - 65 Full
15 Junior and Cadet

/continued.

- 5 -

"Secretary's Report"

The number of dinghys in the Club is a little higher than last year, at 150, and the number of cruisers about the same as last year. This means that the lost members came from the non-sailors, and is possibly just failure to rejoin the M.A.S.C. when the new subscriptions were introduced.

The arrangements for O.O.D. duty have been carried out well, and the introduction of a Race Officer rota into the sailing programme has brought about a considerable improvement in this duty.

The number of Associates permitted was fixed early in the year by the M.A.S.C. and because the final date for subscriptionsto be paid is the end of March, and therefore we cannot know vacancies until then, it'sdifficult to finalise Associate admittance until fairly late.

The committee have been concerned about the use of the site by unaccompanied non-members, and have continued the occasional gate checks. However, we cannot afford these every weekend during the summer, and O.O.D's have found it impractical to identify interlopers.

Two of the proposals on the agenda are designed to improve these points.

Sailing Secretary's Report

Sailing at the Club at the moment is going through a period of change. More and more helmsman are travelling to attend open meetings held by other Clubs and whilst the Club's name gains in stature, entries to Club races this year are down on last year's figures. The Helmsman of the Year, although still successful, attracted a total of 106 entries as opposed to 127 last year - a drop of 16%.

The three main fleets points series remain well supported. Enterprise Spring Points attracted 41 entries, main points series 89. G.P.14 Spring Series attracted 29 entries and the main points series 46. The Hornet Series attracted 29 entries.

This year has seen the first staging of a Mirror Points Series which attracted a total of 17 entries. Next year's entry will be double this figure I am sure.

The Handicap Fleet, as such, failed again to produce a series this year, although a number of non eligible boats sailed in the races. This, I believe is a reflection in our Club of a national trend away from handicap racing towards class racing. The Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships next year, for example, will be run more along class racing lines and whilst retaining the final Cock of the River races, should prove more attractive to

/continued.

- 6 -

"Sailing Secretary's Report"

the modern dinghy sailor. Our own Saturday Points series faltered this year - the total entry was 8, and the entry to the Cadet Points was down to 22. I think we should be aware of this trend and attempt to cater for it in the future.

The re-organised Ladies Points was a success with a total entry of 30, the only disappointment being that not one crew found himself eligible for the crew's prize!

Talking of Ladies Points and crew prizes, I think it worth noting that it was at this meeting last year that both these innovations were suggested.

The open events staged this year proved to be as successful as they have done in the past. The Regatta was a success as were the Enterprise East Coast Area Championships, and most agreed the discotheques provided the best atmosphere we've had a Stansgate Parties for years.

In spite of unattractive weather conditions, the Challenge Cub attracted 45 entrants this year a drop of only 6 on last year's figure.

The Blackwater Inter-Clubs Cruiser Championships boosted our Cruiser Cup entry to 14. Dabchicks S.C. won the Championships but it was nice to see one of our own members - M. Owers - win the Cruiser Cup.

Team racing on the river is at a low ebb and we are no exception to this rule. The only successful scheduled team race this year was against Saltcote.

At least the Hornet Fleet thought it successful as they once more won the trophy. Our Enterprises could'nt field a team to race against B.B.C.'s Ariel S.C. and M.Y.C. failed to race against us in G.P.14's. Although the G.P.14's did put up a very good show in a three cornered team race at Stone by beating both Stone and Thorpe Bay in the final analysis.

Individual achievements this year have been more notable than last year. Simon Darney came 2nd in the Hornet European Championships and 3rd in the Hornet National Championships. 6th in the Enterprise World Championships at Weymouth was Julian Bigden. Well done both!

The rescue boats have done us well this year, but it would be nice to have a guard launch that goes faster than a close-hauled dinghy for these gate starts!

Races have been well managed by the Race Officers and assistant coxswains supplied by the fleets this year. For our Club I believe we have hit on the right scheme as far as race management is concerned.

Finally, as I'm not standing for office again this year due to a posting abroad, I want to thank the whole Club not only for everything they have done towards making my job as Sailing Secretary easier but also for the valued friendship they have offered me particularly in times of personal stress. I'm sure you will make my successor feel very much at home in his new job and I wish the Club every success in the future and hope to manage to fit in the odd visit to Stansgate every now and then.

Peter Crick.

TWO SEASONS WITH A MIRROR

The second season of sailing a Mirror from Stansgate is over. If the first season was spent in learning the rudiments of this fascinating art of sailing a small boat, this season has seen an introduction to the two equally attractive worlds of cruising and racing.

/continued.

- 7 -

Our season started, as the next one will, at Easter. We took the boat to the Norfolk Broads and camped near Norwich. The main problems were a surfeit of wind and the tent zips freezing up!

The Regatta was extremely enjoyable. We camped at the club and the slowly freshening conditions of the three days were ideal. We did not do very well and it became apparent that even a Mirror can be tuned.

The Spring points did not get off the ground, however several of the Summer points have been sailed, and it is very true to say that a tremendous amount can be learnt in races against similar boats about tide, wind, tactics and tuning.

The pleasures of cruising have been sampled. A particularly enjoyable trip is to sail with the last hour or so of the tide up Lawling Creek and to call at the Maylandsea Bay Yacht Club for refreshments before returning on the first of the ebb.

And so to next season, more racing, a spinnaker perhaps? Certainly more cruising. The more adventurous of the Mirror Fleet have already ventured to Mersea and there is much of interest in that direction. Till Easter - time to dream.

Geoff. Farnie.

Sail Training Association:
Schooners "Sir Winston Churchill" and "Malcolm Miller"

The Sail Training Association schooners "Sir Winston Churchill" and "Malcolm Miller" will be providing a full season of cruises next year and the Committee have previously agreed to reserve a number of berths for Essex young people in the series of cruises and to offer grant aid to those who are selected.

Details of the cruises on which berths have been requested are set out overleaf. The cruise fee will be £60 and the Committee offers grant aid of 50% of this fee. Young people selected to take up these berths will be expected to meet their own cost of travel to the point of embarkation and home from the point of disembarkation.

The "Sir Winston Churchill" and "Malcolm Miller" are schooners of 300 tons Thames measurement, 135 feet long, have a beam of 25 feet and a draught of 5 feet 6 inches. They are rigged three masted schooners with a Bermudan mizzen and gaff sails and top sail on the fore and main; in addition there are square sails on the mast; the top of the main mast is 98 feet above deck. They have two auxiliary diesel engines each of 135 horse power which will drive them at 9½ knots and they have central heating installations for use in cold weather.

In each permanent crew there is a Master, a Chief Officer, a Bosun, an Engineer and a Chef. In addition, there are three experienced Watch Officers, three Watch Leaders and 39 trainee crew on each training cruise, supported by a Navigator, a Purser, a Bosun's Mate and a Chef's Assistant. TRAINEES DO NOT REQUIRE ANY PREVIOUS EXPERIENCE OF THE SEA OR OF SAILING.

The three-watch system is used on board, each watch consisting of:-

A Watch Officer.

A Watch Leader between his 17th and 24th birthday.

13 Trainees who must have reached their 16th birthday on the first day of their training cruise but must NOT HAVE REACHED THEIR 21st BIRTHDAY ON 1st MAY 1971.

The rules and requirements for the cruises for girls, including the age limits are exactly the same as for boys. On girls' cruises, the Watch Leaders are girls and two adult ladies are also on board.

The trainees will spend a fortnight on board. The majority of the time will be spent at sea but there will be opportunities to go ashore. Whenever possible, each training cruise will include a visit to an overseas port. Apart from this intention, it is not planned to establish any detailed itinerary, each day's programme being arranged to give the best possible sailing as dictated by the weather.

The young people on board will be part of the ship's company and as such will take an active part in the care and maintenance of the ship and standing and running rigging, as well as their watch duties as look-out, steering, galley work and ship cleaning.

Life at sea in a sailing ship is traditionally one of the hardest that a man can undertake. Although this taste of it will last but two weeks, it would be idle to pretend that the Sail Training Association's Schooners provide an exception to this or that those on board will not be very fully extended.

Those who show the requisite qualities during their training cruise may be offered the chance of further cruises as Watch Leaders, Bosun's Mates or Chef's Assistants.

SOCIAL SCREED

We all talk about the weather, so why not learn something about it?

Come along to "Clouds and Weather" at the M.A.S.C. on Friday 29th January at 8 pm. when Mr. Ken Pilsbury, A.R.P.S. from the Meteorological Office at Bracknell will try to teach us the significance of cloud formations and their changes, with the aid of about 100 slides and diagrams. He may also try to sell you an excellent book he has written on the subject. Cruisers - if you want to know when to reef the burgee, this is the man to tell you! Racers: Don't be a depression, katabatic winds may give you an extra knot. Photographers - Mr. Pilsbury has exhibited photographs at many international exhibitions. This should be a very interesting evening so I hope as many as possible will come along. Also during this evening a member of the St. Johns Ambulance is coming along to demonstrate resuscitation and discuss hypothermia.

You will remember some time last summer a Mr. Forbes from Musto and Hyde (Sailmakers) coming down to Stansgate to talk to some of us. His visit was so well received he has agreed to come along to Beehive Lane on the 19th Feb. to talk to us again and answer many of our questions.

Finally, I am trying to form a Social Committee to enable us to have some very successful 'do's' this year. If any of you are interested (male of female) I would be pleased if you could contact me.

G.P. PATTER

G.P. 14 Fleet Meeting 17th Nov.

Midst the plush opulence and polished plastic of the M.A.S.C. Committee room, the Fleet met to discuss its past and future activities. Articulate mumblings went on until about half past Doom Watch hour, and the following is a condensed report on our deliberations.

Sailing Past.

Generally regarded as rather glorious.

Sailing Future.

It was agreed that the Spring and Summer Points Series were sucessful, and should continue unchanged. Despite the rather poor showing in the Saturday Points Series members felt that it should continue, and some promised support for '71'. Midweek racing was also considered a must for next season.

Cruising. Two dates to appear in the programme, one up river venue and one down river (See Gunga Drapers' write up "G.P.70" in this issue). Those cruises will be organised only so far as the date&start time are concerned. Where to go will be decided on the spot, on the day.

Inter-Club Racing

Maldon/Marconi Team Race. We will try to arrange a team event with the Maldon Y.C., arrangements as before, i.e. 2 races at home and 2 away.

Osea/Marconi Team Race. It was decided to pursue last years policy and arrange an event against Osea S.C.

Stone/Marconi Event. We will not be team racing against Stone S.C. this year. Instead we will have a type of "invitation points" series. On certain dates we will invite Stone S.C. to participate in our points races, and they will offer a reciprocal invitation to us. Each club will extract from the result points for its own series of races; each race being two races in one. There will be no formal prize offered to the winner of the invitation points, the idea is to provide a change of opposition and a chance to meet other G.P. sailors. Unlike team racing this will not be limited to 3 boats on each side - everyone can have a go.

General.

Various types felt that we might encourage more participants in our races if we made the courses more interesting. "Interesting" in this case being something like a figure of eight course round the two islands. Anything like this would of course have to be arranged on the day, and I have requested that certain dates in the Yearbook are marked with an asterisk. On these occasions we will arrange our own courses in consultation with the race officer of the day.

Courses were further discussed with an eye to handicap points series (Helmsman of the Year). Basically the argument was this. If a spinnaker carrying boat is to sail down to her handicap number, then she must be raced on a course which permits the correct amount of spinnaker work. Three out of four classes sailed within the club carry spinnakers.

Taking an Olympic type course as the "right course" the ratio of beating, reaching and running approximates to 1:1:1/3. It is very rare that this state of affairs exists with our present selection of courses.

It is not difficult to arrange courses with the 1:1:1/3 ratio. I have devised some for all the main wind directions and submitted them to the committee for consideration.

That, apart from a few swift halves, ended the meeting.

continued over./

- 5 -

7532 has not had a chance to rest her aluminium bones yet. Tony and I have been flogging her round in the Leigh on Sea Winter Series. Conditions have varied considerably from strong "swimming type" breezes to "where the 'ell are we" type fog.

We found that the bottom of the Thames appears to have a strong magnetic attraction for the masthead - it is quite probably that if the Thames were the Jordan then Tony and I would be the two most Holy chaps in the land.

The winter series culminated in the Brass Monkey Trophy Race, sailed on the 27th December. The fact that this was the coolest December day for thirty-two years probably had something to do with the fairly low entry of 27, it certainly had a lot to do with the way we performed - very carefully. The winner of the trophy was the Fleetwind Nat. Champ sailing his boat LOLITA, we were 12th.

Our position in the winter points series was more comforting, we ended up 2nd overall, GLASS AUK sailed by H. Kemp of Leigh was first.

What happened to you all for the beginning of the Winter Jugs Series? If it had not been for the timely arrival of Peter Crick we would not have had sufficient entries for a start. As it was Dave and I had a number of practice starts and would surely have sunk if it were not for our very efficient self bailers. The next in the Jugs series will be on the 21st Jan. at the Royal Oak starting at 8.00 pm. (The Royal Oak is on the Danbury/Maldon road just before the crossroads).

G.P. 70.

A personal viewpoint on progress of the G.P.14 fleet at Stansgate during the past season.

Cruising

Fleet members have taken part in a number of spontaneously arranged up-river cruises.

continued overleaf/

- 6 -

It appears that organised cruises are out of favour.

A drawback to the spontaneous-type cruise is that potential participants may miss out simply through lack of knowledge.

Some intended to make a long day of it and sail up the Colne to Wivenhoe and back, but pressure of racing events prevented this. A pity.

Ken Beavins, surely the club member who gets most use out of his boat, has sailed round to Brightlingsea a couple of times, but none of us has been further afield - by water anyway.

Racing.

Racing has improved tremendously in quality, if not in entries. In 1969 racing tended to be processional, with Norman Palmer usually clear ahead, and occasional place swapping at a respectful distance behind him, although he was beaten outside the Points Series.

1970 in contrast, saw frequent place changing in every event. In some races each entrant was at the front for a time. It is no longer possible to make mistakes and get away with it. For example, in the last 2 races in the Summer Points, one boat made one error in the morning race and one error in the afternoon race - resulting in 3rd in the series instead of 1st.

As a direct result of the keener competition, spinnaker techniques have greatly improved. Now more regard is paid to wind direction and less to wind strength. Some have used the beast in every race this year when the wind has been abaft the beam.

There have also been some spectacular capsizes!

The ability of a G.P. to carry a spinnaker successfully with the wind forward of the beam, a surprise to many, was convincingly demonstrated during the Pilot's Cup.

On a close reach from Bradwell to the Bench Head, G.P.4035 trailing somewhat after another late start, tried the spinnaker on the basis of having nothing to lose. The result was to make up two places and pressure other boats in to setting their spinnakers. Those that did not set their spinnakers fell behind.

Several Helmsmen have had crew problems. Peter Bains damaged his crewing faculties mid-season and deserted Dave Draper for the rescue launch.

One gentleman has had eight different people crewing for him in races. Even if he had best friends, they would'nt tell him!

Now, tribute to the most successful partnership of the season, yer actual Pat Black and Tony Cockrell with G.P.7532, winners of Spring Points, Summer Points and the Pilot's Cup. A change of boat from 1969 seems to have done the trick psychologically and they are now hard to beat. Currently they are sailing in a Winter Series at Leigh-on-Sea, and doing well against the best G.P. competition in the area. Well done each!

And now a word about the boat. The National Championships were won by G.P.830 with G.P.8830 second - a remarkable tribute to the careful updating of the rules that has taken place without outclassing the older boats. The only innovation essential for competitive sailing is the genoa.

The fibreglass G.P. has proved to be of equal performance to wooden boats and adequately strong without resorting to an increase in hull weight. The great reserves of strength in the original design have proved their worth in a way not envisaged by Jack Holt when he drew up the specification originally.

It is noticeable in a number of other clubs in the area how enthusiasm for G.P.'s is far greater than at Stansgate with the helmsmen and crews of all ages from swinging youth to senior citizens.

continued overleaf/

Pe ge

Stone S.C. for example get a higher percentage turn-out with G.P.'s than any other class and fleets like Leigh-on-Sea make an impact in all respects wherever they go. Perhaps money is the answer? G.P.'s are the most wanted Class second-hand as the 'Wanted' columns of the Sailing Press prove. The competitiveness of older boats keeps prices stable at a fairly high level. I know of one boat that has changed hands three times in the last few years for virtually the same price each time.

Are G.P.'s sailed hard? In our Regatta when it blew up a bit only Yew GP's retired from a fleet of 25, whereas some recognised racing machines Led half their fleets retire. This was not done by touring round under reduced s=il since a number of theoretically faster boats were passed (again!).

The G.P. National Champion also won the National Finn Finder competition
this year - indicative of the standard of top level G.P. racing as is the failure
of certain sponsored 'name' helmsmen to make a decent showing in G.P. Area
Championships.

Let them all come and may the class prosper - especially at Stansgatet

Gunga Dir.

the police was given that an endeavour would be made to enforce the eight-knot speed limit. Social Evening 29th Jan. 1971.

We were treated to a very interesting and instructive evening when Mr. Reader from Marconi's St. John Ambulance came to tell us how to treat a person who had been immersed in the sea to the extent that he was apparently drowned. Using a life-sized dummy, he was able to demonstrate to us the method of mouth-to-mouth resuscitation which has now superseded all the older methods previously practised. His assistant, Cadet Margaret, helped and refreshed Mr. Reader's memory with details about timing, etc.

After an interval for refreshments, Mr. Ken Pilsbury from the Met. Office at Bracknell gave us a talk about weather forecasting with special reference to the interpretation of cloud formation affecting yachtsmen. He showed us many beautiful coloured slides of the various types of cloud, which he had made over the years from such distant parts as Malta and Jamaica, and members should now take a special interest in identifying clouds they see during the coming season and in endeavouring to forecast the weather to be expected therefrom.

Our thanks are due to Brian and Mrs. Bowsher for bringing Mr. Pilsbury along to talk to us and for accommodating him overnight; to Avril Stevens for making the necessary arrangements and to Vic Tate for working the magic lantern in his usual faultless style.

Altogether a most successful evening with an excellent audience.

Our Chairman for the evening was Eric Payne.

MIRROR NEWS

The prospects for the Mirror Fleet in 1971 look very good, if we can't match the skill of the Hornets, Enterprises and G.P.'s, I hope that we will be able to match their enthusiasm for taking part in, and helping run, Club Events.

Racing in the Mirror Fleet is a gentlemanly affair, you will not see protest flags or be bawled at for making a mistake. The only cries you are likely to hear are those of "starboard" and "water", often uttered for your own good. Have no fears about racing with the Mirrors - it's good fun. In fact, the other Fleets are so kind to us that in the Mud Trophy we had Enterprises, G.P.'s and Hornets falling over themselves to let us through.

Taking part in the club racing programme has added advantages. You are allowed into the hallowed precincts of the race box and given considerable power over the other Fleets by running their races. This duty is not as formidable as it appears, there is always the O.O.D. who can advise on courses, and there are usually several other experienced people around who will help the uninitiated. It gives a great feeling of satisfaction to lower the flags and watch even the 'experienced' boys sometimes making a false start.

To provide an efficient racing service we also need from time to time people to help man the rescue boats. This can be a most instructive experience on a rough day and gives useful practice in 'seamanship'.

As a fleet we have much to discuss, and as your Fleet Captain I am your representative on the Sailing Committee - it is my job to put your views concerning Fleet welfare to them.

I hope that you can come to the Get-Together when we can discuss the many matters concerning deriving the most pleasure from owning a Mirror Class Dinghy in the Marconi Sailing Club.

Geoff Farnie.

SOCIAL NEWS.

To start the 1971 Season off the Fitting Out Party will be on April 16th. The theme is "SHIPWRECK". To give you some idea of a Shipwreck Party - people come along dressed as they would be when their boat is shipwrecked. This could be when they are asleep in bed, so they would be dressed in their night attire, it could be during the day when they are sunbathing etc. (we might even be wearing our hot pants!!) or during the evening when they are at a dance and so on, but I'm sure many of you will have lots of better ideas so I hope there is a good selection of different dress. There will be a prize for the person who has the three funniest things one would grab to take with them when they abandon ship.

I hope as many of you will give this a little thought to help make the party a success and I would like to mention here that we want to have more of a party atmosphere this year. Tickets will be on sale in a couple of weeks' time from the usual people. Now that Peter Crick has left Baddow, Julian Bigden will be selling tickets there. Price 50p which includes vittles.

The DISCO Party at Stansgate on May 8th is mainly a party for the younger set. This will be a very informal affair and an entrance fee of 12p will have to be charged. I hope many of you will come along and bring your friends. Bar will be open. If anyone wants transport please contact me. Avril Stevens. Soc. Sec. Int.570. Ext. [redacted]

HOW TO GET THE BEST OUT OF YOUR SAILS

Last June, Donald Forbes from the famous firm of sailmakers, Musto and Hyde of Rayleigh, paid a visit to our club at Stansgate and we spent a most interesting and instructive day, with plenty of practical demonstration, learning how to get the best out of our sails.

In the July issue of Navigans, Eleanor Witter wrote a most lucid and detailed account of the various points discussed and members are urged to make a further study of this article before embarking on next season's racing and to read it in conjunction with this less adequate description.

During Donald Forbes' visit to Stansgate he dropped the hint that he would be willing to talk to us about sails during our winter lecture programme, so our social secretary, Avril Stevens duly arranged this and the meeting was held at the main M.A.S.C. hall on February 19th.

We spent a most interesting evening with a real dinghy completely rigged on the stage to enable Mr. Forbes to demonstrate as his talk proceeded. Some cruiser owners raised various points concerning sails from their point of view, as opposed to the main dinghy coverage.

At one stage in the lecture when Mr. Forbes asked if anyone used spreaders, some amusement was caused when Eric Payne rushed forward carrying an enormous spreader attached to a very ample stainless steel shroud from his Atalanta cruiser, which up to that point, had been discreetly hidden behind the stage and had been brought to the meeting for another purpose altogether.

It was a most enjoyable evening, again with the attendance around the 100 mark, and questions continued to be answered until a late hour and we are most grateful to Donald Forbes for giving up his time so freely on our account.

Our thanks are due to Avril Stevens for organising the meeting so efficiently - to Julian Bigden for lending his Enterprise for the demonstration - to Nick Tovey for lending his sails and to the other members who went to the trouble of bringing their sails and dinghies to the club in reserve.

Our chairman for the evening was Vice-President Eric Payne and the vote of thanks to the speaker was proposed by our Rear-Commodore, John Witter.

DINGHY BUILDING

Would-be boat builders who, for a variety of reasons, are deterred from undertaking a construction will be interested in the boat building class held on the premises of Rainsford Girl's School.

The class is run as a Recreational Class by the Chelmsford Education Committee and the fee for a year's tuition, guidance and accommodation for the project is £8.00, this covers attendance on two evenings per week.

There are currently some 27 boats under construction at the school ranging from a 23ft. cruiser to an 8ft.6in. pram dinghy, the most popular boat being the 13ft. torch dinghy, for which g.r.p. shells are obtainable.

The course is run under the direction of Mr. John Wiffen, who is the Metalwork Master at the associated Boy's School assisted by Mr. Derek Sizeman, Foreman in the Glass Fibre Section at New Street, from whomfurther details can be obtained.

L.C.Kirk.

TO THE WESTERN ISLES VIA THE CALEDONIAN CANAL, 1970

DR. DONALD McKENDRICK

For our summer holiday we usually tow to the Mediterranean but after repeated persuasion from friends we decided to join them this year in the Western Isles. With the Forth and Clyde canal closed it is quite a long haul from the East coast so I arranged to use one weekend prior to our holiday proper to knock off the first hundred miles.

The 'Jayess' is a Snapdragon 27 and although bearing the official number 2 she was in fact the first one built and appeared at the Boat Show in January. She had already proved herself during a gale in our shakedown cruise in March and later during a rough passage to Holland at Whitsun. She has an Albin 12 H.P. auxiliary with the usual navigation equipment which includes a Mercia electronic log. This has the great advantage of being able to mount the speedo head in the cockpit and the log by the chart table. There are six berths and three or four can cruise in comfort for prolonged periods.

On Friday July the 3rd three of us arrived at a cold and blustery Stansgate for the first leg to Wells. I had two of my normal crew with me for this hop - my son-in-law Peter and an old friend Michael. Both would have liked to crew the whole way to Inverness but time would not allow. Peter and my daughter were to spend a week with us later in the Western Isles.

We quickly got the life-raft on deck in its position at the foot of the mast and were under way by 1400 hours, deflating the 10 ft Avon as we went as we had already lost a valuable part of a spring ebb. The wind was NW5 and we reached Clacton before the tide turned and the wind fell light. We had an uneventful motor-sail past the Cork L.V. and Orford Ness, being off Lowestoft by dawn. I decided to close the shore inside Corton sands to cheat the tide and then went below for my first sleep only to be woken in an hour by a change of motion. A quick look at the Seafarer showed we were in 10 feet instead of 4 fathoms, having come a cable or so too far off-shore. The tide turned again off Cromer. In the morning the wind had backed to the west and had given us a good sail, in fact our progress had been so good that I decided we could easily make Wells on the evening tide instead of waiting for Sunday morning as originally planned. Our course during the afternoon turned more and more to port until the wind was on the nose and we finally motor-sailed the last five miles to the entrance. What a help Blakeney Church is in an otherwise featureless landscape. Frequent bearings gave us repeatedly good position lines which combined with echo soundings confirmed our dead reckoning. This was particularly important as off Sheringham the speedo, which had developed a tendency to be rather optimistic over 6 knots slowed unaccountably and then dropped to zero as I was watching it. The diagnosis of the sensor unit rod falling off was easily confirmed by withdrawing the unit. A spare rod only takes a moment to fit but inserting it at sea can mean 2 or 3 pints of water in a locker so I decided to wait till we got to Wells as we would be drying out during the night.

We picked up the Wells buoy at 1710 - ten minutes later than estimated. Like so many offshore harbour entrance buoys this seemed unnecessarily small and difficult to see and we were certainly within a mile of it before we were sure it was what we were looking for. Although the wind of 3-4 against the tide was only producing a gentle chop outside the breakers at the entrance certainly gave promise of what it could do here in a blow. The channel is not well buoyed for strangers. We followed the prescribed route closely, running in under main alone, but fluctuated from 15 to 3 feet and grounded twice, the first time well within the channel. The second time the bow was hard aground so we dropped the hook - but it would'nt go - half the shank was above water! When I discovered that the stern was in 20 feet a quick burst astern put us back in the 4 knot flood to reach the quay without further trouble. There we were greeted officially and kindly by the H.M. Mr. Taylor, berthed alongside and made comfortable for the night. We had an excellent chicken ghoulash, dining on a peaceful summer evening on our cockpit table before turning in. We slept well.

/continued.

- 5 -

On Sunday morning The H.M. led us to a mooring as arranged taking us ashore in his launch from where we returned to London by car. I was very satisfied. 138 miles in the first 27 hours seemed to be a good omen for our holiday and we had a good northing achieved.

Friday, 10th July.

I arrived back in Wells at 1800 hours with my new crew, George, the sanest psychiatrist in the business, and a delight to have aboard any yacht, and John, a young engineer who had been introduced to me by a mutual friend. John has a boat of his own in the Solent but is always keen to increase his experience. He proved to be a most pleasant and extremely competent seaman, and I could not have had a better or happier crew. There was the added bonus that both of them have cast-iron stomachs and as I have never (yet) been sick in a small boat we felt fairly confident on that score.

The 'Jayess' was hard aground on the sands as the H.M. had forgotten to bring her alongside as promised. A friendly yachtsman took us over the water in his dinghy and we took advantage of our unexpected ground to scrub the bottom. We motored to the quay at 2300 hours. There is about 2 ft. alongside at low water so we sat comfortably on our twin keels for an hour while we slept.

We cast off at 0920 on Saturday 11th and were soon at the outer Wells buoy. It was a glorious warm sunny day and with a 3-4 W we made 5½ - 6 knots under genoa and main. The Humber L.V. was abeam at 2100 hours - 52 miles on the log in just under 12 hours of sailing. The wind increased a bit during my watch so the working jib replaced the genoa. When John took over it was SW 6 and a gale warning on the 0640 forecast came as no surprise; so we altered course for Bridlington. With four rolls now we were still being over-pressed as the wind got stronger but lazily we spilt the excess instead of tucking in more reefs as we were near to shelter. We tied up alongside a fisherman, 22 hours out of Wells with 101 miles on the clock. The H.M. greeted us during our bacon and eggs and moved us to a drying berth alongside the quay where we were comfortable enough. The Yacht Club made us very welcome and we wallowed in their simply enormous baths. Gales persisted and kept the rescue services busy. One yacht could not make round Flamborough but was eventually towed in safely and there was a tragic drowning in the bay. I do not normally set sail during gale warnings but by Monday evening we were getting restive and as the forecast was marginally better I decided to press on. We left just before midnight and were soon round Flamborough Head. With working rig and an off-shore force 5 we had another glorious sail on a clear warm night with a few fishermen and the odd coaster for company. During Tuesday afternoon the wind veered and increased to NW6. By 1700 hours the sky looked really awful, storm clouds interspersed with brilliant yellows and sudden squalls. We prepared for trouble, George seeing to the storm jib and putting extra lashings on the other jibs and everything else on deck, while John rigged the trysail and I looked around to see if I could find anything else for them to do. (Not entirely idle, I was trying to keep the ship fairly steady!) The 1800 forecast was NW8 imminent so we downed the jib and motor sailed like hell for Sunderland which we reached at 2050 before the trouble started. This is a very easy entrance which would obviously offer shelter to a yacht in just about any conditions but the masses of empty quays made it seem a sad and rather derelict harbour. We spent a peaceful night alongside a ship quay although we would have been better to have joined the yacht moorings (which we did the next morning, Wednesday) but we could find nobody about in the whole harbour to tell us where to go.

I should mention here that I do not in fact have a trysail but I do have deep reef points in my mainsail. By rolling loosely down to this point and lashing the cringles with the boom topped we get a very serviceable storm sail. The reef points are just below the numbers. If a trysail is not carried I think some arrangement of this sort is essential in a cruising yacht as even with a well tapered boom there is a limit to the number of rolls which can be put in without the boom dropping too low. When beating with this rig I think it is probably worth while keeping the topping lift just tight enough to take a little strain out of the leach.

continued overleaf/

- 6 -

With regard to watches, with a three man crew I prefer three hours on and six off. This of course shifts the watches and allows for four hours sleep at a stretch (enough at my age). I always do the navigating on my own boat so seldom get more than 2 - 3 hours consecutively anyway. We were "on a 66" (Yacht Passage Form) and had a long chat with the coastguard in his station who advised us to stay in Sunderland. However time was beginning to get a little short and northerly winds were not going to be any help so we left on Wednesday at 1450 under trysail and engine with a fair tide, waving to the storm cone as we passed the C.S. station. This was not foolhardy as we could safely have run back to Sunderland had this proved necessary. In three hours the wind veered and eased to NE5-6 so the storm jib went up and we sailed into Blyth for dinner and to await the next fair tide. We were greeted by the club boatman in his launch who put us on a mooring, booked a table for us at the best local restaurant and even arranged for a club member to run us there in his car. Such kindnesses really are appreciated.

Our night in Sunderland was to be our last night in harbour before Inverness although head winds from now on were to mean much motoring and hence calls for petrol.

To be continued next month.

HELP! salty but not quite caustic comment from the Commodore.

IF ANYONE IS LOST FROM OUR CLUB -

I know it's a dreadful thought - but possible if we do not observe Club rules and use common sense - I give warning therefore that -

If you have a life jacket - WEAR IT

If you have'nt a life jacket - BORROW ONE

If you can't borrow or buy one - then the Marconi Sailing Club cannot afford YOU as a Member.

Please don't embarrass the Officers and other Club members with foolhardy behaviour when you go sailing, especially during the early season when the water is so cold.

Watch the experienced sailors, not only are they wearing life jackets at this time of year but also expensive wet suits. Additionally their boats are fitted with buoyancy to Class rules which makes them almost unsinkable. Thus, not only are the crews protected against exposure hazards but they have a craft which can be recovered after capsize, quickly emptied and sailed back to base.

Now let's all be sensible and wear Life Jackets until we feel the heat of the sun upon our backs, and only then, if we are good swimmers, should we go to sea without wearing them, although still ensuring that they are in the boat.

Cadet Members of course must always wear life jackets when they go to sea.

Think about it - YOU I mean.

You know it makes sense.

Stan Allerton.

SAILING PROGRAMME 1971.

The sailing season has got off to a very good start indeed. The weather has been fine and the entries high, as you can see from the Results Page.

The programme this year is similar to last years, but a few more races have been squeezed in. The Ladies points has been increased to six races and the Summer Points Series to twelve. The Hornet Invitation Series is to be sailed at Stansgate with both Stone S.C. and Saltcote S.C. competing. Also some of the G.P.14 Closed Series are to be sailed as Invitation events with Stone S.C., with races at Stone and Stansgate (denoted by I in the Programme).

Support was lacking in 1970 for the Saturday Series, and it was with some doubt that we decided to include it again this year. Come on all you Saturday Sailors, try your hand at racing and make the efforts of the Coxons and Race Officers worthwhile!

The Local Open Events pages are packed with information and many helmsman will be carrying the Marconi Flag to these meetings.

Another feature is the inclusion of two dates when it is hoped that Informal short Dinghy Cruises can be arranged. Pat Black has offered to help with these.

One final request, please help your Fleet Captains and the Race Organisation by doing your share of the Rescue and Race Officer Duties.

R.G.Greygoose.
Sailing Sec.

THAMES BARGES - DESCRIPTION AND FILMS

A very interesting evening was had by about 30 members of the Club at the M.A.S.C. on 12th March, when Mr. Sam Poulton described the build and rig of the Thames barge and Mr. Milton showed films of the Barge Race in 1968 and 1969.

Mr. Poulton, who is Commodore to be of the Maldon Little Ship Club, described himself as being no expert on barges, but had owned one (Black Eagle) for 29 years! His description of hull and rig was of great interest, particularly with regard to the technique used by the crew (2 men) to lower the mast all-standing- and raise it again? On being questioned, he believed that some of the barges sailing at present had 20 years life left in them, and then the sailing barge would be gone for ever.

/continued.

- 3 -

Thames Barges - continued.

The films were produced very professionally by the Maldon Cine Club, and the 1968 race demonstrated the difficulty of being O.O.D. of a barge race when the wind dies completely off Bradwell. The 1969 race made the Wallet Spitway and the finish at Maldon. On being congratulated on recording the Spitway bell, we were told that the sound of a small glass bell was recorded at home and then replayed at half speed!

The guest speakers were introduced and thanked by our very able host Eric Payne, and our thanks are also due to Avril Stevens and Terry Hallam for arranging the meeting.

B.A.Bowsher.

HANDICAP FLEET

Do you feel that something ought to be done to put more life into the Handicap Fleet?

Do you want to take part in races but think that your lack of knowledge of the racing rules debars you?

Do you feel that your boat is the wrong sort for racing or that lack of a current measurement certificate debars you?

Do you want to race occasionally but think that courses are too long or at the wrong times?

Would you race if you knew a few chums who also wanted to race? Does lack of crew prevent you from entering club events?

If you own a Handicap boat and if your answer to any or all of the above questions is yes, then come along to the bar of the M.A.S.C.Clubrooms, Beehive Lane, on Tuesday 20th April at 8pm. and lets get acquainted and talk it over.

I hope we will be able to discover that racing can be an enjoyable pastime and that one's sailing skill can be improved by competition without having to learn a host of abstruse rules and without necessarily owning the fastest boat at Stansgate.

The Wednesday evening races, particularly, are very pleasant, with congenial company, nobody seeming to care very much whether they came first or last. It is usually very well worth the evening journey.

Don't forget, too, that the Sailing Committee is interested in fostering a thriving Handicap Class. They recognise that recruits for the main fleets very often come from the Handicap Fleet and indeed, sometimes new classes grow in this way.

So, whether you come along for the chinwag or not, please think about joining in and supporting the club activities and racing events this coming Season.

Lets show the other Fleets they don't have a premium on enthusiasm!

Eddy Edwards.
Fleet Captain.

ENTERPRISE FLEET NEWS

The fleet has got away to a good start to the season with five boats sailing in the tuning-up race and eight boats sailing in the Spring Points.

Arthur Hodges in his new boat "Ad Ventum" is sailing extremely well, and is obviously making sure of a good place in the Spring Series. A welcome newcomer to the fleet, Norman Ritchards and his crew Alex, have already made their presence felt by coming second in both the first and second Spring races.

Some new gadgets have appeared this year, Nick Tovey has a "Saylon" winch fitted to his boom to control the clew outhaul. Over centre levers for the jib halyard are now allowed in the class and one or two boats are fitting these.

Tim Bigden has fitted his boat with wide gunwhale, kicker winch and other goodies, and showed great promise in the Spring Points until he got tangled up with a mooring buoy, loosing about three places, hard luck Tim.

THE SHADOW AND THE FUTURE

Perhaps I ought to commence by apologising for keeping you in the dark -
perhaps.

At the A.G.M. last November I concluded my report by making the statement - "It is your Club and your decision". Perhaps in any Club such a statement should be treated with a certain amount of reserve but within the context applied I felt, have felt during the following months, and still feel that the decisions made in the “report” I am about to give were and are indeed your
decisions.

It was at that same meeting you all accepted without contradiction the need for the Marconi Sailing Club to exist and flourish at Stansgate and to that end agreed to pay the new rent upon a course of “succeed to buy or bust".

Turning back to my opening remark therefore you can now understand why I have-not previously come forward with news of the state of negotiation, such news has either been “subject to further negotiation" or I have been in a hurry because of fear of “Busting”.

As so many of these negotiations have by their netaoe been delicate I would like to pay tribute to the faith and patience of my fellow officers i allowing me the freedom to negotiate “in the dark" and for supporting me to the present stage where we await permanent planning approval before the contract Ky is signed and our Sailing Site is purchased.

My appreciation also goes to the Chief Executive of the M.A.S.C. and the Chairman of tho M.A.S.C. Committee also, especially to the Company Property Officer = Mr. A. Hi dset

Under unmentionable threats from The Madam Ed. and a great awareness of my duty to Club, class, and the culteral revolution, I take up my pen to scribe this the first epistle of 1971.

H o l t! who goes there.

In the beginning there was Jack and he looked upon the waters and said "Let there be life". And there was life, and now we are up to our necks in G.P.14's, Enterprises, Hornets, and the odd Solo.

Jack saw that this was good, and as the royalties began to roll in he realized that it was truly marvellous. But Jack was lonely and so he invented Allen and they prospered and multiplied and sent forth many fittings and the sun shone out of Jack and upon all the waters and the fleets were happy.

/continued.

- 4 -

Many were the benefits bestowed by Jack upon the fleet for he wrought miracles with polyamide and fibrous glass that bustith only sometimes.

And it came to pass that all was not well upon the face of the waters, but the sun still shone forth mightily from Jack and so he suffered one Harlot to travel unto the Antipodes to do battle with the tribes of Cobblers that lurketh there. Fair of form was she with smooth black bottom and swinging spreaders and her stays were of stainless steel. For half a moon she tarried there vanquishing many of the Cobblers.

Thus heard Jack, and he spake unto the P.R.O. man, and unto the Ad. man and unto the Bank man and they rejoiced and feasted and stood on Putney Bridge at midnight and threw snowballs at the moon. For it is written that he who smiteth the Cobblers shall have snowballs.

HANDICAP FLEET NEWS

The Handicap Fleet season started well with an encouraging turnout for the first meeting held in the M.A.S.C. bar lounge on Tuesday April 20th despite competition from the M.A.S.C. Annual General Meeting.

Discussion revolved around finding some of the answers to the questions put to the fleet in the April Navigans, with some of the conclusions summarised below:-

Most fleet members considered themselves to be in the beginner or "not terribly skillful" class. This meant that, if racing were to be encouraged and enjoyed, lengths of courses and the prevailing conditions if adverse might deter many helmsmen from racing. It was concluded that more laps of fairly short courses (similar to those for Mirrors) would be advantageous and would enable boats to retire if their crews became fatigued. Racing might well be abandoned if conditions were not suitable even if more experienced fleets were racing.

/continued.

- 7 -

Most handicappers were family sailors whose sailing involved the fairer sex and youngsters who should not be scared off by "hairy" racing. There should be a weaning in process based on gentle initiation.

Very few of the fleet had any experience of racing and fewer were well versed in the racing rules. Many thought that this lack of knowledge meant that they would make a poor job of racing or that others might not want to race with them. All felt that, for them, racing should not become so competitive that there would be a risk of damaging boats. It was concluded that, as long as the normal safety rules were observed (i.e. the Starboard rule) and competing boats otherwise kept clear of each other, there should be no reason why racing should not be enjoyed by even the novices. In other words early racing should be akin to all competitors pottering in one direction, with the formality keeping pace with the increasing skill of the participants.

All agreed that not the least important part of fleet activity was the social side and camaraderie among the fleet (and indeed club) members should be encouraged.

It was decided to hold a further meeting at 8.30 pm in the M.A.S.C. Bar Lounge on Tuesday 18th May to discuss mutual problems and to try and sort out some of the technicalities. It is hoped that the meeting will be well patronised.

TRIALS AND TRIBULATIONS

It's not difficult they said, a quick up and down with the flags, a couple of toots and they are away. It was our turn to do Race Officer duty. We were there an hour before the race, but have you ever noticed how quickly the time goes at the Club, and it was all done in a rush.

Which course? - there are so many in the book, however a long standing and much respected member came to our aid, 'Give 'em plenty 'o laps, you can al'us shorten the course'. Then there was the signing on forms and collecting the things from the safe. The method of correcting the clock seemed very complicated, lift the glass and push the hands round! Still that's what we were told to do.

It seemed as though we had only just arrived, but it was time that we were at the Race Box. It is a surprisingly long way from the Club House and by the time we had sorted out our combinations (the lock), the course letters and the flags, we were a little late with the 10 min. gun.

The start itself was quite easy, one hand on the hooter, one eye on the clock and two more hands on the flags, the difficulty came in deciding who was across the line! There followed a pleasant undisturned rest, since neither the Radio or the telephone seemed to work, ---- and then someone remembered that we had not put out the declaration forms.

They were about half way round the second lap when we decided that two laps would be enough. So we hoisted the appropriate flag and making the appropriate sound signal we prepared to 'finish' the fleet. I think that everyone returned, the only mistake we made was to hoot someone who had made a false start and who had not returned to restart correctly. Technically he still had another lap to do.

We were packing up and were nearly ready to go when a G.P. member came in with a Protest against a member of the Enterprise Fleet. Well this eventuality was not covered in the 'Lazy Man's Guide for Race Officers', or perhaps it was and it was the Race Officer who was lazy and had not read it. All was resolved when a committee of three was formed by the Hornets and they passed judgement.

By this time we were quite worn out and pleased to pack everything up and go home.

Anon.

EDITORIAL

The Regatta weekend once more went off very well, with entries high again. The weather was rather a spoil sport but completely out of our control, and going by people's faces and remarks it did'nt get the better of us.

Would you please all note that the area beyond the race box is "out of bounds" to all our members, and very shortly will be fenced off. Please see that no damage is caused to this fence.

Lastly, please note that there will not be a Navigans in August, but I shall be pleased to receive any "bits and pieces" for the September issue, anytime after next month's issue. Why not use the extra time to think up something unusual?

Mary Greygoose.

SOCIAL SCREED

Raffle Ticket No. 320 (white) for the Regatta raffle was not claimed. Could the winner please contact me. The prize is a sun lounger.

The barbecue this year is on Saturday July 10th at Stansgate. Tickets are 40p each, available from the usual people. This price includes your food, dancing, bonfire, bar etc. As usual we are asking for helpers. This involves cooking, stoking and serving. If anyone would like to help during the evening, even if you only come for an hour, it will be a big help to us. Last year some 400 people turned up so something like 200 sausages and 200 beefburgers were cooked and served.

Lets hope that the weather will be as kind to us this year as it was last. Do try and get your tickets early to enable us to estimate how much food will be required.

TO THE WESTERN ISLES VIA THE CALEDONIAN CANAL, 1970

DR. DONALD McKENDRICK

Continued from Issue 3.

We left Blyth at 0250 on Thursday morning. As dawn broke to a beautiful day we came across some cobles one of whom led us well over a quarter of a mile along his floating salmon net to pass the eastward end. They obviously have to patrol their nets all the time they are down - even though we appeared to be the only other shipping around! Soon afterwards we were delighted to be met by three dolphins who frolicked round the bow turning on their backs and grinning at us as they did so. They escorted us past Holy Island when, duty done, they gave final leaps in the air and shot off. We were well outside the Farne Islands with Longnose lighthouse just visible, but the mainland not, when I decided to put into Berwick for petrol. Here again we received kindness from a local yachtsman who ran us to the garage for our petrol and took us by a short cut for some excellent fish and chips. But what a harbour! It was calm. We motored in with the breakwater lighthouse and the town hall in strict transit as suggested in the C.A.Handbook, keeping an anxious eye on the breakers to port and starboard. The sounder showed depths dropping rapidly from 7 to 3 feet - and we were in - to be confronted round the first bend by fishermen with salmon nets right across the river. These had to be hand-winched in to allow our passage both on our way in and out. After a two hour stay we were off again with a useful tip to turn 45 degrees to starboard when 30 yards short of the end of the breakwater. This I did and was delighted to see the echo sounder continue to register a steady 6-7 feet, and watching that was nearly the cause of disaster. John suddenly shouted "head up" and I looked round to see a comber just about to break on the port bow. I managed to head up enough for it to break under the boat but this pushed our head round and with the next one we were not so luck; it broke on the port bow, throwing us over and soaking the cockput, the two aft berths and of course John and myself. George was delighted that a moment before I had asked him to go below to secure something. He was quite dry and emerged grinning, completely unscathed, wondering wat I had been playing at. It was my own fault and we were lucky it was so calm and the 'Jayess' so buoyant. I have never seen a breaker coming at me like that when in a boat before - and I don't want to again. We were now through the breakers and found we were surrounded by serious bearded faces all rather sad and definitely disapproving of the way I had crossed the bar. Seals are such delightful creatures. It is such a shame they break the fishermon's nets and have to be destroyed.

After a complete change and general tidy up we motored a while until the wind piped up 4 from the west and we had a lovely reach across the Firth of Forth to the Inchcape rock (Bell Rock lighthouse) which we left a mile to port. By 0800 on Friday we were motoring again on a warm and sunny morning. All our wet clothing came on deck and we dozed in the cockput while the Q.M.E. kept us on course although motoring. At 1210 we sighted the first yacht we had seen on passage since leaving Wells. Indeed during the time we left the Cork L.V. till we arrived at Inverness we only saw four sailing yachts and one motor yacht at sea - and two of these were in the Moray Firth. There is certainly plenty of room for sailing in these waters.

It was now Friday afternoon and as George had to be in Munich (not in his sailing clothes!) on Monday we put into Aberdeen for him to catch the evening plane. We were charged 7/6d. for the privelege of letting him ashore alongside some filthy piling quite unsuitable for yachts while small boys bombarded the dock with dead fish. We were glad to leave. John and I now went on to four hour watches and we had a peaceful night past Buchan Ness and Kinnaird's Head. As soon as we were in the Moray Firth it suddenly blew up to NW7. With six rolls, no jib and the engine ticking over we were just able to lay along the coast making 2½ knots in a nasty short sea. I was not too happy with this as we were virtually on a lee shore but I held on till the tide turned against us as I thought we could make it back to Fraserburgh without too much trouble if we had to. John had a plane to catch next day in Inverness and luckily with the turn of the tide the wind dropped and the sea calmed down. We were short of petrol once more so we put into Buckie.

/continued overleaf

- 6 -

The entrance is narrow but having avoided the East, Middle and West Mucks - nasty reef with a beacon only on the W.Muck - there is no bar and this makes Buckie available in all weathers - which is more than can be said for any of the other small harbours on this attractive but inhospitable coast. It is the cleanest harbour I ever remember visiting, with a most friendly and helpful H.M.. All the many fishing boats seemed newly painted and in tip-top condition and we would have dearly liked to spend the night in this pleasant place. However after some bacon and eggs ashore washed down by six cups of excellent tea we sailed at 1840 on the last lap of the first leg of my holiday. As the Moray Firth began to narrow the night was enlivened by the odd sudden and occasionally vicious squall. At the entrance to Inverness Firth there are a number of unlit buoys but they are not too serious a hazard as it never gets really dark in this part of the world in the summer. The navigation is easy if one keeps Coversea light open astern and steers on the fixed red T.V.mast lights which are not shown on the chart and had me puzzled for quite a while. The overfalls and whirlpools in the narrows look as if they would be really something in a blow. Inverness Firth itself was boiling with porpoises, some of them looking more like whales they were so big. At 0710 on Sunday we dropped the hook off the sea-lock at Clachnaharry, having sailed 718 miles from Stansgate. We had taken just under eight days for the 580 miles from Wells, of which nearly three days were spent gale bound in Bridlington and Sunderland. I got John ashore soon after 0800 hours as there was not enough water for the sea lock to open for another hour when I was warped gently into the Caledonian canal. After a bit of breakfast I undressed and climbed into my sleeping-bag.....

The head winds for so much of the trip had been a nuisance as we had a strict time-table to keep, but really we were very lucky with the weather - no rain, hardly any fog and mostly sunny and warm. Our sea-boots were never out of their locker and my souwester only on my head twice. I did'nt take a single radio fix but the North Sea Pilot, vol. 2, (especially in the Moray Firth) and of course Reed's proved invaluable. The C.A. Handbook with its harbour plans and passage notes was as helpful as it has so often been in the past but there is no warning of possible hazards at Berwick (!) and Buckie receives only a curt three lines.
