THE ROYAL YACHTING ASSOCIATION A.G.M.

The annual general meeting of The Royal Yachting Association was eventually held on May 6th; after having been postponed from the original date of March 17th; because of the postal strike. By a referendum previously held, it was decided to start the meeting at 1730 instead of at 1430 as heretofore, in order to enable members to attend after leaving their work, but this did not appear to have been effective as the Caxton Hall was only sparsely filled with little over 100 members or half the number attending last year; out of a membership of 33,000 from some 1,500 clubs; the average age of those attending appeared very high.

The routine business and elections passed off quickly enough, but when it came to the increase in subscriptions, argument began. Some members said that the removal of S.E.T.should help the finances while someone mentioned the rent of the present premises at Buckingham Gate was well over £8,000. The present rate of £2.2s. had been maintained all this century and it was finally agreed to increase it to £3. It will be remembered that the subscriptions from clubs had already been increased two years ago, and it was agreed that the subscriptions of life members should be upgraded.

The committee wanted to make R.Y.A. membership compulsory for all who entered races or to impose a levy on race entry forms or introduce a fee on all racing boats but this was vigorously opposed from the floor and the difficulty in collection of these fees was appreciated, so finally,after much discussion, it was agreed to refer this matter back to the committee.

/continued.

- 7 -

The National Coaching scheme was discussed and it was agreed that this should be conducted on a regional level with greater involvement by the local clubs, so that all who wished to learn or improve their ability should benefit.

The R.Y.A. was pressing for the inclusion of sailing in the Commonwealth games and choice of classes to be used is to be considered.

It was pointed out that about half the association's finances are devoted to racing.

It is interesting, and not without significence, that while Jack Knights gave a full report of the meeting in Yachts and Yachting, Yachting World published just a paragraph about it, while Yachting Monthly did not even mention it!

Eric Payne.
R.Y.A.Liaison Officer.

HORNET NEWS

NATIONAL JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP 71, AT CLACTON S.C.

The National Junior Championships for 1971 completely surpassed all expected proportions with an absolutely massive entry of 21 year olds and under competing from all over the country.

It was interesting to note that a large number of clubs had to hold their own elimination trials before sending their helmsmen. This seems to point very favourably towards an extremely active second generation of horneteers - who everybody realises are the class's future.

The Juniors originally were to be run in conjunction with the Clacton Splash, but it soon became apparent that the size of the programme would curtail this event in favour of the Juniors, and we oldies would be committed to becoming 'fringers' on the shore, relagated to shouting at our respective boats, and praying. A good response to boat lending ensured that only two heats, each competing twice for a place in the final, had to be run.

In contrast to Saturday's force 3-4, Sunday was practically flat, racing was slow and tedious, however enthusiasm grew as the final began,resulting in the Clacton verandah becoming jammed with advice giving helmsmen. Brett Dingwall and John Heslop opened up a large lead from the bunch, only to fall to 4th position on a particularly flukey spinnaker reach. With only two beats left (by now the bets were being made on the shore to be evaluated in pints later) Brett remained undaunted and commenced the next beat with 100 yard deficit. Superb sailing put them 50 feet in front once again, a lead which they improved by another 50 ft. at the finish! - Well done, Brett and John.

G.P.PATTER

To recap, dear reader, you will remember how three boats and umpteen persons trailed to Broxbourne for the first of the Traveller's Trophy Meetings on 2nd May, now read on.

Forty-two boats came to the line - and it was crowded. The lake is shaped roughly like a kidney bowl, the narrow part being about 30 ft. wide and the whole area being something like our dinghy and car park joined together. The wind adopted guerrilla tactics - it was very frustrating - Blackjack retired during the second race. Norman Palmer and Dave Draper continued and secured 12th and 9th overall places respectively, Blackjack taking 18th position in the 1st race.

There were numerous capsizes caused by sudden gusts which although not particularly strong came from totally unexpected directions - they were invariably followed by a flat calm. Typical observed incident - two boats were running side by side on opposite jibes with spinnakers set - sudden gust - one boat capsized and the other shot straight up the bank into a blackberry bush. Our general opinion was that pond sailing probably has its good points, the chap in the blackberry bush certainly found some, but we could not.

On the following Sunday the 9th May, the same group of persons visited Leigh-on-Sea S.C. This was just a social visit really although we did join in one of their points races (20 boats on the line).

This was a much more enjoyable affair as far as Blackjack was concerned, we finished 3rd. Dave and Norman dithered about a lot and then blamed me for not pointing out where the marks were, which was rather unfair since I put in a great deal of effort in order to show them the way round - part of the burdensome load of high office, I suppose. Tempus fugited on and paused awhile whilst Norman Palmer won the Saturday single handed race. During this event Ken Beavins managed to successfully set his spinnaker - as far as I know even Elvestrom has not tried single handed spinnaker work in a dinghy.

The last two races of the spring points series held a double interest. The first was that Blackjack had to beat Hanging Five in both races to win the series; the second was that these two races were part of the invitation series with Stone S.C.

Blackjack won the first race but capsized after overtaking Hanging Five in the second, a rapid recovery and some superb sailing by the crew of Blackjack took her right through the 12 stong fleet to finish 3rd, one place behind Hanging Five. Consistency pays - congratulations to Dave and Gary on winning the Spring Points series. (I hear that the ban on that hat has been lifted as a result).

The Stone G.P. fleet enjoyed their visit and we look forward to meeting them again. Stan Atkins 7531 managed to break his tiller extension and soon afterwards went overboard when a toe strap broke, he made a rapid recovery however and only lost one place. Gordon Parr caused Norman to capsize a "C" mark, Anne bruised her ribs and Gordon in fear of his life retired to the safety of the Stone S.C.

Somewhere I have managed to miss out the Pilots Cup. So - Pilots Cup won by Dave in Hanging Five, Norman in third place, the race being sailed in very light airs and taking 6 hours to complete.

Regatta

Very enjoyable. Hanging Five gaining several places to take 8th overall. Blackjack gained 6th and 17th on Sunday and retired through lack of wind on Monday. Ken Beavins set off in his boat on Saturday with son Nick and cruised round to the River Crouch, spent the night there and sailed back again on Sunday morning - I have not seen Ken to enquire about the trip but it must have been a wonderful downhill ride back along the coast.

Peter Baines has purchased N. Palmers boat "Whiplash", and another new boat in the fleet is 6278 owned by Geof Wright - we look forward to seeing them both on the line in the near future.

Pat Black.

J.H.Gill

Members will be grieved to learn of the death in The London Hospital of Joe Gill, one of our oldest members, who was in fact, a founder member and our Honorary Secretary from 1950 - 1954.

Joe was always a keen sailor and his wife Joyce and his daughters Anne and Helen, often sailed with him in his cruisers.

He owned a gaff-rigged Dauntless, Puddleduck, and later a plastic Signet, Tufty Duck, which now lies disconsolately at its moorings at Heybridge awaiting a new skipper. Joe was a clever mechanic and made an anemometer and weather vane which he mounted at his masthead and a log mounted on the transom, all conveying electrical impulses to give indications on the instruments in the cabin. One of his favourite haunts was the "secret waters" of Arthur Ransome on the Walton backwaters and as the names of his cruisers indicate, his visits were very much family affairs.

Most of Joe's time at Marconis was spent in the aeronautical division, firstly at Writtle and latterly, at Basildon.

Eric Payne.

The starting proccedure is basically simply, 10 mins. before the start a 'gun' is fired and the class flag is hoisted (NO. 6, a long thin flag for Mirrors). At 5 mins. another 'gun' and Blue Peter, flag P, is hoisted. At the start both flags come down and another 'gun' is fired. If however one or more boats is over the line at the start, there will be two 'guns' and the class flag will come down half way until the offending boats have returned to cross the line correctly. After that - good luck!

Although the Mirror is a delightful boat to sail and possesses few vices, its' true character is at last beginning to come to light. If it is displeased with the helmsman in heavy weather it does not capsize but leans over and fills up with water !!! A most alarming tendency!!

CLUB SAILING - A PERSONAL VIEW.

It has been suggested that the support this year for Club points racing is lacking and that this may be due to there being an excessive number of races in the programme. A study of the results show that support this year is similar to that of last year, but the interest in some fleets is ascending whilst others are declining. The Saturday Points series however, is proving to be a dismal failure, and unless more support is forthcoming it is unlikely to be repeated next year. Your views on this and racing in general would be helpful in planning next years' programme.

I know from experience that the best and quickest way to learn to sail is to race, and that no-one need be put off by a lack of a detailed knowledge of the racing rules. Our Club is unusual in that we have a very large number of sailors who do not race. I believe that the strength of a club hinges on the team spirit of its members and this only comes from sailing together, in organised races or cruises.

Now that the fine weather is here come and join in the remaining races, your Fleet Captains will welcome you with open arms.

Your Sailing Secretary,
Ron Greygoose.

continuing TO THE WESTERN ISLES VIA THE CALEDONIAN CANAL

Monday, July 20th. After springcleaning the boat in the morning I was ready to receive Evelyn (my wife), Michael (medical student son) and younger daughter Sally, aged 17. They had driven the Landrover and trailer to Dumbarton, coming on to Inverness by train and taxi. After a reunion lunch we motored up to Muirtown basin (through the first lock) where we filled up with water and petrol and made arrangements to enter the Canal proper the next morning. We were up early on Tuesday and just after passing through the lock at 09.00 hours the engine stuttered and stopped. This was obviously due to a block in the petrol supply. We found the carburettor to be filthy and the From G3 petrol line filter indescribable. As it was impossible to get a replacement Michael spent half an hour rinsing it through with petrol in reverse and we had no further trouble until we got to Crinan a fortnight later when we had to repeat the performance.

We entered Loch Ness through Dochgarroch Lock in the teeth of a S.W.5. It was squally, rather bleak and very cold. After motor sailing for an hour or so the wind veered a bit and we were able to beat the remainder of the 25 miles to Fort Augustus. Loch Ness in this weather was rather lonely and we were not sorry to reach Fort Augustus at 18.30 hours where we climbed the five locks, tying up for the night an hour later, six hours in all from Dochgarroch. There is a bank in Fort Augustus where we were able to get some much needed cash on Wednesday morning with the help of our bank cards. At 10.15 we motored through a most attractive part of the Canal, passing Kytra and Cullochy Locks until we reached the lovely Loch Oich. Here we dropped the hook in ten feet of water outside the very narrow buoyed channel while Michael and Sally set off for a mountain climb. Evelyn and I sat in the cockput in the cold sunshine until they disappeared from view. At the top they had a magnificent view of the whole 60 miles of the Caledonian Canal, only a third of which are Canal cuttings, the rest being natural lochs.

Wednesday night we spent at Gairlochy - another delightful spot in this lonely and beautiful countryside. We were awoken the next morning by the degaussing vessel Thatcham - a large, rather dirty Naval ship with very smelly exhaust - with which we had to share the remaining locks during our trip through the Canal including the descent of the Banavie Bank (8 locks and a bridge altogether). The whole Canal is well maintained and the locks all electrically operated and efficiently worked and at a cleat of £9 it seemed to me to be remarkable value. One cannot pass through on Sundays although the sea locks are opened at weekends to allow vessels in (for an extra charge of £1.) The minimum passage time for a yacht is 2 days.

At 14.40 hours on Thursday we anchored off Fort William for a couple of hours to do some shopping and fill our cans with petrol, Muirtown and Fort Augustus being the only places where we could get petrol in the Canal. We sailed six miles to Camisasaig, just above the Corran Narrows, for the night but the wind shifted to the east while we were asleep and I awoke at 06.00 hours to find us dragging onto the rocks. We were up and away in a few minutes. It was a filthy morning with tremendous and continuous rain brought down on us by a strong following north easterly wind of 5 to 6. This meant we had to have the wash boards in and the hatch cover completely closed, a most unusual state of affairs in the "Jayess" as in nearly all conditions the sprayhood keeps the cabin dry without any other protection. We ran on the genoa alone down the side of Mull in very poor visibility but by lunchtime the rain stopped, the sun came out and we wailed into Castle Bay. Here we had a glorious walk on the lovely Isle of Kerrera before motoring the last five miles to Oban where Michael and Sally were to leave us. We picked up a council mooring off the Great Western Hotel on which there was a large notice telling us the cost of the mooring was 7/6d. a day payable to the Harbour Master on the pier. We tried to find him four times but never succeeded so I'm afraid we still owe Oban 7/6d. After a welcome bath at the Columba Hotel we had dinner ashore at McTavish's Kitchens, reputed to be the best eating house in Oban. We had a good night, although rolling rather uncomfortably to begin with.

On Saturday I rowed Michael and Sally ashore for the London train. Evelyn and I were now on our own for a week. We took it gently and had one of our happiest ever weeks afloat. There were a number of highlights - ghosting

/continued

- 7 -

into Easdale Sound off Sail Island; a most happy evening with some young men returning from the Tobermory race; the most heavenly sunsets; the excitement of drifting through the Dorus Mor with a 6 knot current with whirlpools turning the boat in all directions as there wasn't enough wind for steerage way; watching the seals in Loch Craignish, slight anxiety in "rock reading" at the entrance to Loch Swen; and the beauty of Tayvallich which was in one sense our journey's end as here we met the friends who had persuaded us to make this trip in the first instance. They had just arrived after what sounded like a wonderful cruise to the Outer Hebrides.

On Friday, 31st July, our daughter and son-in-law (Janna and Peter) rounded the headland in their car. At the same moment the rain of the last 24 hours ceased, the sun came out and we had hot Mediterranean weather for the remaining ten days of our holiday. We sailed to the Fairy Islands where we watched the terns protecting their nesting grounds from an inoffensive gull that just wanted to sit and watch. We picked wild raspberries. And we sat and soaked up the peace and beauty of this lovely part of the world. On Saturday we pottered in Loch Swen and on Sunday we sailed north again to enter Crinan basin in the early evening. Another bath, this time at the Crinan Hotel followed by an excellent dinner in their beautiful mirrored dining room joined by our friends who came from Tayvallich by car to make a memorable evening.

We started to pass through the Crinan Canal at 06.40 on Monday travelling with a 9 metre which had no reverse and only a trailing bucket to hold her back. As there was a Force 3 leading wind, this had its moments of excitement in the locks. There were dozens of yachts coming the other way but even so we were through the Canal and its 14 locks by lunch time and out in Loch Fyne soon afterwards. We picked up a mooring for the night in East Lock Tarbert, a dirty commercial port so different from all our other resting places. So we left early on Tuesday and had a good sail to the Kyles of Bute, stopping at Port Druishaig where we bought some stores at a village shop delighting in the name of Port Druishaig Emporium. We anchored off Colintraive for the night having another excellent meal, this time at the local pub, food every bit as good as the Crinan Hotel but prices considerably less.

Wednesday we spent in Ormidale bathing, lazing in the dinghy and clambering in bikinis in a lovely mountain ghyll. By Thursday it was time to go. With a predominantly north-easterly 4 - 5, we reached and beat with the genoa and three rolls till we were off Grennock where we entered the narrow channel of the Clyde but here the tide turned against us so we motor sailed the last 22 miles to Dumbarton. I had no chart of this area and we nearly came to grief on our way to McAlister's yard as it was not at all clear which was the right buoy at which we should turn off to enter the creek - and I chose the wrong one. However we found the channel again and tied up at 17.00 hours on August 6th - 959 sailing miles from Stansgate.

We got the mast down that night and the next morning were lifted onto the trailer. Peter and I brought the boat back by road leaving Dumbarton at 10.50 on Friday and arriving home at 20.40 hours on Saturday while Evelyn and Janna collected Peter's car from Lochgilphead, making their own more leisurely way home.

The holiday was such a success that we are already planning our next visit - the temptation being to go west-about if only one could rely on 10 days without south westerlies. We will certainly return to the Western Isles.

WEEKEND DINGHY CRUISE

When I sold my Wayfarer and built a Mirror 16 several people expressed surprise and were obviously of the opinion that the Mirror was somewhat inferior to the Wayfarer. As we don't all aspire to be a second Frank Dye, and least of all myself, it would be difficult to prove one way or the other, but I hope that this account of a modest weekend cruise in "Sobraon" will go a long way to convince readers that she can more than hold her own alongside other boats and that the deficiencies are more with helmsmen and crew.

With only a weekend free and wanting to cover as much fresh ground as possible I planned to launch Sobraon at Leigh-on-Sea, sail out to the Whitaker Beacon and then either over to Walton-on-Naze or up the Crouch to Burnham, the choice being a question of time and/or weather. The final leg being the run home to Stansgate.

It should be possible to leave the Ray Gut, Leigh at high water and reach the Whitaker before the tide turns but to allow for contingencies, a Friday evening start and a two hours sail to Shoeburyness would put us well on our way by Saturday.

Snag number one, my crew, Mick, caught the wrong train home and finished up at Colchester which put us well behind schedule and by the time we arrived at Leigh it was too late to sail that night, in fact there was barely enough light to launch the boat. We said our farewells to Joan and Linda who took the trailer back, and, putting the boat cover over the boom, were soon asleep.

Saturday dawned clear, with a light westerly wind as we set off at 0830 hrs. making good time on the ebb, or so we thought. At Shoeburyness we estimated our speed at 4 knots, hardly fast enough to reach the Whitaker by low water, and the wind was dying on us, the burgee gyrated round and we barely had steering way.

Resorting to the auxiliary (Micks' muscles) we paddle/sailed past the Blacktail Spit and keeping the N.E.Maplin buoy to starboard we closed the shore slightly where two keel boats were sailing in a moderate breeze. Hot with our exertions we removed waterproofs and jumpers, retaining our lifejackets. We found the wind at about force 2 and headed for the Whitaker Beacon, the tide had turned by now and the wind was heading us so that we were beating, but making good progress. The wind rose rapidly to 4 or 5, very squally conditions, and we regretted removing our waterproofs. It needed all our concentration to sail the boat and after the first wave over the top it seemed irrelavent anyway to bother about waterproofs, we were soaked through.

We failed to notice that the keel boats were no longer to port, wind and tide had put us further over the Foulness Sand, the wrong side of the Whitaker and on a lee shore. In the shallow waters we were unable to keep full centreboard down and beat our way off, so hove to whilst deciding what to do. Beyond the Whitaker Beacon larger boats were experiencing difficulties and we thought it prudent to make for Burnham, not so easy though as we now had a large sand spit between us and the Whitaker Channel. We both felt very cold by this time and rather than wait for water we jumped out, pulled the boat against wind and tide to a point where we could cross into the channel and sail up to Burnham. Eleven hours after leaving Leigh we landed at Admirals Hard, up river from the town. Dry clothes, fish and chips, and so to bed.

The wind turned 180° during the night and we awoke to a westerly once more, blowing in the open end of our cover. After breakfast, with everything stowed, we donned waterproofs and at 0900 hrs. ran down river, but not for long, the wind headed us and we were soon tacking in order to keep close to the north shore. Out of the Crouch we headed north just before reaching the Crouch buoy and tacked across the Ray Sand, the Buxey Beacon was visible but we failed to see the yellow and white Ray Sand Channel buoys and wondered if they were still in position. Wind about force 3 and rising giving us good sailing past Dengie Flats. We kept outside the wrecks to avoid getting caught on St. Peter's Flats on the falling tide and by the time we were abreast of Batchelor Spit the wind was blowing nearly as hard as the previous day but less

/continued.

- 5 -

squally. From a position just north of the spit we altered course to enter the Blackwater and on a broad reach planed past St. Peters on the Wall and Sales Point. Into the Blackwater and comparative calm, a gentle run to Stansgate where we landed at 13.30 hrs. just 4½ hours for the trip from Burnham.

Our verdict on the Mirror 16 was all to her credit, her stability at all times was unquestionable and we felt no lack of confidence in her ability to respond to the helm. Lighter than the Wayfarer, she planed easily and the self draining cockpit that works on all points of sail was a boon in the rough conditions.

I am not sure that I like a centre mainsheet whilst cruising, it clutters up the thwart and although it undoubtedly benefits the helmsman, Mick's comment was "It was never designed with the crew in mind". There was plenty of room for sleeping, our two airbeds taking up no more than half the available floor space.

In retrospect it might appear ludicrous for two dinghy sailors to be pulling their boat across the Foulness Sands almost surrounded by water, but soon that privilege will be denied us forever as will the route through Havengore Creek. Make the most of it while you may.

Fred Partlett.

GOOD SAILING (TV) (Colour) Tuesdays 7.00 pm BBC-1 (six programmes).
2 November - 7 December 1971.

AIM OF SERIES This series provides instructional material for sailors at a fairly advanced level. It assumes that the greater part of the audience can handle a boat and is now ready to develop this basic competence into real skill. Topics such as chart reading, understanding of buoyage and tides, and coastal navigation procedures will be covered. The programmes will also provide information about the four main types of sailing - dinghy sailing, dinghy racing, cruising and ocean racing.

PROGRAMME CONTENT.

1. Sails (2 November) - The sail is the power unit of the sailing boat. This programme recapitulates the basic theory of sail working and goes on to look at one or two experimental sail designs - the wingmast of C-class catamarans and the revolutionary 'Planesail' rig, and includes interviews with this designers.

2. Dinghy Handling Techniques (9 November - Elementary dinghies, on which most people begin sailing do not possess the modern equipment of the faster racing boats, particularly the spinnaker and the trapeze; nor can the techniques of planing in strong winds or tilting in light airs be applied effectively to them. The National Champions of the 505 Class, Larry Marks and Richard Hughes, demonstrate these techniques with further dramatic illustrations from the 1968 505 Championship races.

3. Racing (16 November) - After a brief introduction to the different types of racing available and the racing rules, the major part of the programme is devoted to the analysis of a six-boat race specially sailed for this purpose by the Hamble River Sailing Club with Merlin Rockets. Critical points in the race are examined by the use of models.

4. Cruiser Handling Techniques (23 November) - Whether a person has sailed before or not there are certain basic techniques which must be mastered before he or she leaves a mooring with a cruiser. These include the ability to return to the mooring in different wind and tide conditions, the ability to reduce sail, the ability to cope with a man overboard. The programme is introduced by Alec Miller, Head of the Educational Dept., The Merchant Navy College, using Trident and Nicholson 38 cruisers for demonstration.

5. Coastal Navigation (30 November) - The two fundamental requirements for coastal navigation are knowing howto read charts, and make proper allowance for tides. Exercises included are (1) a journey through the Medway buoyage system in a cruising catamaran and (2) entering the rocky harbour at Barfleur by chart and leading marks. The programme also includes a brief explanation of the use of the sextant.

6. Going Foreign (7 December) - The programme is devoted to a trip from Cowes to Cherbourg, a popular first 'foreign' voyage, in a Nicholson 38 cruiser, illustrating the navigational, tidal and wind problems encountered, the Customs procedures at each end and on return, and some of the delights of cruising.

SUPPORTING MATERIAL

A set of twelve illustrated cards, encased in a clear plastic wallet giving quick, easy reference to the kind of information every yachtsman needs, e.g. knots, signal flags, charts and tides. Price 62½p, available from BBC Publications and booksellers.

THE SITE IS OURS - WHAT ABOUT A CELEBRATION?

Yes, it has all happened, the Marconi Athletic & Social Club are the proud owners of the Sailing Club at Stansgate and the Sailing Section become the permanent tenants with planning permission. The Deed of Surrender was dated the 9th of September. Contracts have been formally exchanged and completion is due on October 7th.

All the living on a knife edge is over and we may occupy our great Sailing Site at Stansgate for as long as we are capable of running The Marconi Sailing Club according to the rules and for the objects laid down.

I Sincerely hope that all of you who read this will reserve some effort to ensure that our future at Stansgate remains bright and that our headquarters may be seen to be of a very permanent nature as quickly as possible.

AUTUMN LEAF TROPHY - 1971.

The Club entered a team of three boats to compete for the Autumn Leaf Trophy at Wraysbury Lake S.C. on the 23rd and 24th October. The event was sailed in Enterprises and our helmsmen were Julian Bigden, Roger Hance and Mike Taylor.

The competition was very fierce and although we failed to make the semi-finals our team put up a good fight in very trying conditions. The eventual winners were Grimsby and Cleethorpes Y.C. with FelixFerry S.C. second; both of whom were experts at roll-tacking in absolutely no wind. The several members and families who travelled with the team were made very welcome by the Wraysbury Club, and were able to sit in the sun enjoying the creature comforts whilst the team got lost in the fog or tangled in the trees!

LAYING UP DINGHIES AT STANSGATE

I expect that as in previous years, many dinghies will be left at Stansgate during the winter. A little effort now can save a lot of work and possible trouble later on.

High winds and rain may be expected during the next few months and dinghies should be made safe and secure so the most important thing to do is remove masts. Please do not leave these projecting into gangways where they may be damaged or worse still, cause damage. If possible take them home, if they cannot be stowed under cover, either tie them to the leeside of a vertical drainpipe or secure alongside a garden fence or wall supported at several places with either cord or brackets.

A dinghy will winter quite well turned upside down supported on some old tyres. Securely tie down some sort of cover, canvas is better than plastic as it is not so prone to condensation. If necessary, secure trolley on top.

Should the boat be left on its trolley, use an old boom or piece of timber to raise the cover and let air circulate. Covers should have extra lashings over them and under the boat, even good ones can be damaged by the wind getting underneath, frail and old ones may be torn to pieces. Take a look around the dinghy park now, there are some wonderful examples of the right and wrong ways of laying up!

N.J.James.

ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING

The Annual General Meeting of the Marconi Sailing Club will take place on Friday, November 19th, 1971 at 8.00 pm in the M.A.S.C. Hall, Beehive Lane.

This is the occasion of the year when members have the chance to discuss the running of the Club with the retiring Committee and to make suggestions for changes and improvements for the new Committee to consider.

The new Committee and Officers are of course elected at this meeting and to do this volunteers for Committee are required. To this end a nomination form is included in this issue of Navigans, and we would like to see many of these returned to the Secretary with suggestions for potential Committee members.

If you feel you would like to serve on the Committee and nobody has suggested it, don't be put off, just fill in the appropriate bits and wave the form in the air, and the other formalities will soon be completed. Or more seriously, return it to the Secretary as an indication of your willingness and he will do the rest.

20th HORNET WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS

SOLINA - POLAND.

The amount of paper work that one is required to produce for a visit to a Communist country, is incredible. Although we began our enquiries at Whitsun; three weeks before our departure we were still uncertain of an entry, even though we had a file eight inches thick with the 'necessary' forms.

The trip was relatively uneventful across Belgium and West Germany, and it was'nt until we reached Helmstedt on the West/East German border that we began to have doubts. At the Allied checkpoint is a model of the East German border security precautions; three barbed wire fences, one minefield, completely devoid of vegetation and further fences punctuated with machine gun searchlight posts. On entering the Eastern sector we had to purchase our transit visas and vehicle insurance, as well as declaring all our currency. Naturally all the forms have to be filled in duplicate, the whole operation to clear the border, for the four of us, taking about two hours. The visas stated quite plainly that you are not allowed to deviate from your route, I could'nt help wondering what would happen if we broke down or over ran our visa time.

Our first mistake was, obviously, to get lost. To correct our route we had to cut back around Berlin via Potsdam and here we had our first surprise. Potsdam is still in a state of semi-desiccation. There are still huge bombsites with rubble lying in the streets, almost as if the war finished yesterday. Obviously at one time the architecture was superb - but all these buildings were now covered in shell marks. It occurred to us that this was not the place to be found with boats with Union Jacks on their sails; as it was, the locals made it fairly plain that they either disliked us, or were frightened to be seen talking to capitalist British. One or two pointing guards made it plain that they too did'nt take kindly to us driving past their barracks, so when we were eventually back on our stated route, we all breathed a sigh of relief. (To emphasise the tight security, one of the Dutch competitors became completely lost. Minutes later a helicopter flew over head and five minutes after that the military had stopped him).

Poland was extremely pleasant after East Germany, the people are friendly and the roads are good, with the exception of the towns and villages which invariably are still cobbled. The cobbles started our problems, slowly the trailer wheels grew nearer to Father William as it curled up like a bean can. Two wheel studs broke off like carrots and the mast support broke clean away; with six masts, (4 British team spares), this presented quite a problem.

Eventually we arrived, Solina at last! Fortunately we had no accommodation problems as the Poles had awarded two British boats and two Dutch boats free lodging - "Father William" being one of them. Solina on a sunny Sunday looked good. The sailing area was a dammed up river, producing a lake about 4 by 1½ miles, with a few small islands scattered here and there. Solina was obviously being turned into a tourist centre, and a lot had gone into it for the World Championships benefit. The concrete hard for the boats was on the verge of being finished, and likewise the hotel, which had been built originally for the workers on the dam, and was now being given a face lift. People milled everywhere, holidaymakers, sightseers, T.V., bandsmen etc. Dozens of helping hands unloaded "Curved Air" from "Father William", and then hundreds of faces solemnly watched over the barrier wall as boats were rigged and tuned.

/continued.

- 7 -

In the afternoon the opening ceremony commenced after the abandonment of the practice race. The brass band played - the flags all went up and everybody marched round in pairs - as per true Olympic style. Eventually a rowing boat left the shore bearing a flaming torch which was to light the main torch on one of the islands. To round off six Russian parachutists dropped from an ancient aeroplane, which had been circling overhead, trying to land on a white lifebuoy on the lakes surface, it was all very impressive. The British and Dutch naturally followed up with their own ceremony - an absolute rave party at which we all got smashed on vodka.

Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday the Poles showed us how devastating their windward performance was. They all sail extremely freely, we would describe it as close reaching. This technique has obviously been developed to combat rapidly shifting conditions and fresh water. Another factor was that, to date, they had 12 elimination trials and 30 days of sailing at Solina, with the peculiar wind refraction from each shore and from the islands, one had to have a set formulae made out for the windward leg - the Poles knew it backwards! Off the wind British and Dutch boats showed complete supremacy particularly spinnaker reaching, however owing to the shape of the lake the course was predominately beating and running, all 3 days, which did not allow for the fast reaching ability of the British and Dutch to show. 'Mojo' and 'Yabadoo' both managed to get to the front - but only 'Yabadoo' was consistent. (Wind strength 4 gusting 4½ with occasional lulls at force 1 or less!)

Thursday brought a lay day, strictly against Hornet rules, but the Poles had organised a trip to some stately home. This was not really Hornet material, as you can guess, except for the zoo, the monkeys fascinated quite a few Horneteers!

Friday came and the wind howled. During the night it had backed 180°, and was 6 gusting 7. 'Father William' blew clean off the launching trolley with no sail up at all, however the wind had steadied and at last the British and Dutch high pointing ability began to pay, 'Father William' moved into 3rd position with five of the British force in the first ten boats. The afternoon race provided much the same pattern, the Polish boats sagging away to leward with their peculiar technique, only to be caught by British boats as they tried to tack uphill. On the very broad reach the leading Poles' mast collapsed under the enormous compression strains, allowing 'Father William' through into 1st place, which I'm sorry to say did'nt last very long. Reaching speed differential between the British and Polish could now literally be measured in knots. Upwind was the first time that I've ever heard the wind shrieking over the rigging of a dinghy whilst sailing. We were sheeted so hard the mainsheet blocks were touching, and still the sail refused to feather as we required. A huge gust eventually knocked us flat, however, Smoothy and Tony in 'Yabadoo' grimly held on with their 25 stone, and moved into 1st position only to capsize on the last gybe and finish 3rd.

Generally a superb week, the Pole who won deserved victory, he sailed magnificently all the time, and well done Smoothy and Tony in 'Yabadoo' for salvaging 2nd position for the British team. Just in case we think that we are the greatest Hornet nation on earth, it's estimated that Poland probably has twice as many Hornets as the U.K. and Australia, but she only registers a certain amount, the rest are regarded as trainers. All Polish boats are government owned, if you qualify for a boat its up to the individual to equip it in his own manner, which leads to home made pullies, mainsheet travellers etc. If you do not show promise, your boat is taken back and given to the next chap on the waiting list - take note all ye with grass growing through your c/b slots!

Our one criticism of the week were the commissars on duty night and day, they were everywhere, dark glasses and all. These people are definitely not connected with the sailing but with the party, and just watch all the time. In our hotel there was always a commissar on duty, although there were no Polish crews in our block. Several of us found the female versions very friendly - but sooner or later they started "Where do you work"?, "What do you do"?, the friendly line just being a starting point.

/continued.

- 8 -

Technical information.

Centreboards - Considerably larger than ours about 17" across and parallel with angle cut tip.

Masts - A few alloy - mainly wooden without spreaders. British masts were all, naturally, alloy, and it is interesting to note that spreader lengths were virtually identical and, with the exception of "Dry Bones", positioned in the same place, 6" above centre. (Between deck and hounds).

Sails - Polish sails on the whole were good. British sails predominately Holt mains and a fair number of Goodwin genoas. All the spinnakers Polish and British were well undersize, seven inches in some cases.

The Poles are trying to introduce a very rounded aft hull section, where, according to the plans, the bottom should be flat ply. They were told quite plainly that these boats were not 'Hornets' and would be disqualified if brought to England. The Hornet committee is now altering the rules to prevent this in future boats.

Generally the week was superbly run, the Poles did their best to ensure a good time for all. The prizes were extremely generous and the money spent on the hotel etc. must have been enormous. A full length television film was made of the whole week and we are hoping to get this to show over here.

British Boats Finished:-

2nd. - Yabadoo - Mike Holmes (Smoothy), Tony Canning.
6th. - Dry Bones - Alf Reynolds and Cecil Tuc (Dooley).
9th. - Mojo - Dane Dorry and 'Ollie' Hollingmouth.
10th. - Father William - Bruce Long and John Heslop (Youth).
12th. - Spartacus - John Boon (Zoomer) and 'Biggles'.
Canned Air - John Hales and Jane Long - (Haggis Trophy - best mixed boat).

Apart from Yabadoo these results may be slightly inaccurate - following them in Polish is'nt easy.

Bruce Long, J6, Baddow.

M.A.S.C

Minutes of the Sailing Section Annual General Meeting held at 8.00 p.m. on Friday, 19th November 1971 at the M.A.S.C. Beehive Lane.

Chairman Mr. S.R. Allerton (Commodore)

Number Present 87

1. APOLOGIES FOR ABSENCE Mr. R. Waller and Mr. J. Pletts apologised for their unavoidable absence.

2. MINUTES OF THE LAST A.G.M. Copies were provided to members at the meeting. Adoption of the minutes was proposed by F.J. Savill, seconded by G. Charlton and carried unanimously.

3. MATTERS ARISING FROM THE MINUTES Nil.

4. THE COMMODORE'S REPORT The Commodore presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans" December 1971). There was a brief discussion on points concerning the extent of the site that had been purchased, and also about the building plans. The Commodore re-iterated that a planning sub-committee would be formed by the new Committee. A previous investigation carried out in 1968 into the cost of a new clubhouse had indicated a sum of about £17,000. A vote of thanks to the Commodore for his report, coupled with special mention for his work of completing the site negotiations was delivered by K. Beavins and seconded by E. Payne.

5. THE SECRETARY'S REPORT The Secretary presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans", December 1971). The adoption of the report was proposed by I. Tate, seconded by G. Farnie and carried unanimously.

6. THE TREASURER'S REPORT The Treasurer provided copies of estimated accounts to members at the meeting and explained various items. He emphasied that the account included the rent for the site for both 1971 and 1972, but that it would still show a small surplus. In reply to questions of detail, the Treasurer pointed out that the account was an estimate and the detailed final blanace sheet would be presented to the Committee at the end of the year. It could, of course, be inspected by request. The report adoption was proposed by M. MacArthur, seconded by G. Charlton and unanimously adopted.

7. THE SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT The Sailing Secretary presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans", December 1971). This not only dealt with details of the years sailing programme, but also presented an outline of the work of the sailing sub-committee. Adoption of the report was proposed by J. Bigden, seconded by P. Black and unanimously carried.

8. COMMITTEE PROPOSALS These related to the offices of President and Vice-Presidents; it being proposed that they should be subject to election and re-election on a three-year term, and that they would be eligible to vote at committee meetings. T. Hallam pointed out that the amendment to rule 9(a) excluded permanent officers from committee meetings, but it was realised that this was in error, and that the proposal should read "Rule 9(a) delete the words "--- but shall not vote". The Committee proposals were then unanimously accepted.

9. ELECTION OF OFFICERS AND COMMITTEE The election of officers and committee as per agenda (by Rule 10g). Mr. E. Payne took the chair and proposed that the officers be accepted en bloc. This was seconded by D. Byatt and unanimously approved.

There were more nominations for the Committee than vacancies, for both ordinary and associate members, and six out of the eleven ordinary members were elected by ballot. These were I. Tate, G. White, B. Long,

- 2 -

Miss D. Renshaw, T. Bigden and D. Boswell. The two associate representatives elected were W. Standing and K. Beavins.

10. ANY OTHER BUSINESS There followed a general discussion on the size of the club and the facilities. The Commodore pointed out that family membership included wives and children, and there were in fact about 500 persons in the club. With the new site and a new clubhouse, this could be increased. In answer to questions on fund raising the Commodore pointed out that we had a start with £1,600 in reserve, and that the proposed Planning sub-committee would give attention to this point.

John Witter remarked upon the development requirement to landscape the site and proposed a Tree Planting Fund.

Mr. Huartson reminded members of the need to take care when towing boats, as his son had been injured by a trailed boat at Danbury. The Commodore said a note would be put in "Navigans" as a reminder.

Mr. Hance asked about possible increases in Associate Membership. The Commodore said numbers had to be governed to a large extent by the level of Company members.

J. Wild said there was still an impression that we only had the site from the M.A.S.C. for five years, and the Commodore emphasised the fact that we would have the site, and the support of the M.A.S.C., for as long as we could run the Sailing Club.

Mrs. A. Stevens said that there was some concern over the increasing costs of the Laying Up Supper, and asked for comments.

After a range of opinions had been aired, 52 members voted in favour of staying with the Heybridge against 20 in favour of the M.A.S.C.

S. Campbell proposed a vote of thanks to Jack Reeves, for his services in the bar, and to Mary Greygoose for her efforts in editing "Navigans".

Ian Tate commented on the noise from the adjoining lounge, and asked if we could request less interference next year.

Peter Foreman referred back to the proposed voting rights for Permanent Officers, and felt there could be a danger here in future, but the Commodore said he personally welcomed the move.

A. Adam proposed a vote of thanks to Robbie Sims for introducing the club to the Stansgate site. The Commodore warmly supported this, and added his thanks to Arthur and Maggie Adam for their help also - to a round of applause.

The Commodore then thanked all members for their attendance, and support over the past year.

The final annoucement was of Working Parties for the next three Sundays - voulunteers with gloves, nail pullers, hammers, post boorers, flame throwers or hedge trimmers especially welcome.

The meeting closed at 10.00 p.m.

D.W.G. Byatt.
Hon. Sec.

THE 1971 ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING

The A.G.M., held on Friday 19th November, was once more very well attended. The Sailing Section can give itself a pat on the back occasionally, and it can certainly be commended for the great interest shown by members on this occasion. COMMODORE'S REPORT

Members of The Marconi Sailing Club

A year ago I stood before you to deliver my report and at that time I paid tribute to the efforts of my fellow Officers and Committee. On this occasion the excellence of their work is again commended with special emphasis being directed to those members with whom it has been my privilege to work for several years and who for various reasons are not accepting nomination for office next year.

I refer of course and say a special thank you to Dave Polley, John Witter and Dave Draper who because of their excellence in the posts they have filled cause the Club to be that much greater because of their efforts.

To the remaining officers and committee members who are either seeking higher office or continuance of office with myself, through Committee recommended nomination I would say 'Thank You' for all your good work and the compliment you pay me by accepting such nomination. To those who are not continuing as members of the Committee, may I say thank you and perhaps we may see you again in some other helpful capacity.

Tonight I have no intention of making a lengthy report as the general business and activity of the past year will be reported by your other officers.

I must say that after reading the minutes of the last A.G.M. the questions and answers session in cold print looked like an inquisition. Although unperturbed at the time, when reading through the "script" a year afterwards it certainly sent me into a cold sweat. I could however understand your worries

/continued.

- 4 -

and perhaps now that we have our Sailing Site you can understand why the answers to questions appeared guarded and appreciate the complications which had to be overcome to reach our objective. Let no one doubt the seriousness of the situation as at that time and since we could so easily have had the Site sold over our heads. Any important news on this subject has been reported to you through 'Navigans' but I will add that we are indeed a very fortunate club to find ourselves agreeing to pay increased rent to the tune of £1,000 per annum at one A.G.M. to become owners (through our Mother Club) of the Site by the following A.G.M.

Further - that for at least another year no proposals for increase in subscriptions have been tabled as your Committee consider purchase repayments are adequately covered at this years income level.

Planning permission is held by us to develop the Site. Such permission includes that of demolishing the present building in favour of erecting a new club house with dinghy and car parking facilities. This permission becomes subject to renewal if not taken up within 5 years.

The formal agreement is currently being drawn up by which the Sailing Club is granted licence by the M.A.S.C. in accordance with the terms already reported to you for the next 5 years.

The plan which is exhibited in the hall tonight shows the areas purchased and the positions of the facilities relative to the planning permission received.

Your Committee, having accomplished - with a lot of assistance from a lot of people - the first stage of Operation "Secure Stansgate" now instruct Stan to open the Gate in order that constructive views and ideas may be received from you.

I will, if re-elected be forming a special Development Sub-Committee in January and would ask that your contribution of ideas towards financing developing and building on the site of our permanent home be forwarded to the Secretary for consideration by that body.

The important question of Working parties to secure the Site boundaries by erecting fencing will I hope be discussed and arranged later in A.O.B.

We should all be delighted to see the current unprecedented number of applicants from the younger members to fill the Committee vacancies.

When elected it is the duty of the membership to give them the encouragement needed to ensure the successful advancement of the Club by unselfishly accepting the basic rules of the Club and by adhering to present and future bye-laws which may be introduced by them.

It is very necessary for our Membership to jealously guard the privileges which have been won for them by challenging any rule breakers and rejecting all non-members from our facilities excepting those properly and personally introduced, signed in and accompanied by members as their guests.

If these remarks appear pointed to a particular section of the membership then I make no apology.

Whether we be dinghy owners, cruiser owners or non-boat owners, as either Ordinary or Associate Members, as good club members we all have the same responsibilities.

We have won the Site - now let us secure it - for ourselves.

I hope you will forgive the digression.

The year 1972 holds much in store for the Marconi Sailing Club as we reach that magical figure of 21 years young and really get the key of the door. Although the records are slightly blurred I am told that it was in 1951 that the Club was founded by 15 Stalwarts who operated from a riverside shed at Heybridge. In 1956 they, with quite a few more, were posted over the sea

/continued.

- 5 -

wall to the barge MAMGU which remained the Club's headquarters until 1962 when activity was transferred to Stansgate which it is now within our power to maintain as our permanent home.

The object of planning total site development, including the building of a Club House in character with our image and the additional objective of planning and working to secure the finance required to make this possible is presented to us as a challenge for this 'coming of age' year.

Can we meet the challenge of this special year?

I feel we can - but first send in your ideas and suggestions - we have a long time before fitting out and sailing again, perhaps we may use this time to benefit our Club and ourselves.

Thank you for listening to me, if there are any questions remaining unanswered I will be pleased to try to answer them.

S.R.Allerton.

SECRETARY'S REPORT 1971.

I am pleased to report that the proposals accepted by the members at the last A.G.M. have been carried out, with results close to those predicted.

We anticipated a reduced membership this year resulting from the increased fees, but the reduction has been lower than feared. Nevertheless, the membership of the club has decreased slightly in two successive years. The figures for this year, 1971, are

* Marconi Members - 230 - * Associates - 70
" Cadets - 37 - " Cadets - 10

(* Note this is now frequently husband and wife)

Now that we are assured of a more promanent future at Stansgate, we feel sure that membership will increase; a membership drive might be worth considering for next year.

Bringing forward the subscription final date to the end of February was a great help particularly with regard to associates applicants, who previously had to wait well into the season to hear if they could join.

The number of dinghies sailed from the club was similar to last year, at 150, and the number of cruisers has remained constant, and so once again, our reduced membership, although slight, has come from our non-sailing members.

Committee meetings have been held on the first Monday of every month, and an exceptionally high attendance percentage has again been maintained, the lowest attendance was 13 members.

The meetings early in the year dealt mainly with club organisation and committee structure, for example, the appointment of Clubhouse Secretary, Cadet skipper, Dinghy Park Secretary, to name but a few. There was also considerable effort by the Sailing sub-committee in preparing the sailing programme and for the regatta.

A main theme running through all the meetings is, of course, the site negotiations, so ably handled by the Commodore, the outcome of which you have all heard.

There is also, however, another issue that arises from time to time, and that is the problem of dealing with interlopers, both accidental and intentional. We are sorry to note that the car parking label idea has only been partially successful, in some instances over 50% of the cars in the park did not display a ticket, although on checking many of these had in fact paid a parking fee.
/continued.

- 6 -

There have also been a number of rather blatant cases of members introducing an excessive number of guests. We do urge everyone to please ensure that guests are "signed in" in the visitors.book.

The Commodore and I did not have a chance to compare notes until just before this meeting, so I hope any repetition will emphasise these points.

There have been comments that sometimes the committee seems remote from the members, although this last year there has been much more participation by members in club affairs. However, it is obvious that we shall need to form a number of active sub-committees next year, and it would be encouraging if many of the members of these could be co-opted from those of you willing to help in specified areas. In this way, you would not only be involved and in touch with the workings of the committee and club, but also help to share the load on the basis of many hands make light work.

Finally, I would like to report that the clubs material possessions have been re-insured as follows:-

1) Club premises and contents £1,730 for fore.
2) No. 1 (16') Rescue boat - £400
3) No. 2 Walker fisherman - £167
4) No. 3 Walker '8' pram - £40
5) No. 4 (24') Rescue boat - £350.
6) 'Brazil' £150 plus £25 trailer.
7) 2 Radio Transceivers £100 each.

All boat policies also carry third party indemnity.

In conclusion, I would like to thank all the officers, committee members and fellow members for their help and understanding over the past year, thank you.

Dennis Byatt.
Non. Sec.

SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT - 1971

Some members may not be aware of the organisation and work needed to bring you your sailing each year, and before I report on this year's sailing activities, I shall outline it briefly to you.

The Officer responsible for sailing matters is by tradition, the Rear Commodore. To help him with this task he has a Committee known as the Sailing Sub-Committee which is composed of the six Class Captains, the Cadet Captain, the Bo un, the Coxswain, the Race Equipment Officer and the Sailing Secretary, plus the other Flag Officers and theHon Treasurer as ex officio members. Typical of the jobs involved are the fitting out and maintenance of Club boats, moorings and race marks; the preparation of the Year Book and sailing programme; the provision of Race Officers and Rescue Crews; and the organisation of principal events.

We have tried to provide you with the organised sailing which we believe you want, but if you are dissatisfied in anyway or have some suggestions for improvements you should tell your Class Captain who will present your proposals at the regular monthly meetings.

Sailing this year started early and finished late, and whilst the enthusiasm and performance of the active dinghy racing members has undoubtedly increased, the actual members racing in Club events has fallen slightly compared with 1970.

Entries for the Helmsman of the Year fell from 106 to 89 and attempts to increase interest in the event by the use of Committee Boat starts failed after the first two races.

/continued.

- 7 -

The Enterprise Spring and Summer Points Series both attracted more entries than last year, whilst the G.P.14's fell by half. A bright spot was the Mirrors whose entries more than doubled from 17 to 47, making them second only to the Enterprises.

The Hornet Fleet however, makes up in quality what it lacks in quantity, although this year - the first for many - the fleet has grown in size. In relation to fleet size more Hornets races than any other class, their entry averaging 1 in 3 of the fleet.

Bottom of the racing stakes were the G.P.14's where the entry was less than 1 in 8, with the Enterprises 1 in 4 and the Mirrors 1 in 5.

In spite of the strenuous efforts of the Handicap Fleet Captain there was no support for the Dinghy Handicap Points Series. The Saturday Points Series was also a complete failure and should not I consider, be continued next year as it is unfair and demoralising to Race Officers and Rescue Crews when they have to make a special journey to Stansgate.

The Regatta this year was bigger and better than ever, or perhaps worse than ever depending on whether you are a sailor or a worker or both. Our policy of confining our open trophies to this one event has been hotly debated on many occasions, but it is obvious that saturation point is near.

The Cruiser Cup and the Dinghy Challenge Cup were 'blessed' with such fine weather that re-sails were necessary. The Challenge Cup re-sail was almost as unlucky with the race having to be finished at the 3rd mark after 1½ hours. Total entries fell from 45 to 39 with only 11 competing in the re-sail. The Cruiser entry was 16 with 12 appearing for the re-sail.

Interest in Cruiser Racing, although low in the earlier part of the season, showed signs of revival towards the end and promises well for next year.

Interest in team racing also revived towards the end of the season As well as achieving the annual victory by the Hornets over Saltcote, the Club entered teams in the Enterprise East Coast Area Team Championship and for the Autumn Leaf Team Trophy at Wraysbury. This form of racing should be encouraged as it provides an opportunity for Clubs to sail against each other, and the chance for individuals to represent their Club.

We can now boast some of the best helmsmen in the country and their numerous successes have included; a 2nd in the Hornet Nationals, a 10th in the Hornet Worlds, a 5th in the Enterprise Worlds, a 1st, 2nd and 3rd in the Enterprise East Coast Championships, the Blackwater and Colne "Cock of the River Trophy", 1st, 2nd and 4th in the Enterprise Nimbus Trophy and many other wins and places at Open Events.

It has been suggested that the presence of top class helmsmen discourages beginners and less skilled members from sailing in Club points races. The sisuation is not quite as bad as it seems however, as the top helmsmen usually seek the stiffer competition available at open meetings and may not complete the points series - mind you many would like to do both, but I believe this is both impractical and wrong. Nevertheless it is something to be considered when planning next seasons programme.

The rescue facilities have worked well, thanks to the efforst of the Bosun and Coxswain and their many helpers, but the club boats are far from ideal and require a great deal of maintenance. We should urgently consider changing our rescue boats to minimise these 'chores' and also provide a more reliable service - something we will need should we extend the sailing into a Winter Series.

Finally, your retiring Rear Commodore - John Witter and I, would like on your behalf to thank the Sailing Committee and the many others who have provided us all with such good sailing in 1971.

R.G.Greygoose.

LOOK BACK WITH PLEASURE

This past year has been a memorable and successful year for the M.S.C. being crowned by the acquisition of the Freehold of 10 acres of land beside the River Blackwater at Stansgate.

This great achievement has been brought about by the tenacity of your Commodore and the business accumen of the Trustees of the M.A.S.C.

I am sure that many, if not all of you, will be greatly relieved to know that for the first time in the history of the M.S.C. we can look forward to a future of sailing from our own shore and not be wondering where we shall all be sailing the following year. To me this is a great step forward and one which I feel I would like to mark in a small way.

It was with this in mind that I proposed at the A.G.M. that we should start a Stansgate Tree Fund whereby members who felt that they would like to have some permanent record of their association with the Club at this time could make a donation or present a tree to be planted at Stansgate.

When Stansgate was purchased, it was with planning permission for the erection of a permanent Club House on the site. There was however, one clause in the planning approval which has not generally be published and that is that trees have to be planted on the site during the development. This fund makes a start on the permanent development and as trees take longer to grow than bricks and mortar to build, we cannot start too quickly.

Opening this fund was approved in principle at the A.G.M. and any contribution - no matter how large or small - will be gratefully accepted by the new Treasurer, Frank Savill. Some members have indicated that they already have trees they would like to donate and I shall be pleased to hear from any of these members.

We propose to consult the planning Authority and to seek advice from tree experts to ensure we have a correct balance of trees in approved positions. In the meantime we will be placing markers on the South East boundary and anyone with trees for planting may plant them beside the markers.

The scheme has got off to a good start and all interested will be kept informed both personally and through Navigans.

I.Y.R.U. AND R.Y.A. NEWS

At the meeting of The International Yacht Racing Union recently held in London it was decided that as the Enterprise dinghies which did not comply with the original design may be faster than those according to the present class rules and measurements, probably because of their finer bows, they would not be eligible for entry in national championships or other international events after 1st January, 1972.

The Enterprise Association is not altogether happy with this decision and considers that the I.Y.R.U. has been too hasty in their decision - obviously the last of this has not been heard!

On the other hand, the modified Solings do not appear to be appreciably faster than those conforming to measurements, although such experts as Messrs. Hobday and Patton dispute this, and they are being allowed to compete.

The Committee dealing with International regulations urges the introduction of a simple international yacht identity document.

The introduction of international insurance certificates is also recommended.

A sub-committee has been formed to consider the practice of helmsmen and crews wearing many layers of absorbent clothing, which when saturated, increase their weight and consequently aids the windward performances of their boats. Also from the safety point of view, it considered that the practice should be banned. The question of enforcement would present difficulties.

Eric Payne.
R.Y.A. Liaison Officer.

ENTERPRISE NEWS

The Annual Fleet Meeting was held at the Marconi Sailing Club on Friday, 3rd December, 1971 when your Captain, Julian Bigden, said that he did not want to stand for election. He has filled the position for 5 years, during which time the Fleet has gained strength and he had encouraged many new members. He is handing over an active racing Fleet, but whilst he will no longer be Captain in the forthcoming year, his experience will not be lost and in fact he should have more time to advise the beginner. I would like to thank him on behalf of the Fleet for all that he has done for the Class.

I have been elected as your Fleet Captain and hope I can keep the Fleet as strong as it is now. Dennis Boswell was re-elected as Secretary so there will still be one officer within The Marconi Company.

There was some good discussion at the meeting and it was pointed out that we have 31 boats out of which 20 entered one or more races during 1971. That is pretty good but the strength of the Fleet is in racing, which is the only way to learn how to be a good helmsman and during the forthcoming year I would like to encourage more entries in the Points Series.

It is quite understandable that beginners are put off by the high standard of some of our top helmsmen, especially now that we have Roger Hance, who was World Champion in 1970. They sometimes feel that they are not in with a chance and therefore do not make the effort to get down for the Points.

A suggestion has been put forward that we have a 'Second Division' which would work roughly as follows:

All boats start together, racing for the Points Series and the Race Officer would record the positions in the normal way. Our Racing Secretary would then pick out the Second Division members and allocate points in the finishing order within that Division. A helmsman could therefore be 6th for example in the points race but be first 2nd Division man and therefore receive ¾ points towards the 2nd Division prize.

To be eligible for 2nd Division a helmsman must elect to be considered and this would be agreed upon by a small committee. It is anticipated that the 2nd Division would be reasonably small, comprising beginners, helmsmen with boats not quite up to peak standard, helmsmen who want to take things a little more easy and anything else you can think of.
/continued.

Better late than never - Here beginneth the first installment of Margaret Campbell's log of their Summer Holiday - 1970.

This was to be our first trip foreign complete with family on board our 24ft Gallant Class Cruiser "Pepito", therefore our plan was to make the shortest possible crossing i.e. Ramsgate - Calais. The crew consisted of Stan Campbell (Skipper), Margaret Campbell (the Writer) and Juniors - Ian aged 10 and Jimmy 8.

The week prior to our holiday, "Pepito" had been sailed around to Leigh on the first stage of the journey from the Blackwater. We were sailing in Company with friends from Leigh, and for us it was a convenient point of departure being only about five miles from home.

On the evening of July 24th, after numerous trips with necessities in the dinghy we appeared to have everything we needed for our 14 day holiday and turned in for an early night.

Our aim for the next day was Ramsgate and after an overnight stop there, on to Calais on Sunday - however, this was not to be. During the night the wind steadily increased and by morning a full gale had developed.

Saturday, July 25th.

On waking and hearing the wind howling and the rain lashing down, the youngest crew member peeped our of his sleeping bag and said "Perhaps something exciting has happened like our dinghy has blown away or sunk!" Ten minutes later when we decided to take a look outside, we discovered that our dinghy had indeed filled with water in the night and sunk, and of our oars there was no sign. Uneasy thought - is our younger son a Jonah? Lesson learnt, make sure oars are securely lashed in future.

Since it was high tide and the water looked most uninviting we could'nt get ashore yet anyway, with or without oars, so the only alternative was to get the cards out. Thoughts of making for Ramsgate had already gone, if it was like this in sheltered waters, the open sea was certainly not for us today. At midday there was only a short stretch of water to cross, so with the aid of a stout stout piece of wood discovered on board, we ferried out way to the shore to stretch our legs and hunt our oars (unsuccesfully) though one turned up later, apparently picked out of the water by our friends from "Waratah" in the early hours of the morning.

The rest of the day was spent uneventfully, new oars were purchased and we turned in hopefully for an early night and a better start the next day.

Sunday, July 26th.

0630. Awake, and the wind seemed to have moderated somewhat. However, with wind strength 5, 6 or 7 still forecast, we decided we would have to change our plans again. We felt that the longish haul to Ramsgate was not a good idea in view of the forecast, but instead we could at least cross the Estuary and go through the River Swale in comparatively sheltered waters and at least be on our way.

1030. Slipped from Leigh out into the Thames and sailed via the end of Southend Pier, No 4 Sea Reach Buoy, More Swatch Buoy and Sheerness. It was a hard beat into Queenborough with a series of very short tacks past Queenborough Spit Beacon with one eye permanently on the Echo Sounder. However we did not go aground and made quite good time.

1430. Dropped anchor off Queenborough and cooked lunch.

/to be concluded next month.

Continuation of Margaret Campbell's log. ...

1530. Left Queenborough to take the inland route through the Swale. Made a very fast passage, no delay at Kingsferry Bridge, which opened immediately for us to pass through.

1830. Turned to Starboard up Faversham Creek where we were to spend the next two days tied up alongside several other boats also awaiting an improvement in the weather. It was a good berth with a very welcoming pub nearby and our stay was most pleasant. The only fault to be found was the smell from the "Bone Factory" about a mile away!

Wednesday, July 29th.

The wind had now dropped away to nothing and we realized if we were going to get to Ramsgate we would have to motor sail. Why was there no happy medium in the wind strength?

1000. A nice civilized hour to leave our pleasant little creek on a hot, sunny and practically windless day. We sailed close inshore to the Kent coast passing Pollard Spit Buoy, Whitstable, Herne Bay Pier, South Margate and South East Margate Buoys to the Longnose Buoy. From the Longnose Buoy we rounded the North Foreland and thence via the Quern Buoy to Ramsgate Harbour. We gazed at all the Kent resorts with their beaches black with people like flies and were very glad to be able to do our sunbathing in private.

1600. Entered Ramsgate Harbour.

Thursday, July 30th.

Made an abortive attempt to reach Calais. Left Ramsgate at 1030 but after beating for three hours in a Force 5 we knew we would not reach the South Goodwin Light Vessel by the turn of the tide, So decided in view of the very poor time we were making we had no alternative but to call off the attempt that day. We were back in Ramsgate Harbour in half an hour.

Friday, 31st July.

We now made another change of plan and decided that an afternoon departure would be to our advantage. The only disadvantage appeared to be that of arriving at a strange Harbour in the hours of darkness, but this did not seem to be of great importance as a place like Calais was obviously well lighted.

1600. We again left Ramsgate Harbour, this time with a favourable wind. We turned South and sailed via the Ramsgate Channel and the Downs to the Goodwin Fork Buoy and thence to the South Goodwin Light Vessel, which we left to Starboard and the South Goodwin Buoy to Port. We then steered a course 107 degrees M. for Calais Breakwater. This time we knew we were well and truly on our way. Visibility was good and in a very short while we could see the vague outline of the French Coast. We passed close by the Dutch Fleet sailing down Channel and numerous Townsend Ferries, Tankers etc. but although extremely close they did'nt give us any cause for anxiety.

2115. We sighted the Flashing light of Calais Lighthouse. Gradually the one light became dozens strung out all along the coast and it seemed we were very near. However it was still a long time before we sighted the red Breakwater Light amongst the hundreds of shore lights and not until we were about a mile off did we spot the green light on the other Breakwater, but at 0100 we passed between them. The boys slept much of the way across, but we had promised to wake them as we went in, which we tried to do, but they sleepily opened their eyes and decided they had no wish to see Calais until the morning. We arrived just too late to lock into the Inner Harbour so resigned ourselves to a night in the outer Harbour. We poured ourselves a drink and at this time were not unduly worried that we had a decidedly uncomfortable berth. There is a very nasty swell in Calais Outer Harbour and the Townsend Ferries pass extremely close causing an unpleasant rolling. However, we were not complaining, we had reached our objective even if we were five days later than anticipated.

(Sorry folks, I shall have to leave the rest until next month.)
