Continuation of Margaret Campbell's log.

1140. Lock Gates open. We start our Seagull and chug around awaiting our turn to pass through, then unaccountably our motor faded and we were left drifting helplessly around the harbour. We slung out our anchor and the Skipper started dismantelling the Seagull, unfortunately, by the time the motor was showing signs of life the lockgates had shut and the Inner Harbour was as far away as ever. Eventually we did get in and spent three days very comfortably with every facility close at hand. We decided this was the best moneysworth we had encountered - just 9/- per day.

We found everybody very friendly and the people at the Club most helpful. We had the Seagull looked at, but were assured there was nothing wrong with it so forgot the incident and set about enjoying our stay in France. The day after our arrival thick fog decended and for the duration of our stay Calais Harbour was wrapped in a thick blanket and we were to hear the mournful sound of the foghorn right up to the day of our departure.

Tuesday, August 4th.

On Tuesday afternoon we locked out of the Inner Harbour in readiness for the return journey the following day if visibility improved. This however was optimistic - the fog persisted for two more days and we spent two very restless nights in Calais Outer Harbour. Our complete crew are champion sleepers on the boat, regardless of wind or exposed conditions and I can only say that this was an entirely new experience for us and one we won't forget.

Friday, August 7th.

The first thought that registered was that something was missing - at last the mournful sound of the foghorn had gone. We switched on to the Shipping Forecast at 0640 and sure enough visibility was given as good and a nice healthy Force 4 to 5 forecast. The wind direction given was North West, but this in fact turned out to be a South West which could'nt have been bettered. We left Calais at 0810 along with a whole fleet of boats, all of which had been, like ourselves, waiting for the fog to lift before going out into the Channel. The destination for all of us was Ramsgate, it was therefore with some surprise that we noted that the rest of the boats (with the exception of Waratah, with whom we were in company) were making to the South West rather than North West on an entirely different course to ours. Somebody's navigation was at fault, ours or theirs? TheSkipper was convinced we were right, our course had been gone over very carefully, so we continued on 350 degrees M. which although nearly a Northerly course was the course we had to steer to make the South Goodwin Light Vessel owing to an average tide of 3½ knots. which was setting us to the Westward.

In the event we did the right thing and arrived in Ramsgate well ahead of them. We could only assume the first boat out had not allowed for tide set and the others had followed behind. We ourselves were set down more than anticipated but they must have had a very long run up the coast. We had a most enjoyable sail across the Channel and in no time at all picked out the White Cliffs in the distance. Again we saw a lot of interesting shipping. The sun shone for us and it was certainly a day worth waiting for. We rounded the South Goodwin Light vessel and closed the shore to avoid a foul tide, sailing reciprocal courses of those sailed on outward bound passage. Just before 1600 hours we approached Ramsgate Harbour Entrance and lowered our sails and started the motor preparatory to going in. We had had a beautiful day and everything had gone as planned, when to our horror just as we reached the Harbour Walls our Seagull gave a cough and a splutter then left us helpless again. There was some frantic pulling, swearing and dashing about for a few minutes, but help was coming in the shape of an enormous Motor Cruiser, fortunately for us coming in from the North just behind us. They slung us a line in a most seamanlike fashion and in no time at all we were entering the Harbour in style towed by a floating Gin Palace. We were told later by those who saw the spectacle that we had such a large bow wave we looked like a submarine! Really our motor does choose the mastiest times to let us down. With the weekend close upon us our immediate concern was to get ashore and get our wayward Seagull seen to before we continued our homeward journey. We found somebody willing to do it that night and return it to us the next morning.

To be concluded next month.

THE R.Y.A. ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING

The annual general meeting of The Royal Yachting Association was held on March 15th; in the dismal atmosphere of The Caxton Hall at Westminster, and this atmosphere seemed to dominate the proceedings. Out of an estimated two million people in the U.K. interested in sailing, only 35,000 are members, of which a mere 150 or so stalwarts of a high average age attended. The number of members actively interested in racing was thought to be about half the total number.

The election of officers was a mere formality, Owen Aisher again being President, all being elected without opposition. Only the election of council members was by vote, A.C.Stock was nominated but not elected although he received the three votes allocated to our club.

Two major proposals were made, one suggesting the formation of a special committee with a paid secretary, with the object of increasing membership by improving public relations and the forming of regional and area associations each with its own paid secretary; the second proposal was that the existing associations should be recognised and represented on the council. Although these proposals were passed, there was opposition from Tony Morgan and Charlie Stock who contended that regional associations do exist and that the council has already power to enlist professional help when required.

The question of the £9,000 rent for the H.Q. at Buckingham Gate was again criticised but the finance committee was considering whether it would be an advantage to move out of London.

Eric Payne.
R.Y.A. Liaison Officer.

Hornet sailors have long been ridiculed on the puny size of their spinnaker and until recently have firmly retorted that this enables them to 'fly their kites' in most weathers. DINGHY HANDICAPS

The handicaps used in Club handicap and all-in races are those agreed by the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee. At this year's meeting it was agreed that handicaps in BJRC events would be the same as last year, but suggested that both Maylandsea Bay and Marconi sail Enterprises at a PN of 100 in closed handicap races.

The Sailing Sub-committee considered this proposal but felt that any change made should be by one point only at a time, and after further discussion it was decided by the other Class members that the Enterprise this year will sail at a PN of 99 in all closed handicap races, i.e. at the same rating as the G.P.14. The R.Y.A. states "The continued success of the Portsmouth Yardstick depends on constant revision, and this in turn depends on the active co-operation of participating Clubs. There is a tendency to accept all Yardsticks without question, but Clubs are urged to check any Primary Yardsticks suspected of "drifting", all Secondary Yardsticks regularly and all Portsmouth Numbers every race. If re-rating is found necessary, the revised figure should be used locally and reported at the end of each season in the R.Y.A. annual questionaire".

The modification of any handicap rating is always a little contentious as it causes a 'loss of face' to a demoted class but gives it a new competitive edge, whilst the other classes face stiffer competition.

For several years now it has been apparent at Stansgate, that the G.P.14 is at least as fast as the Enterprise and it is hoped that with both racing on equal terms it will add extra spice to the rivalry between those two classes and promote more support for Club handicap races.

OBSERVATIONS!!!!

There was much muttering a few weeks ago over the decision to improve the Enterprise Handicap Number.

Although there had been a strong feeling among the 'E' folk for some time that the G.P.14 handicap number does not fully reflect the advantage conferred on that boat by its genoa introduced five years ago - a feeling which is reflected in our Sailing Secretary's article in last month's Navigans, and which has apparently prevailed in the B.J.R.C. - this view is, I gather, not shared by our G.P. fleet, who simply do not believe that their boat is as fast as the Enterprise.

I understand that the change came as a complete surprise to them and that there was for some weeks an indeterminate though strong feeling that a fast one had been pulled. It seems now however, as though they have philosophically accepted their fate, so perhaps there is nothing more to be said. Except perhaps to ask whether it is not possible that the decision would have been taken in a happier atmosphere is there had been some prior informal chat with all of the interests most affected.

Interesting to juxtapose all the G.P. moans about racing handicaps with the fact that the first three G.P. points races were not sailed for lack of entries. By contrast the 'E' men have been their usual energetic selves, some of them making a good start by covering themselves with considerable glory at Waldringfield over Easter - as noted in last month's issue.

After at least one April Points race, which ended with fleets becalmed and drifting helplessly towards the North Sea, we can, I hope, expect increased emphasis by R.O.'s & O.O.D.'s upon Rules and Sailing Instructions.

The connection with drifting towards the North Sea? Take a look at Sailing Instruction No. 5.

The approach of our annual Regatta is, I am sure, viewed with mixed feelings in the Clubs. One can discern at least three views.

For some members it is with gloom that they foresee an overcrowded club with all facilities grossly overloaded, and people as thick on the ground as on the Costa Brava in August. These members will probably stay at home and dig their gardens.

For many others the Regatta means a weekend of fellowship and sport, an opportunity to test themselves and their boats against friends from other clubs. These people will throw themselves with glee into the whole business, racing and social, and their enthusiasm will perhaps be some recompense for the organisers.

These are the people I have most in mind, for they must surely feel nothing but apprehension at the inevitable approach of their annual shindig. I refer not only to our Flag Officers and Committee who carry the responsibility for the whole exercise, but to the tent arrangers, the prize buyers, the latrine men, the bartenders (two sides of the same coin!), the rescue launch crews - to say nothing of the many people involved in organising the racing itself.

I am sure these good people consider that it is worth all the hard work they have to put in, but they can be forgiven if they hope for more active and reliable help with the more menial tasks than they usually get from the brighter stars in our racing firmament, and for more interest and support from the stay-at-homes.

Thursday 30th March

Launched at Dixon Kerly and motored to Stansgate in a rather fresh wind, anchored off the hard to collect Walter who had travelled down by car. Jobs to be done and of course sleep before the last member of our weekend crew was to arrive by boat at 02.00 in the morning.

Friday, 31st March

Kyle of Bute sailed straight past and into the night with the skipper shouting instructions as to where they would anchor. Off Stone we thought he said - and in fact we never did meet our extra crew. It was bitterly cold and with a good fresh S.W. wind at 07.30 am sails were hoisted and a course set for Harwich and perhaps Holland. As the day drew on we succeeded in convincing each other that a cross channel trip so early in the season would probably cure us of the sailing habit for good. It is difficult to recall how cold it was that weekend and just to keep warm the primus cooker was kept going full blast all weekend when we were moored or anchored. Before long we were heading up the Orwell and glad to pick up a mooring at Pin Mill still with only a handfull of yachts in occupation.

Saturday, 1st April

After a couple of trips ashore for food and fittings we were only too happy to sit in the fug caused by the cooker being full on for warmth, till a feeling, probably of guilt, made us hoist sail for Walton Backwaters. The day was brilliant sunshine but still cold and most of this short trip was occupied with determining the compass deviation which is as much as 30°! A bouncy sail into the Backwaters and an evening ashore pertaking in the legendary night life of Walton (one half of bitter in the Yacht Club). We were glad to clamber into our sleeping bags and let the warmth seep back into our bones.

Sunday 2nd April

A very early start to clear Pye End buoy well before low water. With a draught of 4'9" and a charted depth of 3' in places we succeeded with only one incident where we touched. Once clear of the shoals we sailed till we were between Medusa and Walton Tower and there hove to for breakfast whilst the tide sorted itself out.

With the wind freshening, we turned our bows into what was to become a healthy force 7 (against the tide). Jonelle ignoring these facts of nature, put her best foot forward and off we went with stanchions rigging and at times the cabin combings half submerged. For the greater part of this journey the Aries self steering gear did most of the work without hesitation or causing the yacht to miss her stride.

Eventually, we had to send up our smallest jib and a sense of proportion gradually returned, the cabin sole was where we always wanted it and we could now wipe the footprints from the desk head.

The motion in the Blackwater was not much better than out in the bay with a few gusty squalls lurking about ready to welcome us home. With a sigh of relief we picked up a mooring at Stansgate and disappeared below for tea and soup.

So ended our shakedown and warm up cruise which was to be the first stage in our plans to sail Jonelle to the Mediterranean. A few little jobs were still to be done but Jonelle inspires much confidence with her ability to take on the rough seas which we all face with some trepidation.

Tony Porter

Letter to the Editor of Navigans. 12th June, 1972.

NEW CLUB HOUSE

As an Ordinary Member I feel entitled to answer Peter Foreman's comments in the last Navigans in an Ordinary Member's capacity.

Peter's thoughts are in accord with my own. The original idea (born 1968) was for a single storey Club House built on pillars (storage etc. underneath) with a commanding view of the river from the lounge.

Other facilities included would be adequate changing rooms, toilets and showers, also bar and galley facilities, in fact this was the type of building included in our planning application last year. I feel that - as Peter suggests - the building should be adequate but not large and built only for summer or seasonal usage.

The point raised re building on the river side of the sea wall would never be entertained. In fact even if we were able to get over the dead bodies of the Wentworth Days in the area and build we would certainly suffer from shifting foundations.

I have been an advocate for finishing races off the hard for some time but of course this does mean a control in two places due to the unfavourable conditions for starting races from the shore anywhere but as at present.

(Signed) S.R.Allerton.
Commodore.

Planning and Development of Stansgate Site

It is said that a little knowledge is dangerous. Maybe this is so but unfortunately knowledge and opinion so very often get mixed up and this is where the term of "getting hold of the wrong end of the stick" came from.

Mary, in her Editorial last month, drew attention to an article regarding the new Club House which was very welcome and will it is hoped provoke others to follow suit, indeed the "murmurings in the bush" are beginning to be heard, so much so that "secret plans" and "decisions without reference to membership" are being referred to. "Getting the right advice" has also been mentioned, but I am sure that all of this is well intentioned and feel that the following facts and detail will fill you all in on what has been happening during the last six months.

A Planning & Development Sub-Committee was formed as agreed at the Annual General Meeting. This Sub-Committee first met in January when agreement was reached as follows:-

"That the objectives of the sub-committee would be to plan for 'Development of the Stansgate Site' to the benefit of the Marconi Sailing Club according to the terms of the Planning permission within five years. Further extension of Planning Rights would also be considered.

The development plans shall include:-

(i) Clubhouse - size, design, facilities etc.
(ii) Precincts (all factors).
(iii) Launching facilities, hard and foreshore.
(iv) Moorings.
(v) The use of large field.

/continued.

- 3 -

Implementation plans and methods would be considered against

(a) Membership numbers/potential/required or acceptable to Members.

(b) Finances - i.e. willingness of members to subscribe to development by additional subscriptions.

(c) Time scales - relative to the above".

Many meetings later and with a great deal of work outside of Committee having been accomplished, a first report was presented to the Main Committee (at the May meeting). It would be ridiculous to suggest that all of the ground mentioned in the foregoing terms of reference have been covered but the following are extracts from Committee Minutes:-

(i) The development required depends upon the size of the Club and a fee paying membership of 300-350 is indicated by past figures.

(ii) Information will be sought in relation to development of large field for use by caravans within our club membership (this could produce a large revenue source).

(iii) The position of the new Club House is as detailed in the Planning Development Permission granted, the building of which must be commenced by July, 1976, or further application made.

(iv) A single storey prefabricated (partly) building (as covered by Planning permission) has been suggested, or a more elaborate two storey building which would be subject to planning application.

(v) A detailed presentation would be prepared for the A.G.M. in November.

(iv) Other proposals presented and accepted by the Main Committee were as follows:-

(a) That the triangular field on the left hand side when entering the site should be the car park.

(b) The small field should be for the new Club House.

(c) The dinghy park should be as present.

(d) The cruiser park should be at the bottom of the dinghy park.

All above are covered by Planning Permission

(e) We have no Planning Permission for the large triangular field on right hand side of entrance to site.

(f) Access to large field.

Two bridges were proposed and accepted and have since been built. Another bridge immediately outside of our property to divert farm traffic to Ramsey Wick, and thus enables boundary fence to be completed near Race Box, is yet to be built.

The foregoing covers very broadly the facts without going into the mass of detail which has been gone over to enable an evaluation of the situation.

The proposals which will be made to you - the membership - will be based on fact. Such proposals are very incomplete and need your assistance, we want to know what you want, how much you are prepared to pay, how much you are prepared to work.

Remember - without prejudice - that whatever we build can only by built with our money and will belong to the Sailing Section of M.A.S.C.

/continued.

- 4 -

Remember - without rashness - a decision to raise subscriptions by £8-10 per year per subscribing member (that's roughly the amount required on present membership to build a £10,000 Club House within four years (approx)) could deny membership to someone else.

Remember - with gratification - that we must continue to pay our dues in amounts of £1,000 increasing by £100 per year for the next four years to our parent club against the debt of £21,300 incurred for purchase of site, which, without their help would by now have been sold over our heads.

Remember - without flamboyance - the need for a "Club House in character with our image".

Now- HELP US - with your opinions and ideas.

(Signed) S.R.Allerton.
Commodore.

Letter to the Editor of Navigans.

Dear Madam,

May I express to your readers, and through you to the Main Committee, some of my views on the future of our site?

1. I would like to see one of the two triangular fields kept completely free of motor cars, boats and other vehicles, (except on specially congested occasions like the Annual Regatta) so as to provide an open space, free of oily car droppings, for the many young club children under sailing age. Special play equipment is not wanted, only clean grass and open space. The same area could also be used for family picnics thus relieving the pressure on Clubhouse accommodation and the beach.

2. The tree planting scheme is a great idea, but, in addition, I want to see as much as possible of the existing hedges and trees and grass retained. Concrete and bricks can be laid in an afternoon but it takes years for a hedge to establish itself.

3. I agree with Peter Foreman that in any new Clubhouse good toilet and changing facilities are essential, but for sailors, please, not caravanners and campers.

4. My final and most important point is that I am firmly opposed to any suggestion that caravanning or camping by members or anyone else, should take place at Stansgate, except at the one annual 3 day Regatta, and also, of course, to any idea that planning permission should be sought for these activities. To allow these activities at Stansgate will inevitably turn an open airy and pleasant spot into the sort of waterside slum which is all too common along the Essex rivers and coast and would show an irresponsibility which would be little short of criminal. I would urge those of your readers who agree with me on this point to make their opinions heard now to nip in the bud this disastrous proposal.

Whilst writing may I say a word of appreciation for Navigans and the work that goes into it? I have always looked forward to its appearance, and have particularly enjoyed some of the thought provoking items in recent issues.

(Signed) Ken Beavins.

Letter to the Editor of Navigans.

I write to draw your attention to the inaccuracy of a statement in the May, 1972 issue of Navigans. Writing on the lack of response to the Commodore's call for suggestions for total site development, including a Club House, you say - '"Until this issue of Navigans not one idea had been received"'.

My architect son (who often visits the Club) and I are very interested in this subject, and during one meeting at the "Cricketers" we had a discussion with Peter Foreman, during which we put up some suggestions. These included that the Club House should be raised high enough for sailing to be seen from the lounge, and that the starting box should be part of the Club House. Subsequent enquiries as to the progress of these suggestions brought forth answers that neither of them could be adopted. The reasons given were something to do with planning permission.

Several times since then my son has enquired whether an architect has yet been appointed, and what fruit one's suggestions were likely to bear. I replied that I did'nt know about the architect, but that I had got the impression that the whole thing was cut and dried and it was'nt much use putting up any suggestions.

Peter Foreman's article in the same issue of Navigans leads me to believe I may have been wrong. If so I am delighted to hear it. Be that as it may, I think that it is clear that the lines of communication between the powers that be and ordinary club members leave much to be desired.

I suggest, therefore, that this important matter should be the subject of a special general meeting with two items on the Agenda.

1. To explain the present state and future plans for the Stansgate site, and particularly the new Club House, and to discuss the matter fully.

2. To decide what future action is needed to enable ordinary members to be informed of progress, and to express their views.

Yours sincerely,

J.W.Pletts, Baddow. 1.6.72.

OBSERVATIONS

If one can judge from several complimentary remarks by visitors, the Regatta seemed to go off quite well. Apart from one race in which one Class's difficulty in finding No. 4 mark led subsequently to the abandonment of that race for their class ( - but why did'nt they follow the other classes?), organizationally all seemed to go well.

However, the strong winds throughout the weekend were certainly such as to disabuse our Regatta guests of any misconception some may have had to the effect that the Blackwater is just another river. During the points races it was unambiguously THE SEA. Some helmsmen were deterred by the conditions and did not start, others were forced to retire, sometimes with breakages, and I suspect that many of those who managed to complete the course were grateful simply to have done just that.

One interesting and noteworthy Regatta incident occurred when the (Marconi) crew of the leading boat in one of the races left his boat and deliberately entered deep water to render urgently needed help to a family of two adults and two very young children, whose Mirror had capsized. T. Bigden is particularly to be congratulated for his part in the incident, and the nice thing is that the following boats in the race, who had of course caught up with the erstwhile leading boat, then deliberately delayed so as to allow it to resume its former position after the rescue operation had been completed. The incident reflects credit on all concerned, except (it has to be said) on the helmsman who took two small children for a sail in such patently adverse weather conditions.

Observer.

CRUISER SECTION NEWS

The second May meeting which should have continued serious discussion of our trip to Walton was rather overshadowed by the weather forecast which proved to be accurate. Worst Bank Holiday on record!

However, the following was gathered for would be Walton wanderers.

1. Best wind is off-shore i.e. N to W. Avoid trip if Easterly especially N.E. because of exposed nature of shoreline (i.e. nowhere to run if you get fed-up).

2. Must make Medusa buoy by turn of tide to take you round Pye End buoy to anchorage off Stone Point; if necessary motor sail up coast from Brightlingsea.

3. A copy of East Coast Rivers by Jack H. Coote gives navigating details and other useful hints.

Let's hope for better weather for the weekend planned in August (25th-27th).

Congratulations to Alan Huartson who has passed his Yachtmasters (Coastal) certificate.

FLEET 60 NEWS
2 PINT POT - THORPE BAY 13-14May.

With the lure of World Championship qualification, Marconi's were well represented for Thorpe Bay's 2 Pint Pot - one of the events being used in Marconi's World Championship elimination events. Unfortunately the total meeting - being run in conjunction with a Fireball open, was virtually a failure owing to the appalling weather.

Three Marconi boats were on the water on Saturday. In a varying force 2-4 N-Easterly disaster first struck at Geoff and Jane, in their new "Orangade", with a broken mast, unfortunately sustained by another boats stupidity, they were eliminated half way through the race. This left Bruce and Gory to finish 4th and Lemon in his new boat "Seeker" to finish 7th.

Sunday - needless to say, was a disaster right from the word go. With the wind still NE and screaching up over force six. After an hour of sitting around well out to sea waiting for the start and weathering the squalls as they occurred. The rescue facilities were overstretched before the Fireball start, after the Fireball start it was chaos - plenty of firewood everywhere! Eventually after more waiting and the occasional wave washing boats from stem to stern - literally, we all breathed a sigh of relief when the cancellations flag was hoisted.

This decision came none too soon for "Seeker" who had run into trouble with a faulty rudder fitting. Simon and crew were taken off until their boat could be retrieved again leaving "Seeker" securly tied to another moored Hornet. Rescue boat bungling was then responsible for "Seeker" being cast adrift and

/continued.

- 7 -

allowed to disappear towards the pier - (we all know its a crummy colour, but most of us agreed that this was a bit much!). Judging by Lemon's morose expression even he thought he'd never see it again, however some hours later "Seeker" was recovered by one man in Thorpe Bay's No. 1 launch - single handed off the pier - which must constitute a very high standard of seamanship! - A lot more than can be said for the rest of Thorpe Bay's rescue fleet which was virtually non existent!

The weekend was brightened by a superb pie, beans and mash supper on Saturday night, and an extremely good disco - but Marconi's Championship decider still remains open.

Bruce Long.

CLUBHOUSES

A new Clubhouse! One's mind immediately sees a large impressive building with a huge lounge and a portrait of the Queen over the bar. Not to mention the hot showers, maybe a bath or two and perhaps even a washing machine (as per Colne Yacht Club, Brightlingsea).

At Thorpe Bay they have a Commodore's Bar and bar billiards; at Hayling Island a drying room for clothes and a baby room; Sussex Yacht Club has a bar just like your 'local', and at the Royal Corinthian they have a Submarine Bar, a dining room, dormy houses and "ties will be worn after 7.00 pm.

The buildings have characters of their own. But clubs take on the characters of their members too. At Clacton they have a clubhouse in much the same class as our own except they've got a verandah and an upstairs, but the people are super and friendly.

This used to apply to Maylandsea Bay until they erected the 'Great Disaster'. Anyone who has known the club for some years will tell how it has changed from a jolly, "glowing", who's-going-to-be-Race-Officer Club - much the same as our own - into an uninteresting, spiritless place. Why? - they built a new clubhouse. Oh yes, they have nice changing rooms with hot showers, but go upstairs and there's a huge bare expanse of floor with stark walls and an uninviting bar. And that's all - except the usual small tables and uninteresting chairs. No pictures (not even Her Majesty), no visiting clubs' burgees, no cosy corners, no interest, no character.

I think our club is super - the members make it so. I always curse there being no showers or even hot water. I am always yelling "shut the door"! when I'm changing as, when it's open, it exposes half the tiny Ladies Changing Room to full view. And the cess pool smells. But I would'nt swop any of it for a Maylandsea Bay.

Not that I'm against a new clubhouse. I think it's a marvellous idea. When we have visitors we can proudly say "come and see inside". What I hope is never said to sailing members is "you can't come in for a drink - you're wet and you'll ruin the floor". After all it is a sailing club.

I think what I'm trying to say in my ramblings above is what a tremendous amount of thought must go into the planning of the new clubhouse to try to reflect the character of the old club in the new building, and I think it very important that members put forward their own views.

As Bruce is on the planning committee I feel I ought to say that the above is in no way representative of his, or the committee's, opinions.

Jane Long.

OBSERVATIONS

The sad fact is that there just is not enough water and beach to go round in Essex.

On a recent sunny Sunday visit to Stone, I found at the end of the road long queues of cars being directed to already full car parks by a harassed unofficial traffic warden. Things like this make one realize the tremendous pressure that an expanding and increasingly mobile Essex population is inevitably putting on the few places with access to the Blackwater. Stansgate is one of those few, and it can only be a matter of time, months rather than years, before that pressure spills over and makes itself felt at Stansgate. All very well to have a notice which says that vehicular access to our Sailing Club is restricted to members, but it will only be so restricted if we make it so - and if we don't the steadily increasing trickle of uninvited gatecrashers we have always had at Stansgate will become an unmanageable flood.

/continued.

a ere

The precise form which is to be taken by our measures to avoid this is very important and is not just a matter of detail. We need a system in which each member must play his part, however uninterested he may be in such mundane things as gates and keys. The practical answer does not lie solely in periodic gatechecks, but in a gate with an integral lock from which a key cannot be withdrawn unless the gate has been shut and locked, with a key for each paid up member. :

One can take some heart from some of the recent Navigans Letters to the Editor which suggest that some members realize that our leisure world at Stansgate is no more free from environmental pressures than is the real world Outside. The difference is that at Stansgate we can exercise real control over those pressures, if we have the will to do it.

Observer.

Letter to the Editor.

A Plea for Campers

"Whilst having every respect for Ken Beavins' views-against campers: end caravanners, I would like to put in a word for hopeful, future campers at Stansgate. tae

Last year and previous years some of our most pleasant times at the club were Saturdays and Sundays spent in the peace and tranquility of the summer evenings, after the early-burly of the sailors =nd racers had gone.

This year the weather so far has'nt encouraged one to stay on much longer, but on these wonderful evenings at the club how much nicer it would have been to put up 2a.tent and stay the night, than to drive back home and spoil it all. Many times we have wished this were possible.

Of course, regular camping, as on the scale of the regatta, would be Getrimental t the site. Any other camping would have to be severely restricted in some way sc as not to spoil this “pleasant spot into a waterside slum".

Restrictions might include tent sizes, numbers of tents allowed, (possibly as few as 3 or 4) and definitely members only.

Comments on Future Club House

A single storey building on pillars, as suggested by Stan, seems a good idea, with *storage etc. underneath". Does the “etc* include changing facilities, or will sailors have to wade upstairs to discard their wet
clothing"?

- 4 -

Letter to the Editor.

Caravans

"I have read one of the most bigoted and conservative letters which it is possible to write on the subject of preventing people from enjoying themselves after their own fashion without interference with others. There is actually a claim to represent 'sailors' as a class apart - one of their main attitudes is to establish a spirit of self reliance where each man takes his own course but perhaps this is more the attribute of those who venture on deep water. Since when has a caravan caused an obstruction on the Blackwater?

We have all seen monstrosity on water usually in backwaters floating in their own sewage but fortunately the Blackwater tides deal with these problems - which is probably a pity to some of our chair bound week-end sailors which I am afraid most of us are - so lets not put on priggish and pretentious airs about being 'sailors' - your real sailor would'nt even bother to spit by way of comment. Still let me reply to the points raised a little more constructively.

Point 1 Clear Open Spaces

Young children under sailing age 3-7 don't like four acre fields - they do not go there but stick to edges and cubby holes.

They like to feel secure and close to mum. Short grass on partly bumpy ground over a space of not more than 40 yards square with an old tree is ideal.

Point 2 Hedges

Why state the obvious.

Point 3 Loos for "sailors" only

Not very good for the bar trade.

Point 4 Touring caravans and Tents make a remarkably happy combination to dinghy sailing providing overnight accommodation and warm dry place for changing and rest which is an asset both for weekends at Stansgate or "away" fixtures.

The suggestion that caravan users invariably turn a pleasant place into a slum I find personally offensive and is in complete contradiction of the facts. There has never been any filth at Stansgate as a result of people camping or caravanning - in fact there is almost a horror with all the people I have ever met of leaving any trace behind of their stay.

There is a case against the improper use of caravans as anything else and the use of a caravan as a static shed with all its attendant rubbish is as bad as the missuse of a cruiser in the dinghy park for the same purpose.

This is easily resolved by a club rule that caravans, motor caravans and tents if brought to the site should (a) not be allowed on the premises for more than 14 days (or similar). (b) Be moved at least every 4 days to allow the grass to grow. (c) Be only allowed on permission from the committee or nominee after the payment of a suitable fee (ensuring standards and income). (d) If a caravan - be fitted with integral toilet arrangements. (e) Institute a maximum number allowed. (f) Ensure that as a condition of use that work (a rare element not popular with 'sailors') on site upkeep be part of the fee.

It follows that, if properly organised a small caravan/camping facility could be a very welcome asset to all our members on occasion and that it would be very popular even with 'sailors'.

/continued.

- 5 -

To diagress onto a further topic as regards the new club facilities which we are encouraged to comment upon, I would like to make a few points.

The Clubhouse is only used to effect at weekends during the summer. The present one apart from special occasions copes with the numbers using the site, therefore we do not need one much bigger although showers would be welcome.

A toilet - wet block etc. is probably needed, could we not make what is effectively an ablutions block somewhere and fit a flat top to it. On top could be fitted a SWIFT PLAN building such as at Baddow or other similar types of structure to make a clubhouse. This would be a reasonably economical one as we are committed to fairly heavy running expenses by the acquisition agreements.

It would beinteresting to know what our 'image' is - to see ourselves as others see us - or should we remain enchanted with our own reflections.

The facts are that we are running the club on a shoe string with heavy overheads and exploiting the willing few to run or ruin a valuable asset."

(Signed) Tom Gaskell.

OPEN DAY

The Open Day, on Saturday June 1st, was arranged in order to "show off" the club to our Marconi colleagues, and also to try to get some new Marconi members. The weather was kind, with enough wind to give some exciting sailing. Before the event, we felt that ten new members enrolled would be very satisfactory. In fact we attracted twelve!

All the "fleets" participated. There were dinghies on show for inspection, with owners in attendance to give details of costs etc. The sailing demonstration of each main class was followed by a sample handicap race, won by Frank Savill in a Mirror - our fastest growing small boat class. The commentator - our own Kenneth Wolstenholme - Bigden (Jack to his friends). This was followed by boat trips for visitors and then Marjorie Allerton, the Commodore's wife, drew the winners for the Raffle.

Our thanks to all those who helped and those who just came to visit - especially the new members! Certainly everyone seemed to be enjoying themselves!

Dennis Byatt.

CRUISER SECTION NEWS

The July meeting was varied in content.

I should like to thank Stan Allerton for coming along to discuss site development plans.

Chris Cooper tried to prevail upon would-be racers to sign on and off, and the route for the postponed Barnacle Points race was discussed.

A small but keen entry enjoyed a superb sail on the 15th. The course Chris chose was an excellent length to encourage more people to participate.

The question of adequacy of moorings available was discussed, some members wished to extend the moorings outside our present limits. It was stated that the Crown Commissioners would not short term lease the mooring rights until the future of Ramsey Marsh was decided. The possibility of extending the other side of the hard was not discussed.

The amateur lawyers then took the floor when John Hooper lodged a very strong complaint about the number of odd boats picking up his mooring. (Perhaps that lovely big red buoy is irresistible!). He made it quite plain

that he had had his share for one season and asked us to co-operate by not directingpeople there. John Gibbons and Ron Sunderland then gave chapter and verse on the foul deeds done at Maldon to their mooring. Apparently there was no law to deal with the matter. Really, I thought they were kind fishing folk up there!

Three cruisers have now been badly holed so I have written a general appeal to the dinghy people in this Navigans.

Cruisers are going off together when the weather permits outside the official accompanied cruises, if you are interested check with Vic, Stan or myself on Saturday morning. They tend to be pretty spontaneous!

Duke) presenting the prizes expressed his thanks to the Marconi Sailing Club for putting the Site at their disposal and making the day a great success. Minutes of the Sailing Section Annual General Meeting held at 8.00 p.m. on Monday 27th November 1972 at the M.A.S.C. Beehive Lane

Chairman - Mr. S.R. Allerton (Commodore)

Number Present - 98

1. APOLOGIES FOR ABSENCE Mr. R. Towell, Mr. R. Waller, Mr. W. Standing, Mr. S. Campbell and Mr. T. Condon apologised for their unavoidable absence.

2. MINUTES OF THE LAST A.G.M. Copies were provided to members at the meeting. Adoption of the minutes was proposed by J. Witter and seconded by A. Nash and carried unanimously.

3. MATTERS ARISING FROM THE MINUTES None.

4. THE COMMODORE'S REPORT The Commodore presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans" December 1972). The adoption of the report was proposed by D. Polley, and seconded by J. Bigden and carried unanimously.

5. THE SECRETARY'S REPORT The Secretary presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans", December 1972). The adoption of the report was proposed by T. Gaskell, and seconded by P. Foreman and carried unanimously.

6. THE TREASURER'S REPORT The Treasurer presented his report and explained the breakdown of the account. T. Hallam questioned the very high profit on the Bar to which D. Byatt replied that we had very low overheads and had very low stocks. J. Bigden queried the very high rental on the telephone. D. Polley queried an item under Car Park of £22.50, it was pointed out that this was the cost not the income, which was £163.00, J. Witter indicated that Claud's Wages had not been mentioned, these are presented in the General Account, J. Terry asked for the income on the Rescue Boat Account, the Treasurer replied that this was £50.00 from the sale of the old boat and £169.00 from the Grand Draw.

Adoption of the report was proposed by G. Charlton and seconded by Mr. Terry and unanimously adopted.

7. SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT The Sailing Secretary presented his report. (The text was distributed in "Navigans", December 1972). Adoption of the report was proposed by Mr. Clayton and seconded by D. Polley and carried unanimously.

8. COMMITTEE PROPOSALS Proposal 8(a) related to the new clubhouse and there was considerable discussion as to the necessity for, and style of, a new clubhouse. It was pointed out that we only have temporary planning permission on the building we have at present and that it would be advisable for us to take up our permanent planning permission as soon as possible. A plan and drawing of the proposed new clubhouse was presented for discussion. Costings were presented based on a precast concrete "Wet" block and timber lounge. The siting was queried, however we were limited as to the positions for which we would be able to get detailed planning permission. It was not envisaged initially to start and finish races from the new clubhouse.

Proposal 8(b) related to increasing the fees. The proposal was intended to provide a fund of £2500.00 and an income of £1000.00 p.a. to finance the new clubhouse. No instructions had been received to date on the effects of V.A.T. Considerable discussion was aroused by the unequal charges for Dinghies and Cruisers. Stan Allerton indicated that he wished a two thirds majority for proposal 8(a) and that amendments could not be accepted from the floor.

Proposal 8(a) was put to a vote, 50 in favour, 34 against.

The necessary two thirds majority was not obtained.

Proposal 8(b) was put to a vote, 25 in favour, 51 against, the proposal was rejected

- 2 -

Proposal 8(c) related to the purchase of a new rescue boat, after some discussion in which D. Boswell thanked the Cruiser Fleet for launching the rescue boat fund, the proposal was unanimously accepted.

9. ELECTION OF OFFICERS AND COMMITTEE Mr. E. Payne took the chair and proposed that the officers and committee members be elected en bloc. However F. Savill indicated his unwillingness to continue as Treasurer. The proposal was seconded by N. Tovey and unanimously approved.

10. ANY OTHER BUSINESS There was a suggestion that, when the club premises are handed over to visitors, we should have a rescue boat available.

Mrs. E. Witter expressed some concern that if we did not raise the fees in the next month or so that we would have to wait a year before anything could be done.

T. Gaskell proposed a vote of thanks to Avril Stevens for the excellent Laying Up Supper.

A Vote of thanks to the Committee for their work was proposed by T. Hallam and seconded by P. Foreman.

The Meeting closed at 10.55 p.m.

G.H. Farnie,
Hon Sec.

COMMODORE'S REPORT

As last year, and indeed as at any A.G.M. any year, this report must pay tribute to the Officers and Committee who have managed the affairs of your Club.

The past twelve months have been exceptional in that the action and intentions of the various elected bodies have been under the scrutiny of general membership through the participatory nature of the business involved, the reports made and the active hindsight of the figure who has so relentlessly filled our Navigans pages under the pseudonym of "Observer".

I am very much tempted to repeat part of my reply to the admirable toast given to the Club by the M.A.S.C. President - Mr. Robert Telford - at our Laying up Supper recently. This explained my feelings for the Club and its Officers. I must however contain myself to a purely business approach and say on your behalf to them - without exception - you have done a good job this year able supported by many splendid members. You have worked hard and played hard producing steady progress of a general club nature and exceptional results of a Sailing nature - whilst most others were busy complaining about the weather.

Before I leave the tributes I must mention again the names of Avril Stevens and Mary Greygoose for your special commendation for the work they have performed over several years and who now leave office for a well deserved change in activity.

Our business tonight is so important that it is difficult to avoid reference to the obvious climax to your Committee's year of work. In view of this and the reports which are to follow I will but mention some important highlights.

A long time aga now, but do you remember the admirable Winter sessions?

Our Regatta, although not quite so well supported this year, was no less successful or enjoyable than its predecessors.

/continued.

- 4 -

The Open Day was a grand success and responsible for stirring up interest in many people, not just those who have joined subsequent to and because of this event, but in more mature members who found a new interest.

The Barbecue was probably one of the best yet and to end this particular commentary our Laying up Supper was the best that many of us can remember.

A fund was introduced by the sale of the large launch for a new Rescue craft. This fund was ably supported by the Grand Draw organised by Peter Foreman and now amounts to nearly £250. Your new Committee will hold a mandate to provide a new launch and members will no doubt be encouraged to support the fund further.

Advice was sought and plans are in hand to erect a 'faggot' breakwater on the east side of the hard to try and prevent further break-up of the hard by holding in a protective shingle bank.

The very active Cruiser Section have plans for erecting scrubbing posts and for building steps over the sea wall near the recently demolished race box. The race box was of course flattened by the recent gales and is to be replaced by a "Poulton portable" with aid and assistance from the willing hands.

I would now like to commend our "caretaker" Claude Emerson for all his useful work which the Committee recognised from the financial viewpoint during the year.

Many of our Members spent very active and enjoyable days during last Winter on site development by hedging, ditching, fencing and bridge building across the dykes. Boundary gates were erected and trees planted. This work is as yet incomplete but members will have the opportunity to complete most of the work in a couple of weeks time.

During this year - and as our Secretary will report - our Membership has grown to 350 Subscription accounts and to a total head count of almost 900.

Our Treasurer also has a very good report on the financial side.

My friends, I now come to the meat of my report which obviously concerns the propositions to be put to you later.

At this time a year ago I reported fully the acquisition of the Site which we now occupy on licence from our Mother Club. Reference was made also to the outline planning permission which was obtained on your behalf and details were given of the Site and the areas allocated within such planning detail. Details were also displayed of the new Clubhouse location and a type and shape of building which did not offend either Essex County Council, Maldon Rural District Council or B.A.C.S.P.A. (representing river users and Clubs generally).

My words at that time were - "I will, if re-elected, be forming a special Development Sub-Committee in January and would ask that your contribution of ideas towards financing developing and building on the Site of our permanent home be forwarded to the Secretary for consideration by that body".

Having borne the constant worry and burden of the site negotiation alone, due to the delicate nature of the business involved, I deeply desired the fullest participation of any and all members in the planning which was to follow if we were to develop naturally and fully as a club with a good home and a proud bearing.

I would therefore ask you to remember those words of mine and the opportunity offered to all. I would also ask you to remember how we have tried to keep you all informed during the year on our work and deliberations and quote the reminders as follows:-

In February of this year I reported the formation of the Planning and Development Sub-Committee, stating terms of reference and asking for ideas and comments.

/continued.

- 5 -

In May you were asked by the Editor of Navigans "Where are your ideas and suggestions?" making special reference to the challenge given by me in relation to site development, planning and financing and I quote these words - not mine - "If you are interested in the future of your Club, please make your voice heard by conveying your opinions, ideas and suggestions to your Committee members".

At this time letters to Navigans commenced.

In June I gave a detailed report of the development and planning activity entered into by your sub-committee members who had met many times and were responsible for the detail after many hours of thought, research and work.

I now quote words from such report:-

"The foregoing covers very broadly the facts without going into the mass of detail which has been gone over to enable an evaluation of the situation".

"The proposals which will be made to you - the Membership - will be based on fact. Such proposals are very incomplete and need your assistance, we want to know what you want, how much you are prepared to pay, how much you are prepared to work".

"Remember - without rashness - a decision to raise subscriptions by £8-10 per year per subscribing member (that's roughly the amount required on present membership to build a £10,000 Clubhouse within four years (approx), could deny membership to someone else".

"Now help us with your opinions and ideas".

In July I attended the Cruiser Section monthly meeting and set myself up to answer questions and discuss development plans using the same basis for discussion and making the same appeals.

By September the last letter to Navigans appeared on these subjects.

On behalf of the Planning & Development Sub-Committee I would now thank most sincerely those few members who did help us with their ideas, suggestions - yes - and even their arguments. Conclusions must be drawn that in view of the notice given, the questions asked and appeals made that the remainder of the membership will be confident in and satisfied with the proposals placed before them tonight by virtue of their silence - which - with all the opportunity given - can but imply commendation.

Details of progress made was regularly reported by the Planning & Development Sub-Committee to the Main Committee culminating in unanimous approval by that body for the proposals placed before you tonight under items 8(a) and 8(b).

In another direction, assistance towards financing the erection of new premises at Stansgate has been sought from the M.A.S.C. and we have received an idication that such request will be considered within the framework of M.A.S.C. development plans generally.

This then brings the situation to date and completes a report which tells of a long hard year of work for my colleagues and myself.

I trust that you will reward their effort and confirm your confidence in those whom you wish to re-elect to Office tonight by accepting their proposals which are based on reason, research and fairness to all.

This is the time when, sadly, I stand down from Office and responsibility. Thank you all, once more, for the way you have accepted the leadership which you bestowed upon me and for the support my colleagues have given me throughout the past 8 or 9 years.

It has been my privelege to be at the helm at a time when we, the Marconi Sailing Club - have established ourselves at Stansgate and to have led the planning of what will be the best Sailing Club Site and premises on the Blackwater. I am deeply grateful for that privelege but more-so for the friendships which I have known and will continue to enjoy.

/continued.

To my successors I say "Good Luck". There's a fine team coming along - help them - not under cover but openly. Give them the support they deserve.

Thank you for the presentation made to me at the Laying Up Supper. This gives me a great deal of pleasure and will be in constant use either on my boat or at home where it will remind me of the fair winds I enjoyed as your Commodore and aid me in avoiding the pressure of storms in the future.

Stan Allerton.

SECRETARY'S REPORT 1972.

The main committee has met at the beginning of each month and attendance has been very good with a minimum of 11 people.

The various sub-committees have been active both in the running of the Club and in the planning of future activities. The Sailing Sub-Committee continued to organise the Clubs sailing activities efficiently, and a Social Sub-Committee was formed to assist Avril in organising the Social Functions. The results of the work put in by the Planning and Development Sub-Committee will be presented to you tonight.

This work done outside the Main Committee forms a large part of the successful running of the Club.

Suggestions and ideas have also come from the Cruiser meetings that have been so well supported this year.

The O.O.D. rota has been well adhered to and there was only one occasion when there was not an official O.O.D. on duty.

SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT - 1972

The year taken as a whole has been successful, despite the atrocious weather conditions that prevailed for much of the time, and whilst our most experienced sailors revelled in the conditions - breaking a lot of expensive gear in the process - the less venturesome, or perhaps saner, members stayed on dry land.

The sailing programme arranged for the year, in the main followed the traditional pattern. Exceptions, however, were the revival of the Barnacle Points, a new formula for the Helmsman of the Year, and as recommended at this meeting last year, the scrapping of Saturday Points races.

The Spring Series were particularly effected by the bad weather - the G.P.14's did not manage a race and the Mirrors only one. Surprising perhaps, but entries for the Summer Points all showed an increase over those of last year - although yet again the Handicap Points failed to materialise. Entries for the Regatta fell to 113 from the previous high of 185. This reduction was caused chiefly by a mid-day high water which enabled some of the up-river Clubs to hold competing events, gale force winds and the absence of the Hornet fleet. - Next year should see the entries back near the 200 mark.

Dinghy Challenge Cup entries fell for the 3rd year running to only 21 - less than half the 1971 figure. The Cruiser Trophy sailed on the same day attracted 18 entrants, - 1st and 2nd places being taken by Marconi boats.

The interest in cruiser sailing and racing, promised at the end of last season, continued to grow - and with better weather conditions would have been very much greater. - Several cruises and 2 Barnacle races were in fact completed.

Our top helmsmen have collected an even more impressive array of hardware this season and those of you who attended the Laying Up Supper saw just a sample on display - Successes include a 2nd in the Hornet Worlds; 1st in the Enterprise Worlds; the Enterprise East Coast Area individual and team Championships; and the Nimbus Trophy; the Cock of the River Trophy for the 2nd year running; the Herne Bay Long Dog and many other open meeting trophies.

The Hornet Invitation and Team events with Saltcote and Stone were thoroughly enjoyed - particularly by Saltcote who took the trophy for the first time. The Enterprises invited and just managed to beat a strong team from Broxbourne, - it is hoped that this will become an annual event. It is also hoped to arrange invitation series next year for both Mirrors and Enterprises with our neighbours Loughton and Steeple Bay.

The Helmsman of the Year, in spite of the new format, was poorly supported, but it did provide two active handicap class men with an opportunity to race - and take 1st and 2nd places in the final into the bargain.

A major problem this year has been the provision of an effective rescue service. The sale of the No. 4 launch and the failing servicability of the No. 1 has meant that some races have been sailed with only the Fisherman 14 in attendance.

Even more of a problem has been the manning of the Rescue Boat - although the Fleets have provided Assistant Coxswains we seem unable to find or organise a group of regular coxswains to assist the club coxswain - our thanks go to him and his helpers for their many hours of service. It may be necessary next year for the fleets themselves to provide the bulk of this effort. Perhaps when we manage to buy that new boat the picture will change - we shall see!

Finally I would like to thank everyone for their support during my term as Sailing Secretary and hope that you will give similar support to my successor.

R.G. Greygoose.

Royal National Life-boat Institution

"Dr. Jones informative letter in the November issue of Navigans may well give the wrong impression. The River Blackwater is covered by the activities of the Maldon Branch of the R.N.L.I. with representation from all of the villages bordering on the river as far down as Bradwell on the South side and Tollesbury on the North side and including villages in the hinterland as far away as Southminster and Purleigh.

OBSERVATIONS

Some may tell us that the defeat of the outgoing committees' proposals on Clubhouse and subscriptions at the recent A.G.M. is a sign of a healthy and active democracy in the Club. On the other hand it may simply have been the effect of active pre-meeting lobbying among an already fairly tightly-knit and highly articulate group of members with a common interest. Certainly there could be no doubt of the strength of the antipathy with which cruiser people viewed the proposal that their Hard Fees should in future be greater than those for dinghy sailors.

One suspects, however, that they may have felt just a little abashed at the ease with which they succeeded in toppling the Establishment, or (choose your own flavour) rejecting the carefully thought-out work of the Committee.

One could have forgiven the committee men up for re-election if they had withdrawn in the face of rejection of their proposals. We are lucky that most did not feel it necessary to do so - had this not been the case we would have been in a constitutional pickle. As it is, with proposals for Clubhouse and means to pay for it defeated at the A.G.M., we have no policy on these matters.

However, nature abhors a vacuum and I do not think it will be long before the new Committee comes back to us with an unaltered Clubhouse proposal and somewhat modified subscription proposals.

It cannot have been a very easy A.G.M. to conduct and no-one will have envied our Commodore his task, particularly as it came at the end of a three year period in office which had thrust upon him peculiarly heavy responsibilities which most of his predecessors had been spared. Eric Payne's nicely turned motion of thanks for Stan's work was well deserved.

This Navigans is the last to be edited by Mary Greygoose. Her editorial wisdom and guidance have been much appreciated and her choice of contributors impeccable - and I shall be very cross with her if she chops this bit.

Observer

Constitution and Rules of the Marconi Sailing Club

1. NAME

The Club shall be called the "MARCONI SAILING CLUB".

2. OBJECTS

The objects of the Club shall be the promotion of Amateur Sailing, the encouragment of social fellowship amongst all those interested in the sea, and the provision of all possible facilities to this end.

3. The Club shall be constituted as the sailing section of the MARCONI ATHLETIC AND SOCIAL CLUB in accordance with Rule 19 of that Club.

4. STATION

The Club shall operate on the River Blackwater from "Stansgate Abbey Farm" or such other premises as circumstances may require.

5. COLOURS

The colours of the Club shall be Royal Blue and White. The Club Burgee shall be White with a White Tern on a Blue Ball. The Commodore's Flag shall be the Club Burgee in rectangular form with swallow tails, the Vice-Commodore's Flag shall be the same with a Blue Ball in the hoist, the Rear Commodore's the same with two Blue Balls in the hoist. The Club Tie shall be dark Blue with a representation of the Club Burgee at intervals over it.

6. MEMBERSHIP

(a) Every candidate for membership must intend to take an active interest in sailing or boating.

(b) There shall be the following forms of Full Membership:-

(i) Ordinary Membership. All Employees over the age of 18 of the Marconi Group of Companies and its Associates shall be eligible for ordinary membership on application to the Honorary Secretary provided that they are members of the M.A.S.C.

(ii) Associate Membership. This shall be open to all other persons over the age of 18 whose application is sponsored by two ordinary members and approved by a simple majority vote of the Committee and Gen ral Committee. Associate Members shall have no voting rights and may hold office in an advisory capacity only.

(c) Honorary Membership. Honorary Members may be elected by a two-thirds majority of the members of the Committee present and voting.

(d) Temporary Membership. Persons deemed suitable by the Committee and visiting Members of other Yacht Clubs recognised by the R.Y.A. may be accepted as Temporary Members for a period fixed at the discretion of the Committee.

- 2 -

(e) Cadet Members. Young persons between the ages of 10 and 18 shall be eligible on the same terms as for those of 6.b.(i) and (ii) except for age, for Cadet Membership, subject to the written consent of parent or guardian, which must be enclosed with membership application.

7. RIGHTS AND DUTIES OF MEMBERS

(a) Members in joining, undertake to be bound by the Constitution and Rules of the Club, which shall be sent to them by the Hon. Secretary on acceptance, and shall acquaint themselves with the Club Bye-Laws.

(b) Full Membership shall be terminated only by resignation, death, expulsion, or under Rule 13(c) regarding the nonpayment of dues.

(c) A member wishing to resign shall give written notice to the Hon. Secretary before 1st February, otherwise he shall be liable to pay the subscription for that financial year.

(d) Suspension. A three-quarter majority of the Committee present and voting may suspend a member from the Club for breaches of the Constitution, Rules or Bye-laws, or unseenly behaviour. The member concerned shall have the right to be present, and to defend himself, at such a Committee Meeting.

A member suspended by the Committee under this Rule may demand an Extraordinary General Meeting under Rule 11 except that the number of signatures required for such a demand shall be only four. Suspension, for the period decided by the Committee, shall nevertheless take effect immediately. The M.A.S.C. General Committee to be informed of action taken.

(e) Expulsion. A member may be expelled by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting at a General Meeting. The M.A.S.C. General Committee to be informed of action taken.

(f) Cadet members must comply with the Rules and the Bye-laws of the Club, together with any special Cadet Section Rules.

8. OFFICERS

The officers of the Club shall be divided into four groups.

(a) The President and an indefinite number of Vice-Presidents shall be elected by ballot at the Annual General Meeting of the Club, and thereafter require re-election every three years.

(b) The Flag Officers shall be the Commodore, Vice Commodore and Rear Commodore.

(c) The Honorary Officers of the Club shall be the Secretary, Treasurer, Sailing Secretary, Social Secretary and Clubhouse Secretary.

(d) Junior Officers of the Club may be appointed by the Committee, e.g. Editor of Navigans and Cadet Section Representative.

(e) The Officers, other than the President and Vice-Presidents, shall retire annually at the Annual General Meeting, but shall be eligible for re-election. Flag Officers shall not serve in the same rank for more than three consecutive years. Members must have served for at least one year on the Committee within three years immediately preceding election to Flag Rank.

- 3 -

9. THE COMMITTEE

(a) The Club in Annual General Meeting shall elect six Ordinary members who, with the Flag and Honorary Officers shall be the Committee. The Permanent Officers may attend Committee Meetings.

(b) The Committee shall include at least one and not more than two Associate Members, who shall serve in an advisory capacity only.

(c) The Committee shall have power to co-opt Junior Officers and may also co-opt an appropriate Member to fill any vacancy which may arise. Co-opted Members shall have full voting powers, except in the case of Associate Members.

(d) At least one Committee Meeting shall be held in each calendar month.

(e) Committee Meetings shall be convened by the Hon. Secretary or Commodore only and shall be notified to Committee Members at least two days in advance.

(f) Seven Committee Members, including at least one Flag Officer shall form a quorum.

(g) Unless otherwise specified herein the Committee shall act by simple majority the Chairman having no vote other than a casting vote. The Senior Flag Officer present shall normally preside.

10. POWERS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee shall be the authorised agents of the Club and in pursuit of the objects of the Club shall have the following powers:-

(a) To make and rescind contracts.

(b) Make and amend Bye-laws which shall govern the conduct of members.

(c) Fix remunerations, if any.

(d) Suspend members as provided in Rule 7 (d).

(e) The Committee shall appoint Sailing Social and House Sub-Committees and such others as it may see fit. The composition of these Sub-Committees shall be as set out in Rule 14, subject to the discretion of the Committee. The main Committee shall give to each Sub-Committee on its appointment, a statement delineating its powers, functions and financial arrangements. The Sailing Sub-Committee shall be regarded as the Club's Racing Committee for the purposes of the R.Y.A. Rules and the only appeal from its decision on racing matters shall be to the R.Y.A.

(f) A resolution passed by the Club in General Meeting to rescind a decision of the Committee shall not take effect retrospectively, except as provided by Rule 7(d) (Suspension).

(g) The Committee, at a meeting held for the purpose, shall if necessary nominate members of the Club (who consent to serve) for election at the Annual General Meeting to all posts falling vacant. These nominations shall be published as required by Rule 11(e).

(h) Subject to the direction of the M.A.S.C. the Committee shall control the financial affairs of the Club except as provided by Rule 13(b) and shall elect a Treasurer whose duties shall be to arrange payments, advise on expenditure, receipt all income, apply Rule 13(b) if necessary and present a Statement of Accounts at the end of each financial year.

- 4 -

(i) The Committee shall appoint Trustees, who consent to serve, for such transactions as require trustees. The Committee shall arrange such insurances or other safeguards as would have been considered necessary had Trustees not been called for.

(j) All written contracts entered into by the Club (except where Trustees are required) shall bear the signature of two of the following: The Flag Officers, Hon. Treasurer, Hon. Secretary, acting on the authority of the Committee.

(k) Contracts entered into by Trustees on behalf of the Club shall bear the signature of those Trustees, acting on the authority of the Committee.

(l) Minutes shall be made of all the proceedings at meetings of the Committee and any Sub-Committees and the attendance recorded.

11. GENERAL MEETINGS

(a) General Meetings shall include Annual and Extraordinary General Meetings. Twenty Ordinary Members shall form a quorum. In the event of failure to obtain a quorum at an A.G.M. the Committee shall remain in office and continue to function until the next General Meeting at which a New Committee shall be elected as laid down in Rule 11(d) and (e).

(b) The Annual General Meeting of the Club shall be held in November of each year.

(c) At the Annual General Meeting the Officers and Committee shall submit for approval reports on the state of the Club, its finances and activities.

(d) At the Annual General Meeting the Officers and Committee shall be elected for the coming year, in accordance with Rule 8 and 9.

(e) Nominations for posts to be filled at the Annual General Meeting shall be sent to the Hon. Secretary not less than 14 days before such Annual General Meeting with the written consent of the nominee and the signatures of two supporting members. All such nominations, together with the list prepared by the Committee under Rule 10(g), shall be circulated to members at least seven days before such Meeting.

Notwithstanding the above, any defeated candidate for office may be nominated orally for another office or the Committee. Oral nominations shall also be accepted if an unopposed nomination is withdrawn.

(f) The agenda for the A.G.M. shall include Any Other Business.

(g) Voting at any General Meeting shall be by show of hands, except for contested elections to office or on request of a majority of members present, when it shall be by secret ballot. The President, failing this the Commodore or Commodore's nominee shall preside and shall have a casting vote only.

(h) An Extraordinary General Meeting shall be called by the Hon. Secretary on request of the Committee or of 12 full members in writing. A two-thirds majority of members present and voting shall be required at an Extraordinary General Meeting for any resolution.

(i) At least 21 clear days notice of any Annual General Meeting or 14 days notice of any Extraordinary General Meeting shall be given to the members by the Hon. Secretary. The notice of the A.G.M. shall include the first sentence of Rule 11(e).

- 5 -

(j) Ordinary members shall be the only persons entitled to vote at General Meetings.

(k) The Agenda of any General Meeting shall be sent to each Member at least seven days before such Meeting, and the business at the Meeting shall be confined to that Agenda.

12. NOTICES

(a) All notices required by the Constitution to be sent to a Member in writing shall be deemed to be correctly served when posted to the Member at his last known address.

(b) The Club News Letter "Navigans" shall inform Members of any notice placed by the Committee on the Club Notice Board, situated in the Clubhouse.

(c) No notice shall be placed on the Club Notice Board without the authority of a main Committee member or Club Officer who shall also sign the document and, at his discretion, submit it to the Editor of "Navigans" for publication.

13. SUBSCRIPTION

(a) The Subscriptions shall be:-

£
Ordinary member including husband or wife and children under 15 yrs. - 3.00
Associate member including husband or wife and children under 15 yrs. - 6.00
Cadet member aged 15-18 yrs. - 0.50
Honorary & Temporary members - gratis
Hard Fee (all boats sailed from the club by members over 18 yrs.) - 8.00

Car Parking for vehicles parked at the club by members - 0.50
JOINING FEES - Adult Ordinary Members - 0.50
Associate Members - 5.00

(b) Subscriptions fall due on 1st January each year (except on joining) see Rule 13(d). If any Member fails to pay his account by the end of February his name shall be brought before the Committee and if he fails to pay his account within 14 days of a final notice, he shall be deemed to have resigned without prejudice to the right of the Club to collect all outstanding dues.

(c) Members accepted after 30th September in any year shall not be required to pay any further subscription until the second January after acceptance.

(d) Every applicant for membership shall remit the amount of an annual subscription with his form of application.

- 6 -

(e) Subscriptions for non-employees to agree with M.A.S.C. policy.

(f) An Associate Cadet who joins the Club before his or her 17th birthday and remains a paid up Cadet will not be required to pay entrance fee on application for Associate Membership.

14. SUB-COMMITTEES

(a) The following Sub-Committees are appointed under Rule 10(e): Sailing, Social and House Committees.

(b) The Flag Officers and Hon. Treasurer shall be ex-officio members of all these Sub-Committees.

(c) The Sailing Sub-Committee shall further include the Hon. Sailing Secretary, Cadet Section Representative, Club Bosun, Rescue Launch Coxswain and Representative of such Classes as may, from time to time, be decided upon by the General Committee. The Class Representatives, who shall be Ordinary Members, shall be elected by the owners of boats of that class at a Fleet Meeting or, in default, be appointed by the Committee.

(d) The Social Sub-Committee shall further include the Hon. Social Secretary and three others appointed by the Committee.

(f) No member (other than the Flag Officers and Hon. Treasurer) shall serve on more than two of these Sub-Committees. All Sub-Committees may co-opt two further members who shall have equal voting rights.

15. LOSSES

The Club cannot be held responsible for any loss or damage sustained by a member or his visitors.

16. SUGGESTIONS

Members wishing to bring suggestions for improvements to the notice of the Committee shall submit them in writing to the Hon. Secretary, who shall acknowledge them. The suggestion, and details of the decisions of the Committee or appropriate Sub-Committee taken at the meeting immediately following the receipt of the suggestions shall then be published in "Navigans".

17. VISITORS

18. FLOODBOARDS

See Bye-laws.

19. CLUBHOUSE

The Club facilities shall be available to Members subject to such limitations as the Committee may impose from time to time.
