20. CLUB PROPERTY

No member shall remove, or borrow for his own use, any item of Club property without the permission of the appropriate official or Committee.

21. OFFICER OF THE DAY

An Officer of the Day shall be appointed on all appropriate occasions, and shall act as the executive officer of the Committee in all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of members and Club premises during his day of Office.

22. INSURANCE

All boats normally sailed from the Club shall be adequately insured against third party risk. The M.A.S.C. will not be liable for any form of claim.

23. BOAT REGISTER

All members shall be required to register with the Club all boats which they sail as members of the Club. The Form of registration shall include a declaration which shall be re-affirmed annually, that the boat complies with Rule 22.

24. ADVERTISING

Members shall not display gross forms of advertising at the Club or on or about boats registered with the Club.

25. BUOYANCY

(a) All dinghies normally sailed from the Club shall be fitted with buoyancy to class rules or as the Committee may reasonably require.

(b) Members sailing from the Club should wear personal buoyancy at all times when the red flag is flying, and at all other times personal buoyancy should be carried aboard the boat.

(c) Cadet Members shall at all times when sailing from the Club wear personal buoyancy.

26. RACING

All Races sponsored by the Club shall be sailed in accordance with the I.Y.R.U. and R.Y.A. Rules.

27. Any matter arising out of the Club Constitution, Rules or Bye-Laws or lack thereof shall be referred to the Committee.

28. AMENDMENTS

Amendments and additions to the Constitution and Rules set out above shall be made only by the Club in General Meeting, and shall require a two-thirds majority of full members present and voting. Such proposed amendments shall be sent to the Hon. Secretary in writing at least 14 days before a General Meeting. The Hon. Secretary shall give the members at least seven days notice of any such proposal. The General Committee must approve amendments to Rules.

- 8 -

29. LICENCED BAR

(a) Bar Sub-Committee

Not less than five members of the Committee shall be elected to the Bar Sub-Committee, and shall be responsible for the orderly conduct of the Club and Bar, to the General Club Secretary of the M.A.S.C. in accordance with the current licencing laws, including the purchase for the club and the supply by the club of intoxicating liquor.

(b) Hours of Opening and Closing

The Club Bar shall be open as directed by the Committee within the permitted hours in accordance with current licencing laws.

The committee have the power to alter the times of opening and closing of the Club Bar on special occasions within current licencing laws, by resolution at a prior Committee meeting, such resolution to be posted on the Club Notice Board, and the General Club Secretary of the M.A.S.C. so informed.

Excisable liquors shall be supplied to members except those under 18 years of age.

The sale of intoxicants shall only be in the permitted hours in accordance with the current licencing laws.

(c) Introduction of Guests

Only members as defined in Rule 6(b), (c) and (d) shall be permitted to introduce two persons to the Clubhouse (this shall be varied at the direction of the Committee who must give at least seven days notice on the Club Notice Board of their intention to do so).

The name of the visitor who shall not be an employee under the Marconi Group of Companies and its Associates in the Chelmsford Area, unless a member of the M.A.S.C. and that of the member by whom he is introduced, shall be written in the Visitor's Book kept for that purpose, by the member introducing the guest.

Members must accompany guests, introduced during their stay in the Club. No visitor shall purchase excisable liquors provided on Club premises. Should he do so, then he shall be required to leave immediately and the member concerned shall be expelled on the fact being duly proved. It will be the duty of any officer or member of the Club to report such breach of the rules at once to the Secretary or the Committee.

(d) Misconduct

No unauthorised gambling, bad language or other misconduct shall be permitted on the Club premises or on organised visits to other premises and the elected officers of the Club have the power to suspend any member guilty of same until the next Committee Meeting.

Any member charged with misconduct shall be given notice before the Committee.

The Sailing Club Social Programme is hotting up for the new season, the Fitting Out Dance should be good but I wonder how many people will actually have their boats ready by then. I know one person who wont.

Still there is loads of encouragement, especially after those superb films of Jonelles trip to the Mediterranean, shown at the last Winter Social Evening, lets hope for weather like that this Summer, and get down to painting and varnishing in anticipation.

COMMODORES NOTES.

Since my last note, the clubhouse planning sub-committee have had another meeting to issue the plans for more exact estimates of both a prefabricated (but permanent) building and a traditional brick building. We should get these costs later this month, and then be in a position to consider submitting more deatiled plans to the M.A.S.C., and then to the planning authorities.

Roger Towell, as you may know acted as Cadet Skipper last year, but regrets he is unable to continue this year as he has work commitments likely to take him abroad for longish periods.

We would be pleased to hear from anyone who would like to take on this important task. It is not particularly demanding, many cadets are well organised in crewing for parents or friends, but some of the younger, or new members can be encouraged to join in functions, to help on various occasions, or have some sailing arranged for them. It is obviously usefull if there is someone who can act as a focus for these activities. Any volunteers please.

Incidentally, Roger is without a boat this year, and although he hopes to get another cruiser in the future he has given up his mooring.

It has been suggested that as there is now quite a demand for moorings, people who have had moorings but are without a cruiser for a year or two should be encouraged to relinquish their mooring, and go on a priority waiting list. At present, there is a possibility that some members might be tempted to hang on to their moorings as an isurance, and in the ridiculous limit, we could have a mooring area with no boats in it.

SOCIAL SCREED.

This is not a cruiser only night but planned to interest dinghy wanderers as well.

Due to a date mix up the March meeting has had to be moved to Wednesday 28th. March.

Mr. Reader of the St. Johns Ambulance Brigade will repeat his popular talk on - Resuscitation and the Treatment of Exposure -. The evening will include the showing of the film - The Pulse of Life - and a chance to practice the theory on - Resusci Annie -.

SAILING PROGRAMME 1973.

Sun 1st April - a.m. Preparations. 14.30 Practice race.

Sun 15th April - First two Spring points races. (all fleets)

It was decided in committee that there should be more regular dinghy racing at the club. To that end all fleets are scheduled to race even when they have to supply the race officer etc., also the Helmsman of the Year qualifying races are to be combined with six specified points races.

All this will give about a dozen Spring points and twice that number of Summer points races. In fact there is dinghy racing scheduled for everyone on every Sunday during the season, so come along and support it - the weather may be good this year.

- 4 -

HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR 1973.

There are once again 6 qualifying races, each helms best 4 results calculated on handicap will count. Then the first and second from each fleet will qualify for the final, which is again to be in one class of dinghy. However if any fleet averages more than 10 entries in any 4 qualifying races, the third helm can compete in the final. More than 15 allows a fourth and so on. One essential change from 1972 is the qualifying races will be sailed in conjunction with afternoon points, one per month between April and September, with the final in October.

The Helmsman of the Year (Costain Cup) should be about the most coveted award in the Club and as there are plenty of helmsmen at Stansgate, let friendly battle commence.

John A. Weedon.

To Cruiser Social Secretary.

Your tilt at Observer in January Navigans was somewhat unwarranted. Why you should have felt it necessary to sideswipe his anonymity and exhibit hurt pride at his suggestion of pre-meeting lobbying at the same time, only you will know. Regarding the latter there is more than one of us who at least hold partially to that theory.

What Observer could have said, in addition to what he did say, was that to a pottering dinghy sailor such as myself, you have played a not inconsiderable part in getting subscriptions (for dinghies) raised by some 55 percent- and this is a large raise even by present day-standards.

It is somewhat unfortunate for those of us who logically consider the above mentioned raise, that the last two years of <squeeze and freeze> appear to have left you and those who voted with you, financially unscathed. The one fact you have not grasped is that the ordinary people of this country now tend to value their meagre possessions a good deal more than before this era. In other words they now try and make the work of one penny do the work of two. And, in this case, what has been done is to successfully equate a 10 foot dinghy with a 25 foot cruiser. You and yours are indeed behind the times.

I cannot say that I am sorry for not being included in your band of <fair minded dinghy owners> and I sincerely hope that the issue (not necessarily divisive) will be raised again. No doubt subscriptions will continue to rise (what had you in mind for next A.G.M.) but may I add a plea for such fair proposals broadly along the lines of those originally mooted but thrown out at the last A.G.M.

Meanwhile, our new Club House - which we all want- may it successfully go ahead. And many pairs of hands will be needed to dig the footings.

Ron. Doubleday.

At the last meeting (17th Jan.) , during discussion on the coming seasons race programme,race officers and Mirror dinghies in general , it admitted by several members (myself included), that we new very little about the racing rules. You will not be alone as Roger Mance, Julian , Mike Taylor , Arthur Hodges , Ron Greygoose , Dennis Boswell, Norman Richards and Jeff Soseg will all be there , to name but eight boats, nine including my own.

If you would like more details give me a ring on Chelmsford [redacted].

If you feel a little more ambitious there is always the World Championships in Vancouver 1 - 24 August. There are possibly three Marconi crews going - Mike Taylor, Roger Mance, and Julian.

Spectators are very welcome in fact the Vancouver Y.C. may be arranging cheap accommodation for spectators.What is more the return air fare may be as little as £100? . Sounds an excellent way to go abroad for a holiday.

Don't forget to look in - Dates for your Diary - FOR SOME INTERESTING ENTERPRISE DATES.

Jim Bigden.
Fleet Captain.

CRUISER SECTION NEWS.

Thanks are due to John Dodds for his shots of Jamaica and the lesser Antilles . I think I would rather get stuck on a sandbank once or twice than drown in a mile of water only 1/2 mile offshore.

I shall be sending off the order for antifouling within a few days so anybody else interested should contact me immediately.

At the next meeting we ought to plan a few cruises and races. Also I should like to put up some ideas for using moorings which people do not require for a year or two, guaranteed to produce a lively discussion.

LETTER TO THE EDITOR

Can we drop the gimmick of very personal "open letters", and revert to the accepted form of 'Letters to the Editor'? There is really no such thing as a public, private letter!

Peter Foreman, in correcting a rather oblique paragraph in the December "Observations", may have taken deeper umbrage than was justifiable; but he did keep his facts accurate. I am sorry that Ron Doubleday (February) was much less careful. May I have space to untwist some of his more perverse statements?

The increased fees, he surely knows, are required to finance the new club-house, which he says "we all want". We mostly do; but it was evident at the AGM that many members had grave doubts whether, also, we could afford it in this year of financial squeeze. He appears to be phasing those doubts after "seeing the bill", but fails to remember that it was Mr.Foreman and the cruising members who started the discussion on this point; although members with most types of boat joined in. Our choice is not a simple one: the deadline on our planning-permission is already extended, and if we can build now it will probably be cheaper than in, say, 1975. On the other hand, finding the money is certainly not painless and the estimates already allow for some do-it-yourself economies.

Can anyone really believe that Mr.Foreman and those who voted with him are "financially unscathed"? Their increase of dues is the same as Mr.Doubleday's, and their income is just as frozen. Does he infer that their pockets are as good as bottomless? He must be joking!

In keeping the Hard Fee the same for all classes of boat, what is being done is to equate the value of the service provided by the Club to a 25 ft. cruiser and a 10 ft. dinghy. The Club has, in fact, regarded this as fair justice ever since its foundation: if we were to change dues as a percentage of a member's total sailing budget (if that were possible), the top rate would be paid by the keen dinghy-racing man who travels to open meetings. It's not on - thank goodness.

In 1962, as Commodore, I worked very hard to get the Stansgate site because it was the finest dinghy site on the Blackwater. Many of the cruiser owners, then based at Heybridge Basin, were none too happy about the site for themselves, because of its exposure. I hope doubters will satisfy themselves on this point round the bar (half-a-pint of ale is quite cost-effective in cooling an argument) rather than in General Meeting. The Club was founded to help keep sailing within the means of Marconi employees, whatever type of craft they favoured.

Arthur Adam.

ROYAL YACHTING ASSOCIATION A.G.M.

The annual general meeting of the R.Y.A. was held at The Caxton Hall, London, on March 14th, when there was an exceptionally good attendance, partly due to the fact that the meeting started at 4 p.m. instead of at 2.30 p.m. as previously but largely perhaps, because of the controversial nature of the proposals on the agenda and because the meeting was well publicised beforehand.

The R.Y.A. is greatly in need of funds and a firm of management consultants had been requested to examine the whole structure and suggest ways of improvement. A member asked whether this report could be published but this was refused on the grounds that it was too voluminous and too difficult to summarise anyway.

The main proposal was that all members of clubs who were not themselves members of the R.Y.A. should subscribe 30p. per annum and that this should be added to the fees which clubs already pay and which are based on the club's membership. While it was agreed that all keen sailors, specially the racing enthusiasts, and those who go to foreign parts and visit other clubs, should be members but the family man who potters and undertakes perhaps one major cruise during his summer holiday and social members without boats, feel that with the increased subscriptions they already have to pay to belong to their clubs this should be a sufficient contribution. The difficulties of administration and the additional burden on our heavily-worked treasurers, should this proposal be adopted, were stressed.

Consequently this proposal was overwhelmingly rejected, some clubs even threatening to relinquish affiliation should it be passed, and the matter was referred back to the committee for further consideration. An alternative suggestion was that the present clubs' affiliation fee should be reduced by 50p for each member who himself became a R.Y.A. member but this was also rejected.

A further suggestion that all club fees should be doubled was received with derision.

For the new committee, our votes were cast in favour of Charlie Stock of B.S.C. and Sammy Sampson of the W.M.Y.C. who were the only candidates known to us, but neither was elected.

A considerable income was admittedly derived from sponsors and although no names were mentioned, most members were well aware of their sources.

Public relations were criticised and it was thought that the work of the R.Y.A. was not appreciated and that clubs should be informed at their A.G.Ms and in their bulletins of what is being done. The members then adjourned for cocktails.

Eric Payne.
R.Y.A. Liaison Officer.

A boat which acknowledges breaking a racing rule shall get clear of other boats and then make 2 complete turns (both in the same direction) while on the same leg of the course. EDITORIAL

This is the time of year for social functions, the Fitting Out Dance seemed to go very well; I hear the Disco Party was quite a success, and before we know it Regatta Weekend will be upon us again.

Can anyone help John Witter find a home for his mini-meter?

I'd like to draw the Cadets' attention to the article Jimmy James has written and to wish him the best of luck as our new Cadet Skipper, I hope lots of us will be able to help him with the loan of boats, as I'm sure there are many boatless keen cadets!

Are you wondering, like me, what has happened to those astute observations that favoured these pages last year? They could always be relied upon to promote 'lively' conversation amongst the members, and I for one would welcome them back.

Dot Renshaw

COMMODORE'S NOTES

You will, I'm sure, be pleased to hear that we now have a Cadet Skipper. In spite of his many commitments, Mr.N.J.James (Jimmy) has offered to arrange some activities and help cadets to become involved in club affairs - so come on cadets - contact Jimmy!

The long and involved negotiations and planning for the new clubhouse are nearing an end, and we hope to complete the remaining details and submit our plans in the next few weeks. As I previously indicated, no plan will meet with 100% approval in such a large club as ours, but believe me there are few aspects that have not been gone into in fine detail, bearing in mind all the constraints. We still have the final hurdles of planning consent and financial sanctions, so keep your fingers crossed as any further delays could jeopardise the project through rising costs.

Thanks are due to those of you who came to the last two working parties, ably organised by John Witter. The bridges have now been concreted and the site cleared up - so please help us keep the club as neat and tidy as we can.

Finally, I would like to appeal for volunteers to help with the Regatta, and the preparations. The main working party will be on Wednesday May 23rd at 6.30 p.m. Help would also be welcome on Friday evening, the 25th.

There is also a need for assistance during the Regatta in the Bar, with the organisation of Entries and Racing, Car Parking arrangements and Beach Marshalling. As usual, many hands make light work, so if you're not taking part in events and would like to be "involved" contact myself, or any committee member. Ladies, of course, especially welcome.

Lets keep this, our major event of the year, its usual success.

Dennis Byatt

DINGHY EXHIBITION 1973

Once again, the winter is seen to end and dedicated class sailors gather to discuss, inspect, spy and deride all other classes but their own. Pictures, pamphlets, and every manner of exhibits are studied to compare with the individual's own boat and problems. Hornets have a new, very much enlarged spinnaker and it is rumoured certain horneteers were seen near the 505 Fireball display, studying their spinnaker arrangements, but this fact cannot be substantiated.

The day culminated for many of the Hornet fleet present, viewing a film on the Australian 18 footers, of particular interest now Alf Reynolds 18 footer is sailing with its four hornet crew. The film was very moving (did someone whisper frightening?) as the huge sail area engulfed the screen. As the hornet 140 sq.ft. spinnakers begin to arrive, one wonders if these awesome feelings will be repeated in the first blow of the new season. Burnham cruisers look out!

To the Editor of Navigans.

CLUBHOUSE AT STANSGATE

Although the new drawings of the proposed clubhouse at Stansgate are not yet available it is understood that the arrangement is to be approximately as shown in the sketch plan.

All the interest and activities of the club take place on the hard, at the opening in the sea wall, the starting line, the boat park and the cruiser moorings, which, with the present layout, can only be seen, if at all, obliquely from the north windows of the lounge. We therefore think that the building should be the other way round with the lounge overlooking the hard, with windows facing north, south and east instead of north, south and west, as at present proposed. If anybody asks why it is important that the activities mentioned above should be clearly visible from the lounge, the answer is that this is what the Sailing club is all about.

Several reasons have been given why the lounge at the western end is preferable.

1. Wet sailors will use the lounge as a passage to the changing rooms this seems unlikely as it would mean going up and down steps. If it does happen, and cannot be prevented by a notice, it would not be difficult to put a small piece of fencing, for example, to make this route from the hard to the changing rooms less attractive.

2. The view westwards towards and beyond Osea is very attractive.

Certainly the Club is extremely fortunate to have such a good outlook. It is more fortunate to have another attractive view eastwards towards Bradwell. We believe that the interest in Club activities, all to be seen towards the east, far outweighs any preference there may be for the Osea view.

continued...

- 7 -

3. The lounge must be at the western end to allow room for possible future enlargement.

The eastern aspect could be kept by moving the clubhouse far enough westwards to leave room for extension towards the east.

4. It's too far for wet sailors to walk to the changing rooms.

As the proposed entrance is in the middle of one of the longer sides, turning the clubhouse about, as we suggest, would not make any difference to the distance to be walked to any part of the clubhouse. Moving the clubhouse westwards as suggested in the comment on 3 above, could increase the distance from the hard by ten or fifteen paces.

For the reasons set out above, it would be a bad mistake, and an avoidable one, to build the clubhouse with the lounge to the west.

We therefore most earnestly plead that, before it is too late, every member, and particularly those who have been most closely concerned, should pause, try to clear their minds of details, and ask themselves whether they really want a clubhouse turned away from club activities. If they come to believe, as we do, that this could be a bad mistake, and would spoil the Sailing Club atmosphere, we hope that they will let some committee member know without delay.

Alan Batchelor
Jack Pletts
Geoff Wardell

P.S. The above letter was prepared and submitted in good time for the April Navigans, and I was very surprised when I got my copy to find that it had not been included.

However the Commodore's notes did refer to the occasional reports from the Planning Committee to members over the last two years. Unfortunately it seems to me that these reports have not had the effect of bringing home to members that the proposal is for a clubhouse turned away from club activities, which I regard as extremely controversial.

I hope that the above letter and this postscript will make members aware of what it is proposed that they shall get for their money, and that if it is not what they want, they will let the Committee know clearly and without delay.

J.W.Pletts.
3.5.73.

BURNHAM EASTER EGG

Wet suits were well and truly aired this weekend as over 30 Hornets from all over the country travelled to Burnham for the Burnham Easter Egg Open Meeting. New boats were modified involuntarily, old boats hit form, prominent horneteers celebrated too enthusiastically, tempers were lost, but all enjoyed the meeting with the new spinnakers performance a major topic of conversation.

On Friday's race, Reg Evans from Clacton and the Barnes brothers from Stone, came 1st and 2nd bringing success to our part of the country. Bruce Long was 5th. On Saturday the wind was very flukey and turned the fleet back to front several times, ending in a win for Stuart Korth from Medway and R.Hampson (newly Marconi) came 2nd. Bruce was 4th.

On Sunday the weather was ghastly, with the wind gusting force 8, but even if we could see the weather for the rest of the day, and knew before getting out of bed, that sailing would be cancelled, we would have gone just to collect our chocolate Easter Eggs, left magically in the boats in the dinghy park.

So with no racing on Sunday, all hinged on Monday. The start was very confused and due to this problem, several boats were coming back to the starting line when the final gun was heard. Malcolm Goodwin, last years World Champion won this race and went on to be first overall. Reg Evans was 2nd and Stuart Korth 3rd in the final positioning, and all received most attractive traditional glass-wear for their prizes.
continued...

- 8 -

Marconi was well represented by three boats, Simon Darney and Bob Fisher having opted out of a twosome for a slightly sturdier Soling. Bruce Long with Biggles did very well by coming 6th overall, while Geoff White and Garry Constable, John Tillotson and Mike Turner seemed pleased with their boats potential performances, and look forward to the coming year.
Annette Horne.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

What a difference the sun makes! The weather was really kind to us for this year's Regatta - some change from last year. Everyone really enjoyed themselves - and said so! Both the Saturday Pennant Race, and the Class Races had record entries - the final count was 199 boats.

The Club looked magnificent - a credit to Claude and all those who helped to prepare for the Regatta. These events really do take a lot of effort to organise on both the racing and social side, and our thanks are due to all those who worked so hard to make the weekend such a success.

As the publication of this Navigans falls during the 'Open Day' weekend, we must wait and see how we fare then.

We have an interesting new event on Saturday, 23rd June, when some colleagues from the Avionics Company at Rochester are coming to Stansgate for a Handicap Challenge Race, and an informal Social get-together. I hear that some of their cruisers are hoping to sail round from the Medway for the weekend as well.

VISITORS TO STANSGATE

Every year, particularly in the fine weather, we get a fairly substantial number of uninvited visitors. We ask Harry Holt to "man-the-gate" occasionally, and members are asked to bear this check with fortitude, and remember that as many as twenty car loads of casual visitors have been turned back on one day.

It would be of considerable help if members ensured that they either came with, or were at the club to greet, their own guests. It is in fact a club rule that members are allowed up to two guests each, but they are responsible for them.

Please refrain from making casual invitations to "look us up at Stansgate sometime" as there have been instances of genuinely interested Marconi visitors being upset at being turned away - and we need all the new members we can get!

Dennis Byatt.

R E S C U E !

Easter Monday saw our new Rescue Launch make its first live rescue. Roger Laver and Chris Kingsley, manning our launch, brought the helmsman and crew ashore from a capsised Hornet (not one of ours) when it became obvious that they were not going to right their boat. Pat Black and Tony Cockrell were then put aboard the drift dinghy and with the aid of the launch first removed an anchor from the masthead before sailing the boat back to the hard.

The following letter was received a few days later.

22, [redacted],
Hornchurch, Essex.

25-4-73.

Dear Sir,

I am writing to thank your club for doing such a grand job last Easter Monday in rescuing myself and my crew from my Hornet No.629 after we had capsized in front of your club.

I am a member of Stone Sailing Club and was out for a mid-day cruise. After we had capsized two of your members manned your rescue boat in order to come to our aid. After rescuing us they then returned, righted my boat and sailed her into your clubhouse from where I later towed her back to Stone.

I would also like to thank the various members of your club who leant us clothing, gave us brandy and hot coffee, and drove us back to Stone.

I hope the relationship between our two clubs is furthered in the future and that we may give the same help to your boats should they require it. Without your help I'm not sure how the episode would have ended.

Thanking you again most sincerely.

Yours gratefully,

(signed) Paul Derrick.

MARCONI SPRING BANK HOLIDAY REGATTA

The Spring Bank Holiday Marconi Regatta was one of the most successful yet with a record turnout of over 200 boats. Many of them having travelled many miles to attend the event.

Sailing commenced on Saturday afternoon with two practice races, one for handicaps under 100 and one for those above. The under 100s was won by Julian Bigden in Midwich Cuckoo, an Enterprise of the Marconi Sailing Club. The over 100s was won by R.Partridge, sailing Ivers Bird, a Mirror Dinghy of I.P.C. Yacht Club. The day was brought to a very successful conclusion with a Disco party held in a Marquee erected especially for the occasion.

On Sunday the class racing started in earnest, with Enterprises mustering 41 boats, Mirror 11's 28, Fireball and GP 14's both with 25 boats, Hornets 24, Finns 12, Handicap 13, Kestrel 7, Solo 6, and Flying Dutchmen and 420 with 5 each.

Throughout the weekend the weather did not let the sailors (or sunbathers) down once, added to that there was a fairly stiff breeze on all three days.

LETTER TO THE EDITOR

I was pleased to read a letter concerning the lay out of the new Club House.

I suggest that the presence of the ditch parallel with the sea wall should not inhibit us from choosing a square building or even constructing the building with its long axis at right angles to the sea wall.

I suggest we sailing members wish to be able to sit in the lounge and look up and down the river as well as across the river (that is, West, East and North). Only to a lesser extent do we want to observe the car and dinghy parks to the South. Excellent vision over the sea wall all round could ensue if the bar and galley were in an island site in the lounge (like all the best modern kitchens!).

I further suggest that such an arrangement, especially if there were bridges to the sea wall and hard, would appeal to non-sailing members too.

The site to the west of the entrance to the hard (as indicated by four pegs) is too close to the entrance to the hard and should be half-way between the eastern boundary of our sailing site and the entrance to the hard and its approach road.

We must get the siting and basic shape of our building right from the beginning and make sure it is capable of being expanded in future. In these inflatory days we must not be afraid of borrowing money on a gilt edge investment.

Yours sincerely,
(signed) Dr.R.T.Jones.
6, [redacted], Basildon, Essex.

CADET NEWS

Response to the request for loan of boats and sailing help for Cadets has been most encouraging. A Heron, several Mirrors, Enterprises and GP14s complete with crews have been offered for the Cadet Races. There have been requests for Cadets to crew in other races and also to sail in cruisers.

Any of our hundred or more Cadets who would like to take advantage of these offers please let me know of their sailing preference. I will then be able to put them in touch with boat owners so that suitable dates and times and if necessary, transport arrangements can be made. Later on a list of helpers and boats will be put on the Club notice board.

The last two Cadet Races were not started because of lack of entries, disappointing for the one or two who were keen to sail. A minimum of three boats are required for a race, with the help of our other members and the warmer weather, a good entry should be possible.

Children under ten may helm if accompanied by an experienced crew, although they would not qualify for major awards. There is no age limit for crews in those races.

Some Cadets may not wish to sail just yet, there are a number of ways in which they can take part in Club activities. One of these is assisting the Race Officer, helping to start and finish races, hoisting and lowering flags, watching out for capsizes and anyone in trouble and several other interesting things.

I am hoping to arrange a special Cadet Day which will include a "rescue trip" in the new launch.

Telephone in the evenings please.

[redacted] or see Mrs.James or myself at Stansgate.

Jinny James
Cadet Skipper.

MIRROR NEWS

I think everyone will agree, it was the best weekends sailing we have had this season.

It was good to see so many of our own club Mirrors sailings at the Regatta, and also plenty of competition from other clubs.

I think the keenest one was the lad who arrived on the hard with his Mirror at 8 o'clock on Saturday morning and asked, "When does the racing start?" He had sailed his boat down from Harlow S.C. starting out at 6 a.m.

A word of thanks to all the Mirror ladies who so ably carried out the various tasks allotted to them - thereby allowing the menfolk to brave the hazards of the Blackwater - Thank you ladies.

The three Marconi Mirrors that went to the open meetings at King George S.C. on 19 & 20th May enjoyed some keen racing with about 40 boats competing. The wind varied quite a lot in strength and direction, but it made a change not to have the tide to contend with.

The only capsize of the meeting was very neatly performed by - yours truly - with the boat still tied to the pontoon. Don't ask me how I managed it. I'm still trying to figure it out myself.

- 8 -

We are now well into the sailing season and there are still a lot of Mirrors in the fleet that haven't been out yet this season. I know the weather hasn't been very kind to dinghy sailors - but the water is getting warmer. So let's see more Mirrors out on the water for the remainder of the season.

Stan Oaker.
Mirror Fleet Captain.

EDITORIAL

Due to the fact that 'Navigans' is a little late this time, I can tell you that the weather blessed the Barbecue yet again, all the tickets were sold and it was a great success.

The surprise innovation of the fireworks was great. The midnight swim was almost crowded - a pity the Commodore could run faster than Vic Tate and Stan Campbell!

Open Day seems a long while ago now but I'd like to welcome the new members who joined us then, those of you without boats remember you can put your name on the board in the club house if you'd like to crew for someone else.

Please note next month's issue will be late as well, because I'm off to Penzance for the Enterprise Nationals!

Dot Renshaw.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

In spite of the fact that we did not hold our Open Day when originally planned, it was certainly most successful in terms of enjoyment, weather and new Marconi members.

We changed the date to avoid clashing with the M.A.S.C. Barbecue, and then discovered we'd clash with the Essex Show, and several away meetings. I must admit I was apprehensive half way through the afternoon when Geof Farnie told me he'd only had one application, but thereafter business was much more brisk, and we were delighted to end up with at least twelve new members.

Many thanks to all our helpers, sailors and organisers. The sailing demonstrations were well received, and the boat trips exceedingly popular.

Incidentally, Jack Bigden's appeal over the P.A. for new members was heard by the crew of a passing cruiser, who came ashore and asked for an application form! For the benefit of our Associate Members, the main idea of the Open Day

- 2 -

is to "show off" the club to Marconi people, in order to attract more ordinary members. This, incidentally may also allow us to take more associates, whilst still maintaining our membership ratios.

The detailed plans for the clubhouse have now been completed, and submitted to four builders for quotations and to various authorities. There are likely to be some modifications regarding siting, but at present these don't seem serious. By far the most important consideration is the cost and we won't know this for a week or two yet.

The weather has been most kind to us this year, and this has been reflected in the sailing activity. In particular, the cruiser fleet has been much more active. The 1st Barnacle points had a record entry of seven boats, and the cruise to Brightlingsea (dare I say Pin Mill?) was a great success.

Dennis Byatt.
Commodore.

SOCIAL SCREED

The KENNY BALL BARBECUE was a great event and all those who assisted Robbie are to be congratulated, let's hope for similar weather and success at our own Barbecue.

Open Day was also very enjoyable and I should like to thank all those who helped in any way to make the day go so well. I heard the story of one person taken for a dinghy ride who said there was nothing to this so the helmsman, with the help of some force 5 gusts gave him a good tousing with which the recipient was delighted. We got 12 more members with a few more promises so it was all worth it.

Peter Foreman, Soc.Sec.
Section 12, E.E.V.Co. Ext.333.
or [redacted] [redacted].

OPEN DAY

The "Boat Trip" side of Open Day was well supported both by boat owners and visitors. About 5 dinghies, 7 cruisers and the new Rescue Boat took over 50 adults and over 40 children out for a sail or motor. Other members lent lifejackets and as a result of all these efforts several families have now become sailing club members. The visitors were very appreciative of the kindness of club members in taking them out for what for many of them was their first trip in a smallish boat.

Eleanor Witter.

THIS AND THAT!

The warm sunny weather has encouraged many more swimmers this year, especially as the Blackwater really does seem much cleaner now. The children, especially, have enjoyed themselves. However, please note that the tide rip can be very strong past the hard, and when dinghies are coming in it can be hazardous, especially when races are finishing. We recommend that at busy times, swimming is safer from the shore east of the hard.

Incidentally, the average speed of cars down our road seems to be increasing. Not only is this dangerous, but it tends to break up the road, which we have to help maintain, either by volunteer labour or cash. Please keep your speed down to 15 mph!

Again on motoring, many cars do not display their car park stickers. This makes security checks difficult. We're sure most people have them so please make sure you display them.

We have now brought the club rule book up to date. Initial copies (stencilled at present) may be obtained from Geof Farnie in the next few weeks. Final printings will be done next year.

Dot.

- 3 -

'THE WATCHING EYES'

Having read the views of various members I am beginning to wonder at the deep concern expressed as to what they will see from the new club house.

What is it that is so interesting that goes on on the hard? Surely people come down for fresh air and sailing. If the weather is find they should be out there and if bad, there will be no one to watch. There is of course the dinghy park, but can that compare with the magnificent natural sweep of water up river? With the club house set at the slight angle it has been given the ladies will still be able to see some of the racing if there is a cool wind blowing.

Is it not time someone started to think of the more practical details such as who is going to wash up all the extra tea-cups and beer mugs that will have to be catered for? I am sure my wife will be delighted to have decent facilities at last but already she finds it as much as she can cope with and what was a pleasant little change is becoming too much. I feel sure that the bar workers are beginning to find the same problem. With a lot of members finding it too much trouble to return their empty cups or mugs, let alone help to wash them up, isn't it time a little thought was given to these problems instead of where will the eyes watch from. I too pay my full subscription and am prepared to do my bit, but it seems too many are taking the work of a few for granted.

A last word, the anonymous writer may mean well but I wish he (she) would stop it. After enjoying the quiet beauty of Stansgate for 30 years it only needs an anonymous watcher to turn it into something like a concentration camp.

Hoping this helps to clear the eyes.

Yours sincerely,

(signed) Alfred Cottam.

OBSERVATIONS

Several notable changes are to be seen in the dinghy fleets this year. P.Black has returned home to GP.14 after his brief sally into the Hornet fleet. Frank Savill is now sporting a Y.W.Solo, and Arthur Hodges a Laser, another single-hander.

I observe that there are several erstwhile regular racing competitors who now spend most of their sailing time in their two-man dingies sailing single handed, usually very competently. I suspect that these folk just could not face the trauma of seeking out and training a new crew now that the faithfully family crew is no longer available. Could not some formula be devised to allow such helmsmen to compete single handed in closed club races, perhaps in the Handicap class" Don't ask me what Handicap number should apply for example to a single handed GP.14 - we have experts on that sort of thing, don't we?

SURFACING
BY THE GRIBBLE

This could be a vintage year for cruising; before the end of June there were two Marconi entries in the Calais visitors' book. The winds have been reasonably kind and my only complaint has been sea-fog, which is less frequent in the later months, anyway.

Reminders for anyone going foreign for the first time:-

Carry - a Red Ensign,
a "Q" flag
and a small "courtesy" ensign of any country you expect to visit (generally stocked by yacht chandlers in the usual ports of departure).

Hoist - a radar reflector; experiment beforehand to find out how to rig it without chafe - it's disconcerting if the thing saws through its own halyard just when you hear a hovercraft approaching.

Customs - foreign - may or may not be strict about clearance. Home ones definitely are.

Compass - check it as well as you can, as by steering visual courses known from a chart, and comparing with the compass reading obtained by a crewman; do this whenever you can, on different courses.

Write - it up for us afterwards - you could win the MAMGU Trophy.

A groundmanship

"Well, I didn't expect to see you stuck on Thirslet Spit! And you were putting on antifouling last week, surely?"

"Dammit, man, I'm checking my compass for heeling error."

THORPE BAY TWO PINT POT

With the weather getting more and more gorgeous, (wind and sun) sailors and sailing widows alike, looked forward to this weekend's Hornet (and Finn) open meeting at Thorpe Bay Yacht Club. On Saturday a force 4 wind gusting 5 prevailed for those sailing, with temperatures in the 70's for those left behind. Although I'm told it was too cold for a bikini in the committee boat, those involved in the organisation proved themselves very efficient, and, with their olympic courses, ran an excellent meeting. The first race began at 11.15 a.m., rather difficult for those with long distances to travel, but none the less there were 36 entries. The result was a first for Malcolm Goodwin in Revolution, second was a local boat, the dread of the result sheet writers, Doremi Fasol Latido, and third was Mike Smoothie Holmes in Yabatoo. In the afternoon's race the leaders results were much the same. Malcolm Goodwin again first, Boremi Fasol Latido second, but with Jeff Furlong in Sea Boots third. Bruce and Biggles would have done even better if some of Bruce's patent inventions hadn't started shedding themselves.

On Sunday there was a more variable force 2-5 on occasions and not so much sun. The water seemed even more polluted and revolting and the Cat Cracker of the Shell oil refinery made an unusual background for the courses. In the morning's race, Revolution did not have such a good start and was well down on the first lap, with Bruce leading a lot of the way. However, he fought back to win, with Yabatoo second. Then the afternoons results? Surprise, surprise Revolution was first, and local Yabatoo second.

- 5 -

The final results were Malcolm Goodwin and Julian Lord in Revolution first, Yabatoo second, Doremi Fasol Latido third, Sea Boots fourth, and Father William with Bruce Long and Biggles fifth. The two other Marconi boats of John and Mike in Easy Rider and Ray and Tony in Lazy Jack came well up. Easy Rider came 10th overall with one 6th and some unmentionables, Lazy Jack 12th with a best of 8th.

During the prize giving, as well as the main trophy of the 2 Pint Pot, a two pint potty was presented. In addition two free pints of beer were presented to each of the 8 pairs of prize collectors and as the bar was closed at the time, they were the most envied prizes ever. It is expected that next year's competition will be even fiercer.

Annette Horne.

CRUISER TENDERS

Would cruiser owners please 'park' their dinghies on the West side of the hard entrance (i.e. where we hope the new club house will appear) for the last week in July and first week in August, so that Claude can cut the grass.

Thereafter, it would be safer to keep all tenders on the East side of the hard (dinghy park) as we hope the bulldozers will be starting the foundations of the new club house then.

EDITORIAL

Well this is my last issue of Navigans. I seem to have been editing it for such a short time, and now I hand over to Brenda Tate, best of luck Brenda and I hope you enjoy the job, I certainly have, especially once I sorted out those printing problems!

I have a new job in Paris so it would be rather difficult to carry on from there - thank you everyone who helped, by sending me all the 'insides', the new address is on the top for future copy.

I look forward to seeing you all in the new clubhouse at some future date.

Dot Renshaw.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

I'm sorry to record that this is the last "Navigans" to be edited by Dot, who is leaving us for the dark lands south of the English Channel. It doesn't seem long since I encouraged Dot to join in the Sailing Club, and she bought her Enterprise "Anomolous", which she learned to sail with commendable skill. I'm sure you would like me to wish Dot all the best in her new job at Eurocontrol, and to insist that she visits us whenever she comes home.

We are most fortunate that Brenda Tate has agreed to carry on the Editorship of "Navigans", Brenda has only been associated with the M.S.C. for about a year, but in that time she has really become one of us, and I know she has the welfare of the club very much at heart.

My report on the new clubhouse is still only of slow, but we hope, sure progress.

We are meeting with the Essex River Board on 21st August over some problems regarding siting, but if these can be overcome, we should be able then to move ahead more rapidly.

- 2 -

All our major sailing events have now been completed and we can look forward to at least a couple of months enjoyable sailing, especially if the weather continues to be so magnificent.

Dennis Byatt.
Commodore.

P.S. Just to remind Cadets (especially juniors) that the Garrett Memorial Trophy is presented each year to the most promising and/or helpful cadet. We have our eye on one or two of you, so keep on the ball!

CECIL STEBBENS, DECEASED

Members will be sorry to hear of the passing of their old friend Cecil Stebbens, Water Bailiff and river pilot up to the time of his retirement some two years ago: he was 71. He was closely associated with our club since the early fifties when we used an old shed on the seawall at Heybridge basin as our clubhouse and he constructed a fine ramp of planks from an old barge, down to the beach. Later, when we used some allotments further down river towards the Blackwater Sailing Club for a dinghy park, he constructed in the same way, a ramp over the sea wall, which served us very well for quite a time, although we were severely limited by the state of the tide, and members who stayed sailing a little too long often had to push their dinghies back over the mud! Cecil's motor boat towed the barge Mamgu round to Heybridge on Sunday 20th April 1958, and moored it off the original clubhouse; he constructed with considerable ingenuity, an access gangway, the last section of which was hinged to allow for the rise and fall of the tide, so we were able to board the barge at any time.

Mr. Stebbens was a Trinity House Pilot holding locences for the rivers Crouch, Blackwater and Colne and also a sea licence out to the Sunk light vessel.

He was awarded the life-saving medal for jumping into the Crouch, fully dressed in his uniform and rescuing a little girl.

During my term of office in 1957, Cecil presented us with a handsome trophy, The Pilot's Cup, for the winner of an all-in race, which we still sail annually.

Cecil will be greatly missed at the Basin and we offer our condolences to his widow, Mrs. Stebbens and his sons, Cecil and Darby, who are well known to all who frequent The Jolly Sailor.

A wreath was sent on behalf of the club to Mrs. Stebbens by our ex-Commodore, Jack Bigden, who was Cecil's brother-in-law.

Eric Payne.

PROFESSOR N.K.ADAM, M.A., Sc.D., F.R.S.

Members will be grieved to hear of the passing of Ex Commodore Arthur Adam's illustrious father and we tender our sincere condolences to Arthur, his mother and Maggie in their bereavement. Professor Adam was keenly interested in sailing and in the early days of the Club, he sailed from Heybridge in Arthur's cruiser Goose.

Eric Payne.

NICE GESTURE!

Whilst sailing off the estuary the other day, I encountered a violent thunderstorm with torrential rain, so decided to put in to West Mersea for the night.

I travelled a long way up the Ray channel before finding a vacant mooring which I took and whilst making fast, noticed a jam jar secured to the strop; this contained a message saying that visitors were welcome to use this mooring if they were off it by a given date when the owner's yacht was due back. I enjoyed a peaceful night without the fear of someone coming along and claiming the mooring, just as I had turned in for the night.

FRAP THOSE HALYARDS!

It would be appreciated if owners of cruisers, especially those having metal masts, would secure their halyards well away from their masts with either elastic strops or even pieces of codline, to reduce that continual clanging when there is any breeze.

It is exasperating to have to lie alongside a yacht making this din especially at night and the continual flapping cannot be much good for each mast or halyard.

In cases where electric cables run down inside the mast, unless the inside is filled with plastic foam, the cables should be drawn as tightly as possible at the point where they emerge at the foot of the mast.

At some clubs, the steward is instructed to board a yacht which has its halyards flapping or has its burgee left flying and rectify matters, the owner of the offending yacht having his account debited with a fine.

- 3 -

THE EXPANDED RIVER

Discovering that the season was nearly over without any major event - apart from races etc., Frank Savill and I decided to have a 'grand potter'. (Perhaps I should explain that two years ago we had reached a similar decision, being proud new owners of Mirrors, and made elaborate plans - and provisions, for a trip to Brightlingsea, dropping in at Mersea. This started off in a force six gale and we were glad to seek the shelter of Mersea, where we picnicked and explored the creeks, then made our way more slowly back, having to walk the last hundred yards.) This time it was Brightlingsea or bust.

Saturday morning came and by ten o'clock we were on the hard and the usual gale blowing. Casually remarking to the gathering throng (two small boys and one man) that we were just going for a trip down to Brightlingsea, we set out at low tide, Frank in a nice fitting wet suit and I in the few odd things I call my sailing gear, but proudly clutching a new life jacket I had bought for the sake of convention. With a force six behind us and a turned tide against us it was one long run, Frank holding the boom and I manning the tiller and clutching my life jacket. The sun shone and it began to feel like surfing in the South Seas and in 2½ hours we were off Brightlingsea.

We decided to put in to the bank opposite, have a cup of coffee and make ourselves respectable for the grand entry - Frank never having been to 'B' before. On the beach we chatted with the sole occupant, a beachcomber type who said he had worked on Osea for a few years and had left, selling his boat to Mrs. Pye of Steeple. He said he now earned his living as part time artist and boat repairer. We remarked on the few people about and he said all the robots were packed away on Bank Holiday Monday. The salt on us fairly glowed. Crossing over to the harbour - after a friendly warning about getting back up river - we were glad there were few about as there was little room to get even a Mirror in. With the friendly loan of a trailer from the club, we left our boat well up the beach and walked to the boating pool to have our sandwiches etc.

The sun shone, it was nice and sheltered, in fact a Shangrila and I suggested we rang up and said we were storm bound, but Frank, who is the conscientious type, reminded me of the beachcomber's warning and reluctantly we made our way back to the club beach, to find our boat floating nicely in a foot of water all ready for us - untethered.

Leaving the harbour at about 3.45, we soon met the wind and seas and a lump came in my throat as the little old tub complacently ploughed her way through it. She was aptly named 'Frantic'. From then on it was one long hard beat after another, with one on the helm and the other bailing and we realised we were going to have to pay for our hilarious morning. By the time we reached Bradwell I was beginning to envy Frank his wet suit as we slowly and painfully edged up the river, the wind and tide pressing us stubbonly back. After effecting another of our acrobatic changes of duties, we decided on smaller tacks, which helped for a while but fearing the mud flats we went back to the longer beats across river. Slowly the Stone came nearer as darkness began to fall and by the time we were opposite it was dark and we were glad of the friendly lights.

I suggested meekly to Frank that perhaps we ought to put in there, but the gallant fellow was not to be beaten and so out we went across the river again. Coming back, having decreased the distance to the clubhouse by some 100', we began to notice the burst of activity at Stansgate. Lights were being lit and several cars could be seen streaming down and there was a general hub-bub. I suggested to Frank that it could only bw a large scale rescue operation and began to feel warm again with importance. Slyly I pointed out that we shouldn't waste the time of police etc. or put our wives to further misery when we could drop in at the Stone and telephone. At this blow below the belt he capitulated and thankful for the friendly gleam of the Stone Sailing Club's lights, we sank our bow into the soft sweet mud and stepped ashore.

continued...

- 4 -

At the Stone Sailing Club a large dinner party had reached its second course and there were a few raised eyebrows as we blundered in. Quickly two members came to our aid and we were offered everything except to sit down at the table and join in.

First the trolley to get our boat in, then the telephone to Stansgate. 'No' said a rather puzzled voice there were no anguished wives on the hard, but they would ring Margaret and ask her to pick us up. Margaret (bless her) was quickly on the scene (before we could finish the hot showers and coffee) and warmly and smoothly we made our well-lit progress up river to collect our things at the clubhouse.

Here we found a brazen air of normality. The noise was not that of wailing wives but of a disco and the flares and carlights for a barbecue we hadn't heard of. Quickly we adjusted ourselves to the hard and thoughtless world.

Now we know our river and that it is not just for light entertainment, not only that, we have seen the mouth of another one.

Hope we make the clubhouse next time Frank.

Alfred Cottam.

BANK HOLIDAY CRUISE

Seven cruisers from the club enjoyed a very pleasant August Bank Holiday in the Walton Backwaters. The holiday for Snowgoose began on Friday, when with a scratch crew, Mary, Vic and I, we tacked our way against an easterly wind, up to Stone Point. Here we met the Perkin's half-way through a fortnight's holiday and were royally entertained on Angele.

Saturday morning we picked up our official crew from the Yacht Club, Robert, looking very smart in new gear. We spent the day lazing on the beach at Stone Point searching the horizon for the M.S.C. burgee. Just as we had given up hope and we were eating a very late lunch, they all arrived. Segla, and Coppelia, commodores past and present. Thundercloud, Carousel and last but certainly not least, Karina with Bobbie and George. Roulette had started too but was last seen off Clacton Pier. Travelling in convoy down the Walton Channel we picked up moorings or found a safe spot to anchor near the landing steps. Then we repaired to Walton for fish and chips and beer. (The cruising man's staple diet.)

The following day we returned to Stone Point. The children swam, although it wasn't very warm and the adults lazed about or went for long energetic walks along the tide line. In the evening there was a cheerful gathering on Snowgoose, and we enjoyed a huge bottle of Cianti - the Commodore's duty free.

Monday we had to say goodbye to Segla, Thundercloud and Carousel, who had to return to Stansgate. Snowgoose had gained an addition to her crew, a lesser spotted Swinton (Jayne). Angele, Coppelia and Snowgoose had decided to leave the backwaters and go up the Deben. We wished Karina luck and a safe and easy passage home and tripped the anchor at 3.0 p.m. and motored across to Bawdsey. We had no trouble crossing the bar, it was almost slack low water. Our only worry was a large steel Dutch barge that appeared to be going sideways in front of us.

We picked up moorings in Ramsholt. It is the most picturesque spot. The water was as smooth as glass, the moonlight clear and bright and the phosphorus gave us a sparkling bow wave. Next day we went on up river to Woodbridge, passing Sirius anchored at Waldringfield. We took a berth in the Marina and the opportunity to stock up on provisions and fuel. Vic and I enjoyed a chat with Terry Hallam and Queenie, whom we met on the waterside. They had some shopping to do.

Our skipper decided that we were a very motley dirty crew so in the afternoon we all had a hairwash under the hose pipe on the pontoon and gave the mullet a bubble bath. We stayed overnight and the next day dropped down to the

continued...

- 7 -

Rocks, a place which has many happy memories for Snowgoose. This is a curved sandy beach shielded by rushes and trees. It is topped by a pinewood that is inaccessible by road. We spent a happy twenty-four hours there just mucking about. The children sailed the dinghy or scrambled up and down the slopes, which left Steven Perkin's suffering from an attack of the dreaded yellow peril. The sand gets everywhere, but eventually the bilges.

We left at lunch-time Thursday dropping down to Felixstowe ready to return to Stansgate on Friday. The engines on Snowgoose and Coppelia both had the gremlins. Stan was fighting the weed, and our magneto fell off but was quickly repaired. Thursday night we had supper at Bawdsey Ferry and a quiet tate-a-tate on Angele. Friday we crossed the bar and came home. By Clacton pier we saw the familiar shape of Roulette. Had the Foreman's been there all week?

Brenda Tate.

Well, the sailing season is rapidly drawing to a close but the social one is just beginning. The informal party was certainly different, and very enjoyable. I am looking forward to the Laying-up Supper and a chance to take off my gum-boots and put on some make-up, and, yes folks, I am actually going to have my hair done. I hope I shall meet you all there. By the way, perhaps the Bigden's had better look to their laurels. I took our dinghy out single handed for the first time last Sunday and only gybed her once. Enterprises next year?

Brenda Tate.

SOCIAL SCREED

I should like to thank all the wives who brought food to the Informal Party and made sure we did not go hungry, while the bar satisfied our thirsts. I had planned a party with a difference but it was way beyond any expectations! The pianist, Charlie Hurst was not only a great success but was essential because we had no electricity for most of the evening, he played, for at least an hour in what can be best described as murky visibility! He was also playing very hard to try and compete with the Megawatt psychodellic lighting provided at no extra charge!

We look forward to another enjoyable Laying-up Supper this year. Tickets are now available from:
Dennis Byatt at Baddow.
John Witter at Basildon.
John Weedon at New Street.
Peter Foreman at E.E.V.Co., Section 12.
Jack Reeves at Cromptons.

- 2 -

I have repeated the tear-off slip at the back of Navigan's to show the information to help with the table plan.

The children's party this year is being arranged differently, in that we are trying a professional entertainer for the whole time, so that help is needed only for the food. I should appreciate offers of help to cover the food to offset some of the cost of the entertainer. The slip return was 100% successful last year so please fill in the slip at the end of this Navigan's. The age range is from as young as they can be left without crying (!!!) to about 10, older ones are welcome, but they tend to become helpers!

Peter Foreman, Social Secretary.
Section 12, E.E.V.Co. Ext.333 or
Chelmsford [redacted].

COMMODORE'S NOTES

We had a magnificent turn out to repair the road, and in spite of a high wind which kept blowing out the flamethrowers, the result seems most satisfactory. Our thanks to the helpers and the Essex River Authority who loaned us the flamethrowers and John Hooper who gave us the materials.

The M.A.S.C. have approved the new clubhouse and subject to a suitable agreement between the M.A.S.C. and the M.S.C., work should begin in January for completion by mid-summer 1974.

This will be the last Navigans before the Laying-up Supper. We have carried out the wishes expressed at the last A.G.M. and repeated the arrangements of last year, when we had a most enjoyable evening. We are aware, of course, of the increased cost, but for an excellent meal, wine, and dancing until 1 a.m., it represents good value at todays prices. So we hope that as many as possible will come along to support our major social event at the end of this grand sailing year.

Dennis Byatt, Commodore.

CRUISER SECTION NEWS

The cruiser meet was held as usual at the Cricketers. The drinking was interrupted for a short while to show my slides of the Calais trip, next month I'll bring along the movies which are not very professional, due to a motor fault on my camera, but do show us enjoying some good sailing breezes as opposed to the calms on the slides.

I was very disappointed having to start my motor to finish the Cruiser Race course but the Force 6 dropping certainly favoured the fast boats. I knew I was in for trouble when I saw Amity tacking several times to make the Inner Bench and watched with envious eyes her roaring back out to the Bench Head while I plotted a course across the shoals of Colne Point to avoid the dreadful combination to my boat of Wind and Tide. Even then I had to tack across the channel once to get from just downstream of the Inner Bench to just upstream.

Never mind I thought, I won't have the tide so strong against me up river, and I hammered back to the Bench Head. However thereafter my luck really ran out because the wind while veering easterly, which would have helped considerably, proceeded to drop until just past Bradwell, I resigned having calculated an E.T.A. of 8 p.m. Never mind, it was a good sail.

Peter Foreman, Social Secretary.
Section 12, E.E.V.Co. Ext.333 or
Chelmsford [redacted].

THIS AND THAT

Congratulations to John and Vanda Tillotson on the new addition to their family.

Pandora's are popular. Ken Bevin's has just purchased one. Mike Sisson's has taken a leaf out of John Swinton's book and has bought a Pandora hull, is building it at home this winter to replace his Dragon sold earlier in the season.

Peter Bentley would like to thank all person's concerned in retrieving Caurosel's rudder, which was apprently lifted off by the bad weather. It is now attached by both lanyard and split pins pending a more permanent modification this winter.

Do you know ... that if your tender is not named it may not be covered by your insurance. Please note that all tenders should be clearly named.

Do you know ... about the new regulations regarding trailers bought in on 1st May this year. Under the new law the speed limit for boat trailers (not above 30 cwts.) is increased to 50 mph except where a lower general speed limit applies.

There are also the following conditions:-

1. the relevant weight of the trailer must not, if fitted with brakes, exceed the kerbside weight of the towing vehicle or, if unbraked, exceed 60 per cent of that weight.

2. The towing vehicle must be clearly marked with its kerbside weight either inside the vehicle or externally on the left side or nearside.

3. The trailer, if it is either a caravan or a trailer carrying fixed equipment, must be clearly marked with its maximum gross weight on the external nearside.

4. A plate with the number "50" must be fixed on the trailer in a vertical position facing squarely to the rear.

Combinations not complying with these regulations are restricted to 40 mph. on all-purpose roads.

EDITORIAL

It was so nice to see everybody looking so smart, especially Dot, home on a flying visit from France. Thanks also to the Helmsman of the Year, who extended his hospitality to all of us who wouldn't go home to bed.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

The year really does seem to be drawing to a close - the 1973 Laying-up Supper has now come and gone. However, we still have the Christmas Dance, not forgetting the A.G.M., to come. The Laying-up Supper, ably managed by Peter Foreman, went off most smoothly, and by all accounts was very well enjoyed.

Mabs and I have had the privilege of attending the Laying-up suppers of several of our neighbouring clubs, and there is no doubt that ours compares very well with the best. However, we are all concerned about the rising cost, and you will see that we have a proposal to discuss at the A.G.M. that we should move to the M.A.S.C. next year. I hope that as many of you as possible will come along to put your views, especially if you do or would come to L.U.S's and vote on this at the A.G.M. Please remember that only ordinary members may vote, and that the count will be taken on membership cards.

We have only one nominee from members, (the associates) for a committee member. We had hoped for a representative from the ladies, but perhaps we can "co-opt" one of you for the new committee.

I'm sure you will be pleased to hear that the committee have asked Sir Neil Sutherland to become an Honorary Member of the Sailing Club. Sir Neil, as most of you know, put much effort into building up the M.A.S.C. and was responsible for the establishment of the M.A.S.C. at Beehive Lane. I am delighted to say that Sir Neil and Lady Sutherland are pleased to accept and look forward to visiting us at Stansgate in the future.

Dennis Byatt.
Commodore.

MOORING CHAT

We now have a long waiting list of people requiring moorings in 1974. Three of these are Company members with boats needing a position in A row. It has been suggested that we move all moorings on A row closer together so as to squeeze another 3 in.

The Orange No.1 launch with winch is now ready to lift moorings and will remain in the water for the next 4 weeks until 8th December. Will all A row people please co-operate and lift their own gear before the beginning of December so that we can re-position and re-allocate at the beginning of next season.

A Cruiser fleet working party will be required to fit out our No.1 launch ready for a very early start next season. Please may I have a list of names for volunteers to do this task which will take place on Sundays in the boat-shed. The Cruiser fleet is the largest fleet in the club so I hope that the response will be good.

It is necessary to remind all members that if they are the last to leave the site it is their duty to make sure the club-house is locked and all secure, the floodboards are in position with their bars and the winches are padlocked.

Vic Tate.
Cruiser Fleet Captain.

The best time to transplant shrubs is before Christmas. M.A.S.C. CAR DRAW

Do you know that a new car draw series has started? This is a venture organized by the M.A.S.C. to raise money for capital projects for the club. If you are a member of the M.A.S.C. or an employee of GEC-Marconi Electronics, MIMCO or EEV Co. you are eligible to join. And if you join through the Sailing Club, then 10% of what you spend goes to club funds.

All you have to do to join is to agree to subscribe 10p per week for 10 weeks and at the end of that time you are eligible for the big draw. Each Sunday at 8.30 during the 10 week period there is a draw for small prizes of approximately £50 value and all paid up members are eligible.

The 10 week periods have just started and you can join at any time during the period up to the next major draw by paying the back payments and continuing up to the end of the period.

If you are not already a subscriber why not see your local agent, or better still become an agent and support your club.

If you want any more information, do not hesitate to contact me.

If you have left a boat at the Club for the Winter, you are advised to make a trip and check that it is properly prepared for bad weather.

COMMODORE'S REPORT,

i i have eas very fortunate in my first: year of Office in having
two great assets. The most important has been the support of a...
magnificent committee, and the goodwill and friendliness of members...
ip Sa second has been .the grand weather which has enabled us. to hold so many successful events. This statement is entitled the Commodore's report, but of course, we all know that the items covered represent much hard work by many people. I shall try to deal with the main events in chronological order, and some of these are, of course,. actions arising from our last A.G.M. and the Extraordinary General Meeting of last December. ) . = nt

Inevitably, the approval given for provision of a permanent .club- house at Stansgate has been uppermost in our minds. The planning sub- committee was reformed and a series of meetings took place at which we were aided by a few co-opted members with building experience. It
became evident that for a modest increase in price, we might be able|
to raise the lounge and provide a large amount of necessary storage and working Space, and we arrived at a unanimously agreed outline thanks design. At this point, I would like to place on record our great, to Ron Rider, who translated these sketches into workable plans, complete with a detailed specification. Copies of the layout were pinned up in the clubhouse for the benefit of . members. The plans and spec were offered to five builders in the locality, and 1 am pleased to inform you that Subject to signing the final agreement, the chosen builder on both price and provisions:
was Mike Taylor. This was approved by. the M.A.S.C. We were, of course, in close collaboration with M.A.5.C., and I would like to acknowledge the help and encouragement we have had from then.
In July, we submitted the plans to the Maldon R.D.C. They referred them to the Essex County Council Planning Authority. As the location of the buildind falls within the jurisdiction of the Essex Rivers Authority, we also submitted plans to them in parallel, in order 4 we hoped to speed up the process. It was ‘there that we discovered that all new permanent buildings had to be at least fifty feet from the sea wall which would have put the clubhouse in the main car—park. We won a concession to reduce this to thirty feet, but even this required a re-drawing of some of the plans. I had hoped to be able to report at this meeting that everything was signed and settled, but alas it seems I was ‘too optimistic. It was only at the beginning of this month that the H.C0.C. got around to studying our plans, and inevitably, I suppose, have requested changes. These are :comparatively small,such.as.thickening up the facia boards, re positioning the windows and providing a second fire check door, but it again involved Ron;Rider in a re-drawing excercise. This, he carried out at great apeee and the new drawings are now back with the E.C.C. We'‘have made urgent requests to the planning people to ensure that these are submitted to the Maldon Planning Committee Meeting on December 4th. If this comes about, we should be able to start the excavations in

continued.

-4-

January, hopefully for the building to be complete in July.

The cost is rather higher than we had hoped partly because of the 50% increase in usable area, and partly because of rising costs of materials. For example, timber prices increased by 60% in the summer. The M.A.S.C. have approved an allocation of £19,000 for the clubhouse and as soon as planning approval is received and the agreement signed with the builder, we shall be negotiating a new rental agreement with the M.A.S.C.

In spite of our disappointment in not having all the formal actions complete, we might bear in mind that at the beginning of this year we were still thinking in terms of a three or four year project.

During the year, we also worked out our project income, and prepared a series of budgets. I don't want to steal our treasurer's thunder, but I know he is looking forward to reporting that our budget for this year has been well met.

We are obviously not proposing to increase fees this year, and we hope not in 1975 either, but this must depend upon factors outside our control such as continuing inflation and of course, the size of our membership. I should mention here that next year our basic membership fee and car parking charge will all be subject to V.A.T. which will have to be added on. Fortunately, our hard fee and mooring fees are not subject to V.A.T.

We were instructed at the last A.G.M. to proceed with the purchase of a new rescue launch. The foundations for this purchase had already begun in 1972, and we were fortunate in obtaining our magnificent 'Mariner' from the Boat Show at a good discount, and we also got a good-discount for the 'Crescent' outboard. I'm Sure you will agree the new boat is a real asset to the club, and a great releif to those who spent weeks each season refurbishing the old boat.

Last December, we took active steps to protect our hard with the brushwood breakwater, which has not only reduced the errosion to the East, but mysteriously seems to have consolidated the mud at the bottom of the hard.

Early in the new year, the new racebox was erected, and has been well used for its first season. The road has been refurbished, and the bridges virtually completed.

So far, this has sounded more like a building firms report, so with some releif, let me say a few words about sailing, which, after all, is what we're most interested in.

The 1973 Regatta broke all records - 200 boats took part. The organisation of the sailing and festivities was very good and every race was sailed in fine weather conditions. It was obvious, though, that our resources were pretty strained, but in spite of this, all reports I've had from visitors were enthusiastic, and we are likely to have a large turnout again next year. We must, however, be prepared to pay out for some extra facilities.

The Open Day was quite successful, in spite of a clash with away events, and a number of new members joined the club.

One new unofficial event took place in the summer, a friendly challenge match against some of our colleages from Rochester. By popular request, we shall be repeating this in 1974.

The fleets were active, the enterprises have won the Nationals, the Area championship and the Club's name was carried to Canada with an excellent result. The Hornet team have done well and the Mirrors go from strength to strength. The G.P. 14's appear to having some

difficulty with numbers, which is a pity as the G.P. is a good boat for the estuary. The Cruisers have had a very good year, and have emerged as a strong sailing group, with a number of fleet events successfully carried out. We are becoming rather worried about the demand for moorings, and some arrangements must be made to increase the utilisation of our moorings area in the near future.

Speaking of the future, it is Marconi Sailing Club's turn to organise the 1974 B.J.R.C. championship at stone on 14th July 1974. This is an event on a par with our Regatta and we shall be grateful for assistance with a number of tasks.

Before I conclude, I would like to pay tribute to those members retiring from the committee. Geoff Farnie has valiantly carried out the duties of Secretary for two years, and we have been most grateful for his efforts. Dot Renshaw, our ex editor of 'Navigans' and dinghy sailor par excellance put in a lot of hard work most cheerfully.
