OBITUARY

W.E. LENDERYOU.

Older members of our club who knew Bill Lenderyou will be grieved to hear of his passing at the age of 72 years. He was a Founder Member of the Maldon Little Ship Club in 1930 and served for 15 years on their Committee. He was Commodore for three years in the fifties. His fine motor cruiser SUCCESS was used as Committee boat for all B.J.R.C. events after racing was resumed at the end of the War until this last season, when illness prevented him from coming to the starting line. The Blackwater Joint Racing Committee, of which he was Chairman for several years, presented him with a Silver Salver in appreciation of his services to racing.

He received a Royal Warrant from the London Little Ship Club which entitled him to fly the defaced Blue Ensign. In 1966 Mr. Lenderyou founded the annual Barge Match which has been an attractive event on the Blackwater ever since. He was an Honorary Member of the Blackwater Sailing Club and always used SUCCESS, moored off Osea, for starting their all-in race for the Dyer Cup at the end of each Season.

Bill was owner of Essex Radiators at Great Baddow and many of our Members have had their radiators and petrol tanks repaired by his firm and will remember his very pleasant personality.

We offer our sincere condolences to his widow, Mrs. Lenderyou and to the M.L.S.C. He will be greatly missed by all of us in the sailing fraternity.

ERIC PAYNE.

SAILING BARGE HOLIDAY.

In August I joined the sailing barge Marjorie at Maldon for a 4 day cruise. Marjorie is a common sight on the Blackwater as she sails to and from the Hythe Quay, Maldon, with charter parties aboard and is easily recognizable by the white cross in her topsail.

She is a coasting barge built for R & W Paul of Ipswich in 1902, with a length of 86 ft. and a beam of 20ft. The hold has been fitted out to provide cabin accommodation for 12 charterers, a spacious saloon and a well-appointed gallery. The crew (skipper and mate) live in the traditional skipper's cabin but eat with the charter party(who supply and cook the food).

The barge has a ketch rig, the mizzen being sheeted to the rudder blade to assist steering and counteract the force of the foresail and staysail.

Our party consisted of 5 chaps, including myself, the rest of the party having backed down. There is a moral there for anyone interested in organising a charter party. However, the smaller party is an advantage as it gives plenty of opportunity to be involved in the sailing and working of the barge.

We were towed away from Hythe Quay at 5.20 am. on Monday August the 20th. by a small tug. The tide had just started to ebb, but the wind was almost non-existent. All the sails were set off Heybridge, we charterers being given various ropes and told to pull, and the tug cast off. We drifted rather than sailed down Colliers Reach and some extemely strong language was used to attempt to 'whistle up a wind'. It became apparent as the days progressed that little could be achieved in or around the barge without the use of certain quaint old barging phrases and sayings, although no harsh words were ever directed at the barge herself, she being almost sacred among vessels. Such was the rate of progress that we had time to start cooking breakfast off Northey Island and to be washing it down with a cup of tea whilst passing Stansgate. At last the tide turned at Bradwell and it started to rain, and we anchored to catch up on some sleep. The wind freshened in the afternoon and at 4pm. we hoisted sail and raised anchor. The barge set off towards Mersea at a grand space. A few of us climbed into the barge's dinghy and spent some time circling the barge taking photos as she sailed. She looked splendid under sail, close-hauled, and I took some fine colour slides. That night found us anchored off Brightlingsea in company with Dawn, Walter Cook's other charter barge.

Next morning we left Brightlingsea at 9.30am. and headed down the Colne for the Spitway. There was a fresh easterly breeze blowing and Marjorie ploughed her way out of the Blackwater estuary. Heavy rain and rough water made navigation difficult and it was a comfort that at least the crew appeared to know the way. The seas in the Spitway were quite rough and confused and the old barge creaked and groaned below decks. It was the first time I have ever made tea when the cups wouldn't stay where I put them. Our cruiser colleages are, no doubt, used to this. We had to go about twice in the Spitway to clear the

/ continued.

-11-

the Buxey sands, this was quite a memorable experience in the conditions prevailing. Once into the Swin we freed off and ran 'Up Swin' into the Thames, crossed over to the Medway channel and anchored off Gillingham 6½ hours after leaving Brightlingsea. Certainly a journey for a dinghy sailor to remember.

Wednesday we spent anchored at Gillingham where we weent ashore for a few hours in the morning, and went up to Hoo Marina in the dinghy in the afternoon. As the tide was to turn about 6pm. it was decided to move down river to Stansgate Creek (near Sheerness) that evening. We had a fine sail, tacking down the Medway with the tide in our favour. We were graced with a fiery sunset, and the lights from the navigation buoys and tankers at the refineries made a colourful picture. It was quite dark when we anchored in the entrance to Stansgate Creek but by now I knew my way around the deck well enough to avoid tripping over the umpteen bits and pieces that are required to make a barge go.

Next day, Thursday, was our last day and we had to be at Southend Pier by the afternoon to change places with the next charter party. Marjorie was to stay in the Thames as she was to sail in the Southend Barge Match the following weekend, Thursday morning we up-anchored (a back breaking bu siness, by far the worst job on the barge), and headed back into the Thames. Once clear of the Medway I got my chance to take the wheel under the guidance of a watchful barge skipper. This indeed was sailing in grand style as we tacked our way down river just off the Kent coast. The sea was choppy and the breeze fresh, and the wheel kicked like a mule. I soon found it was better to let her have her own way when she kicked making alterations in between times. I continually cast anxious glances from the bob to the sails, ever conscious of the gaze of the crew. Putting the barge about was certainly different to tacking my GP 14, but the principle appeared to be much the same. A hearty 'Lee-Oh' to warn the crew tending the foresail bowline, then helm hard down and around she goes. The foresail is backed by means of a bowline which pushes the barge's bows cleanly through the wind. Once on the new tack the bowline is let go and the foresail whips across the horse and away she goes. All good things must come to an end and the barge was handed back to her crew and course set for Southend Pier via the South Shoebury buoy and the Essex coast. The holiday was over when the barge dinghy landed us on Southend Pier with all our gear, 4 days and 60 colour slides after leaving Maldon.

If my tale has whetted anybody's appetite and tempted them to organise a charter party, I would make the following suggestions, one is to book early as chartering is very popular and the second is to be sure of your party and see the colour of their money before you commit yourself. Being left with half your planned-for party can be very expensive.

RAY BALL

MOORING MATTERS.

Unusual astromical coincidences that occur only 20 times in 300 years are causing freak high and low tides this year. The sun and moon will be pulling the oceans in the same direction and the moon will be even closer to the Earth than usual, affecting tides even further, The result will be higher and lower water levels along our shores than any in the past 12 years. The effects along the East Coast will be dramatic. It has been predicted that the village of Dunwich, once a flourishing port, 20 miles south of Lowestoft, until overwhelmed by the advancing North Sea in the 10th Century, should be on dry land again for a short time.

It also means that if you have a mooring on A or B row you will be able to pick it up and inspect it with considerable ease! The date and time to note in your diary is Saturday 9th., February at 7.30am. This is the ideal opportunity for all deep water mooring holders to make sure that they relay their moorings in the new positions as marked on the new mooring charts.

PRINTED BELOW IS THE WINNING ENTRY FOR THE MAMGU TROPHY 1973.

A SMALL ODYSSEY,
by KEN BEAVINS.

In the early summer of 1973, an increasing diserchantment with dinghy racing ( perhaps not unconnected with a conspicuous lack of success since 1972 ), together with crew problems, led me to consider wider sailing excursions in my GP 14, Lady Clare.

What follows has, I hope, sufficient of the characteristics of a log to qualify it as a Mamgu Trophy entry, but it is priorarily a piece of personal writing.

The choice of crew presented a problem. Nik and I have in the past made several successful short sailing/camping trips, the most recent having been in 1971, when we visited Burnham and Foulness Island. But this year he was not available. The only other person with whom I have achieved that instinctive, intuitive, rapport in the boat which is essential was also not available, so I concluded that this trip would have to be single handed.

The planned trip was a five-day north easterly excursion up the Essex coast. The first and last nights would be spent, sleeping in the boat in the general vicinity of Colne Point, and the other two farther North at pre-arranged accommodation ashore.

The planned times of departure, passing and arrival, taking into account tidal flows were set down on paper in terms of High Water rather than clock times in order to allow (prophetically, as it turned out) for slippage of dates. Each day's sheet of paper also had a column in which I was to log the actual times. That column remains blank to this day- and the paper looks as though it had seen more sea water than ink..

By converting the HWD based times to clock and calendar times, I found that the only suitable dates when I could be free, were between the 6th and the 10th of August, and in mid-July I committed myself by giving to a somewhat incredulus wife and family a statement of my intention and to the Almighty a fervent prayer for good weather.

Because of the planned overnight stays in the boat, a sleeping bag, the boat cover, rudimentary cooking gear and two thermos flasks were to be taken. Food would include milk, coffee, sugar, soup, orange juice, biscuits, cheese, nuts and dried fruit. Each morning the flasks would be charged one with coffee, and the other with soup for consumption at the end of the day. Midday food would be contained in a plastic airtight box and consist of biscuits, cheese, nuts and fruit. Brandy would also be taken.

I planned to take extra sailing gear, including the small headsail, a second anchor, all the spare line I could find, a small compass and my knife/marlin spike which doubles as an identity disc. The latter two items were worn around my neck. I borrowed Clare's M.W. transistor radio and took a list of BBC M.W. weather forecast (23.45 Radio 4 is best). I also purchased a red hand flare. (Use when aircraft or vessel is sighted). It remains unused. I did not take the spinnaker. I wore my wet suit and bouyancy jacket all the sailing time. I have included the foregoing details because they were the subject of much thought in the planning stage which absorbed

/continued.

-8-

my spare time attention for some time before the trip and on which to a large extent the outcome of the trip depended.

In the event, most of this logistic planning was successful, but the one thing I could not plan, of course, was the weather. Force 6 wind on Monday the 6th August, reinforced on the Tuesday by heavy rain made a start impossible, or at least foolhardy. By Tuesday morning, with no comfort to be had from a telephone weather forecast featuring force 5 to 7, I had decided to cut my losses and return to work on the following day, unless there was a significant improvement. When I rose the next day in readiness for work, I tried the telephone forecast again, just once more for luck. Joy, oh, Joy! It had a 3 in it "3 to 4 S.W." the lady said. A hasty reassembly of the gear and food proceded my departure for Stansgate.

DAY 1

With the wind WSW force 2-3, genoa rather than jib seemed to be in order, and I left Stansgate at 11.35 in gentle broad reaching conditions. The sun shone from a patch of blue sky between grey-edged clouds, and I was already finding the wet suit to be very warm.

By the time I passed Stone a few minutes later the wind had a little more west in it, giving a very free sail. At 11.50, having passed Thirslet Beacon five minutes previously, I was running down a rippling grey Blackwater which changed miraculously to a pure green when the sun came out, and the water was chuckling merrily along the side of the boat when the sudden onset of an involuntary gybe woke me from my reverie and served to remind me of the need for constant single-minded alertness..

At Bradwell I was interested to see coming towards me the Maldon- based steam tug, Chriane, towing another tug up to Maldon making three altogether on the Blackwater now. Keeping fairly close to the south shore, I made for the sewer beacon East of the Power Station, and then passed Sales Point at 12.35. By now the wind had freshened to force 4. At 13.00 about half a mile West of Bench Head Buoy, there was just a touch of cream on the tops of the waves, and fifteen minutes later, I was a quarter of a mile North of the Bench Head in a longish rolling swell.

I had intended to stop overnight at Colne Point, but in the freshening wind I began to see that the lee shore presented by Colne Point would be less than hospitable. So, finding myself well upwind and midway between Colne Point and Bar Buoy with some twenty minutes of ebb tide still to go, I decided to go on a little further up the coast, and landed at pretty well dead low water at St. Osyth Beach at 14.00.

The beach here is sandy and, apart from the occasional boulder revealed at low water is quite a suitable overnight berth for a hauled-up dinghy. On the subject of the buildings on the sea wall, and the caravan site, fish and chips, bingo, and so on behind the sea wall I had better confine myself to saying merely that together they constitute one of the most striking examples I have ever seen of the sort of waterside squalor in which, regrettably, Essex seems to specialize.

With the sails taken off, and the large anchor out, there followed a period of about six hours in which I ate lunch, snoozed on the bench and, from time to time, shifted the anchor as the tide crept up.

At high water (20.27) with the boat hauled up just above high water

/continued.

-9-

level, I could settle down to supper and rest of a sort in this boat, under its boom-up cover, and after listening to the 23.45 inshore weather forecast (S/S-W F4-5) I retired to sleep.

However, despite a liberal swig of medicenal Brandy, I slept only till 0200 whom I was woken by the freshening wind and the slapping of the one piece of menning rigging which I had forgotten to tie clear of the mast. Therafter, I dozed fitfully and very uncomfortably. (One of the GP14's vices is that only small children and midgets can stretch out fully on the bottom. If a normal adult should be foolish enough to attempt to sleep in the boat, he has no option but to wedge himself in with shoulder between centre-board case and side seat, and head on the thwart- and this is as uncomfortable as it sounds. To be fair, though, Jack Holt did not intend that the boat should double as a bedroom).

DAY 2. The next morning ( 9th of August).

I was glad to rise with the daylight at 0500. By 0700, all was stowed away, flacks filled and sails up- genoa again. I was ready to go, but because the boat was about thirty feet from the water, there being two hours to go before High Water, there was much heaving and grunting before I got her to the water, bows on to the breaking waves.

During the night I had had considerable doubts ( encouraged, perhaps, by my physical discomfort) as to whether to go on or return to Stansgate, and in the morning, the sight of that grey sea and sky and the full of the force 3-4 south westerly wind, did nothing to reassure me. I postponed the decision until after I had a sail about on all points (as well as giving one the feel of the wind and water, this checks for possible errors in rigging). Launching was a trifle tricky, and I was almost (but not quite) forcibly beached by the quartering sea, but once out, conditions felt tolerable, and, the decision made for me, I found myself five minutes later broad reaching East on starboard tack past Martello Tower No.3, Imray, Laurie's chart Y6 already a little damp despite its plastic envelope.

By the time Jaywick had been passed (Tower No.4 0725) the wind was fresher, I thought 4-5 and there was now a tendency for the waves to break over their tops. The boat was moving quite fast, although I still felt fully in control. I began to realize, however, that if I was to avoid dead-running ( which in the rolling swell now building up would have been asking for an involuntary gybe and capsize) I would have to harden up a little on the wind. This would take me further out to deeper and perhaps less agitated water. Clearly, I could not hold this course indefinately, so I decided to tack down wind between a mile and half a mile from the shore. At each change of tack I went "right-round" not caring to risk a gybe, not even an intentional one in what seemed to me by now to be a very heavy sea with large waves, some of which blew over while at their tops. I passed Clacton Pier at 0745 when, to quote verbation my words from the tape there was "along, rolling, horrible, nasty sea running."

I do not know whether fear is a good thing. The answer, I fancy, was some dependence upon the cause. Perhaps, though, in a well-ordered world in which one normally does nothing more dangerous than crossing the road, a touch of real peril and the attendant cold clutch at the pit of the stomach is no bad thing, a chastering purge of fear, setting the rest of life in perspective. I hope this is so because for

/continued.

-10-

a while I was afraid.

At 0800 the sun came out for what looked like being a long spell. It was very welcome indeed. The exercise had by now become one of keeping way on (not difficult as most of the boat was planning), and keeping the right way up. To this latter end, both dead running and exposure of the boat to beam seas were equally to be avoided. I found I had to give every part of my attention to the boat, there was now little opportunity to record time, nor for thinking about anything but the next few seconds of the task in hand.

Mentally ticking off the land marks as they slipped by (and they could have been on a desert island for all the sign of movement that were to be seen ashore)- 0825 Red cliffs, 0850 Frinton Block of Flats- I realized that I had began to get the hang of it. This was as well because tacking down wind became increasingly necessary as my desired course became more northerly, although it also meant noticeably less progress over the ground than a dead downwind course would, on the face of it, have given. My resistance to the temptation to dead run was stiffened by rememberance that on the four occasions I had capsized in the past, three had been assiciated with dead running (subsequent events were to alter that statistic).

So it seemed to take a very long time to get round Walton Piar although in fact it took only 35 minutes to cover the entire distance from Frinton to Naze Tower, including rounding the Pier. After this chart Y6 was displaced by Y13 which showed in greater detail, the remaining part of this leg.

Once past the Naze (0925 Naze tower ), the wind was less strong and the water much smoother. On a broad port readh across Pennyhole Bay to No. 4/5 bouys on the Pye sand, I realized that it being 1000 and high water being 1004 there was enough water over the flats to make it possible to cut the corner and make straight for Walton Stone Point. I reached Walton channel No. 8 buoy at 0955, and noticed (but did not note details) that not all the other marks shown on my chart in that vicinity were in fact there.

It had been my plan to wait at Stone Point, pulling up on the sand and (hopefully) dozing in the afternoon, waiting for the tide to turn and in the late afternoon to flood into the Walton Channel. In fact, I had arrived at Stone Point just slightly less than a whole tide earlier than planned, and although the ebb had started, there was still enough water in the channel (entered at 1005) to tempt me up to Walton itself, despite the wind- now perversely shifted to south- which necessitated tacking all the way. Past Twizzle Creek very short tacking was needed because of the small effective width of the channel, the outer edge of the apparent channel being only a few inches deep over soft mud.

This was my undoing. At about 10.30, within a cable of my destination when attempting to go about, the already partly retracted centre board fouled the bottom, and with a dreadful, ponderous inevitability, as though she felt that she had done enough for one day Lady Clare capsized, depositing the great deep water dinghy sailor into six inches of water and about four feet of soft mud.

I was able to right her by the simple expedient of picking up the mast end. Nothing had been lost as most things were tied on. The boat floated, and in other circumstances could have been sailed dry. However, like Lady Clare, I too, had very nearly had enough. So when having got the sails down, I was preparing to bale, my

continued.

-11-

usual reluctance to ask for help was overcome by an overwhelming desire to get myself and this boat on to dryland, and I cadged a tow for the last few yards, from a passing motor boat.

I pulled up on the Yacht Club hard, took a much needed swig from the medicinal brandy bottle, and commenced the tedious task of baling and drying out. After this was done I allowed myself the luxury of a taxi to my pre-arranged quarters ashore and a much needed sleep. (The only casualty from the capsize was the tape recorder. A little water had found its way through the hatch seal into the forward bouyang compartment with disasterous results for the recorder stowed there, through not for the tape).

DAY 3.

The original plan for day three had been to go from Walton up the Stour past Harwich/Felixstowe to reach Manningtree for the night, but as I had lost two days this leg had to be omitted and Friday the 10th of August had to see the start of my return voyage. I was a little worried lest on that day, the high SW winds of the 9th should return. The forecast was force 3-4, and when I left Walton at 08.45 against the last of the flood tide (HW10.08) the wind was 3, West and a gentle relaxed beam reach took me to Stone Point, and there over the edge of Pennyhole Bay, broad reaching to Naze Tower, standing well out to avoid the store obstruction running out from the shore in the vicinity of Cormorant Creek ( I asked myself, without satisfactory answer, why I had not seen these on the previous day).

Past the Naze Tower the wind seemed more S.S.W. and nearer F4 than 3, and in the fairly stiff tack up to Walton Pier, I began to fear again that the wind would freshen to the strength of the previous day, and just before I passed the pier I was perplexed and a little worried by the firing of two maroons from the Coast Guard Station- but then I saw the lifeboat setting out to seaward from the pier.

At about 10.30 after clearing the pier, the tide was discernably ebbing Northwards, and in order to keep in what I hoped would be slack water, I decided to keep in shore as much as the groins would allow. This ploy was aided by a wind back to south, although it fell steadily in strength as I progressed down the coast.

After passing Holland at 12.20 I was able to make a series of incresingly long fetches with occasional short tacks away from the shore. Around 13.00 (about three hours after H.W.) the strength of the ebb and the fallen wind strength meant that I lost a little ground on the short tacks, but apart from this, I made against the ebb tide all the time.

All the way to Colne Point, the sun shone, the wind blew in acceptable direction(s) and strength(1-2-3), and I had a thoroughly relaxed sail, during which I was able to consume at leisure my simple lunch whilst carting a benign but aloof eye over the holiday makers ranged in large and noisy numbers along the beaches. It was a complete and welcome contract to the previous day's conditions and I passed Colne Point at low water, and at the correct time, as planned, to start up the Blackwater with the rising tide. The wind by now was SE 3-4. Chart Y6 was now discarded in favour of the home waters chart, Stanfords No.4.

A thick haze to the west made it impossible to see marks in the Blackwater, so I sailed on a broad reach west, with Colne Point bouys 1&2 in live astern, and by the time I could no longer see the

continued.

-12-

Colne Point marks, the familiar bulk of the Power Station had loomed up. During this leg from Colne Point to Bradwell, the wind went round further to E.S.E. and the boat planned very readily, the long swell, as usual, helping to start the plane. Inside the shelter of Sales Point the wind eased, and I found that the boat would almost sail herself on a reach with genoa set and main left free, and I was able to spend twenty minutes or so making written notes ( I missed the tape recorder).

Passing Bradwell at 16.25, and Thirslet at 16,50 (wind S 1-2), my little trip finished with my arrival at Stansgate at 17.30.

The total voyage distance must be about sixty miles, of which thirty were covered in nearly nine hours continuous, if easy, sailing on the 10th of August, about seventeen miles in rather more robust conditions on the 9th and the remainder on the first day.

I had enjoyed it all immensely, and regretted only the nedessity of omitting the planned Stour leg to Manningtree- but there's always next year.

K.S. BEAVINS

18 FOOTERS.

IN THE BEGINNING

The predecessor of the present-day Eighteen Footer was the keeled open dinghy of 15-20ft. sailed in Sydney Harbour in the nineteenth century. At the turn of the century, most of thesewere 18ft. long by 8ft. beam and carvel built of cedar planking. The Tempest-sized mast of solid Oregon carried an 18½ft. gaff, and the boom measured 30ft. With the 40ft. spinnaker boom and other spars the total length of spars was 157ft. and, with spinnaker set running before the wind the boat could span a modern six-lane highway. Unrestricted sail area meant that 3,000 sq. ft. of Japara cloth was often carried in the mainsail, balloon jib, and romantic-sounding squaresail and raffee, ringtail, topsail and water sails. The weight of the crew alone with as many as 20 people on board amounted to over one ton. However, if the wind dropped, some of the crew members were discarded in mid-harbour and forced to swim home. The solid spars, hundreds of feet of natural fibre ropes, and steel centreboard weighing as much as a present-day bare hull, make us look back and wonder how they kept afloat. Indeed, capsizes were frequent, sometimes even caused by their competitors.

In the early 1930's the first 7ft. beam boat "Aberdare" was built in Brisbane and proved much faster than the wider beamed boats. A couple of years later "Arrawatta" appeared with a 50ft. bermudan rig and ran circles round her sisters. Consequently the gaff rig gradually disappeared as the advantages of the planing hull were realised and, instead od striving for maximum displacement speed, the boats became lighter, crew numbers were reduced (particularly after the advent of trapezes) and sail plan rationalised. From the boat!s evolution we have inherited a true thoroughbred, still retaining the breathtaking spectacle and dare-devil excitement of its sires.

Today an Eighteen Footer must be between 17ft.9in. and 18ft., not less than 6ft. wide with a minimum depth of 20in. from shearline to the deepest part of the hull. There is no minimum hull weight but spars and hull together rarely weigh more than 230-250 lbs. Sail area is still unrestricted, but most have found 1,600 sq.ft. to be the ultimate. The ideal is to have three complete rigs of different length masts and sails to choose from to suit the particular wind strength. If you want to win, you put up as much sail as you dare. In light airs a 36ft. mast would be used, setting a sail area of 380sq.ft. plus a 1,200sq. ft. spinnaker. All the crew members, whether three or four including the skipper, use trapezes. There is a minimum of three crew, but no maximum and no longer are crew members allowed to be discarded when the wind drops!

COMMERCIAL BACKING

Most of the Eighteen Footers sailing in Australia and New Zealand have commercial sponsors who, in return for providing the large amounts of cash required to finance an Eighteen, obtain enormous advertising benefits from the boat carrying the company's name on it's sail. This does not mean that the skippers are professional in any way, the sponsors' money being spent solely on the boat. Sponsors are often organisations which normally have no connection with the sailing world, such as hotel chains, newspapers, car accessory manufacturers, and so on. This form of sponsorship is relatively new in Britain but part of everyone's life in Sydney, where the Eighteen fleet is followed by spectators launches, and full reports of every race with spectacular photographs are a regular feature in the newspapers.

continued/

-4-

Sponsorship was introduced in 1919 when the Plume motor spirit company in Australia had its name on an Eighteen's sail. Today, in Europe, other sports such as football, cycling and tennis receive large amounts of money from sponsors. They find that, for example, it is better value and more rewarding to have a banner at a televised football match than to buy the same amount of time on an advertising spot. There are places in Britain where the same kind of spectator interest will be created by the Eighteen Footers as in Sydney Harbour and the opportunities for sponsors, particularly the first ones, are self-evident.

NOW FOR THE BRITTS IN THE BLACKWATER.

As a result of the appearance of the first British Eighteen Footer "Alfrodisiac" at various important open handicap meetings in 1973, many column inches in yachting magazines and national press have been devoted to its performance. Because of the enthusiasm created around this one boat, at least four others will be ready to sail in the 1974 season, after appearances at the Earls Court Boat Show (by kind permission of Jack Holt Ltd.) and the London Dinghy Exhibition at Crystal Palace.

These four were cold-moulded from a design by the expert Australian Hugh Cook, the mould and four hulls being completed by their intended crews in ten weeks.

The fleet will be based on the River Blackwater but will be appearing at major events on the south and south east coasts. Eighteen Footer Championships and trophy races are also planned.

The 18 Foot Skiff Club of Great Britain was inaugurated in March 1973 to conrdinate the affairs of the Class and to liaise with the World Championships Board of Control in Australia. The Club is now affiliated to the R.Y.A.

A CRUISE TO KENT
by Andy & Sue Dixon. Sept.1973.

INTRODUCTION

This account.is constructed from the day-to-day working log of SUZANNE-MARIE, our Drascombe Lugger, and covers our holiday cruise from, 16th. June to 29th. June 1973. The aims of the cruise were to explore the Kent coast from the Downs to the Medway, and if circumstances permitted, to pop across the channel to Calais. The fact that these aims were not quite fully realised did not detract from a very enjoyable and successful cruise -.not the least because we actually. had some sun this year!

SATURDAY 16th. June.

The Sailing Club Open Day - also the first day of our holidays!
& fine morning gave promise to a successful Open Day, which indeed it was. We dutifully did our bit by taking prospective members for a spin in SUZANNE-MARIE but by 1630 we could dally no longer, and md slipped off downstream with a salty beat into the fresh easterly .. :
breeze. Our first night destination was only Tollesbury Fleet, so it-was not long before the Nass was rounded and we were running up to the Leavings, where we brought up at 1815.We were glad to get our tent strung up between the two masts, as the breeze and the thickening haze had made it decidedly chilly for the last hour-or- so,

SO we settled down to-our first night of the cruise - always, I
think, the most exciting whilst still getting accustomed to the motion of the boat again, and with the prospect of the holiday before you. And especially as tomorrow we were hoping th make the long haul down to Ramsgate, Also

SUNDAY 17th. JUNE.

Up at 0500 to be greeted by the first accident of the holidays — I had slept on my spectacles and broken one of the arms!. Luckily. I had actually thought to bring a spare pair with me- a thing I usually forget.

The day promised fair again, although the wind had veered SW overnight, and a lot of altocumulus cloud was in evidence. We set off at 0620 ghosting down Tollesbury Fleet whilst receiving a reassuring shipping forecast -—- S, F3-4, veering W.. Round the Nass we had a fresh sail in a strengthened breeze for a while,- until it dropped right off again. To maintain our schedule we had to start the motorw to take us over the young flood to the Spitway,, from whence we continued under sail again. At 1020 we rounded the Barrow Beacon and set off in the gentle SW breeze to crab across the channels and shoals that radiate out from the Thames. The sea was mori the sun was warm, not another boat in sight and life was
good

‘Inspite ofa developing haze pilotage was easy - a matter of--
buoy hopping, allowing for tidal drift by keeping two buoys in transit. However, as we were crossing the Black Deep, life became not so good! The wind had been falling steadily so we resorted to the motor again, but before -long it coughed and spluttered to a halt. Whilst I was effecting temporary repairs to a spark plug connector, a tanker loomed out of the haze towards us and caused us to heave ‘to and have lunch while it passed. All the time the cloud cover had been increasing, trapping a sultry atmosphere under it,

vessel ele

-9-

and in particular the blackness amassing in the Kent direction made us somewhat apprehensime. However, the motor working again, we set off to enter the S, Edinburgh Channel. Suddenly, we found ourselves wallowing in a wave system of outrageous proportions! We were in fact cutting across some shoals to beat the last of the flood tide, and had not realised that the tide at this point flooded at least an hour or two after HW. Also, the channel doing a neat right angle bend here, the tide tends to take a short cut over the shallows, causing these alarming overfalls. We battled through with no mishaps, but were glad the engine did not falter again!

The tide was against us all the way down the S. Edinburgh, but once out of it the going was easier, although the motor remained on until the N. Foreland was close to. It was still overcast and sultry, but sufficient breeze piped up at this point to get sailing again. The peace and quiet was most appreciated after hours of motoring.

The last stretch was a pleasant close reach along the coast and at 1730 we motored through Ramsgate harbour entrance with a feeling of achievement that is only possible with a small open boat, and were directed alongside an old fishing boat in the outer harbour. After getting our clearance and paying our dues, we celebrated the successful voyage with a slap up meal ashore and a stroll along the prom. in the evening sun ( the clouds having cleared again!).

MONDAY 18th. JUNE.

Our first night in Ramsgate was not a success! Our little SUZANNE-MARIE was being smashed up against the rusty old fishing boat (alias salvage vessel, I believe) by the swell in the harbour; there seemed to be a party on a nearby yacht; and then the lifeboat maroon went off right over our heads. This all resulted in us seeking refuge in the inner harbour at 0030m when the gate was open for HW. Here we did eventually get to sleep,in spite of the trucks trundling along the quays loading cargo at all hours of the night.

The day was a lazy affair, although I got to know Ramsgate quite well whilst searching around for a replacement part for the outboard motor. It was ideal holiday weather - indeed so hot that Sue actually succeeded in dragging me in for a swim! Ramsgate is lucky in having a good beach so close to the harbour.

TUESDAY 19th. JUNE.

Having gone to bed early the evening before, our plan was to lock out on the midnight tide in readiness for the cross channel trip during the day. However, an 0030 shipping forecast of S, F5-6 was enough in our heavy-eyed state to persuade ourselves to stay where we were.

So another day was spent ashore, mainly in shopping and a stroll along the cliff top into Pegwell Bay. The day was fine again and the F5-6 never materialised, so we were somewhat kicking ourselves for not locking out. In the late afternoon it started becoming overcast and cooler, but we still went to bed early again with the hope of locking out in the night.

WEDNESDAY 20th. JUNE.

All thoughts of locking out were quickly dispelled by a crack of thunder at 0020. The wind was a good F6 now, even in the inner harbour, and the rain was bucketing down. On top of this, the forecast was gloomy again, so back to sleep!

continued/

-10-

The rain had eased off in the morning, and the wind with it. We were beginning to get fed up with Ramsgate by now, and were determined to lock-out with the early afternoon tide. Besides, the continual noise around the harbour, SUZANNE-MARIE was slowly being buried under a layer of Russian peat moss dust from a recent cargo stacked close by on the quay. So at 1350 we puttered out behind a continental coaster loaded with Fordson tractors (it seems we do export something!), and set off for Sandwich as it was too late to think of channel crossings in our little boat today. After negotiating the rather alarming swell at the harbour entrance, we motor-sailed against a light headwind, wanting to negotiate the shallow unknown River Stour before the tide fell too far. Whilst changing a fouled up sparking plug (the bane of my life!) misfortune struck again and took the spark plug spanner down to the sea bed with it! After that the engine had to run with the clean spark plug screwed in only hand tight.

After one small argument with a sandbank at the entrance, we headed upstream to discover a very attractive and unspoilt river. When we reached it at 1600, we thought the same of Sandwich too, except for the burden of heavy through traffic that quaint little town suffers.

A quick rush around the town reulted in another plug spanner, which of course, could not be made to fit the intricate recesses of our outboard motor. Attempted modification with a broken hacksaw blade brought no improvement so we resigned ourselves to another idle day whilst I tried to solve the problem tomorrow.

A drink ashore in the evening was followed by a much more peaceful and pleasant night than we had experienced in Ramsgate.

THURSDAY 21st. JUNE.

Even Sandwich had its noise problems - we were woken up at 0830 by the shriek of circular saws in a mill beside the river. The morning was spent solving the plug spanner problem. A visit to a nearby engineering works resulted in even more drastic modification of the spanner - all to no effect, but the final successful solution was to attack the engine covering itself, allowing the spanner to drop neatly into its slot.

The rest of the day was spent in exploring Sandwich and its environs, although we were hindered by a thick hazy mist which blanketed the soft country scenery. We would probably have run into fog trouble at sea anyway, if we had attempted our channel crossing today.

FRIDAY 22nd. JUNE.

Up at 0500 to attempt our belated crossing, setting off at 0640 after a favourable forecast, except for poor visibility.

We motored downstream into the wind, enjoying the fine start to the morning. However,approaching Pegwell Bay, we could see fog banks rolling in lazily from the sea, and what with a growing halo round the sun, we regretfully turned back and gave up all ideas of crossing the channel.

The northerly breeze gave us a fair wind to help punch against the tide up the Stour again. The tide runs strongly in the Stour, and at Sandwich ebbs for nine hours out of every twelve! The river twists like a demented snake and is very shallow in places, but we managed to sail nearly all the way back to Sandwich, only using the engine on a couple of unfavourable reaches.

-11-

We were back at Sandwich by lunchtime, and after a quick shopping spree we set off to explore the upper reaches of the Stour. This meant lowering the masts to go undder the occasional bridge, but after one long reach where the river doubles back on itself almost to the mouth again, we raised the mainmast, stopped the engine, and proceeded to sail the rest of the way up the Stour. The sky had cleared again but the wind had increased steadily during the day, and as we sailed inland, strong gusts would hit us and send us creaming along at an exhilarating pace between the narrow banks. We were now sailing from an O.S. map instead of a chart, and were glad to know when to expect bridges so that we could drop the mast in time!

We sailed through lush rural countryside, raising a few angling eyebrows, then the Kent coalfield, and then a reservoir! Above the reservoir the river became progressively choked with water lilies and barely three miles from Canterbury we came to a cloggy halt, and returned back to Groveferry, a pretty little spot with riverside moorings and a pub. We drew up by the river bank and retired to the pub for refreshment, only to be disturbed by the water bailiff who wanted us to move SUZANNE-MARIE. It would seem that we'd moored up at the prize angling spot of his stretch of the river!

SATURDAY 23rd. JUNE.

This was the second black night of the holliday! The Stour would appear to be above all an angling river, and an all night fishing party insisted on getting as close as possible to us, and despite entreaties, kept a shouting conversation going all night. I thought anglers were searchers of peace and solitude too! We had intended to spend another night at Groveferry, but it was first necessary to find a quieter mooring. An alternative berth suggested by the bailiff casually remarked that he was expecting ten coach loads on the following day. This was all too much for us, so we quickly set off and motored back downstream to Sandwich for the night.

SUNDAY 24th. JUNE.

We were beginning to yearn for the open sea again, and fortune smiled on us with a clear sky but little wind. We set off from Sandwich, motoring downstream against the last of the flood, but on reaching Pegwell Bay we hoisted the sails and beat our way up the coast past Ramsgate. There was some swell from yesterdays strong winds, but todays wind was light and when the tide turned we had to resort to the moter to push us round the N. Foreland. Once round the Longnose buoy, the northerly breeze gave us a good beam reach along the Kent coast, and the warm hazy sun made it a very pleasant sail.

As the dominating landscape of Margate drew astern, a more puzzling sight developed ahead. A conglomeration of sailing dinghies and speed boats were in our path, and yes, people could be seen walking about. The only strange thing about this spectacle was that it was a good two miles offshore! Our course brought us close alongside the Margate Hook Sands which were obviously a popular playground at low water.

We sauntered along the coast and eventually picked up the entrance to the Swale, running up it with a freshening wind behind us. Although locating this channel might present problems in hazy weather, all we had to do was follow the host of other Sunday sailors. We picked out Faversham Creek leading off to the port, and sizzled into it to find shelter at its junction with Oare Creek, a spot with the quaint name of Hollowshore. Although it was a fine day still, we were

continued/

-12-

glad to get the tent up to get out of the chilly wind that had built up, and after a deliciousmeal of risotto, we retired to the Shipwrights Arms for a noggin before bedtime.

MONDAY 25th. JUNE.

We woke up to a warm and windless morn, with full cloud cover and a fairly thick mist making nearby power pylons crackle. Apart from these pylons, Faversham Creek was a very charming and unspoilt spot, and with very few yachts to choke it up either!

After a leisurely morning we strolled into Oare for a Ploughmans lunch and on to Faversham to do some shopping. Whilst there, we found the reason for the emptiness of Faversham Creek. Jack Coote in his book, EAST COAST RIVERS, stated that the occasional barge uses the creek, but what we saw was a tanker! Small as tankers go, but a fair giant for this little creek. On returning back to SUZANNE-MARIE our first priority was to move inshore a little - a thing requiring careful judgement as only a narrow gut carries any water at low tide, and the exposed banks are steep too. However, during our evening meal, this coastal tanker, BP HAULIER, headed downstream and passed us somewhat too closely for comfort. The skipper evidently thought so too, and gesticulating madly, said he would be back on the morning tide. We then had the choice of trying alongside a yacht in Oare Creek, which is not a suitable thing to do with SUZANNE-MARIE if the mooring dries out, or trying to find a hollow in the mouth of Oare Creek away from the tanker path. Whilst attempting this with a leadline, we confused another yacht sufficiently for him to ground on the nearest sandbank. Luckily a passing local pulled him off and then offered us a mooring for the night, a drying one admittedly, but he thought it was not too steep at that point.

After another evening at the Shipwrights Arms, incidently a quaint olde-worlde place miles from anywhere by road, we retired to bed, but not to sleep, as very soon after the boat leaned right over at a terrible cant and we spent the night at about 45 degrees!

TUESDAY 26th. JUNE.

After the previous night it was definitely going to be a move-on day. Whilst getting breakfast, a heavily laden BP HAULIER came literally scraping up with the tide - going backwards! There was definitely no turning room upstream.

It was another calm misty day, but as we set off a light NE breeze developed which soon freshened sufficiently to push us over the foul tide up the Swale. The warm but misty weather made pleasant sailing, but hid most of the scenery from us. By midday we had reached the Kingsferry Bridge and had to stooge around for half an hour until the bridge opened. We did not need to hoist the special signal of a bucket in the rigging, as another yacht had already done so. When at last the bridge opened, what a feeling of power as along queue of cars developed while three yachts passed through!

We now had the tide with us and were soon passing Queenborough with strengthening gusts of wind giving us some exciting sailing. At last we entered the Medway, hoping that not too many big ships were charging around in the poor visibility. We headed upstream and turned "first left" into Stansgate Creek, and at 1345 dropped anchor in a remote and sheltered spot at the head of the creek.

continued/

-13-

Again we were glad to get some shelter, especially as the cloud was thickening. The rest of the day was spent relaxing and reading as the weather got greyer outside the tent. Then at 2100 it broke, with a great peal of thunder and a really violent downpour - so bad that some water actually got inside the tent!

WEDNESDAY 27th. JUNE.

Another misty day - visibility as low as 1/4 mile. At 1115 we weighed anchor and sailed into the mist. A light NE breeze took us out of Stansgate Creek and just about pushed us over the strong ebb tide as we headed up the Medway. Visibility was such that we were glad to hoist a radar reflector that we had bought in Ramsgate. We buoy hopped up the Medway, any scenery being for the most part blanketed from us. We encountered surprisingly few ships considering the industrial nature of the Medway. In fact, the first vessel we met bore the familiar emblem of the sailing barge KITTY on its topsail!

The engine was required for a while to help us over the tide, but by 1500 we were off Gillingham, where we picked up a buoy and went ashore to do some shopping. On returning, we found that the air had cleared a little and the wind was brisker, giving us a good sail up the next reach to the Medway Yacht Club at Upnor. Here we picked up a buoy close under the stern of T.S. ARETHUSA and settled down for a night at one of the prettiest spots on the Medway, with wooded hills sweeping right down to the waters edge.

THURSDAY 28 th. JUNE.

Yet another grey cold day, but not so misty. However, by the time we had got the tent down and set off at 1100, it was raining quite steadily. The wind had gone southerly today, and we beat upstream with the last of the flood to have a look at Chatham and Rochester from the water. The towns look rather pleasant, perched up on a hill, but don't live up to one's expectations when ashore!

We then ran back downstream with the new ebb, and coming out of the shelter of the Rochester hills, found a fresh breeze. We took a short cut over the flats into Hoo Marsh Passage, cutting off Gillingham Reach. It was lucky we did not go aground with a strong wind behind us and the tide falling rapidly by now. A rip roaring reach all the way down to Stansgate Creek followed, the wind veering right round to NW and increasing to F5. We could now see the scenery we missed on the journey up - perhaps it was better with the mist! We nosed our way to Sharfleet Creek, and dropped anchor in a nice sheltered spot at 1350. It was a lonely spot with marshy islands and salting all around, and it was difficult at low water to believe that we were bound on three sides by a busy industrial port.

The afternoon was spent relaxing and reading,and generally we were glad to stay in the shelter of our tent. However, in the evening the sun broke through, and a ramble on one of the islands brought the day to a close.

FRIDAY 29th. JUNE.

We had set the alarm clock for the 0030 shipping forecast, but need not have bothered! Just after midnight we were woken by a thump and shouting, and found that another yacht that had come to the anchorage in the afternoon had now dragged its anchor down on to us. It was not immediately obvious who was at fault so to save argument we weighed our anchor and motored out of the way. It was very

continued/

-14-

disconcerting because the tide was now in, all but covering the low marshy islands and giving the impression of being right in the middle of the big industrial port!

In the morning we woke to a fine day - it was nice to see the sun again! However, the westerly wind registered a good F5 on our ventimeter and it was with some trepidation that we set off 1020 with reefed main and mizzen, bound back to the Blackwater. Coming out of Stansgate Creek we overhauled another Drascombe Lugger that had evidently spent the night in the creek - we are not only the ones with dinghy camping madness!

Wind over tide in the Medway made for some interesting sailing. We were heading out over the last of the flood, but even so the current was running strongly still and we had to keep to the Grain shore to make any headway at all.

Garrison Point at Sheernes was our point of decision - go on or turn back? The shipping forecast was good, the sky bore no foreboding clouds and the chop should decrease when the tide turned, so we carried on.

Heading down the Medway Channel we had to pass the ROBERT MONTGOMERY - wartime munitions wreck close to port, and as we approached it (superstructure and rigging visible above water) a ship was heading up the channel as well. It seemed to have an escort of miniature tugs - until we got our proportion right and found ourselves staring at a super sized supertanker. We were a bit nervous - with a dangerous wreck on one side and a great monster filling the channel on the other side!

Once out in the Thames, the wind moderated to F4, so we shook out the reefs and set a course for the Blacktail Spit off Maplin. Nearing the Spit, we could see an artificial sandbank on the Maplin Sands, apparently erected to do tidal studies concerning the proposed airport. Having reached the edge of Maplin, it was now just a matter of steering from buoy to buoy up to the Spitway, although we were a bit dubious about the great reverberating booms and accompanying palls of smoke coming from the direction of Foulness!

1620 saw us at the Wallet Spitway buoy - the first familiar sign of home waters. However, the wind had veered slightly and we now had a beat against the still ebbing tide. By the time we reached the Knoll the wind had dropped and become variable, and by 1830 we had got as far as the Bench Head! The tide was now on our side but it still took us another 1½ hours to reach the Mersea Nass. The wind was now very light and evening drawing on, so we furled the sails and motored the last stretch up to Stansgate, picking up our mooring at 2100.

And so the trip from Stansgate to Stansgate made a fine ending to a most enjoyable cruise. It was our longest so far in SUZANNE-MARIE, lasting 15 days and covering 200 miles. The generally fine weather (warmer than last year, at any rate!) helped us to settle down to the rrather spartan life of dinghy camping, although we survived three or so days of heavy rain with no more than the odd dribble to dampen our spirits. Perhaps Ramsgate excepted, we thoroughly enjoyed the Kent coast and have added considerably to our list of places to revisit.

EDITORIAL

Did you spot last month's 'deliberate mistake'. Dinghy transplanting from the Cottam's is on SUNDAY 24th March and not as printed in last month's Navigans. Sorry about that. If you are down moving your boat perhaps you would like to join the working party as well, the start of the season isn't far away now, and there's plenty of tidying up to do now after the winter gales. One person who has worked hard this winter is Claude. He's the chap you never see, who mows the grass and clears up on Monday that soggy mess we all leave in the club house on a Sunday night. Last year he repainted the clubhouse and this year he has help't with the club launches and boats. I'm sure we'd all like to give him our thanks for doing a grand job.

Could I please have some more material from the dinghy fleets. I receive very little dinghy news and now is the time of year when people are buying new boats and a lot is happening. And what has happened to all our correspondents since taking over from Dot I havn't received any letters on club matters or policy at all. So put pen to paper and write me a letter. Food for thought, a club member wispered in my ear that they thought the club was turning into an institution for 'middle-aged potter's'.....any comments.

[redacted].

COMMODORES NOTES

Membership renewals have been coming in at a gratifying rate, and our foolish fears that the general alarm and despondancy would extend to sailing appear to be groundless, thank goodness. Neverthe less, we are anxious to increase our ordinary membership, so do encourage your friends in the company to join us, even if they haven't a boat.

Many of you are aware of the enthusiasm and hard work that Bruce Long has put into building and encouraging the development of the 18' Sydney Harbour Skiffs. However, you may not be aware that these boats are maintained in part by sponsorship, which involves advertising brand names on the sails. Bruce has applied for his boat to sail from the club, as an M.S.C. registered boat, but our club rule 24 states, 'Members shall not display gross forms of advertising at the club, or on or about boats registered with the club.' Furthermore, the R.Y.A. have a similar rule, and we are affiliated to the R.Y.A. We are informed by the Skiff Class that the R.Y.A. are considering a change in their rules regarding sponsorship. Your committee have made the following decision. Bruce will be allowed to sail his boat from Stansgate for this season, without prejudice to future action. We will have to arrange an Extraordinary General Meeting (or at the A.G.M.) to consider the clubs feeling regarding our own rule, and take action accordingly. Our action may be influenced by the R.Y.A. decision.

No doubt there will be plenty of discussions on this point during the season, but most of us felt our decision the best compromise in the circumstances.

DENNIS BYATT.

FALLING IN THE WATER

Compared with the high accident rate of road users, sailing is a relatively safe pastime. However, accidents do occur, and when they do are usually more serious as often rescue is either a long way away or more difficult to obtain. It is therefore more important to take precautions and also to know what to do when an accident does occur.

According to the Registrar General's Statistical Review for I962, there were 898 deaths in the waters around England and Wales, including 72 deaths due to submersion of the occupant of a small boat and 40 due to other water-transport injury by submersion. Total tragedies are not that infrequent in our own Blackwater which compared with many sailing areas, is sheltered, and potential rescuers not far away.

Why do people die when they fall in water. Other than attack by sharks or mechanical injury there are three main causes of death.

I. Hypothermia, i.e. lowering of body temperature due to the cold

2. Drowning i.e. filling the lungs with water, and

3. Vaso-vagal shock, i.e. the shock of water entering the lower pharynx or upper respiratory passages causing a nervous reflex which stops the heart.

To deal with these in turn, the first is by far the commonest cause of death due to immersion. In the unfortunate Lakonia disaster, of the I24 deaths, there is strong evidence to show that apart from II deaths due to injury, most of the remaining II3 were due to hypothermia leading to helplessness, unconciousness and then drowning only as a terminal event. When you consider that the water temperature was 64°F, a temperature never obtained around England, and that help was relatively quickly obtained, you will realise how important is heat loss.

It has been shown that few people survive for more than seven hours in water at 59° F, again much higher than British sea temperatures, and the survival time in water at 32°F is only a matter of minutes.

As on land, the best way of keeping warm in the water is to wear warm clothing. Into this category come 'wet suits' of which I have no personal experience, but which should be the best of all. If you can get out of the water and sit in your dinghy so much the better as unless the wind is particularly cold your heat loss is slower. Contrary to what might be expected, movement in the water accelerates heat loss as the extra heat generated by muscular effort is more than offset by the removal of the warmer layer of water around, and heated by, the body. Therefore unless it is toswim a short distance to a rescue boat or the shore it is much better to lie as stillas possible in the water supported by a life-jacket. As the time of immersion is obviously an important factor, one should stay as near as possible to the pointwhere rescue might be expected. This usually means staying near the boat.

There is no evidence to show that alcohol in normal quantities accelerates heat loss, which may be of some comfort to those of us who imbibe.

In the Lakonia disaster it is known that I5 people died from hypothermia afterbeing picked up so it is important, should you rescue someone who has been immersed for some time , to warm them up as quickly as possible. This is really only important if the rescued is unconscious as conscious people are unlikely to be in danger. The quickest method of warming someone is a warm bath- temperature 97°F-I00°F, but this is only of use if they can be bathed within 20 minutes and is seldom feasible.

continued over.....

10.

A warm atmosphere, hot water bottles, the close proximity of another human body and warm blankets after removal of the cold wet clothing are the usual methods. So if you cannot rescue yourself, wear warm clothing, keep still and make it as easy as possible for your rescuers by staying near the boat or where they expect you to be.

To pass on to the last two headings, prevention is - wear a good life jacket and hold your breath as you go in. Once a person has ceased to breath, irreversible brain damage occurs within 3-5 mins so that any attempt to revive them must be made immediately. If drowning is complicated by hypothermia the chande of successful revival is very small.

Before considering how to revive a person let us consider briefly what happens when lungs fill with water. The water may be fresh or sea water. In the former case the osmotic pressure of the blood causes a rapid absorption of water from the lungs into the blood which so lowers the osmotic pressure of the blood that the red cells burst, releasing a large amount of potassium which the heart cannot tolerate and it stops. This takes place very rapidly, as roughly speaking theminute sacs in the lungs, if all spread out would cover tennis court and they are designed specially to absorb.

In the latter case the reverse occurs as the osmotic pressure of sea water is higher than that of the blood and this causes an outflow of fluid from the blood stream, flooding the lungs and preventing oxygen getting into the blood. The heart can keep beating for a few minutes after this occurs, so the chances of successful revival are much higher.

The treatment of drowning and also of vaso-vagal shock is the same namely artificial respiration. I am sure that the simplest and most effective method is mouth to mouth respiration-perhaps better known as the kiss of life. As with all unconscious people, including unconsciousness due to hypothermia, the first essential is to maintain a clear airway. This is done by hooking the forefingers of each hand behind the angle of the jaw of the rescued and lifting the jaw, and thereby the tongue, forward. If possible the lower teeth can be hooked over the upper teeth.

It is a waste of time attempting to empty water from the lungs of the rescued. It is much better to attempt to inflate that part of the lung which is not filled with water - usually a considerable proportion.. If you kneel facing the feet it is possible to lift the jaw forward, hold the lips together in an airtight joint and breathe gently down the nose. In this position one can watch the chest to see it inflate. Remarkably little effort is required and adequate time should be allowed for the chest to deflate, about three times as long as the inflation period. If the airway is clear, i.e. the tongue is not blocking the back of the throat, the movement of the chest should be gentle and easy.

I don't know how long one should continue this as it is mainly a moral question. If one considers that the brain is dead after five minutes and quadruples this time, I think this is reasonable and is the criterion I have taken on the few occasions I have had to do it.

It is important to realise that if the rescued is breathing it is positively dangerous to give artificial respiration. This will only hinder their own respiratory efforts and possibly inflate the stomach, blowing vomit into their air passages and killing them.

continued.....

II.

It is only necessary to keep a clear airway and keep them warm.

One last point I must mention is the question of vomiting. In a conscious person they will get rid of their own vomit but in an unconscious person they may well inhale it with fatal results. Turn them on their side with the head lower than their waist, and no fluid can possibly enter the lungs.

This article has turned out to be much longer than I anticipated but even so is only an outline of what happens when one 'falls in the water'.

Greater pens than mine have said 'prevention is better than cure' and it is never more true than of sailing accidents.

A. DOCTOR.

The following log was written by Peter and Gill Foreman whose boat Roulette was the smallest of the six from the cruiser section who made the trip across the Channel last season. The other five boats were:-

Stan Campbell's Tijo, Macwester 26, Jack Manning's Jappa
Ken Steven's Carousou, Contest 25 and Vic Tate's Snowgoose I.P.23

CALAIS TRIP July-August I973.

The log of Roulette.

It seemed a very pleasant idea to make a cruise in company to Calais, especially being such novices as Peter and I in both navigation and weather forecasting. The crew was varied throughout our trip on Roulette, but at all times all 2I' was well utilised! At the start the crew comprised Dick Meader, Geoff Farnie and Peter. While we didn't accomplish all we had hoped due to bad weather, it was all well worth while and the following log resulted:-

Saturday July 2Ist.

Wind whistling in rigging, crew drinking coffee and discussing possibility of going to Ramsgate, general feeling against the trip.

04.00. Boat rolling heavily on mooring with a strong tide and N. Westerly fetching up fair waves. Guess wind strength 5+. Set alarm for 6.30am. First mistake, must set earlier than wanted, missed Thames weather, but a lot of force 6 about. No sign of life on the other boats! Seems unlikely to make passage today so decided to sail to Bradwell to familiarize Dick and Geoff with the boat. Set course for Brightlingsea at I7.00. with S.W. force 5-6 blowing. Past Stone at I7.I5 with a good tide under us as well. Full sail was a bit hairy and we made Thirslet Spit by I7.20. where we put in 2 rolls in the main! TheNass was abeam at I7.53. and the wreck at I8.24, No I0 abeam I8.50. Turned away from Brightlingsea by Harbour Master at I9.00 so anchored in Pyefleet Channel and had dinner. Set alarm for I2.30 when Dick was to note weather forecast and reset for 3.00am.

Sunday July 22nd.

03.00 Geoff and I(Pete) decided to motor over to Brightlingsea to search for the others, after a quick breakfast weighed anchor and picked up the red leading lights quite easily instead of the usual stumps. Woke Vic at 4.00, who made us a cup of tea and back to bed. The 6.30am weather forecast, more depressions and strong winds about. Waited making good use of the time to put on a new mainsheet and secure Dennis' Redstart rubber dinghy on the top deck with flares, pump and baler tied within and tucked up out of the way. The I7.55 forecast not favourable so took solace in the pub after fish and chips. One thing one learnt on this trip was that one should never bank on being off on the first day of one's holiday!!

Monday July 23rd.

The first of our crew left the ship! Dick had to return to work having been unable even to reach Ramsgate as hoped!! Having rowed him ashore Geoff and I walked off our frustrations on a trip to St.Osyth. The replacement crew(Gill and Tim) arrived in time for a much remembered trip to Wivenhoe on Snowgoose. All 24 bedraggled and disheartened souls were seen to arrive in one boat to the amazement of the owners of the quay where we asked permission to come ashore. The Pakistani's had nothing on us! Everything was very quiet in the town and one can only assume that the inhabitants stayed behind shuttered windows while the tiny streets were beseiged by such a motley crew! Having circum navigated the town we left at I8.00 and after an excellent scampi and chips at the Freemason's Arms and one pint of cider, the holiday spirit had at last been instilled. Peter sobered up tying the rubber dinghy once more to the cabin top in the high hopes of a start at 5.00 the following day.

continued...

Tides @ Sheerness 07.I7. L.W.I304, H.W.I9.30. Swin H.W.06.47.

I3.30 Engine trouble. Changed plugs, No one noticed our plight although we hooted- later found Jappa had heard but thought we were messing about, suggested that another time one should sound continuous burst and turn at right angles to course. If in real trouble can turn foresail upside down. Revs still not right but continued on our way.

I4.I0 Mid channel buoy abeam. Average speed approx 3½kn.

I5.30 Engine trouble. Cut suddenly but Stan had already turned to check why we were slipping back. Threw us a line but only needed to tow for 2 mins. before engine restarted after changing plugs. Added 2 galls of petrol. Revs restored. Not too much trouble with shipping lanes, had to avoid one shortly after Stan had assisted us, had turn up tide, wake not as bad as the ferries which gave very steep short troughs. Rather like narrows. Either due to delays or wrong estimated course arrived well below target buoy. Cape Gris seemed too close. Big swell in harbour entrance considering no wind and had to race with ferry to get in. Motor seemed to have no revs! Psychological! Tied up in outer harbour and waited like starters in Grande Prix to get into the Marina. Nearly a divorce because Pete wouldn't get in the queue! All in on one trot. Margaret Farnie and kids arrived, cooked the mackeral caught on the spinner en route. We kept seven but could have had many more, threw the small ones back. Had a drink in the clubhouse and then to bed.

Thursday July 26th.

07.00 Up to see the 2nd. member of our crew off, with many thanks for moral support espcially when the motor gave up! and a certain amount of trepidation on Gill's part about the passage home as Ist mate. Talking of moral support, our first trip was a rapid march to the customs to get clearance and our green card for duty free! Our early start was frustrated by the closing of the swing bridge to enable a large cargo boat to come into the Marina. We arrived to find the customs shut but they very obligingly opened again and patiently took all our information, I wonder if our equivalents would have been so long suffering. Once we had put in our orders at Dekkyspotters, a whole-saler we found very easily with the aid of Stan, who had been before, and knew the ropes. We returned to the boat and consumed the last of the delicious mackeral and then set about clearing our prop shaft which we found to be fouled by engine room cotton. Presumably thrown overboard by the Sea Link that came very close immediately before we seized-up! Five stalwart men balanced on the bowsprits which allowed the stern to rise enough for Richard to clear the prop from his dinghy. Took the boat for a trail run up and down the Marina until the captain was satisfied then settled down to a lazy afternoon and a lively evening aboard Tijo.

Friday July 27th.

Dull and overcast again, after bright intervals. Peter took carburetter off and cleaned out the sludge, also filter while Tim and Gill went into town to sightsee. It is very evident that Calais suffered terribly in the I939-45 war and the old historical town was totally destroyed during the occupation. It has been rebuilt in the modern manner and new industries has improved her economic potential and the lace industry continues to offer employment to a large part of the population. It has become a really important French port with routes from Dover, Folkestone and Ramsgate. We're always horrified at the thought of turning "Navigans" or indeed the club into a "thou shalt not". I'm sure you'll all agree that the only way to run a volutarily organised social club like ours is on the basis of "Courtesy and Consideration", and it is nearly always the small things that help the most. Bringing back the tea cups and beer mugs, and not dropping litter make all the difference. Funnily enough, its nearly always the small things that we get most complaints about. In particular, there have been increasing complaints about dogs running lose and fouling surronds. Even more important is the nusiance and danger caused by cars being driven in the club precincts atquite ridiculous speeds. During fitting out, it is not unreasonable for members to occassionally drive their cars into the dinghy park, but this must be minimised and discontinued as soon as possible. If you do take your car beyond the car park, keep your speed to a walking pace please.

For the rest of this season, you are asked to park your cars in the big triangular field on the right, as you enter the site.

Also, please note that the building site is strictly out of bounds It is particularly dangerous for children, and any disruption of meterials or equipment can only be reflected in delays and increased cost.

Sorry about the sermon, we hope it's infrequent.
