...and took some time to regain buoy. Altered course 235°M visibility still less than 1½ miles.
11.45 Sand end abeam (5½ miles)
12.00 Aground up Oare Creek alongside the Shipwrights Arms, the setting was ideal; The landing stage could only be described as hazardous even when sober, though some amongst us found it was also picturesque! The weather and the feeling of splendid isolation was magnificent we sat and soaked up the sun, at last, and had no desire to go anywhere.

Thursday August 2nd.

Awoke to another beautiful day but at a distant angle, being the outside boat again. The creek had become a mere trickle over night and we were surrounded by a sea of mud. We wandered up to Oare village and remarked at what an ideal hideout, after a robbery this would be!! So if we disappear one day don't show anyone this log!! We visited the chandlers as well as stocking up on food supplies again, and bought a red ensign to replace the one we'd borrowed for the trip. The owners of the chandlers had been in business there for years and had plenty of stories of the modern idiots that went aground in Oare Creek!! We left Oare Creek about 14.20 and motored up the River Swale and under the Sheerness-Queensborough Bridge. On raising a bucket up one's mast the traffic was stopped, a considerable amount by the time 4 boats had gone through; a mile of traffic both sides plus a train. We motor sailed at a fast pace to Queensborough with Gill at the helm on a broad reach and full throttle. Pete went below to make a chaos sandwich and came up to pick up the mooring! (I'd been longing to put the reeves up for the entire trip so on this occassion I got my own way!) The moorings at Queensborough were beautiful, good and strong but too far from the hard for us to bother to blow up the dinghy and go ashore

Friday August 3rd.

Alarm at 4.0am, up at 4.15am, stilldark, cup of tea, the tent down (I must explain once all 3 children were aboard we needed to cover the cockpit in order to have storage for our clothes etc.) and cases stowed inside the main cabin as the children were still asleep. We cleared the cockpit ready for a rough day's sailing- force 4-5 forecast, but from the S.W. so should be a good run or broad reach, Roulettes best tack.
04.40 Left mooring at Queensborough, navigation lights on, we motored out with visibility good with lights and general glow in the sky. No fog was forecast. We set the spritsail and mizzen, but no mainsail as we wanted maximum visibility to pick out the various flashing lights on buoys. We headed past the quick flashing red lights of the rail head towards Queensborough Spit which came abeam at 4.55am, one nasty moment when a pusher barge turnedthrough 90° to head straight for us. Took course 05° for black and white buoy off Isle of Grain Hard. Tide already setting us towards Sheerness side, no traffic about.
05.05am Sheerness Point abeam
05.10 W. Cant to starboard, headed 70° for first starboard navigation buoy. Set roller foresail.
05.25 Grain Edge and 1st channel buoy in line, wind dropped or was right behind. 45 mins for 3 miles, average speed 4 knots.
05.30 Ammunition ship clearly visible. Headed offout of channel
05.35 No.8 abeam, mainsail set, tide slooshing past buoy.
05.45 Midway between 6-4 buoys, navigation lights out. Gill at the helm having pups at crossing the main navigation channel 19 ships visable, some moving, most moored due to dock strike in London.
05.50 No.4 passed, 50 yd wake behind due to tide!
05.55 Altered course 40°M for Sea Reach No1 Now caught up on time completely, 3 miles in 30 minutes- average speed 6 knots, 2½ tide, 3½ boat
continued.. ....

9.

Sea very calm, dead run i.e.S.W. as predicted.
06.15 Took avoiding action with respect to large vessl at Sea Reach No.1(20 mins for 1.6 miles-5 knots) coaster very obligingly headed S.E. turned back on course. Straight for moored vessels aiming for E. Shoesbury buoy- most direct. Listened to 6.30 forecast W3-4-5-in Humber. Latticed tower now built to E. of E. Shoesbury Beacon. Also long spit of land not shown on charts. Visibility good. Heading 0-20 through moored boats quite safely. Black tail Spit Beacon west and warps on the nose.
06.44 In line. Still 5 knots despite gilling about.
06.53 Blacktail Spit E. Beacon and Buoy in line. Over 5½knts. Felt justified in cutting motor, dead run, headed for W. Barrow by mistake at 90°M turned 40°M for Maplin.
07.33 S.E. Maplin and W Barrow abeam still over 5½ knts, delightful sail and help from the tide. Peter did quick calculation to give E.T.A. at various buoys so as to establish that we were not dropping behind schedule.
E.T.A.10.00 Swin Buoy i.e. low water.
07.35 Maplin abeam.
08.05 Maplin Spit abeam-rain- 5 knots still, no need for motor 10 mins ahead of required schedule. Altered course 20°M for N.E. Maplin, however due to tidal set had to alter course again to due N.-20 degrees leeway.
08.10 N.E. Maplin coming up fast Barrow Beacon and W. Swin clearly visible. Wind 2-3 plus spring tide-good.
08.34 N.E. Maplin- Rain stopped.4½ knots.
08.50 S.W. middle abeam, Whitaker Beacon ahead. Altered course 15°M. for S. Whitaker, 35° desired course still fair set due to tide.
09.00 Visibility improved, several fishing vessels.
09.36 S. Whitaker abeam, barely any tide straight for Spitway, course due N. Echo sounder on. Pole taken out of roller foresail. Crossed Whitaker Spit safely, depth dropped from 48' to 20' in about 50 yds.Minimum depth 7'. Other boats seen in the distance, Jappa and Snowgoose very distinctive- presume they left 1 hr behind us, later found 1½ hr behind.....but they had motor sailed! After S. Whitaker Kept N. 350° and Swin came up nicely ahead. Wind strngthening 3 from W.
10.13 Swin Spitway abeam, only 3 knots. Headed 340 through channel on gorgeous broad reach, 7' minimum depth- other boats catching up fast having cleared Whitaker Spit more generously than us.
10.32 Wallet Spitway abeam i.e. 3 knots through the channel.
10.50 Jappa caught us up before the Knoll, sailing beautifully brfore we could get the camera out she passed us, we put motor on full revs but could not hold her.
11.07 Eagle abeam 4 knts- close hauled and motoring, course 320°M
11.05 Carassou passed.
11.20 Thundercloud, Snowgoose and Tijo passed.
11.22 Bar Buoy abeam, didn't make enough allowance for tidal set across the bar.
11.44 Colne Point and Inner Bench in line 4-4½ knots i.e. fair tide. Kept in main channel to take full advantage of the tide and over the measured ½ mile made 5 knots. Beautiful broad reach headed due N. Dropped sails hove to and dropped mainsail at Inner Starboard Buoy. Nearly drifted into fishing vessel so turned motor on and headed into main channel- Brightlingsea.
12.30 On trots at Brightlingsea. i.e. under 8 hrs for 33 miles at over 4 knots. Estimate 1kn overal due to tide, 3 kn on boat. Went ashore straight away after blowing up the Avon. Shopping - and fish and chips at the harbour cafe, excellent at £1.78p and 1 gallon of petrol, glad we took full advantage of the tide and left early. ½ gall. an hour.
continued...

10.

Wind blew up late afternoon and boats came in to shelter. Listened to 5.55pm forecast. Cosy evening read and did log, kids crabbed. Wind blew up in the night.

Saturday August 4th.

Heard 6.30am weather forecast, promised 6-7 later so decided to leave on last of the ebb. Left trots at 1.20 and motored to the end of the creek, raised all sail and went down on tide to No. 10, then 8 but had no wind as we drifted towards Wreck Buoy course 215°M 220°M. No wind, no tide.
11.20 Frustated so put on motor, met more wind towards Bradwell but dead on the nose so decided to make passage by motor. Interested to find that course 245°M approx from Wreck Buoy took us close by barrage and straight up the river to Stansgate. Despite wind over tide(force4) not very choppy at all. Reached Bradwell in an hour 1220, 6knots.
13.15 Stansgate. What a trip, a marvellous experience , now we can do our own navigation!

Peter and Gill Foreman.

To the Editor of Navigans, could the following please be published in April's issue.

An error in the article "Falling in the water", could result in the speeding up of hypothermia instead of the recovery.

The last paragraph on page 9, 5th. line states; "As the conscious people are unlikely to be in danger". How near to unconsious is a conscious person. Everyone pulled out of the water should be considered as a potential case until proved otherwise.

The first line on page 10, "Hot water bottles". Hot water bottles can increase the degree of hypothermia by drawing more heat away from the inner core, therfore they should not be used. Also a warm atmosphere in this part of the world in unlikely to be sufficent.

If ever my life needs saving I hope the rescuers know the symptoms and the correct treatment, and to keep my end of the partnership I have made it my business to find out about all the points of first aid needed in sailing.

C.Leveridge, New Street.

THE VARNE 27- QUICK!

Success if all things to all men; an impossibility to measure in equal terms.

The only certainty is that no matter the manifestation by which we recognize it success is usually the result of a combination of a number of things foremost among these being luck, opportunity and hard work. Given these three ingredients add a dash of expertise and it would be fairly certain that success is assured the intrepid.

So it has been with Varne Marine of Canvey.

A new company- just one year old!- young in ideas and enthusiasm, they are the innovators of an exciting new project in sailing: the Varne 27, wedge shape: fine for'd full aft: low wetted area and quick!

The luck of it!

Following a film show- Sailing in the Med- a few words in conversation between Duncan Stuart, an aircraft designer with ideas about sailing and Walter Standing- both until that moment complete strangers - sufficient to enthuse Walter to bring his particular brand of driving tenacity to bear on the task of providing the financial opportunity from which to launch the new venture.

Premises were found, fitted out and staff engaged during the month of March '73 and the task of bringing the idea to shape began. Discussion, research and experience decided that the requirement was for a fast medium sized cruiser, capable of competing with the best yet offering the cruising man and his family safe passage making; to conform to half ton cup rating yet with modest draught to enable the remotest creek to be ventured.

Above all she would contain quality.

To this end, meticulous detail was included at every design stage, all were conversant with the required standard and work began in earnest. Plugs, for hull, deck structure and interior mouldings were highly finished in six hard working months and the first 27 was launched in January '74.

Trials in the Thames Estuary followed and the idea became reality. It had been very evident during construction that the boat was a "good-looker", a joy to behold. She was now to prove a delight to handle and to fulfil the exacting requirement of her designer. She is extremely close winded and with her relatively short high density keel is expected to outperform current deep draughted fin keel craft. Race winning abilities are confidently predicted in some of this years off shore events and successful participation in July's Round Britain Race is an exciting new project in sailing, the Varne 27' - quick!

Her distinctive red hull will shortly be seen on the Blackwater where her qualities will become readily apparent.

LETTER TO THE EDITOR. (Hurrah!!- Ed.)

Dear Editor,

So there are whispers that we are becoming a club of middle-aged potterers. Would that it were true! I would feel years younger. Here's to the daring young men on the flying trapezees and may they continue to keep the M.S.C. high in the racing records. But don't let us get the idea that this is what sailing is ALL about.

Up with the potterers, hang out a sign "This club welcomes potterers", (from cradle to grave). We should talk more about the fun of anchoring up for a picnic or just lying in the sun. One might sail round Osea Island by accident. It might happen!

The development of the sailing dinghy towards the ultimate of a large water ski with a large sail and a sky hook suspended crew is an exciting and rewarding exercise, but it is a pity when it encourages boats like the G.P.14 or Wayfarer to hang out more rags and suspended bodies in an effort to enter an estate into which they were not born.

Why not a class for old and portly boats with "games" rather than races where the accent is on boat handling rather than gymnastics. They could race on handicaps adjusted like golf (or horse racing!) or picking up dummy "men overboard" etc. so many times in the course of a "race", or anchor and drop sails and paddle ashore to complete the course. These are a few suggestions, but why not just potter.

I offer a second hand trophy for the best potterers log (or should it be diary). The winners first job being to erase the orginal name and evidence of a more energetic past and scratch on his own.

In more serious vein, I think our club has much to gain financially by attracting members with a "pottering" programme, not requiring an expensive boat. The racing men and women will come without being driven. We have room for all and the more members, the lower the sub.

I will now potter around constructing a shelter from the brickbats I probably deserve.

Yours sincerely,

Bill Buchanan.

SPRING BANK HOLIDAY REGATTA

25 -27th May 1974.

Last year our Annual Spring Bank Holiday Regatta attracted a record entry of 200 boats from 34 clubs. If we are again lucky enough to have fine weather, the entry this year could be even higher.

Throughout the year many of our members visit other clubs when cruising, competing in dinghy open events or perhaps when on holiday. Invariably they are made extremely welcome and offered all the facilities of the club.

Our club differs from many others in that we do not hold a series of Open Meetings throughout the year. The Regatta therefore is the one occasion in the year when we can repay that hospitality by sharing our facilities with visiting yachtsmen and also give those of our dinghy fleets who do not travel, the chance to sail in a large competative event. For those who do not sail dinghies there is an oppotunity to view the spectacle of 200 sails across the water and join in the social scene.

Whilst an event of this size does involve us in a lot of work, it only becomes a burden if it is left to a few 'regulars'. MANY HANDS MAKE LIGHT WORK!!!!!- if every member were to give one hour of their time everybody could participate and enjoy the weekend to the full.

8.

THE "MALCOLM MILLER".

by

Andrew Dixon.

A grey friendless sky hung close over the London roof tops, and a chill February wind murmured through the rigging. The silent dockland wharves and cranes added a cheerless backdrop to the scene, and in all made the prospect of setting out for the open sea a little unwelcoming. I was standing on the deck of the schooner "Malcolm Miller", supposedly polishing a large brass winch, but in reality gazing on the latecomers straggling aboard, and meditating on the voyage in the week to come.

The "Malcolm Miller", 135'O.A., is a Topsail schooner belonging to the Sail Training Association, and sister ship of the famous "Sir Winston Churchill" which was at this moment in its own state of bustle just along the quay from us. She is very sturdily built of steel with a good draft of 15½', and can sport up to 14 sails on three masts. She has four headsails, three square sails on the foremast, gaff rigged fore and mainsails and a bermudan mizzen. In addition she can set topsails above the two gaffs, and a staysails between the masts. However, these latter sails are usually regarded as playthings, only to be set on calm summer days when there is nothing much else to do, and at this time of the year (February) even the large mizzen sail has a permanent reef in it.

The schooners accommodate about 40 "trainees", usually 16 to 21 year olds from all walks of life, and the purpose is to give them a taste of adventure as well as to teach them responsibility, discipline and teamwork. A permanent crew of five runs each schooner with the help of adult volunteers to act as watch officers, purser etc.. What then was I, a relative old timer doing aboard as a "trainee". The schooners had just finished their annual two month refit in the West India Docks, and the first cruise they under take is regarded as a "shakedown cruise". As new rigging, etc., is untried at this stage any thing can happen, and the ships are in a shambles after their dockyard sojourn. So adults are taken on for the shakedown cruise to get the schooners in smart and shipshape condition again and to meet any emergencies that might arise. Also, presumably, it is a good opportunity for the STA to select future watch officers etc.

So on a quiet Sunday afternoon we were being initiated in the ways of the "Malcolm Miller". A spell of cleaning, tidying and polishing under the critical eye of the bosun was followed by an instructional session, first to make sure we all knew the basic knots and sail terms, and then to introduce us to the ropes with which we were to become intimately familiar in the coming week. The foremast from which 60% of the sails are controlled, particularly had a veritable maze of halyards, buntlines and clewlines. In addition, there were the yard braces, downhauls and of course the runners. These adjustable backstays are operated by lever mechanism, which when slackened off, allowed a very heavy block to crash around at head level until captured. Controlling this in a bit of a gale struck me as a particularly hazardous operation so I gave it a wide berth! We were also initiated at this stage in the delights of crawling up the rigging and swinging out along the yards. It seemed easy enough with the ship sitting quietly in dock but no doubt it will be a different matter out at sea, with a good heel and large waves to plough into!

After a well earned supper we had the evening off and the more roysterous members of our company went off to explore the delights of the London Dockland.

9.

I decided to have a quiet evening aboard reading and chatting to my enforced companions for the next few days. Our ships company were as complete a mixture as one could wish for. Age groups ranged from the twenties to the sixties, with at least two retired people on board. An equally wide range of accents made communication diffichlt at times West country, Welsh, Irish, Scottish, Yorkshire, Lancashire, broad Geordie and Australian come to mind. Lass than I thought were active yachtsman, only about half having any recreational sailing experience at all, and only few actually possessing a boat of their own. The majority were there just a break in their workaGgy lives, others were ex-proffess- ional seamen and at least two were there "Spying out the land" for sponsoring their firm's apprentices on future crtises. The range of professional status again ranged widely, from bank clerk and artisan to company director and high up civil servants,; the general norm seemed to be professional engineer or equivalent, although we did have with us an author, a BBC radio reporter and an under-butler from Buckingham Pakace!
—

Monday dawned grey and drizzly and we were up at 06.30 as we had
a busy day ahead of us. Sleep had all but eluded me during the night due suppose to strange surrbndings, noises and hard bunks. We, trainees were all quartered in the one mess deck with pipe cot bunks lining the Sides and these squeak atrociously as one turns over. Some were sleeping weel though, if the walrus sounds that reverberated around the cabin were any thing to go by.

We were due to set off in the afternoon, so we were busy performing last minute tasks, and practising sail setting and furling drills. These latter have to be team efforts, co-ordinated by the watch leaders. Several hands are required on each halyard as the gear is of traditional nature and very heavy. This is purposely so to keep 40 odd lively youngsters busy and exercised. As an adult cruise we had a complement of only 24, so there were barely enough hands to go around in a complete sail setting drill.

At I3.15, the last warp was slipped and at last we were away, ~Allowing the "Sir Winston Churchill" through the lock gates. We were motoring, as the schooners always do in confined spaces— the first “aptain of the "Winston Churchill" did a lot of damage with the bowsprit +n his abhorrence of engines! Out in the Thames we met a fresh easterly breeze, which, though it didn't help up and down the Thames was a faar wind for our final destination of Portsmouth. If the easterly wind held, we should be able to get a visit to Cherbourg in between.

The hard work really began now. We got down to one of the more back-— breaking tasks to be done aboard, which was to scrub a layer of lime off the deck that had been put down to preserve the planking during the re-fit period. It had hardened like cement and was a real devil to get off. Taking a breather in the work, I saw the International Code flags "0 Q" flying from the yard arm, and the shore line describing dizzy circles round us, which reminded us that on this the first trip of the season, the compass adjuster was aboard doing his thing.

At 17.30 we went below for supper, after which I had to tog up in warm clothes and oil skins to stand the second Dog Watch. We were split into three watches—- I was in the forewatch, the others being Main and Mizzen watches, named after each of the masts. This meant that when all hands were required on deck I assembled with the rest of my watch in the area of the foremast. In such occasions(eg. setting off, bringing up under sail) my tasks were to help with the foresail of headsails, and the other watches to deal with their corresponding sails.

Io.

If only the duty watch is on deck though, this watch, which ever it is, maybe required to adjust or hand any sail on any mast. We followed a system of four hour duty watches, which in general meant four hours on and eight hours off. This arrangement is complicated by two dog watches of two hours
each, between 14.00 and 20.00 which are introduced so that one does not
keep the same duty watch each day. On coming on deck at I8.00 I was sur- prised to see the lights of Southend on our port beam and Sheerness away to our starboard. The mizzen and foresail had been set by the previous watch, but we were still under power as the wind was almost dead ahead. Visibility had improved and there was plenty of shipping to be seen about. I had plenty of time to look about for the first hour, as I was standby duty. Each duty watch was split into one hour tricks, and one alternated each hour between doing bridge duty and standby duty. On the bridge, as well as the helmsman, port and starboard lookouts are required as well as a messenger. The latter ran errands for the watch officer, and also maintained the rough log book. The standby duty at night had to remain geared up but could sit in the petty officer's mess in the deck cabin consuming coffee and bread and cheese in limitless quantities, unless required for trimming or changing a sail. During the day the standby duty merged with the genere off watch chores of cleaning up the vessel and getting her into ship shape condition. The second hour I was messenger duty, with not many messages to carry, but I was busy keeping the rough log book up to date, noting each change of course and each buoy we passed down the Yantlet Channel. Also each hour a note of windspeed and direction, shipspeed, weather, tempera- ture, etc. was recorded.

Coming off duty I was ready to go to bed, although again, sleep did not come easily. The sea was still calm, but the motion of the ship could now be felt below- a restful unhurried motion that befits the I00' water- line. However, the waves slopping against the steeel bows did give the
feeling of lying in a 500 gallon oil drum! At 22.30 the engines were stopped
and we were a sailing vessel at last. Presumably we had now rounded the North Foreland.

When woken at 03.30 on Tuesday I felt that I had just fallen asleep and it was a struggle to get up for the middle watch at 04.99. On deck we were bowling along with a F5 wind behind us, with mizzen foresail and stay sail set. Shipping twinkled all around us and Cap Gris Nez light house could be seen close to our port. I was on standby duty for the first hour and spent an interesting spell in the chart room where the navigator showed us a few of his navigational aids, such as the Decca Navigator and the Radar (Kelvin Hughes not Marconi!) Beind down below we missed a few interesting moments on deck, where the helmsman battling with his inexperience and a quartering sea, ended up by heading for the landward side of the Cap Gris Nez, now but two miles away! Frantic signalling from the light house, plus some hysterics from the watch officer, soon showed him the error of his ways. The following hour 1 was on messenger duty again, as Boulogne drew abeam. The captain decided it was too early to stop, so we set a course for Cherbourg, a further I40 miles. The third hour saw daylight come upon us, and with it, we set the square topsail to help get us to Cherbourg as quickly as possible. The mainsail was not set, but that only seems to be set when closehauled, or when the captain wants to make a pretty picture. For .v the forth hour I did my stint at the wheel, and found her much more responsive than the Thames barge, the only other sailing vessel of comparable size I've helmed!!! The temperature was 69C so I was very cold and glad of a good breakfast after coming off watch.

11.

However, there was no respite, for the fire alarm went off, and we all had to practice the fire drill. No sooner had we got back below, before the Abandon ship alarm went off, and we had to go through that drill! And then we were informed that "Happy Hour" had been declared. This is the name for an hour each day when everyone trots off to their assigned cleaning stations below decks and scrubs and polishes till the place shines. My assignment was the chartroom, and I kept finding myself diverted by glances down to the chart, or navigational book, or listening to the captain calling up the mainland on the radio.

Then at last we had a break till lunch. The afternoon was free as well, and as it was grey and cold on deck, I lay on my bunk reading and writing most of the time. We were not likely to arrive at Cherburg before midnight, and we might have to stooge around outside the harbour till the morning, so there was the prospect of a busy night ahead.

Back on watch at 16.00, and a definate change in conditions could be seen. Gales had been mentioned in the weather forecast, and the anemometer was now gusting over 40 knots.Black squalls came blinding down on us, and the lee rails were right under water, but still we forged on at 11 or more knots, with all sail, including the square topsail, set! However, after an hour of port lookout duty I had to help hand the inner jib- out on the bowsprit lashing the sail down, I was fervently hoping my insurance policies were all O.K.!!

Fried liver and onions were very welcome after a chilly watch on deck, although at 36° heel, even the fiddle rails failed to keep the plates in place, so the food had an equal probability of landing in one's lap as down the throat. The dinner table was quite deserted that evening- why no-one felt hungry, I'm sure I don't know! While eating the ship jibed (on purpose I presume!) and that posed me with a probelm when it came to sleeping, as my bunk was now on the weather side. A canvas lee-board had to be strapped up to stop me from rolling out.

On deck again for the midnight watch, and it was a surprise to see the French coast close by again and the stars out above. The loom of Cherbourg was approaching, and we were going to run straight in for shelter, After handing the stay we jibed again, and then the square topsail brailed up andthe foresail lowered. Even so we seemed to tear past the harbour lights till we rounded up and dropped the anchor. After battling with the big mizzen sail, we retird below for some welcome rest.

I awoke at 2.30- still fully dressed- after the soundest sleep so far and found it to be a fine sunny day, but cold on deck. We had a busy day before we were allowed ashore to scour the fleshpots of Cherbourg. Actually there was not much chance of that, as the captain wanted to be away again by 14.00hours. After mooring alongside the quay we had another work session on board and got ashore, just as every where closed down for lunch. Perhaps it was as well, after working out a few of the prices in the shops. After a call at a bar or two and a patisserie we were too tired to do much else but take a short stroll round the town and then back to the ship to rest.

When we left at 16.00 hrs, the gale had dropped to a light air so although we proudly left harbour with all plainsail set, we had to use the engines to give us any headway. Fore watch was on duty again at 20.00.

12.

Once we crossed the shipping lanes the engines were stopped, making it most enjoyable as we slipped through the water at a couple of knots. Visibility was good, so on lookout duty I kept a careful watch on the multitude of navigation lights twinkling around us. Before going off watch at midnight, St. Catherines Head, I.O.W., had been sighted. We were due at Cowes the next day, so we were to potter up and down the coast till dawn.

A mad scramble for breakfast, as the last watch had neglected to rouse us, and then on deck for 08.00 watch. The Nab tower was ahead, peering through a grey murky haze. We were attempting to tack up the Solent in a light fickle breeze, but when the tide turned against us as well, we had to resort to the engines. In time the haze melted to let the sun seep through, and the breeze strengthened, so that we were trickling along nicely under sail, as Portsmouth drew abeam. We ploughed right through a naval exercise which expressed its annoyance by letting off a depth charge. The water pressure waves hit us some seconds before the sound waves, and it really sounded as if we had struck a rock!

Soon after lunch we approached Cowes and rounded up to anchor in grand manner. The same second as the anchor hit the water, all sails except the mizzen came rattling down. Of course, the only hitch up had to be the jib halyards, I was stationed at! Another afternoon of scrubbing and cleaning followed, by which time the "Malcolm Miller"was beginning to look quite shipshape, after which we spent an evening doing our best to "live it up" in wintertime Cowes.

Friday morning was greeted with a rude arousal at 06.00hours- extra early because it was my alloted day as galley worker. This meant I was relieved of ordinary watch duty for the day, but instead spent it, spudbashing, dishwashing and serving up food. One is on the go all day, but the work is not strenuous and it is nice to lean out of the galley door watching someone else heaving on the braces. Unfortunately us galley workers (one from each watch) missed another fine manoeuvre as we left Cowes. The sails, including square topsail, were hoisted before the anchor was weighed, and as the anchor broke free the topsail was caught aback to bring the head off the wind so that we could bear away with the fair wind (now southwesterly) for Portsmouth, our final destination. The engines were not used for this manoeuvre in fairly cramped quarters.

We had to enter Portsmouth harbour at 14.00 precisely so the morning was spent out to the Nab tower and back, trying sail manoeuvres and generally showing off the schooner to all and sundry. The day started fine, but as we approached Portsmouth again a black squall came over and we fairly sizzled past the Round Tower into the harbour. A hundred yards off H.M.S.Dolphin we rounded up, there was another dramatic all-sail-down together drill, synchronised this time with the start of the engine, which gently edged us into our berth. The captain certainly knows how to handle his vessel. The Royal Navy always offers the schooner an honorary berth in H.M.S.Dolphin- the submarine depot when visiting Portsmouth. However this means that we couldn't just wander ashore, but had to wait for a special ferry to take us to Portmouth for a last nights revelling.

The galley work was hurriedly finished that evening so that we could catch the ferry and a brief tour of the town night spots was followed by a spontaneous congregation of the ship's company in the Keppels Head pub by the Hard as we all had a last drink with the friends we'd made during the week but whom we'd probably never meet again.

13.

Struggling back on board at 23.30 I found I was "volunteered" for harbour watch duty, which meant standing around on the bridge from midnight till 02.00 in near frezing temperatures, drinking mug upon mug of coffee to keep me warm. What we were to guard against, I'm sure I don't know, as an armed security guard was patrolling the pontoon beside us. Relieved at last, sleep was very welcome, but not for long, as we were all roused at 05.30 for the final clear up below decks before our departure. There was a bustle of washing and scrubbing till 07.00 when we stopped for breakfast. Then at last we signed off and lowered our kit bags into the ferry waiting alongside. As we drew out amongst the silent black submarines around us, we said farewell to the "Malcolm Miller" and hoped that the next occupants of our bunks have as memorable time as we have.

EDITORIAL

Well, the Regatta is over for another year. My best memory of the weekend, is of sitting in the cockpit of "Snowgoose" on that lovely Sunday morning handing out beer to a Hornet crew, slowly drifting by on the tide; as they called, not the usually "Starboard", but a necessary "Reverse"!

This issue contains the Regatta results. Many thanks to Philippa who taught me the rudiments of tabulating last night, so that I could type them!

Dinghy sailors, please don't forget the cruise to Brightlingsea on the 29th/30th. There are many cruisers who would be very happy to accomodate your families, contact Vic or John Weedon.

Please note that George Charlton is now an offical agent for the Marconi Car Draw.

Cover Photograph:- Mike Taylor with his Enterprise.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

Our members can indeed be proud of the club's efforts in presenting the 1974 Regatta. Many visitors came up to me to congratulate us on the Organization and to thank us for a most enjoyable weekend. It was particularly encouraging that nearly 40 of our own members took part in the races including some up to their necks in the organizing!
Occasionally, one hears some complaint that the Regatta disrupts our club. This is true of course, but it is our only open event, and our chance to repay the hospitality of other clubs who entertain our own helmsmen at their open meetings throughout the year. In all, 43 clubs were repre- sented at the Regatta.
It would be inappropriate to single out individual efforts-— everyone at the Regatta must be aware of the hard work put in by those responsible for the sailing programme, the racing and rescue, the social events including the refreshments and bar, and the organization of boats and
vehicles.
Many people commented on the well groomed appearance of the club, a tribute to the working parties and Claude.
Our visitors co-operated handsomely in keeping it that way.
I think the thing that impressed me most was the number of people, both club members and visitors, who came up and offered to help, making the chores almost a pleasure!
We had a few panics of course, like blocked loos, but "modified" drainage arrangements and having the changing rooms in the new club house garages, helped enormously. A few stalwarts stayed on for a few days after the Regatta to clean up the site and by the following weekend the club showed no sign of the massive invasion.
We had another record entry, 235 dinghies took part in the points series— quite a spectacle at the start line!
I must admit that the weather helped, although we had a range of conditions from a fresh northerly on Saturday, through a flat calm and abandonment on Sunday morning to ideal conditions of sun and breeze on
Monday.
However, I feel we must be reaching saturation. I hope we don't get another 25% increase next year in spite of the fabulous bar sales.
You cannot have failed to notice the rapid growth of our new club- house -— it must be well ahead ofschedule. We are certainly lucky in hav:
on the front cover enjoying a little relaxation) who is not only a first class builder but also has the a great interest in the Club's
activities.

DENNIS BYATT. Commodre.

P.S. Thanks to Harry Holts offer to visit the Cambridge Agricultural Sales
we now have a brand new rotary mower at a second hand price.

SECURITY - STOP PRESS

We have just heard that there may have been two Avon dinghies and the 18 footer's outboard engine stolen from the club premises over the last few days. We have not had time to ascertain the full facts but be warned and make sure your gear is secured, or at least covered up. It's a good idea to padlock tenders to an iron stake if possible. NAVIGANS CONSUMER SERVICE..."WHICH BOAT".

There has been much discussion within the club as to whether or not we should have and race another dinghy class.To help anybody thinking of buying a new dinghy, I have asked four club members, with individual dinghies to do a "Which" report on their boats. I would like to thank them for their time and their effort.

Editor.

Let's have a Lark.

The Lark racing dinghy with its fast round bilges and flat after sections is moulded entirely in GRP and can be bought with wooden decks. The only other wooden features are the main thwart and rudder assembly, the centreboard being aluminium, as are the Proctor spars. Designed by Micheal Jackson of National 12 fame and first sailed in 1967, it is moulded by John Baker in Devon. The Lark can be obtained from several South Coast or Midlands builders who will also supply the boat in kit form.

This dinghy is 13'4" L.O.A., 5'5½" beam and the hull weighs a convenient 185lbs. The mainsail is 75 square feet, the jib 30 square feet and the spinnaker is 80 square feet. All this adds up to a two man racer with a P.Y. of 93 (which may go down to 94). There is built in buoyancy below the foredeck and the side benches and transom flaps and auto bailers are allowed. There is a ggod deal of freedom allowed in the internal lay-out to suit the owner and sheeting can be centre-main or transom with sliding horse.

At the January 1973 count there were 1,250 boats registered, some of these going to the U.S.A. where they are very popular,as they seem to be in U.K. Universities. The 1972 National Championship attracted 105 boats.

Eddie Edwards.

CHOOSING A SINGLE HANDER- THE LASER.

My first consideration when choosing a single hander was low maintenance, which menat fibre glass construction and from past experience with other classes, equally important a boat designed for this material. A boat designed for wood and later built in fibre glass is not competitive as there is a weight probelm that can only be overcome by reducing the thickness of the fibre glass, which makes the boat less rigid than the wooden predecessor. This has an adverse effect, particularly in choppy waters and I completely rejected all boats initially designed in wood.

A very strict one design was a must as after the initial purchase I did not want to find drastic 'improvements' allowed that would create expense in keeping the boat up to date. This feature would also ensure a good re-sale value as an old boat would basically the same as one newly produced.

Capsizes are inevitable and I required a boat that could be quickly righted with the minimum of effort. In addition when the correct way up I did not want a boat that held water like a gold fish bowl, as so many do. A dry cockpit and ready to sail away was what I was looking for.

I found all these features in a sleek contemporary boat named the 'Laser'. It is without doubt the fastest growing single handed dinghy in England and at least 14,000 have been registered Internationally. The dinghy is extermely simple, light and easy to handle with a most exhilarating performance.

5.

The carefully designed planing hull shape, similar to the lines of the 'Flying Dutchman', combined with light weight allows the Laser to jump up on the plane long before other boats of its size.

This is not just a fun boat and once the beginner has mastered the basics, racing competition can be found practically anywhere in the world. Many local clubs have adopted the class and transport is no probelm as the boat can easily be car topped for holidays and open meetings.

The statistics are:-
L.O.A. - 13'10"
Beam - 4'6"
Sail Area - 76sq. ft.
Weight - 125lbs.
Positive Flotation - 350lbs.

Price £275+VAT, including all fittings, airfoil shape centre board and rudder, Elvstrom Sail, first year subscription to the Laser Association and deivery. (An order for six would mean 5% discount).

Donald Forbes of Mustoe and Hyde Sails has offered to bring the Laser to the Marconi Sailing Club one weekend if there is sufficent interest.

This is not a difficult dinghy to handle as my children manage without probelm 'How about that then'. If anyone would like to know more my telphone number is Chelmsford [redacted] and Donald Forbes (the expert) is very helpful at South Benfleet [redacted] or [redacted].

Arthur Hodges.

THE BONITO

The Bonito has been designed by the British builders of the Finn to provide a 14'6" G.R.P. single-hander of considerable speed combined with stability, the hull shape bearing comparision with that of a Hornet.

Although designed as a single handed racer, it will also carry one or two passengers and therefore has a considerable appeal to the family man.

It has a simple cat rig sail of 88 square feet sleeved on to a jointed aluminium mast, making it possible to prepare the boat for sailing in under five minutes.

The Bonito weighs only 120lbs and is easily car topped for holidays; I have taken one to Syke for the last two summers for family sailing.

A new Bonito cost approximately £250 but can be bought for as little as £120 second hand, and as the boat requires virtually no maintenance, it makes a relatively inexpensive second boat to buy and keep up. Sailing at the moment off a Portsmouth No of 104, the Bonito may well prove to be under handicapped when sailed skilfully against the more established Solo and Laser.

There are already three Bonitos at Marconi and one or two more would give this promising boat a competitive cnace to show its considerable pace. How about it!

Peter Campion.

THE SOLO

I suppose that we all have our problems at some time or other. In 1972 I was sailing my Mirror with son Mark, then aged 8, as crew. He seemed to enjoy sailing, particularly racing, but after the National Championships at Llandudno he started to rebel. This may have been due to the fact that club racing seemed tame after the Nationals or perhaps he wanted to stay ashore with the non-sailing kids, not seen for some time due to over-lapping holidays.

6.

Of course, he may have finally got fed up with being blamed for my mistakes. Before that season ended we did have some very good and enjoyable racing, however, it was obvious to me that he did not wish to race all the time.

My solution to this probelm was to find some alternative and I set about finding a second boat, a single hander.

Choosing the Mirror in 1970 was simple. Sailing was something I wanted to try and I had no interest in racing. I wanted a cheap boat with good second hand potential. It had to be new becuase I usually do very badly when I try to buy second hand. A Mirror kit seemed the obvious choice, and the fact that the Club reorganized the Mirror Class played little or no part in the decision.

With the new boat the problems were not the same. I was now interested in racing and had there been a singlehanded club class I would almost certainly joined that.

Factors that I considered important included:-
A Portsmouth number between 95 and 105 i.e. not to hairy.
A reasonably well established boat with good second hand potential.
Enough of a boat to cruise with the family occasionally.
A boat that would give me some close racing locally i.e. in the range of the Blackwater and Thames.
A boat that other typical club members might possibly buy in the future.

I decided that a Solo best met my requirements mainly because in 1973 there were twoopen meetings planned on the Blackwater for Solo's. In addition Solo's did in fact sail at our Regatta as a class and also at Stone for the Blackwater and Colne Championships. Boats that I rejected after careful consideration included the Laser, Bonito and the Moth, but of course it would take to long to give all my reasons.

As for price, in 73 I paid just under £320 for a G.R.P. boat with better than average sails and spars. Although at the same time Don Claydon purchased a wooden boat second hand which I thought was very good value at £170.

At the start of the 73 season my new boat took me round the course, but after awhile I felt that I was slowly gaining the upper hand.I enjoyed the larger club handicap events and my cruising extended from Maldon to Bradwell. I was particularly pleased to come fourth out of twenty-one in two of the races at the Harlow Open meeting.

Crew problems! Yes, I still have crew problems, son Mark now complai that the Mirror is not raced enough!

MY ADVENTURe IN THE SOLENT

by
@ very amateur "SAILOR".

It was Easter Monday, and we were "parked", sorry moored in Ports- mouth harbour. The weather was perfect when we boarded the boat at 8.30am Every where was calm and peaceful and hardly a soul to be seen.
An hour later we were on our way, or is it underway, and quite an experience for me- a novice— squirming my way through the hatch with instructions (shouted by my husband) to 2ix the front sail. It wasn't ay fault i put it on up side down=— or was it!
By this time quite a breeze was blowing and we wended our way in and out and around the other boats, had a good look at all the R.N. cruisers etc. anchored around and sailed out of the harbour with me trying to look as experienced as my husband.
Suddenly we were rocking from side to side and I take a quick look at my mate expecting to hear the command "Get ready to jump". His face is as immobile as ever,however, on seeing my stricken look he mutters "Just the swell of the ferry". In the distance the Hydrofoil is bearing down upon us with a roar, but with a flashy glow passes by without causing much disturbance. Then the Hovercraft looms into view and what a beauti- full thing it is and gone by in a flash. Beginning to wish there was just a little rowing boat about, which we could overtake. The old Forts are in sight and soon passed and the navigator:has his charts out and can tell . me the names of all the buoys as we reach them. One of these had a bell inside tolling.
To the left of us is the Isle of Wright and at this time I suggest having our coffee and sandwiches. Unseasoned sailor that I am I travel on all fours to get in the cabin for the lunch bag and out again, and sit with coffee in one hand and a sandwich in the other and wish I had a Spare one to hang on with as we are travelling at a good speed. My first bite of the sandwich is taken while I am low in the water, then whoops I am on high.my food has gone down with a big clunk, leaving me feeling quite uncomfortable. Another thing I must learn- How to eat with the boat in motion.
Osbourne House, Queen Victoria's favourite home is to the left of us. and Cowes Castle, and at last we are sailing just oft Cowes. More coffee etc. well masticated this time, we decide after three to four hours sail-- ing to make our return journey, which my Captain says will take much longer because of the tide. We turn tail, or is it sail — and head for
home.
Across the water I think I can see one of the "Around the World Yachts", returning but cannot quite make out the name through the binocu-
lars.
At great speed now, we are tacking across the water and I begin to feel a bit uneasy again. The water looks very close to me so I crawl across to the seat opposite and hang on for dear life.
Ryde Pier is in sight and we see the train coming out to pick up passengers. The Ferry, Hydrofoil and Hovercraft are still in action, all doing good business that day.
Portsmouth harbour is before us, but we are having a little diffi- culty getting in, after much tacking we make it. Halfway back to the moor- ing a large motor boat roars straight at us, and then we notice someone taking our photograph. The name of a well known Yachting book was written on the side, so who knows we may have our picture in the paper.
Finally we reach the mooring about 7.30pm feeling tired and cold. Get everything shipshape, jump in the dinghy and my sturdy shipmate rows me to the shore. He considers we have sailed thirty miles that day.

9.

Crouching in the dinghy ready to jump out I catch my foot in something and there I am flat on my face on the hard with my face in about two inches of water. What an inglorious end toa most exciting day.

My legs are badly bruised and my knee cap still hurts, so would all lady members of the club please walk with a limp for a while. I should hate being identified as the biggest nit on and off the water.

EDITORIAL

Come one, come all, is our motto on Open Day and they did, including the Sanitary Department, who proceeded to empty the cess pit, adding that extra spice to the wind!! Snowgoose was busy- she is always a favourite for "sixpenny trips around the bay", and it was very nice to see Ian and Frances taking a busman's holiday.

As it was Mid-Summer's Day, we celebrated by dining on cold Christmas Pudding and custard and then joined the 18 footer's for an impromtu barbecue on the beach. Since they are all qualified "cordon noir" bonfire chefs, there was only a minimal risk of food poisoning!!

The combined dinghy/cruiser cruise to Brightlingsea, unfortunately clashed with a visit from Marconi/Elliot's, from the Medway and also we didn't have very good weather. However, five cruisers and three dinghies, the Enterprise Up and Over, Dave Polley and son and F. Partlett's Mirror 16 went down to the Colne. All except F. Partlett stayed the night, Colin and Mike even refused berths on Snowgoose and pitched their tent on the saltings. We all had an enjoyable weekend despite the rain.

DON'T FORGET, to buy your Barbecue tickets for July 19th.

Brenda Tate.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

I hear the Open Day on 22nd June was well enjoyed and we were lucky with the weather again. I missed it as I had the opportunity of a few days holiday and John Witter, with a band of helpers, kindly took
over.
At least six new Marconi membership applications were received and we hear that many of our club members and their families also enjoyed the day, especially the boat trips. There is a suggestion that we change the format next year, and pay more attention to events for our own members- as well as inviting other Marconi people who we hope will join. Any ideas!
Sunday July 14th is an important day for the club -— it is our turn
to run the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships at Stone. The turn of each club comes every 13 years or so; about 150 dinghied take part, so it is almost as exciting as our regatta.
We would be especially grateful of help with Spotting as this is one of the most important factors in ensuring a smooth running race programme. So please, if you can possibly come along by about 9.a.m. at Stone you will be most welcome. It would be useful, but not essential, if you would let John Weedon, or any committee member know beforehand.
It looks as if the new clubhouse will soon be finished at least as far as the building is concerned. The present suggestion is that the formal opening will be coupled with the "Fitting Out Party" in March 1975. However, before then, there will be plenty of chores —- fittings for the changing rooms, curtains, site clearing , paths to be laid and grass to be sown, so we hope that you will all be making a mental note to reserve a day or two during the winter to join in one or other of these
activities.
Turning to be serious matters, I must remind boat owners that it is their duty to inform the owner of any boat that they damage or even just hit. In the case of boats under sail, this is not a probelm, but there have been one or two cases recently where moored cruisers have been hit and there have been delays in reporting. Unless the owners are informed as soon as possible, even more damage could ensue. Names of owners are in the clubhouse, but in case of difficulties the Mooring Secretary, Vic Tate will help. ,
A number of members have asked if the proposed Ramsey Wick Marina will seriously affect the club. We knew, of course, that outline planning approval had been given for the Marina long before we bought the site. However, we must be alert to any aspects which could be detrimental to our facilities, and to this end we are in communication with the owners agent, making sure that our well established usage of moorings, hard, access etc are in no way degraded.
Incidentally, may I remind you that the minutes of Committee meetings are put up in the Clubhouse in order to keep members informed of the business of the club, so please read them from time to time, as there is usually some reference to these things.
Lastly some bad news. I sec that V.A.T. is payable on hard fees and moorings as from Warch 1lst., 1974!!- so thats another 80p to pay next year. I hear that a tax on the wind is being prepared for 1976, at a rate proportional to the Beaufort scale, divided by amount of rainfall multi- plied by hours of sunshine!!

D. Byatt, Commodore.

T.W.HALLAM Esq decd.

On the first day of July 1974 a Sailor and a Gentleman hy the name of Terence Walter Hallam died at the early age of 54.
He leaves a Wife, Children and Grandchildren to whom deep sympathy is extended on your behalf in their sad loss.
Simple and true words and facts behind which lie a great human struggle against a long illness.He suffered and died bravely and this last great quality was typical of the boldness with which he lived and which this brief obituary will attempt to portray. Many others are more qualified than I to write of Terry but this account is of a man known to me first as an acquaintance in business and then as a friend — over more than two decades.
Vy very first sailing experience was on a converted 'smack' which he then owned. We were sailing on a very enjoyable reach down the Black- water when he suggested that 1 take a look forward. This I did, only to turn and find him approaching me with no-one at the helm. To say I felt concerned would be an understatement. Recognising my concern and with "that's all right, mate" he continued his walk around the decks, return- ing to the stern of the boat reaching the helm in time to correct our course and so avoid another boat beating across our bows.
He loved the sea and boats, and , as an expert and audacious sailor would have been in his element in the old days of the buccaneers. Many splendid and sometimes infuriating episodes form the backcloth of my memories of Terry but- at the front of the stage stands the man so many of us admired and will continue to remember with much pleasure and a little sadness.
As a founder member of The Marconi Sailing Club he will be remembered for his organising ability and participation. He was a man of
vision, a builder, a scrounger (in the nicest, legitimate way - let me
hastily add) the latter characteristic being very necessary in the earlier years of a struggling Club. The qualities and Individualism needed to assist in the building of our Club were found by Terry for besides holding many other offices he served as Commodore on two separate occasions each lasting 3 or 4 years. His last period in Office covered the time when vital decisions affecting the club's future were
made and the barge "Mamgu" -—- then our headquarters at Heybridge - was
sold and we moved to Stansgate.
Here under his leadership the present clubhouse was erected and the site opened up with high hopes for the future. His experience and success will never be equalled in the Club, for he lead during the days of "do it yourself" when each member contributed to its work and growth, when unity and friendships were taken for granted.
He was a great ambassador and as a member of other well known clubs and associations on the river brought great credit to both himself and us. His popularity, without question, was well deserved for he was known and :
admired by sailors and friends connected with the sea in all the Essex and Suffolk rivers and many elsewhere.
A happy man, generous to his companions, a man of compassion, young at heart and appreciative of the good things in life, who was devoted to his wife and family.
His cheery "Hello mate" will be sadly missed for he nows sails the seas of tranquility. Some of us will perhaps hear that same creating as the wind billows our sails for a long time to come; and that same wind will bring water briefly to our eyes.
Such was the man.
Farewell Terry - mate.

1974 Police Regatta

The annual Police Regatta this year was again held at Stansgate on
Monday lOth June, when 30 dinghies attended, some coming from as far away
as Hampshire, Sussex, Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, London and Southend. The weather was not brilliant and there were some showers but not enough to damp the proceedings and the visitors had plenty of good sail- ing and altogether, a most enjoyable day. Calm conditions prevailed in the morning, exept for one unexpected squall, which sent the dinghies flying with several capsizes, and the morning race lasted over four hours necessitating the postponement of the afternoon race, Eileen Hodges and Robina Boswell did stalwart duties as race officers in fact, they were in the race box all day and even worked out the results; Crystal was on the flags.
The police launch Watchful moored off the club and served as rescue boat for the racing, helping to bring back the capsized dingies to the hard, the crew coming ashore for refreshments between the races. Malcolm Moore was in charge of the proceedings and attended to the
booking-in.
George Charlton did a brisk business in the bar and Margaret Cottam was in attendance in the galley, and Alf had a swim!
Wireless communication between Watchful, the clubhouse and the race box was continuous and the equipment seemed to function perfectly - probably the police have a depot at their headquarters, which is constantly overhauling the equipment.
It had already been decided to hold next year's Regatta at Thorpe Bay because more over-night accommodation for the visiting crews would be available in that district, but Dennis Byatt, in his address of welcome to the visitors, predicted that they would soon tire of the mud and limited sailing time there and would be back at Stansgate before long. The Chief Constable's Trophy for the best performance by an Essex helmsman was won by Arthur Hodges.
Our Commodore and Vice-Commodore arrived in time to see the Chief Constable, John Nightingale present the prizes and he thanked the Marconi Sailing Club for their hospitality and making their premises available to them.
The organization was superb and the discipline of such a high standard that my duties as 0.0.D. were light, in fact, my wife and I passed a most res tful and enjoyable day.

Eric Payne

Jim Gozzett, deceased. Older members of the club will be grieved to hear that Jim Gozzart of the Maldon Little Ships Club, died last Thursday at the age of 69. He was an active member of The Maldon Little Ships Club and Commodore in the early fifties, He was a founder member of the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee and regularly attended their meetings, he also helpee to organize the Maldon Regatta.

Jim was also President of the local Lifeboat Association and during his term of office he succeeded in raising the contribution from £20 to £3000. He was the owner of many fine yachts including the magnificent Nutcracker, which won many races on the Blackwater.

We offer our most sincere sympathies to his widow, Phyllis and sons John and Peter. His loss will be felt greatly by all of us who sail on the Blackwater.

BRIGHTLINGSEA 13/14th July

Arising on Saturday morning, it was disappointing to find that the rain was still with us, neverthe less the boat was made ready and sails hoisted just in time to prevent the receding tide leaving "Jo" stuck on her mooring. As I was without a crew I gratefully accepted Robert Tate's offer and together we part sailed but mostly motor sailed through very heavy rain to our destination, where Brenda had egg, bangers and mash waiting for both of us. This kind thought was much appreciated.

Having spent Saturday afternoon on "Jappa" and the evening (which was dry) ashore, we returned to the boats. There I had coffee aboard "Tijo" before retiring to "Jo" for the night. Sunday morning was brighter and we even saw the sun. The ensemble again descended on the town and several purchases were made at the chandlers.

"Jo" was cast off for the return trip at 14.00 hours and once again I had Robert for company, we also had a head wind against us although, we were able to sail most of the way. Shortly after leaving the channel, the wind started to get up and the main was reefed down. As we approached the home waters the wind moved to dead ahead and the motor was used to help our passage over the final leg.

Many thanks to all on this weekend cruise for helping to make my first trip to another port! such an enjoyable and memorable one.

Robin Lunniss.

COCK OF THE RIVER - TWO YEARS RUNNING!

Class winners of the Blackwater & Colne Dinghy Championships held at Stone S.C. on July 14th competed for the "Cock of the River" trophy at the Marconi S.C. Stansgate on Sunday 28th July.

Weather conditions were improved compared with the squally conditions prevailing during the Balckwater & Colne Championships, but even so, force 4-5 winds gusting to 6 made sailing distinctly lively resulting in several retirements and capsizes. 27 boats were eligible, during the morning a pratice race was held, the winner being J. Bovis of Maylandsea Bay in his Fireball.

The afternoon final attracted 17 enteries, the event being run as a Pursuit Race, calculated on class handicap ratings. Conditions tended to favour the faster boats and last year's winner, R.Dorks of Stone S.C., really made his Unicorn, a single-handed Cat, speed up and down the estuary to repeat his triumph of last year.

1st. R. Dorks. - Unicorn - Stone S.C.
2nd. G. Reeves. - Hornet - Brightlingsea S.C.
3rd. N. Connelly. - Shearwater - Stone S.C.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

The bad weather we've been having makes it seem all the more fortunate that we did so well with our major events earlier in the season. We appear to have suffered little damage in the recent gales.

The final stages of work are being carried out on the new clubhouse- interior fittings, main supplies, decorating etc., but we are not pressing to use it this season.

Someone asked if we could use the flat roof of the changing rooms as a grandstand. We did look into this during the planning stage, but because of the greatly increased amount of strengthening required, plus railing and emergency access, the cost would have been prohibitive. The sea wall is, of course, only a few feet lower, and makes a very extensive viewing area.

Vic Tate, Ron Rider and myself had a meeting with Bidwells, who are the agents for the new Marina developement. They told us there is still an engineering study to be carried out regarding the whole project, and they assure us that they will consult the Marconi Sailing Club on all details of mutual interest. We emphasised our concern over the access channel, and the possible interference with our well established moorings, and we were again assured that this would be noted- the outline plan submitted would be subject to more detailed study and we would be consulted. I do not think there is much more we can do at this stage, but the committee is keeping a close watch on the situation. It is, however, unlikely that much will happen for several years now.

Il have been known to flood the kitchen out by leaving the plug in the sink and the tap running, over-flowing the washing machine, but never before have I flooded our boat "Carasou".
It all happened on the last leg of our holiday. We had said cheerio to Tony and Wendy Cherry and their family in Brightlingsea and set off a day earlier for our Stansgate mooring, as we were due at a weddings on the
Saturday.
It was a lovely sunny afternoon with a good breeze as we tacked up the River Colne. As we passed the wreck buoy off East Mersea the sky look- ed very ominous ahead. A great black mirk lay right across the horizon. I told Ken, my husband, I didn't like the look of the weather ahead, his only comment being,"We'll just get the edge of it". What a hope, as we discovered later.
The wind got up and I still wasn't happy about the weather around us, so Ken went up and reefed the mainsail, while I took the helm. Then it all happened, the storm broke right over us, lightning flashing, thunder and howling wind. Poor "Carasou" was toboggoning down the waves with their saps being blown off at great speed. All sails were then dropped.
I then got the instruction to go down below and turn off the sea- cocks. (It was all rushing around as far as I was concerned). I managed to do the 'loo' by lying flat on my stomach because of the movement of the boat, and then I thought of the sink. As I turned the sea-cock it didn't seem to be going home, so I turned it the other way, then to my amazement it came away in my hand and the water started to pour in. I grabbed the tea cloth and pushed it into the hole, and then held up the sea-cock to show Ken what I had done. Poor devil went white, and shouted something like "you bloody fool, we'll sink!" (I'm sure I'm not the only crew member that has ever been called a 'b' fool).
All hell was then let loose!! I was put on the helm, (storm still going and wind howling) whilst Ken went below to try to do something to stop the boat filling up. It was no good, turn round and run for Bright- lingsea were my instructions, which I duly carried out. It took all my strength to hold "Carasou" at that time. My only thought was, I think he is trying to get rid of me. This must be why the insurance man called by appointment the other week, Ken knew this was going to happen. I just sat rigid with fright. It was hard to believe that the river had ever been so calm as we sailed up to the wreck buoy.
A minor repair done, ken came back on the helm again and I spent the rest of the journey to Brightlingsea on my knees with my hand over the pipe to stop any further water pouring in.
Back in Brightlingsea we saw the Cherry family. They weren't surprised to see us back: again. We told them about our sea-cock drama. I was immediately taken onto "Ace" by Tony and Wendy’ had a tot of brandy at the ready. She also had the kettle on. Was I pleased to be on "Ace" with Wendy again who was a great help. Tony then helped Ken to mend the sea-cock and mop up.
That night it was decided that I should be sent home before I did any more damage. John Smith was telephoned and asked to come and pick me up, which he duly did. Isn't it nice to have such good friends. On leaving Ken was trying to explain to me how to get the hot water on at home. Tony's comment was, "I wouldn't bother, you'll probably go home and find her sai!- ing around the bungalow in a wooden box".
The irony of the tale is that it wasn't necessary to put the sea-cock under the sink off in any case, as the pipework had been diverted somehow, to prevent water from coming up into the sink.
"Carasou" was taken back to her mooring by Ken the next day, but on coming out of Brightlingsea, he left the helm, to go below for a his sweat- er and ran aground. The boat then lay over for 24 hours, but to make it look deliberate he spent his time over the side cleaning "Carasou's" bottom,
