ROULETTE = EAST COAST LOG 26TH JULY - 11TH AUGUST 1974

Friday evening saw us all at Stansgate where the trip was started in true
cruiser style within the clubhouse drinking to its success. It was a perfect evening and we reminisced over the fateful start of last year's Calais trip. However this definitely felt different and the weather forecast certainly sounded
hopeful.

Despite the fact we had stocked up Roulette with stores to avoid delay on the
Friday evening we still managed to fill our dinghy to capacity without taking any
of the crew aboard!! We were to be five on this trip and I must say I looked on the fortnight confined on a 21' boat with mixed feelings! Last year only three of us attempted the full trip with two extra for the last five days. Also at least three of us had grown since last year. Roulettes water line was well down as ve had taken enough tinned food for a siege and toys to amuse. These had to be cut rather drastically after foolishly telling the children to pack a few things they would like to take! "No not your badminton set Tim or the entire contents of your bookshelves Carol."

After drinking to a successful trip it was moorings away and down to Bradwell to anchor within the barrier and bed by 10.30 p.m. in anticipation of an early start. Peter says he didn't sleep much that night but it did not stop him having to be woken by the alarm set for 04.15. As you may remember from last years log Roulette though a stalwart sailor before the wind does need a bit of waxing to keep up with the fleet which means we usually get two hours less sleep than the others en route. We set out at 04.50 and were pleased to see one other person awake, Stan waved us off dressed for the occasion in his pyjamas. It was quite light with a Westerly force 3-4 blowing as predicted. We watched a superb sunrise at 05.15, one of the bonuses of an early start.

04.50 Motor sailed close to Bradwell bank following 8 knot buoys until we took course 85 M.

05.15 St.Peters Chapel due South, altered course to 115°M for approx. 1] hour.

06.10 Changed course to 95°M, with a good swell running.

06.30 Weather forecast W.5.

06.35 North Eagle abeam. On time, engine cut.

08.10 Gun fleet old Lighthouse and the Red Cliffs of Holland on Sea in line. We were therefore twenty minutes ahead of our calculated minimum speed and on a gorgeous broad reach. We really had to make sure we kept our pace up to make the passage and ensure arrival at the Ore entrance an hour after low water when the flow out of the river would have ceased.
The following sea certainly affected the crew, two breakfasts were cooked but only one eaten and that with great difficulty! The children were still asleep, another bonus when we are aboard they always sleep late.

08.45 Passed Walton Pier, Medusa dead ahead 55°M.

09.05 Passed Medusa fair eddy behind the buoy with the tide sweeping. Wind freshening but the sea still flat, crew feeling less queasy. We were able to lash the tiller and set course 30°M and it was at least an hour before we came to the Harwich Channel.

09.20 Large ferry came by us.

09.40 Chris awoke and decided to get up!

09.45 Carol, reading as usual in her bunk, Tim writing his log.

10.15 North Cork, we had made 5° of leeway from Medusa, so steered 20°M to compensate to Orford Haven.

11.15 Off the entrance to the River Ore, much earlier than expected, really too early, the last thing we had dreamed of. However, the wind had been an ideal one for the boat and for once the rest of the fleet hadn't overtaken us. We had also stood well out to sea in the strongest tide and wind. We had to motor sail against the tide up the river, now with the rest of the fleet, and turned into Butley Creek and anchored together, eleven boats in all, just South of Boyton Dock where once barges collected bricks from the local works. The children were soc ashore, making a camp in the derelict brick barn by the dock. After lunch we went aboard Tijo for a drink and natter and after a short "kip" we went ashore with the Cherry family to explore. Later the younger members provided plenty of spectator sport for us with water fichts in the dinghies. Perhaps J enjoyed it better because my children were not involved and I didn't have to hang out all their clothes to dry on the stays!! Luckily it was a warm dry evening. We were exhausted by this time but could hardly believe our luck at being at our chosen destination on the first night of the trip, ensuring maximum time to explore down the coast. At this time we didn't realise how fortunate we really were for Avril and Ken Stevens couldn't make the passage until the following Thursday!

Sunday 28th July

Sunny morning but very windy, possibly 5-6 W, certainly glad we made our passage yesterday. The Butley proved a very pleasant anchorage and was sheltered enough for the younger ones to sail around in the dinghies to their hearts content which we left Tim doing as we made our way towards the village of Boyton after breakfast. The store, though marked on the map was not there any more, the village comprised only a few houses of various ages and a pub. En route up the farm track and along the lane we saw hundreds of rabbit holes and a lizard, a beautiful pale green, basking in the sun. Carol and Chris were left on the village green to play
on the swings while we continued our walk - they are lazy types - on our return they
had made friends with the 'natives' and Chris had acquired a large pram wheel. We
hopefully tried to dissuade him from carting it back aboard - yet another space
filler - but the locals insisted most generously that he take it. We met a local
retired farmhand on our way back to the boat who told us that once sheep and pigs were the money makers in this area but now everything was being ploughed up and mens work being taken over by machinery. "Brainless lot" he concluded "send out the hedge trimmers immediately the blackberries are ripe!" We lunched in true Ploughmans style on beer, bread and cheese and lovely local timatoes. We loved the atmosphere here so decided to stay on for a while longer when the others set off towards Orford. Je agreed to meet up later. That afternoon all five of us decided to take the dinghy to the head of Butley River and we made good way with the wind behind us. The saltings were swarming with birds, oyster catches, black headed gulls, terns shelduck, heron and many we could not identify. Their cries followed us up the river and we seemed to be the only people around. We went around several times and waited for the tide to rise to carry us farther on our way. We carefully avoided the oyster beds which in recent years have been restocked by the Butley Orford Oysterage and are now yielding a million oysters 4 year. Oyster beds existed here from Roman times until the 1920s.

Having decided we had had enough of the cramped conditions Carol and I wisely chose to walk back to the boat, exploring the countryside around Butley Low Corner farm, and seeing the ruins of Butley Abbey founded in 1171. Tt now stands back from the river but evidently when it was built a fleet of barges were able to bring the stone for its erection to a quay beside it. Records show there was a constant struggle to hold the tides at bay but little by little the marsh land was reclaimed and in 1500 the Priory scribe wrote that the newly walled marshes were only drowned by the occasional high tide.

We came over the hill above Butley Ferry to see the others fighting the tide back. They were tacking, rowing one leg and sailing the other and getting nowhere. We sat on the hill and watched them be rescued by a chap in a motor boat who gave them a tow. We were back to the boat by 6 p.m. and off to Orford and in half an hour were directed by a local boatman onto a mooring opposite the hard. This was 30p well spent for the tide really races up and down this river and we tried to avoid rowing across at other than slack high or low water. It is definitely an advantage to have an outboard motor for a dinghy on this trip.

Monday 29th July

We awoke to a gorgeous clear blue sky behind Orford Castle, a beautiful sicht and we were ashore by nine o'clock. We walked up the pretty main street with cottages to either side but not a sign of life and what peace. The shops seemed hidden too until we found milk and papers in a cottage sitting room and a general stores tucked around a side turning. we finished our shopping and then explored the Castle which is extremely well preserved. It stands high on a hill and commands an excellent view across the river and countryside. Before the lighthouse was built iron baskets with lighted beacons were set up upon Orford Castle. Tradition says that the port was thriving in the 9th century when the town was said to extend far beyond the castle where there are now green fields. The then castle was not built but Orford haven was a snug anchorage and trade and fishing flourished. A fleet of ships brought stone for the new castle in 1165 and berthed at the newly built quays below it.

The children were delighted to explore the dungeons and we saw the banquet hall with its stone ovens and the earliest equivalent of wash hand basins with tunnels behind to shoot the water out, the 'loos' worked on a similar shute principle. The view from the top of the keep was marvellous both out to the river and inland, we could see Sizewell Power Station clearly. We lazed and sunbathed out of the wind all day and enjoyed the local Admams beer pumped by an old fashioned lift pump. We bought smoked salmon from the Orford Oysterage, but did not try the oysters whose beds we had drifted over the previous day. At 4.20 p.m. we left the mooring under motor but soon set two foresails and mizzen and cut the engine. Later we needed the mainsail as the wind appeared to drop. Actually we found we were hammering along so made good time.

17.15 Martello Tower at Slaughden Quay abeanm.

18.30 Joined the "fleet" at "The Oaks" and went ashore for a beach barbecue. Ropes had been attached to the huge trees on the shore line and by the end of the evening it wasn't only the children that were samplin; the swings! We lit a huge fire and cooked sausages and beans and concluded the evening sitting on the hill above in full song!

8

Tuesday July 30th

The "fleet" was on its way but we chose to make our way by dinghy towards Snape Maltings at the head of the river. The route was very twisting and shallow and one could not help wondering how the schooners of the 1800's with their 10 foot draughts navigated the fortuous channel to Snape Bridge. All these vessels were engaged in the coal and corn trade berthing at Iken Cliff where the firm had its coat yard and voyaging as far as Rotterdam, London, Famersham and Chatham. About 1860 ketch barges or "boomies" appeared and replaced the schooners because of their lightness of draught and smaller crew. They traded between the Snape Maltings and Cardiff with Welsh coal. Sprit sail barges used the river in large numbers during the last century, probably some of them carried the bricks for building the Martello Towers at Shingle Street about 1810. The Snape granaries were built by Newson Garrett a merchant and ship owner of Aldeburgh in the middle of the century. The last sprittles are said to have been seen in Snape in 1928. However we were able to pull up beside the barge "Redoubtable" after negotiating the red can, black flagged channel, and climbed up the quayside to view the lovely Malting buildings now the centre of the Aldeburgh Festival. We browsed around the craft centre and had a snack at the "Plough & Sail". Peter and the children set sail again for the 'Oaks' and I walked across the cornfields beside the marshy land. It was very picturesqu but I could hardly be described in the same way once I had waded through thigh high mud to get aboard Routlette! This was one of the hazards of the "Oaks", it is extremely unpleasant at low tide.

15.30 saw us leaving the anchorage, having lost the dinghy off the back of the boat - who had tied it on! - and regained it, thanks to the rapid action of a fellow boat owner with an outboard motor! It started to rain as soon as we left the mooring but we negotiated the narrow passage and with a fair wind only had to motor for a short time. However it died again in Short Reach and we just made it onto a mooring above Aldeburgh when a sudden squall came and it poured.

17.20 Cosy on board cooking up meal, Roulette's smallness is an asset on these occasions. By the time the meal was finished it had turned into a lovely evening.

18.30 Tim rowed across to Jappa to find Ian had gone with a crowd to see "The Three Muskateers" at the local cinema. Ten minutes later we were all on our way! The walk to the cinema seemed endless with the children clamouring to know if they were going to miss the beginning! The cinema was housed in a Tudor styled building reminiscent of a gentile tea house and at a price unheard of in most places Peter plus three children saw the film, the combined price was 65p! I refused to sit in a cinema on a nice evening so met up with some more of our party coming ashore and walked en masse to the lifeboat, the Moot Hall and coastguard look out post. It must be noted that on this occasion we walked for nearly two hours and passed every pub! The others told us of their dire experience when trying to anchor earlier in the day. They apparently set out 10 fathoms of chain in 3 fathoms of water but the wind and current sailed the boats around so that they all went adrift amongst the moorings, all nine of them! So the moral of the tale is don't anchor at Slaughden the ground is not suitable.

The weather looked a little threatening so I hitched a ride aboard Routlette and was asleep when Peter returned at around eleven o'clock. They had enjoyed the film - which I had already been assured of when others of our party arrived from an earlier showing saying 'We heard Peter enjoying himself'. I wonder how they knew he was there! The phosphorescence on this night was marvellous with orange, purple and kingfisher blue light from the water as we sped across the water with the motor on.

Commodore's Notes

In these my first notes as your Commodore and in succeeding notes I will try to continue the policy, so well establish by Dennis, of keeping you as much informed on club affairs as possible. First, however, it is my pleasant duty to say thank you for the hard work done by the members of last years main and sub-committees and particularly those who did not seek re-election at the A.G.M, after several years service, It was a real pleasure to work with you all and I look forward to what I hope will be a successful year with a new Committee on which there are both new and familiar faces and a new Club home,

The first major item of news is that the Clubhouse has now been handed over and has become the property of the M.A.S.C,. and we the Sailing Club members are the custodians of the property and responsible for its management. This event actually took place on Wednesday 27th November.

This custodianship is something your committee takes very seriously and much discussion has taken place on methods of providing the maximum deterent to unwanted guests at Stansgate while still providing the greatest possible freedom for bona fide members of the Club within the constraints imposed by these two aims. As reported at the A.G.M. enquiries have been made to establish the suitability of magnetic locks for use at Stansgate and at the Committee Meeting on December 2nd full discussion was allowed and some conclusions reached, To recap a bit, many of you will know that at least 5 rubber dinghies were stolen from the site during last Season and it is confidently thought that these left by road. Also almost every occasion when members go down outside the usual sailing times strangers are found on the site, ranging from Gypsies trying to find what they can, to picnickers from as far away as London, to Essex residents who claim a right to play in our garden, I have twice in the last two weeks been to Stansgate on business only to find others there uninvited. As you may imagine this gave rise to lively discussion and it was eventually agreed that the only way to keep vehicular traffic off the site (there is public FOOTPATH through the site) and discourage intruders would be to lock the gate, The only practical way to lock the gate and still to provide access to all members arriving by car is to fit a magnetic lock operated by a keycard which is coded, can be produced in large quantities, is uncopyable and returnable if lost without identifying the property to which it gives access. Consideration was then given to access to the Clubhouse and it became obvious that it was desirable to make the same "key" fit the door. It was, therefore, proposed and agreed by the Committee that in the interests of protecting members and club property as far as practical, without placing unacceptable restrictions On members movements, magnetic locks would be fitted to both the gate and Clubhouse and that for this year all members paying a parking fee would be issued with a key which fitted both locks. These locks are expensive and will cost approximately
£325 including installation with a further charge of about £175 for the first batch
of 400 keycards. (There are at present approaching 200 official keys for the old
club in circulation.) This expense will only be justified if members show the necessary sense of responsibility and always lock the Club and gate after them as there will now be no need for members to leave it open for other members without keys, as has been the practice in the past, which lead to the Club being left completely unlocked and unattended for long periods. Further discussion will take place during the year on the methods of issuing keys for future years, the frequency at which all keys need to be changed and the method of covering the cost of these keys.

3.

This is seen as a radical departure from our previous rather lax methods of giving access but it must be remembered that there is not a very large investment in Stansgate made for MSC members and this demands much stricter discipline than previously imposed, and your Committee look for the support and co-operation of all members in making this an effective deterent to our light fingered friends.

Now on to the subject of fitting out the new Clubhouse. The planning sub-committee has now been reformed and will be meeting shortly to continue the process and finalise the plans, so if any of you have ideas about requirements for the club please either drop Ron Greygoose a line or get in touch with your local committee member who will pass on your ideas.

I look forward to seeing many of you at the Christmas Dance on December 14th as I hear the tickets are selling very well. I will close these notes by wishing you all on behalf of the Committee a Very Happy and Merry Christmas.

John Witter, Commodore.

THE MARCONI SAILING CLUB — ANNUAL GENERAL WEETING 1974

COMMODORE'S REPORT

It seems no time at all since we met here at the last A.G.M. The object of these reorts must be to highlight the major events of the year and give members some impression of the way the club is developing. We hope you will express your views freely, because the committee are very anxious to take note of members interests,
I recall that last year, 1 was a little disappointed having to tell you that formal planning permission had not yet been received for the new clubhouse. This year I am, of course, delighted to report that the club- house is complete, and is to be formerly handed over this week.
There is no doubt in my mind that the club did the right thing in voting fot the new clubhouse two years ago. No one could have foreseen the fantastic rise in costs that have occurred in the last year or so- I'm sure we would have been very worried about starting to plan for the new clubhouse now, for completion in two years hence.
Ron Rider has continued to be a great help with his advice, and Bernard Lee has acted as Clerk of Works for the M.A.S.C. throughout the construction. Our grateful thanks to them both. Mick Taylor, as all can gee, has done a grand job, not only with the structure, but also with advice and help with those inevitable associated problems which always seem to crop up.
During the year, your committee took several decisions which we felt cure would be in the long term interest of the club. One of these was to avoid, if at all possible, any change of plans which would increase costs and be unfair to the M.A.S.C.However, it became evident that it would be inconvenient, uneconomic and possibly unsafe to use the existing mains cable for the new clubhouse, so we purchased a new cable and Mick put it in for us. He also equipped the galley and improved some of the electrical services, particularly in the garages. The concrete paths were also extended. We considered these extras to be part of fitting out, and legitimate expenses from the clubhouse and precincts account. The bar has been furnished, including the grill, by courtesy of the brewers.
Several of you have commented about the calor gas cylinder, which we agree is rather an eyesore. This had to be a specified distance from the drains, the main building and be accessible from the road so the choice of position was very limited. We hope to camouflage it in due course with fencing and shrubs.
It is intended to make the Fitting Out party next Spring coincide with the opening of the new clubhouse. I think we should have a small formal ceremony for this milestone, and again your comments would be
helpful.
Now to Sailing - I don't want to steal the thunder of our Sailing
Secretary - but after all, sailing is what it's all about. We can't really
say the weather has been up to much, although none of our events were seriously interrupted. The Regatta was another record — 250 boats this time! Thanks to the most generous hard work put in by the committee and many members, it all went well, and the club received a number of compliments, both at the time and since. At least next year there won't be so much queueing for the essential services.
The management of the 1974 Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Handicaps and Cock of the River, by the Marconi Sailing Club was also most gratify- ing, as not only were we praised for the organisation of the races, but we inherited the event with a deficit and handed over to Dabchicks in credit!

5.

Our own race programme has been well supported and our sailing secretary will be reporting on this.

The cruiser fleet has been very active, no doubt their regular social gatherings have done much to create a fleet spirit. Certainly the armada which sailed on the East Coast Cruise was pretty impressive and the trip throughly enjoyed by all.

A probelm was raised at the beginning of the season by a request from the Sidney Harbour 18 footers for permission to sail from the club. One of our rules prohibits advertising but we decided to waive this for one year, and you have a proposition to modify that rule tonight.

We have, as you know, been somewhat concerned this year about the possible effects on our club of the new Marina in Ramsey Wick, particularly regarding the sea access and its influence on moorings. We have maintained quite a lot of correspondence on this subject and the developers have taken note of our concern. I think that the last letter I received from Bidwells is as much as we can hope for at the present, bearing in mind that as part of the purchase agreement for our own site, the club agreed not to object to planning permission being given for the Marina.

I must now say a few words about subscriptions. When we asked for these to be raised two years ago we said we hoped no further increases would be necessary for some time, and this has been so. We could not have foreseen V.A.T. of course although this was luckily minimised last year by virtue of our separate club and hard fees. I'm afraid that from now on though, V.A.T. is payable on the full subscription. Neither could we have foreseen the rapid inflation and so it may not be possible to hold fees at the present level for many more years.

Nevertheless, as you can see from the accounts, we still have a good reserve, in spite of spending on some fitting out for the new clubhouse, the rates, a new mower, another van etc. We agreed to pay the rates, at least for this year, in lieu of increasing the rent to the M.A.S.C. even though they had to start funding the new clubhouse when building commenced. Incidentally, the rates have risen from £40 to £150 to £660 over the last few years. We are negotiating with the valuation officer for a re-assessment and are hopeful of getting a significant reduction, although this may be somewhat negated by the new clubhouse. The exact contribution we shall pay to the M.A.S.C. for the new clubhouse has still to be fixed, although we have discussed this with them fully and the estimated sum was used to calculate the increased subs two years ago.

One topic of increasing concern is the security of the site and the new clubhouse. As you may know, several inflatable dinghies have been stolen this year, and I'm afraid quite a few people enjoy the benifits of Stansgate without being members. If we are to protect our personal and club property, we must be prepared to accept some small inconviences. The favoured solution at present is toprovide magnetic locks for the main gate and the clubhouse, and for each member to be issued with a key card, the code for which could be changed each year. This would be expensive, but I'm sure worthwhile, as it could also affect the insurance premium for the clubhouse and possibly our own boats if the pilfering is not stopped.

Last year the proposal to hold the Laying - Up Supper at the M.A.S.C. was rejected, but I'm afraid the attendance at the Chancellor Hall this year was not as high as we had hoped. Although the evening was most enjoyable we are worried that the cost for a family is high, and will probably be higher still next year. The final decision for next year's venue must come from the committee but again your opinions will be most welcome.

After sailing, the main activities next year will be fitting out the clubhouse and surronds, and a new planning sub-committee has been set up to tackle this.

Before I close my report, I would like to remind you that this very successful year has been made possible by the hard work and enthusiasm of a magnificient committee and help from many members.

6.

I have been most fortunate in being privileged to work with such a grand team, and to have such kindness and interest shown by you all. I am sorry that i cannot manage my third year, due to several unavoidable factors, but I am very happy to give my wholehearted support to the excellent committee proposed for next year.

I would particularly like to express our grateful thanks to Frank Savill, who has managed our money soefficently for the last three years, as well as maintaining the membership file and distributing "Navigans". He doesn't quite cut-off tomorrow as he will prepare the final account to December 31st, and, characteristically of course, has offered to help the new treasurer settle in.

I would also like to thank Peter Foreman for all the hard work he's put in as our Social Secretary, and for keeping us entertained and well fed.

Our thanks also to the retiring associate representatives. We are sorry to lose Chris Cooper and Clem Michael from the Committee, but both have found it difficult to attend meetings due to changing circumstances. However, the Associates have been very good, and they have nominated four of their members for the two seats on the committee, which will mean we shall have a vote.

I'm sure you will agree that Brenda Tate has done a grand job editing "Navigans", even tho' some of the portraits are better than others. Thank you, Brenda.

Finally, I am pleased to thank Margeret Cottam and Claude Emerson for their unflagging efforts on behalf of us all. We are most grateful for Margaret's devotion in providing us with refreshments virtually every weekend, her bread pud is magnificent. Claude hardly ever misses a day at the club and works very hard not only around the site and in cleaning and painting the clubhouse, but also with boat painting and varnishing.

I mustn't forget Harry Holt, who helps to maintain our security many weekends during the season.

Thank you all and good sailing in 1975.

Dennis Byatt, Commodore.

SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT 1974

The first part of this report covers the club's organised sailing activities, which of course was the published sailing programme. The weather was reasonable kind to us, causing only one occassion when the whole day's racing was cancelled, and even then scratch races were arranged. On the whole the programme was well supported, with the Mirrors emmerging as the largest racing fleet, in fact their summer series had an average entry of over 10 boats. It was pleasing to see big turnouts in the Ladies and Cadets Series. The Handicap fleet had regular racing support this season, which should encourage more boats next year. The Enterprises had similar turnouts to last year and the Hornets slightly fewer. The G.P.14 racing however, was very poorly supported. The Helmsman of the Year final attracted all 10 qualifliers and was won decisively by Julian Bigden.

The more informal events - pursuit races and Wednesday evening races were very popular. Cruiser racing(Barnacle Points) was disappointing, probably due to some bad race management. On the bright side, however, the cruises in company were successful including a fortnight's East Coast cruise with 14 Marconi boats enjoying mixed weather.

Our open events began with the traditional Spring Bank holiday Regatta, which was again blessed with good conditions, had an even larger entry than before. The Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships held at Stone, was organised by ourselves, as it was ourturn, ran smoothly and for that I would like to thank all the helpers, particularly the Ladies. The Marconi Dinghy Challenge Cup was again won by our visitors.

7.

I do urge club members to enter this event as the trophy is an extremely elegant one. The same goes for the Cruiser Cup.

At many local open meetings our members finished up as overall winners including the Hornet Open at Salcote, the Enterprise events at Waldringfield, Maylandsea Bay, Loughton Steeple Bay, Burnham, Brosbourne, Norfolk Broads Area Championships and Loughton Steeple Bay. At National and International level the Hornets, Enterprises and Mirrors were in attendance with Marconi Enterprises again amongst the leaders. A word about the 18' skiffs who provided an interesting spectacle on the occasions they were sailing at Stansgate, many weekends were spent around the country at the invitation of other clubs- and one boat Kwikasair is off to Australia for the World Championships starting January 10th.

The rescue and Race Officer duties on the whole were efficent and it is up to us all to assit when required - one only gets out of the club what is put into it.

Your comments would be welcome on any club matters as it is important that the activities are run for the benefit of our members and they will therefore, be fully supported in return.

John Weedon, Sailing Secretary.

CRUISER SECTION NEWS

I find myself writing this article in my new capacity as cruiser captain- a position I attained in circumstances noneto clear to me, but which reminds me of the soldier left standing when the rest of the troops step backwards on hearing the call for volunteers. However, in more serious vein, I will do my best to further the aims of the cruiser section and the club and will be glad to receive any calls on Danbury [redacted].

The cruiser fleet gathered again in strength at the General's Arms, Little Baddow on Thursday 5th December, and amidst the beer and the laughter, had a most interesting discussion with Gordon Swift, the owner and skipper of the stackie barge "Dawn".

Gordon brought along a photograph of Dawn converted to a sailing haystack and described the trip to London- the need to dig a trench through the stack in order to lower the mast- the return journey loaded with manure- and back to London again with flour. No wonder our bread no longer has character! Gordon very kindly gave an open invitation to visit Dawn in Maldon- or whilst on the River, and of course would welcome any charter parties.

I was sad to read the following article in "Yachting Monthly":-

"While at Ibiza --- --- was joined by another ex-West Mersea craft, the Baltic ketch "Soloeig". Later "Soloeig" sailed to the near by island of Formentera prior to setting sail for South America. The day before her departure she dragged her anchor in a westerly gale and went on the rocks; within twenty-four hours she was a total loss" - a sad way to go.

Many thanks are due to Vic Tate for producing yet another winch from the company archives. Bigger and better than the last, we hope this will reduce the knocking knees and shaky hands of extreme exhaustion from hauling out.

Finally a Merry Christmas to you all, and may your new year be filled with the petrol of your dreams.

Brian Bowsher, Cruiser Captain.

Your committee, at present, has this under consideration and will be discussing at the next meeting the merits of being either a fully Affiliated club or merely an Affiliated club. Briefly the revised membership proposals are as follows. There will be two types of individual member:-
a) Personal Members paying an annual subscription of £5 (of. present £3).
b) Affiliated Members paying through their club, an annual subscription of &1.
This type of member would be contacted by the R.Y.A. through the club.
c) Fully Affiliated Clubs will collect the £1 R.Y.A. subscription from all their
members, except personal members of the R.Y.A., and forwards their fee to the R.Y.A. The club then pays no annual subscription itself.
do) Affiliated Clubs will pay an annual subscription of 4% of the agreed membership income with a min. of £10 and a max. of £300. For the M.S.C. this would be about the same total as we are currently paying.

6.

The log of "Roulette" continued.

Wedn ist Jul

The wind was blowing strongly when we awoke, and we were not at all surprised the others had previously gone adrift for we had sailed around the mooring all night long. Peter had tied the dinghy alongside in desperation for despite a bucket anchor she had bumped for an hour or so earlier. A campaign was mounted after breakfast to get ashore with the minimum effort. We have no motor and the tide was very strong and also we were a good way from the quay. Finally we calculated that we could go over to the nearby saltings and walk along the sea wall to town. We had a very smooth passage ashore and tied the dinghy up. A pleasant half hour walk found us in Aldeburgh and we got all our supplies in a super delicatessen shop and had time to browse in the many lovely bookshops before early closing. Unfortunately by the time we got to the Moot House Museum it too was shut. Obviously another reason to return again in the future. The other reason was the delicious local caught fish and chips which we consummed on the beach in true tradition straight out of the paper, only to be greeted by a past member of E.E.V. staff. He remarked "You certainly look the part, one would never have taken you for an employee of EEV" True praise we felt!

We arrived to collect the dinghy to find we had left it a little late! We hTM* to negotiate three feet of mud to reach the dinghy! But with an assortment of dra.t wood, boxes and planks we achieved our end and it was a much smoother operation than expected! Luck was on our side again for no sooner were we aboard and brewing up a cup of tea when another squall hit us! We had planned to drop down to Butley River but on seeing the Cherry's return to their mooring after setting out half an hour before,we stayed where we were and Peter rowed over to hear how they had got on. They had taken water over the deck in the first leg of the trip with 5 rolls in the main and a storm job! We settled down for a cosy evening and heard on the weather forecast that the winds were force 7-8!

Thurs August lst

The alarm went off at five o'clock and it was very much less windy but still about force 4. We set out for Butley at 5.30 a.m. motoring all the way as the wind was dead on the nose. The sunrise was gorgeous,and made us feel better about getting up so early.

06.30 Listened to the weather forecast off Orford. Gales forecast for Thames
SW5-7, Gale 8 dropping to W4 but increasing later SW5-7. Gallope SW5.
We found the rest of the fleet moored off Orford.

06.50 Pulled alongside Jappa because Jack was on deck. Had a cup of tea and chat. It was hard to believe the gale warnings it was such a pleasant morning but still too late to change our plan and leave for the Deben.

08.10 Left Jappa and though the tide was now reasonably strong against us we managed to make Butley River by 08.50 where we anchored with trip and buoy. We found out unwittingly how they all went adrift at Aldeburgh. We set the tiller to hold towards the bank but in actual fact it enabled the boat to sail. She rode over the trip, trapped it in the propellor or rudder and away we went! Luckily we realised the buoy had disappeared and got worried. Released fairly easily.We sent the children ashore and I tidied up while Peter mended the mizzen where a runner had come adrift. The sun came out and Tim and Chris went swimming, the latter with a life jacket and line on him. After lunch Ace of Diamonds and Whimbrel crews came aboard for a cup of tea. We heard shouting on short and looked out to see Lyn, Dave, Louise and Ian sitting on the bank. They had walked from Orford. They wallowed through the mud and Tim picked them up and with very little free board made their way to Roulette with legs over the side to clean off! Soon the boats appeared and we all went

aboard Jappa.

Friday August 2nd

Peter awoke at 2 a.m. and on glancing out of the porthole found we were alongside Tijo, having drifted downstream past two boats en route! He'd only put out 5 fathoms instead of 8!

Up at 5 a.m. - very misty.

05.40 Left the mooring, motored down on the ebb, very little wind until we were into the main channel of Ore. We put up a mainsail and two foresails but kept the motor going to head better. We found the leading marks hard to see as we were low in the water and the shingle banks were high. However we found them once they were in line, which we felt was a bit late! The course was roughly S.E. with a fair swell coming in the channel. We started to punch the first of the flood which was quite vigorous.

06.20 Passed Ore Channel Buoy and headed down the coast, the wind was on the beam about 3-4. Sea calm with a gentle swell. Cut motor. Woodbridge Haven buoy very easy to distinguish, we aimed for it until the Bar Buoy sighted. We had previously spotted the red can buoy close to shore. Went about almost on top of Woodbridge Buoy. We found we could not hold our heading under sail alone so switched on motor. The course from the Bar Buoy to the Red Can, magnetic North, leading marks dead in line, though we did not realise at first. The A has been replaced by two spades Ww which is orange not black.

This is not an easy river to enter and to be on the correct course one must pass through the roughest water close to the shingle bank. We headed for the red and white chequered buoy on the Horse Shoe Shoal, which becomes very shallow (7 feet) just before it one turns leaving the buoy to port. This despite the fact that the buoy is marked as a middle channel buoy. The shoal was very clearly visible even when we came in 2 hours after low water. We decided that the sails were of no help whatsoever so we motored up on the flood. Just below Ramsholt we spotted a dinghy on the mud, just about to go adrift. There was no sign of a rope anchor or yet footprints away from it, so we pulled up on a nearby mooring and rowed over to investigate. It was just in time because as we took her in tow she floated off the mud. Set off to take her to the nearest yacht club up the river passing Segla and Carasou at Rams Holt. The Stevens hadn't been able to leave Brightlingsea until the previous day. Towing the dinghy was a lark, it scudded from side to side, later Nick Tovey told us we should have dropped the centre plate a little and set the rudder central. We made it up to the Rocks, where the others, who had overtaken us while on our rescue mission, were anchored. We in turn anchored and put out 8 fathoms of chain in 5 feet of water. It was abeautifulmorning and we sunbathed on deck, the children playing happily on shore with ropes on the trees and a sand slide down the steep bank. Most people had a swim. After lunch it clouded over so Peter and I went for a walk to stock up on supplies. We decided we couldn't get to Waldringhamfield, as the path on the 0.S. map didn't look complete so we set out for Shottisham, and were able to do a circular route of approx. 6 miles! The rabbits appeared very tame at first and didn't attempt to run from us, then we realised they were almost blind with bulging eyes, they seemed diseased possibly with myxomatosis.

8.

Partridges by the score flew low out of cornfields or ran under the drops. The farms seemed to specialise in pigs and root crops and we passed a beautiful old tithe barn with grown timbers for the angle beams of the roof. Shottisham was a quiet village with an old church dating from the 135th century. The tower was in need of repair and an elderly lady busy polishing the brass said the population was depleted as the old were dying off and no young families were moving in.

We wanted sausages for our barbecue that evening so bought the store out of them, 8 in all! On the way back we saw hatcheries for the partridges and passed a huge Manor House which caters for shooting parties. Once back at the "Rocks" we collected wood and moved a huge treeroot and trunk in preparation for our bonfire. Meanwhile Roulette went aground and to our horror we found our anchor laid on its side on hard rock, certainly not suitable for anchoring especially near in.
Fortunately we hadn't chosen the bit that shelved steeply to 12', Stan apparently did this one year and landed up at a ridiculous angle. We ate supper and moved to a deeper anchorage with enough anchor chain for a battleship. We rowed ashore at dusk, with a full moon coming up and a huge fire glowing on the beach. What a sight. We once again cooked sausages and also potatoes in the fire and a good time was had by all.

Saturday August 3rd ~Y

After breakfast we set off by dinghy to Waldringhamfield. Jack gave us a tow after we set out trying to sail! We had a drink at the pub and then walked to the Yacht Club to enquire about friends of ours from Woodbridge who were competing in the Deben Week races being held there. Almost immediately Sid appeared and in no time he and Maureen, plus her brother and wife had joined us over another pint at the pub! We told them of our trip but they capped it all by saying they had been out ina Wayfarer outside the bar on Sunday in force 6-7 negotiating a buoy in the middle of the bar! They decided they would like to join us at the Rocks and come to the barbecue so we promised to fetch them that night on Roulette. We sailed and rowed back to the boat with the tide and after lunch Peter went ashore to wash some of the Alde mud off the dinghy. I stayed aboard to do likewise to Roulette ready for the invasion. That evening there was a beautiful wind so we set 2 foresails and a mizzen and did not need any more despite the last of the spring ebb.

We drifted upstream with Carol at the helm and picked up a mooring 20-30 yds off the Maybush Inn. Tim went ashore for water and then ferried our 6 visitors aboard, four adults plus 2 children. They were settled either below or in the cock-— pit and with the main sail hoisted we set off downstream once again. On landing a’ the Rocks we were later told that our party were taken for Pakistani refugees coming ashore! The huge fire was beautiful, someone had even found a hollow trunk to act as a chimney. The only disadvantage on this occasion was the acrid smoke from a
fellow picknickers bonfire - they were burning new wood. At 10.15 p.m. we once again
ferried our party aboard with the kind help of Stan and motored up river, navigating in pitch dark with no moon until we reached a mooring once more off the Maybush Inn. Having ferried our party ashore we were soon in bed with the promise of meeting up with them again in the morning.

SOCIAL SCREED

Winter Meeting :- Two speakers gave interesting and entertaining talks to about 70 people at our first meeting of 1975.

Sam Poulton from Maldon drew on his great depth of knowledge and experience of the Spritsail barges, that often sail past Stansgate, and gave us a glimpse of the characters who sailed and worked them over the years. Sam owned and raced his own barge some years ago. This was brought for the princely sum of £90 (current selling price £6,000), but because of high maintenance costs, he had to have her broken up; a fate which Sam sadly predicts will overtake many of the present barges on the river. He also showed a film of barge races giving a magnificent view of the massed fleets, and incidentally a glimpse of the virile bargeman's dreams- also magnificent.

John Jowers, a fisherman from Mersea, gave the second talk of the evening. John, formerly a University lecturer turned to full time fishing 2 or 3 years ago, I believe. It was something of a surprise to find that this is an expanding business along the Essex Coast. The theme of the talk was that fishermen and yachtsmen can co-exist without undue fricton on the same waters given common sense, and an understanding of the others man's problems. Drifters apparently, shoot out up to one mile of nets and then drift up the Blackwater with the tide. Here the fishing boat can't get out of the way, the drag of ½ mile of net prohibits any manoeuvre. Pair trawling - that is two boats sailing abeam of each other with a massive trawl net in between, is also carried out on the Blackwater - get caught between those and the chances of losing mast, boat and finishing up on a slab at Billingsgate isn't right out of the question it seems.

Our thanks go to Sam Poulton and John Jowers for an evening well spent.

The next winter meeting is again at the M.A.S.C. Main Hall on Wednesday 19th February, starting at 7.45pm. As announced previously we will be welcoming as our speaker Mr R.K. Pilsbury. Mr Pilsbury, now retired from the Met Office, will be giving a talk on the major concern to yachtsmen - the weather. So here's looking forward to another good turn out. Why not bring along a guest?

The start of the sailing season is drawing closer with the opening of the new club-house and the Fitting Out Party both on the same day, Saturday March 22nd. The party is from 8pm. to midnight, with music from the Midnight Sound Group. It is intended to provide a buffet, but in order to minimise costs, I'm hoping that plenty of volunteers will offer their services to prepare food. The cost of materials will be re-imbursed- please contact Audrey or myself. Tickets will be on sale in March, cost yet to be determined but probably around 70p. Unfortunately, it will be necessary to limit numbers to150.

I have just finished a book by Mike Harper, the assistant editor of "Yachting and Boating", called "Through France to the Med."(or Any Yachtsman's Attainable Dream). It is the sort of book for reminding one of the other side of life on cold wet weekends and

There now follows the third and final part of Gill Foreman's log of "Roulette".

Sunday August 4th

Peter awoke at 5.30 a.m. and in pouring rain put the tent over our cockpit up. By & o'clock there was a gale blowing so we lazed in, had a late breakfast watching Ace and Segla going upstream. We set out at noon and in really heavy rain, thunder and lightning we made for Woodbridge. Tim and Peter suitably dressed in all their oilies were in charge and we watched the storm from below. One huge flash we found later had put the O'Hara's (the friends we were meeting again) electricity off. We entered the marina quite well but once in, it becomes very narrow and we made a complete hash=-up of getting into a berth, the wind, which was very strong, kept blowing us into the boats while we were trying to turn round. Luckily, Snowgoose, Carasou and Whimbrels crews were at hand to help us! Once in we packed up the boat, collected towels and clean clothes and made our way to meet Sid who had gallantly offered us all showers. Perhaps that was a condition of going to stay with them on second thoughts, we had been afloat for over a week! We had a wonderful day with them, reliving all our times together in the States, where we had originally met. They too are now happily settled in this country and we couldn't blame them liking their setting in Woodbridge. Perhaps I shouldn't mention our evenings entertainment
in what is meant to be a seamans log - Shush!! We went bowling!! On our return it
was damp and cold and we gladly took up their offer of a bed on the floor for the nighy instead of negotiating the damp, dark reaches of Woodbridge Marina.

Monday August 5th

We slept very well and after breakfast took Neil, our friends offspring, in exchange for Carol, swimming. She envisaged a day on terra firma and Neil certainly seemed to like sailing round the Marina and river with Tin. I went in search of stores again and Peter, and the boys braved the outdoor swimming pool. Rack to the boat for lunch after a drink aboard.

Carasou with Ken and Avril, Peter, Neil and Tim went exploring the other side of the river in the grounds of Sutton Hoo. Chris played with Mary beside the boat most of the afternoon, while I read. Maureen arrived with Carol to swop children again and we had a cup of tea aboard, at 7 p.m. we saw them off as we planned to move on once more tomorrow. They promised to come and explore 'our'river next year. We had supper and went to admire the mullet, a 4 1b one, caught by Dave (Starlight). By the end of the holiday he speared one fish for each boat on the trip and they made a lovely meal.

Chris and Tim went to bed and we left Carol with Ian (Jappa) and Peter and I went for a long walk along the river bank. We came back at ten o'clock to find a party in full swing on Tijo and Thundercloud to meet John Swintons arrival, and a hilarious evening was had by all. Luckily there was no one sleeping aboard the boats in the her vicinity!

Tuesday August 6th

Woke about 9 a.m. to a lovely sunny morning and breakfasted on kippers. After lunch we set out for Ramsholt after watching a hair washing ceremony with hoses on the pontoons? We moored at the Tips, just above Waldringfield. It had been recommended by Sid and Maureen. Peter sailed the children ashore to swim and I sunbathed, it was really hot out of the wind, which was bitter. We went down to Ramsholt later and found Carasou, Ace, Segla and Snowgoose. It was a most beautiful evening and sunset. It was Our turn for the mullet that night and it went down a treat with a bottle of wine. The children sailed themselves ashore while I wrote the log and read, Peter plotted our trip for tomorrow, though the weather forecast at 17.55 was not favourable.

7.

Wednesday August 7th

Woke before 6.30 a.m., the weather forecast was still force 4, rising to 5-6. Decided at least to try to go to Bawdsey and as we only have a 1½ hr passage down the coast we shall probably chance it before the 5-6's set in.

08.30 Left mooring following Snowgoose, with Segla right behind. As we approached the bar a chap who had just come in remarked that it was pretty rough but it didn't look too bad. With the wind at a maximum force 3 we gauged it was safe to go. There was quite a swell, with waves of two to three feet. The minimum depth on the echo sounder reached 4'. In fact with each wave it was 4 foot, seven foot, 4 foot again in rapid succession. Once we were out to sea the waves levelled off and we set course 180°M for Wadgate Ledge. Segla soon overtook us on a close haul. Felixstowe Pier in sight, a really beautifully clear morning.

10.00 Being swept down the coast decided to head straight down 230°M.

10.05 Felixstowe Pier in line.

10.15 Went over the Platters, it showed up as a line of smooth, then rough water, dropped from 16' - 7' very quickly. Platters Bell could be clearly heard. We aimed straight for the Rolling Ground buoy, course still 210°-220°M. At this point we took a photograph of a large coaster going out from Harwich. Another boat, probably a dredger came out but did not keep to the channel. Peter jibbedto avoid and at that moment the wake from the other hit us broadside. We then had to jib again because he headed determinedly across our bow. We passed inside the N.W. Beach and on a beautiful reach with a smooth water roared up Harwich Channel. We noted how attractive Harwich Church looked.

11.00 Entered the R.Orwell approx. ½ hr ahead of schedule. A coaster overtook with no trouble at all.

Off Cullimer Point turned for a dead run and poled out roller jib as a huge ferry came by en route between Ipswich and Rotterdam.

12.15 Turned on the motor to head into the wind and picked up a mooring 100 yds from Boat hard beacon.

13.00 Ashore at Pin Mill after grounding in the dinghy by the barges off the "Butt and Oyster". We enjoyed a drink here for they have a side room where children are welcome and one can buy cold snacks. Here we met up with Snowgoose and Segla crew and after a meal we set out to walk up the lane to Chelmondiston to get stores. We returned to sit on the quay while Chris and Mary played in the Mill stream. The Mill itself is no longer standing, the name however goes back as far as the 14 when the old mill with its millpond or pynd stood in the valley a little way back from the river, where the grass grown banks can still be seen.

8.

Ipswich townsmen used to have their 'main water' supply in the form of a "pennd" from a neighbouring brook flowing into their gardens. Although we no longer use this old word for the stream at Pin Mill, it is still called the Grindle, which is another old Suffolk word meaning the same thing.

The Butt and Oyster is probably 16 and was an ale house and reputed to be a smugglers haunt, it may have been a ferryhouse too. Later when the tide went down we walked in the woods alongside the shore and returned via the shore beneath the huge barges. We found a sandy beach with grass banks and a beautiful view over moored boats on the river to the parkland and manor house opposite. We saw a strange bamboo like growth which I had never come across before and evidently it is a very ancient plant called Horse tails or Equistales and dates from the very early days of the swamplands.

18.30 Back on board Snowgoose and Segla were moving on to the marina at Levinton and told us dire tales of being moored very near the main channel. Peter stubbornly refused to move and after a very bumpy hour or so, once the tide changed, the mooring was very comfortable. We weren't aware of any commercial traffic overnight and after all what the eye don't see the heart don't grieve over! We slept well!

Thursday August 8th

We woke early to continuous rain and it was very overcast. We were undecided what to do. After listening to the weather at 7.55 a.m. which was a bit more favourable decided to up anchor and go down river. We had thought of going up to Ipswich but the large commercial traffic put us off a little.

08.40 Left the mooring and sailed in a light S.W. which developed into a good force 3-4 after Levington which carried us on a nice broad reach down river. It started to rain again. A huge dredger came up behind us and passed down the channel. We noted that Levington Marina had a lightship for her clubhouse.

10.55 Passed Parkeston Quay. Lovely W/SW blowing taking us on long tacks up river, half a mile each tack. We passed Galloper light vessel plus three others which pleased the children. Many of the large liners were loading so it was a very interesting voyage. Luckily none were moving.

11.45 Recognised Ken Bevin's boat heading up for Pin Mill. We had a lovely wind, still 3-4 S.W.

12.15 Mist rolled up and made visibility pretty bad so we decided to pick up a mooring off Wrabness Point and have lunch.

13.15 Mist lifting,on up to Mistley on motor with sprit sail and mizzen set.

13.45 Alongside quay at Mistley beside the warehouses and maltings. We walked into Manningtree passing the remaining two towers of Robert Adam's Mansion built for Richard Rigby, grandson of a linen draper and son of a father who made a great fortune ouf of the South Sea Company and had enormous funds to spend on the Mistley Hall Estate. He became M.P. and Paymaster General of the Forces. The port, which his father had already begun, laid out a shipyard, stone built quays, a timber yard, warehouses, maltings and limekiln together with the amenities of a fashionable watering place, bathing pavilions, swan pool, fountains and a new church.

9.

The swans are still there as we found to our cost. They stood on the only footpath in their dozens and refused to move, so we took our lives in our hands and walked on the road! As we walked a huge black cloud appeared before us so Peter, Chris and Tim turned back and Carol and I went into Manningtree for shopping. "More shopping", was Peter's comment!

14.55 Peter and the boys arrived back at the boat to find it had risen three feet in an hour, no wonder it sluices out on the first of the ebb.

Meanwhile loaded with provisions and wet to the skin, Carol and I saw a neighbour from our estate driving through. They enquired if we were enjoying our holiday afloat! We must have looked the part with oilskins and sou'westers. We hot footed it back to the boat in the midst of the thunder storm.

16.00 Left Mistley, motored off until we picked up the wind off Waift fleet Creek. Headed on broad reach towards Wrabness. It brightened up and we debated going on down to Walton immediately, until we saw the thunder clouds gathering behind us. We were just about to pick up the mooring as the storm broke with hail, heavy rain, thunder and lightning. We decided to stay for the night on a large mooring. The storm lasted for two hours but we were quite content reading and playing cards aboard.

Friday August 9th

09.05 Left the mooring, little wind. The forecast at 06.30 had predicted W.4.

09.45 Passed the Sir Alan Herbert, a Thames Barge, anchored ¼ mile up stream from Erwarton Ness in line with Beaumont Hall. The sun was shining and the wind a steady 2-3.

10.30 Passed Parkeston Quay, the wind was freshening in gusts. We took down the washing - drying from the storm the previous day - to improve visibility!

11.40 Passed the Pye End Buoy. We motored for 35 mins until we turned into Walton channel. The wind had veered S.W. making sailing impossible.

12.40 On a mooring in the Twizzle, having passed Tijo and Jappa on our way in. Once again we tried to sail the dinghy ashore and started off well but it turned into a close haul so took a little longer than expected! One doesn't feel very seamanlike with 5 in a small dinghy, sailing one tack and rowing the other! We walked into Walton and bought fish and chips to consume on the beach as usual. We then made for the Pier and spent the afternoon with the children on the amusements. This was intended as a treat for them alone but Peter used up a lot of the tickets on the bumper cars and I even braved the big wheel! The sea looked fairly calm from the top of the wheel, but at ground level there was quite a swell. We realised that we were also sheltered by the headland. We returned Ian to Jappa and had a council of war to decide whether to venture home.

The weather forecast was predicting Force 6-7 so it looked as if we were going to be holed up after all. Planned to listen to the 6.30 a.m. weather in the morning before making any decisions.

10.

Saturday August 10th

We woke during the night to hear the wind and rain lashing down. On awakening for the 6.30 a.m. weather we turned over and went back to sleep - it was not at all favourable, with W. Gales all around the coast. Peter and Tim went ashore to get supplies and were not back until one o'clock! They had to walk miles because they landed at Foundry Creek hard instead of Colonels Hard nearby. This was a big mistake because they found a dinghy adrift and walked miles to a boat builders to report it. It turned out that they owned the mooring we had taken in the Twizzle and we were advised to move because it hadn't a very heavy anchor. We couldn't help thinking that if it had stood up to the previous nights storm it was pretty safe! Peter returned and looked at the other mooring he had advised and found it had an appallingly thin chain! We decided that the £5.5 fee in the manna would be well worth it if we had to desert the boat. The whole afternoon and evening was interspersed with heavy squalls and we stayed aboard. However by the evening the wind had swung round N.W. which was a favourable wind for the return journey should it die down a bit. To bed to await the morning forecast, though very doubtful we would take the boat home that weekend.

Sunday August 11th

We heard the 6.30 a.m. weather forecast, gales all up the coast, so the decision was obvious, despite the fact that conditions in the river at that time looked favourable. We dropped down to confer with Jappa. Vic Tate was already there, he was wondering whether to take Snowgoose down with Robert aboard sending the others by train. We stated we were going into the Marina to leave the boat to return when conditions were more favourable, probably next weekend. It was a very easy Marina to enter and moor, plenty of room, unlike that at Woodbridge. We left Roulette alongside Segla, Dennis had left the previous day, and set off towards the station, two miles away, looking like refugees with pillow cases of dirty washing over our shoulders! I wasn't leaving that aboard for a week! Once at the station we were lucky to catch the 11.45 a.m. train which was running late and were home in Chelmsford by 1.15 p.m. It is a very easy journey from Walton and I would never worry about leaving the boat there should we need to in the future - very different from the journey home from Brightlingsea when we got holed up there - but thats another story! -

There was still a question mark over our decision as the weather both en route and in Chelmsford looked very suitable for a passage. However later Vic confirmed that conditions had been pretty hairy.

It was disappointing to have to leave Roulette on Walton but why spoil what had been a superb holiday when there was always another weekend to collect her.

CRUISER HANDICAPS 1975

At a Cruiser Handicap meeting of the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee (B.J.R.C.) in February, the method of handicapping for 1975 was agreed.

They will keep strictly to the procedure for allocating and re-rating cruiser handicaps as laid out in the R.Y.A. publication YR2/74, with the exception that yachts with established handicaps will only be re-rated twice a year; once in the winter, and again in mid-season. (This year after the Smith's Cup.)

Yachts without established handicaps,i.e. neither a previous B.J.R.C. handicap nor a R.Y.A. primary or secondary yardstick will be re-rated after each of their first three B.J.R.C. races in accordance with the R.Y.A. procedure which bases their handicap on their average performance so far. After the third race the handicap becomes B.J.R.C. established, and will only be changed twice a year. This adjustment each half-season will be the sum of the differences in performance in the races completed, divided by the number of races completed plus three.

This adjustment will apply to all handicaps, including those of yachts with primary and secondary yardsticks. However, the yardsticks will be maintained for those yachts solely for the purpose of calculating the standard time for each race. (The standard time is the corrected time of the centre-placed yardstick yacht in the race, using her yardstick number, not the handicap.)

This year the B.J.R.C. races are :-

July 20th - Smith's Cup
Aug. 3rd - Maldon Y.C. Cruiser Trophy

Brute force, maybe; but ignorance none. An account of the 1st British crew, Alf Reynolds, Bruce Long and Brian Elry, to participate in the 18' skiff Worlds (Sydney 18's).

"Hello there", typical Aussie greeting we thought, must be in the right place.

"Your on tele, Channel 9's midday sports program - at eleven".

"Yes, that figures ", we thought, "Aussie logic at its best".

This was the way that three superb weeks of sailing, sun, swimming and sightseeing began. (You'll notice no sex - after all, we are British). Suffering from too much British Airways booze and food, we emerged into the Sydney sunshine, pale and forlorn, to be immediately surrounded by brown and brawny bodies, ever had that slightly inferior feeling?

Apres the television, we were whisked away to the New South Wales 18 footers league club, snatched a quick bite to eat in the club's restaurant and joined a private boat loaded to the gunwales with grog ready to watch the opposition performing in Sydney Harbour. Being Saturday, the racing was organised by the Sydney Flying Squadron and this was the last heat, but one, for the Australian titles, so all the big names were on the water. It didn't take long to appreciate the standard was high, very high, and that the new Bruce Farr designs are in a class of their own. Bruce, a young New Zealander, has developed the 18's over the past five years from relative heavyweights to featherweights. Modern hulls rarely weigh more than 160lbs equipped with their basic gear, this added to highly developed rigs, related to crew weight had made the 18's absolutely untouchable in the dinghy field. The new hulls feature a relatively narrow entry in the first six feet, but are formed in quite a pronounce 'U' section to prevent nosedipping. Having kept the entry narrow, the sides then rapidly flare outwards to the gunwales. This is the final stopgap which prevents the boat completely submarining in a big sea. The aft sections run out fairly flat, with a nearly straight chine the length of the boat. The amount of bottom round and thus the amount of buoyancy available in the hull is once again geared to crew weight.

For instance, a light weight crew say 32 stone, will use a design which is considerably narrower in the chine beam and which is slightly flatter all round, than one for a crew of 39 to 40 stone. Science is the new keyword, KB for instance, have a paid aeronautics expert at hand to advise on sail shape etc. and to keep a weekly watch on strech and warping etc. which may affect their performance. Incidently, the KB crew quite happily sail for 2 hours a weekend and devote 25 hours during the week in maintenance and improvement - carefully photographing each stage as they change gear.

The racing on Sydney Harbour used to be followed by five ferries - now only two remain old age having claimed the others but racing is followed more enthusiastically than ever by a huge fleet of private yachts and motor boats.

Our week was spent alternatively working on the new Kwikasair - which we'd borrowed from Phil O'Donnel, sunbathing, surfing and stuffing ourselves with the biggest steaks on earth. "Kwikasair" had been plagued by ill luck since her completion 2 months previously - this we felt was because the builder hadn't followed Bruce Farr's plans. Try as we might there were some aspects which we couldn't rectify or improve, and instinctively felt would be troublesome later on.

The following weekend we flew Ansett to Brisbane, where Jane joined us, leaving Phil to tow the boat up for us. The Brisbane river was our first shock, Horneteers will when I say a "super Shoreham harbour". Filthy with cromate from the tanning factory and blood from the abattoirs it takes on a light brown tinge which is tidal and runs out at about 2 knots. The banks are crowded with docks, a power station, the previously mentioned abattoirs and tanning factory and finally a huge petrol storage area streching either side of the river. However, to compensate the Brisbane 18 footers club was super. One armed bandits are not allowed in Queensland, but nevertheless the club seemed very well off-particularly with an English bar manager.

We were made particularly welcome and eventually stayed with the Commodore in a caravan situated in his back garden. He was also putting up twothirds of the New Zealand team. I think this all got too much for him towards the end of the series- particularly as he'd two young attractive daughters, who were making the most of their ten days of good fortune. There were to be six races - the first was an allcomers invitation with a handicap (pursuit) start.

7.

Kwikasair was favourite to win as we'd obtained a very early getaway but inspite of an excellent windward leg our spinnaker work was shoddy and we eventually went swimming. At the commencement of the series proper, we had to say goodbye to Phil, who was flying to America for his firm, and in his place acquired a proper team coach, Wally Web - complete with speed boat to follow our motley performance. After our first two races Wally was fit to blow a gasket - he'd stand in his little yellow boat shouting and waving his arms, we weren't flat enough, our tacking was too slow, and worst of all - he was right. We had 16th and 13th to our credit and determined to do better in the 3rd race. Suddenly we seemed to hit the go button - the boat came alive to windward and amazed at its performance - wrong selection of kite got us only 14th, but we were improving and beginning to see the light. The fourthrace was frankly a disaster from start to finish. A poor windward leg and the eventual loss of the spinnaker halyard, which meant a capsize to retrieve it put us fair and square at the back. Determined we carried on and started making good ground on the second beat, very flat and fast when an IYE bailer disappeared clean out the bottom leaving a gaping hole into which the water gushed with the ferocity of Trafalgar. It was sink or swim. so with Brian's foot square over the hole we sailed for home. If the fourth race was disheartening the fifth was a tragedy. The wind came up to 25 knots gusting 35, by far the strongest breeze all week. We equipped Kwikasair with her smallest rig, knowing this would deliver more power than we could cope with. We were all conscious of the boat's weak points and the fact that it didn't belong to us, any damage wouldn't be popular, but Wally said, "Sail like... and never mind the consequences", so we did just that. From the gun we flew, Kwikasair felt as if she had a rocket under her, hard on the wind we couldn't stop her planeing, not ideal as we thought it would go faster if we could keep more hull in the water. With the wind shrieking and the main 90% backwinded, we corrected from none to none, with one particularly hard fall into a trough and the three of us hard on the wire, Kwikasair gave a grunt and then the tearing of timber was all we heard as the plate case collapsed.

Wally, all this time had been dancing with glee, as we were lying 7th and whilst not front runners, this promised to be our best result of the week - but alas Kwickasair UK and its three occupants was now sadly settling in the water. Thus ended the series not quite as successful as we'd hoped but packed with valuable experience.

KB won the series with precision power sailing that was totally faultless. We watched awestruck as she deliberately gave up 1st position to the close second runner as she set a 75 square foot extra. For the first half mile afer this manouvre it was too close to see - and her crew let it flog. The competition now were robbed of their opportunity to hoist anything quickly - requiring all their weight outside the boat. As the wind eased at a bend the nearer KB sheeted this sail and powered through, never to be seen again. Well who knows- a British champion in five years - I think it quite possible.

Bruce Long.

March 1975.

PROCEDURE FOR USE OF CLUBHOUSE BY MEMBERS.

As with the old Clubhouse we have made arrangements for all members to use the Clubhouse freely at any time and not to be dependant on the presence of a Club Official. In providing this freedom we have relied on you as members to act with a strong sense of responsibility to the Club and its property by ensuring that the Clubhouse is never left open and unattended. It is therefore timely to remind you of some of the necessary disciplines to ensure the safety and security of the Club and some of the facilities available.

1. Avoid leaving the Club unlocked and unattended at any time ie leaving it open while going out sailing or to the end of the dinghy park to work on your boat.

2. Avoid opening windows or other doors unless it is essential and then always shut them again before leaving club.

3. Avoid switching on electricity unless it is essential and always remember to turn off all lights and main supply before leaving (main supply is on wall just inside front door).

4. Do not put on heaters unless it is essential and always remember to switch off before leaving. Operating instructions are stuck to heaters.

5. Normally during the season Hot water will only be available from the galley water heater during weekdays.

6. Because of the nature of the drainage system members are asked at all times to use water sparingly in the Clubhouse to avoid unnecessary and costly emptying of cesspool.

7. Always remember to carry your cardkey with you as it is necessary to use it to leave the site as well as to gain entrance. Never let people who are not members follow you in through the gate as they may not be able to leave again.

8. Members may use the gas kettles to make hot drinks when the galley is not manned.

9. As and when the Galley is not manned members, in exchange for the contribution shown on the box, may use the Tea, Coffee, Sugar, powdered milk in the top cupboard to the left of the cooker for making hot drinks

10. Please wash, dry and put away crockery etc after use.

11. First aid kit is available in the Galley and members are asked to log items used so that a rapid check of replacement requirements can be made.

12. The key board in the galley holds keys for winches and floodboards and members are asked to return keys after use.

13. A bench, vice and some tools are available in Garage 4 for members use when an OOD or Club Officer is present.

To be distributed to all existing members and to all new members by the Treasurer with their receipt. To be revised as required and reissued annually.

EDITORIAL

That old saying that the man who goes sailing for pleasure will go to hell fora pastime can certainly be applied to some club members, who braved the elements and were sailing in a snowstorm on Easter Sunday.
We have however, enjoyed a few days of sunshine and the Handicap fleet have been the first to take advantage of racing in decent weather. After the discussions about a new class dinghy last year, the problem seems to have resolved itself and we have an increased handicap fleet with everyone "doing their own thing".
A few cruisers have appeared back on their moorings although those in the dinghy park maybe able to sail out shortly, the ground is so waterlogged. Let us hope that the Gods will smile upon us and give us the usual good weather we enjoy for the Regatta.

Brenda Tate.

COMMODORES NOTES
The Fitting Out Party on March 22nd was a great success, if the reports and comments I have heard are any thing to go by; and I would like to thank you all for coming and converting our new building into a lively Sailing Club clubhouse. A more formal occasion is being planned for the evening of Saturday May 17th, when our President, Sir Eric Eastwood, the Officers and Committee will be hosts to invited guests, who have sailing connections with the club or have helped with the planning and building.The evening will be a club function and members who also wish to attend should complete the tear-off slip at the end of this issue, as soon as possible, so that we will have an idea of the numbers wanting to come.
There are still a large number of small jobs to be done in and around the clubhouse to complete the fitting out,and if there are members coming down who would like to lend a hand, for a short period, please, find either Ron Greygoose,
Vic Tate or myself for details of what is to be done.
It was a very pleasant surprise to find that many of the holes in the road had been filled and we are all very grateful to be relieved of this task, by the thoughtful gesture of Mike Taylor, who had some spare material.

John Witter, Commodore.

ASSOCIATE MEMBERSHIP

Bach year we take on a limited number of new Associate members who, by virtue of their connections with the club, the Committee feel are eligible for membership. There are still a few vacancies for the year and while not wishing to have applications from total strangers members are invited to propose for membership friends who already have strong connections with the club, or attend as the guests or crews for members and are already using the club. Application forms are available from the secretary or committee members and if you want to make proposals I suggest this is done quickly.
The fees applicable to Associate Members arei-

Husband and Wife £12.96 including M.A.S.C. fees.
Hard fee for boat owners £8.64. Joining fee £5.40. All fees include V.A.T. at 8%.

OLD CLUBHOUSE —- MEMBERS PROPERTY

The old clubhouse is now in the process of being cleared of all club property and ~—sembers are asked to ensure that all personal property is removed from it byApril 30th. she clubhouse and sheds are due for demolition shortly as part of the conditions of our planning approval. Property remaining there after that date will be considered unwanted and will be disposed of as neccessary.

DISPOSAL OF OLD CLUBHOUSE

The committee is anxious to find a buyer for the old clubhouse, which has served us so well for the last 12 years and if any members know of any organisation that are looking for a structure of this type I should be pleased to hear from them. The only condition placed on the disposal of the building is that the purchaser dismantles and removes, and that the removal is carried out against a time scale acceptable to the committee.

WATER ECONOMY

Although we now have a large cesspool, we seem to be using far more water than we used to. Please, try to be economical and have quick showers and flush the toilets only when necessary as emptying the cesspool costs money.
The drains leading away from the clubhouse were rather unpleasantly blocked because paper towels and other waste, that isn't very soluble in large quantities had been flushed down the lavatories.

John Witter, Commodore.
