COMMITTEE NOTES

Our Editor made an appeal to the last Committee meeting for the contributions to Navigans to be positive and encouraging, but as we progressed through the meeting we became aware that the things we needed to draw to your attention tended to appear restrictive. Unfortunately they must be said, so my notes this month are headed Committee notes. A number of incidents have been reported this season which have included infringements of the Club Rules and are therefore, of a serious nature. Rules have two main purposes, to provide guide lines for the Administration of the Club and to impose some discipline which is for the benefit of all. In the second case it is often also to protect members from themselves, as is the case with insurance. What people may not always remember is that, although they are Prepared to take risks with their property, in the event of an accident somebody could be seriously injured and if not adequately insured the party to blame could have a life long debt both financially and of guilt. We annually ask all boat owners to sign an undertaking that their boat is adequately insured before bringing it to Stansgate and this should not be done without being absolutely sure that there will be cover before bringing the boat.
Members are also reminded that the Club is there for the benefit of the members and — it has been observed that there have been a considerable number of non-members both visit. on shore and sailing and there appears to have been a marked reluctance for these guest's names to be entered in the visitor's book. Under the present rules there are two slightly different versions of rules relating to guests depending on the circumstances. To clarify the situation the Committee passed the following bye law.
"The names of all adult guests brought to the site shall be entered in the Visitor's Book by the introducing member".
Members are requested to observe this bye—law and to ensure that their friends only visit the site when properly accompanied.
We have already heard of anumber of items of members property disappearing since the start of the season. This we find both disturbing and distasteful. As you are aware a public footpath runs through the Club and members are urged to be careful with their property and not put temptation in the way of others. The Club cannot in any way be responsible for the safety of member's property.
I regret very much having to cover these topics in my notes but for a Club of our size to operate successfully on a fully voluntary basis it is essential that we all act with consideration for our fellow members and avoid where possible creating situations which put additional strain on others.

John Witter, Commodore.

SAILING SECRETARY'S NOTES

SAFETY IN DINGHIES A few notes about this subject are appropriate at this time of year when conditions can be cold and windy and most people are out of practice.
First of all pay attention to your equipment. The boat should be checked over to ensure that it is in a sound condition, worn halliards, fittings etc. should be replaced and the buoyancy verified. Clothing also is important and if conditions are such that a capsize is likely then a wet suit is recommended, especially with children who lose body heat quickly when immersed. A good fitting life jacket or buoyancy aid is essential, which must be worn at all times when afloat. (This is a club rule where under 18 year olds are concerned). When you do get into trouble however, keep calm and do not waste unnecessary energy but keep with the boat and try to recover the situation. If all else fails summon help. The universal distress signal of waving your arms up and down by your side may be useful. When there is a strong wind or tide an anchor should be used to prevent you drifting out of sight until help arrives.
Last but not least it is up to each person to decide whether they are capable of coping with the prevailing conditions, if in doubt ask and when the answer is "NO" —- don't go. Of course, if you are practiced at recovering from a capsize and have well found equipment, this will extend the range of conditions when the boat can be used safely.

ENTERPRISE FLEET NEWS
(or THE LONE RANGER WRITES AGAIN)

Isn't the water warm for the time of year. At least I thought so when I was practising for my buoyancy endorsement last Sunday. The first capsize was hardly one at all (I just "walked" round the outside of the transom), the second caught me completely unawares, on the third no-one was looking, and the fourth was just a "dry run" when dicing with Norman. Now though I have perfected the technique so future capsizes should be really good. By the time this article sees daylight the party will have been and gone. I hope it was a great success and everyone enjoyed themselves, but can I say now that I am very grateful to the ladies of the fleet for cooking the recipes of that international chef Gordon Blue. A special thank you to John and “leanor Witter for allowing us to use their home, (especially leanor as head cook) and, well, everything else. Thank you very much. And, of course, thanks to everyone who helped out in anyway, or just came along to enjoy it, for making the evening the great time I hope it was.
But now for some serious stuff. A few weeks ago there were two separate incidents involving damage to boats in which the owners were not insured. Thankfully, no-one was hurt in either case, and they are now covered. I must remind members, therefore, of the signed declaration on their boat registration forms (and of Club Rule 22) that they will be adequately insured for third party risks. I stress that everyone who owns a boat MUST be insured before they sail (let alone race) otherwise serious damage could result.
Anyway, off from that sombre note and on to the future. As we have just had the party and the regatta is at the end of the month when everyone will be busy, I have decided that
the next get - together will be in June on about the 24th. The exact date and venue will be
confirmed in the next issue of Navigane. If anyone else would like to join the Association (you can get good and relatively cheap insurance through it.) I have plenty of application forms. See you all on, or in my case under, the water.

Rob Swale, (capsizes to order - only a few left).

The Log of the "Barbara Starr" continued.

Our boat, a 23' Islander which we have just acquired is certainly being put to the test and so far coming up trumps. All that afternoon we sailed through heavy seas and high winds and arrived at Walton.

5.00pm. After rounding Pye-End buoy and tacking into Walton creek, 21 miles of sailing. Had a nice walk along the sea wall and found a fish and chip shop at the end of it. What ever would we do without this delectable meal? Got chatting to a family who were holidaying in a caravan, very pleasant people, walking back we saw scores of sea cadets hurrying towards the town, couldn't get there fast enough to spend their money.

Wednesday 20.8.75. 9.50am. Raised anchor earlier than planned. We were getting uncomfortably close to the boat next to us. Set off down the Walton channel, jib only. S.W.wind. 11.30am. Harwich harbour and the Guard buoy. To portside several red lightships are anchored. Tug XX12 passing. B.R. cross channel steamer leaving Parkeston Quay for the Hook of Holland. The tug "Egerton" crossing our stern and H.M.S.Ganges at Shotley is sighted. Passing the Shotley Spit buoy to enter the river Orwell. Seas very rough as we pass the mouth of the Stow. The Ipswich Pioneer II car ferry is on its way to Rotterdam. Continue on our way to Collimer buoy with Suffolk Yacht Harbour to starboard.

1.00pm. In very calm waters we anchored at Pin Mill. Cliff went ashore for water, bread, etc, and I with an unusual spurt of energy did some cleaning up. A strange boat came in and used someone else's mooring, expecting to stay there all night. Later the owner returned asked him to move, and in doing so got himself tangled up with the buoys, with the other boat going round in circles watching every move and the squatter getting more and more tangled. Eventually, very red faced he managed to free himself. Motto, "Don't use other people's moorings without permission".

Later we spent a convivial couple of hours in the Butt and Oyster talking to an old salt (and soak) who had, at one time worked the barges. I do wish he had worn his teeth, I couldn't quite grasp all he was saying. On second thoughts I don't think he understood what I was talking about either. That's why we got on so well. Slept very soundly after a few gins and a jar of cockles. 10 miles sailing today.

Thursday 21.8.75. 08.30am. Still in bed I am viewing the panorama through the open hatch. As yet no-one astir, except Cliff who is making a cup of tea, and a few squawking seagulls overhead. To port the smoking chimney of Ipswich power station dimly showing above the trees in the distance, with a line of colourful boats moored in the foreground, or foresea, or foreshore, or whatever. I'd be content to stay here all day, but Cliff has itchy flippers, so I discard my night clothes for my day wear, which is less bulky, and we continue our way up the Orwell passing the Harwich Yacht Club en route. Winds very light. The Ipswich Pioneer II has returned during the night and is now on its way back again to Rotterdam. No time wasted there. (I bet they make a profit). Turn within sight of Cliff Quay Ipswich to take the tide down the Orwell.

16.47. Sailing past Felixstowe docks on our way to the mouth of the Deben. A beautiful evening with the sun brightly shining upon Felixstowe on our portside.

Suddenly and dramatically everything changes. The sky darkens, the heavens open and it rains cats and dogs. The thunder rumbles in the distance, our sails fill to bursting point. All this after a cloudless sunny day, very little wind, and within half an hours sailing time to the mouth of the river. Cliff lowered the mainsail, changed genoa for working jib and started the motor, and myself, knees quaking, at the tiller. In pouring rain, thunder and lightning bad visibility and everything else the heavens could throw at us we entered the mouth of the Deben safely, due entirely to Cliff's navigation. With rain on my spectacles I couldn't see a thing, I should have used my umbrella. Finally we found a safe anchorage opposite the Bawdsey Radar Station, which is, I believe, well known to Radar pioneers such as our own President, Sir Eric Eastwood and others.

Friday 22.8.75. 10.20am. Wind N.W. Lovely sunny morning. All craft anchored around us have last night's wet clothing drying out on deck. Numerous boats moored outside the Ramsholt Arms. Very pretty, set in tall fir trees with fully ripe corn fields on either side. Convenient for the men who do the thirsty work of cutting the corn.

6.

Tacking quietly between the many boats moored at Waldrinfield, we were without warning assailed by an agressive pseudo Oxford accent coming from behind, "Get that bloody thing out of my way". Drawing myself up like a very large figurehead I called back in my broadest Cornish accent, "Have you read your little book about courtesy on the water". We then noticed that this individual was having a private race with one other yacht, so we unofficially joined in and led the way until just before reaching Woodbridge, when they overtook us, but they were bigger than us anyway, and also we were looking for a place to anchor. After anchoring in this very picturesque harbour with the town sitting amongst the trees, and St Mary's Church tower just showing itself above, we explored the town, purchased a few vittals and then sailed back to Shottisham woods and anchored for the night. Eventually four other boats joined us and , as usual in this particular spot a couple of families went ashore and had a barbecue. It was a lovely evening with the water as calm as as a lake. We did just 12 miles sailing that day.

Saturday 23.8.75. 8.30am. Found us up anchor and leaving with some regret this very peaceful and pleasant haven, with our neighbours cheerfully waving us on our way. A bright and sunny morning. Wind westerly. Temperature cooler.

10.45am. The coast line of Felixstowe abeam with its long row of beach huts. Viewed from here they look like colourful tombstones standing on end. Sailed through Harwich harbour to the river Stour as far as Wrabness. Decided it was too rough for anchorage so we turned tail and anchored on the sheltered side of Shotley in the river Orwell. The wind had dropped on us. Sh... had to use the motor to get there. We left a line out overnight and found a hook gone in the morning, so we'll never know how big the one that got away was.

Sunday 24.8.75. 9.45am. Sailed from here on a fine morning but clouds were gathering from the N.W. The wind is S.W. Intrigued by the old Harwich lighthouse which is surrounded by scaffolding. Presumably under repair. Also spot the old black shed where the ancient tread mill operated crane is preserved. We had a look at it some time ago. Apparently it was used in Nelson's time. It being Sunday, we clearly hear the church bells ringing their come hither message from the town centre.

12.15.pm. Sailing past Walton-on-the-Naze with its cluster of beach huts, a feeling of nostalgia overcomes me for my native Cornish coastline. Its beautiful golden sands, and overhanging cliffs, and caves for shelter when the rains come, which they do, all too frequently.

21.00 It was a long sail and at last we reached Burnham on the river Crouch. It was getting dimitty, as we say in Cornwall, so we put the navigation lights on, after fighting the tide. "The strong man", the locals call it. For our last night afloat we moored at Wallasea. We had done 34 sailing miles, 5 motoring.

Although feeling very tired, we go ashore dressed in our usual shabby way and visit the Ward Room. "Ah, special dinner on tonight. £2 per head. Just what we need", and on entering the restaurant we spot an empty table. "Can we have this table"? I asked the lady in charge. With a withering up and down examination she answered, "Sorry madam, all tables are booked". Which, of course, could have been quite true, but I can't help feeling that if Cliff had taken his faded peaked cap off and I had worn my diamond tiara we would have managed to get our dinner. However, not to be out done we ordered an 'open sandwich' at the bar, one of their culinary specialities, which consisted of a slice of toast, with a lump of grilled steak on the top and a salad. All for 55p. Fully recommended by us. After which we had a few drinks, a nice sing song, with a gentleman playing an organ like instrument and then made our unsoberly way back to our boat, along those bobbing pontoons. We slept like logs that night.

Monday 25.8.75. 8.14am. Up and away early. Unfortunately had to motor down the Spitway against the tide. "We were getting nowhere fast". Plagued by flying ants as we left the mouth of the Crouch, and they stayed with us until we reached Bradwell. Became becalmed after passing the Bench Head so reluctantly we used the motor for a while. Called in the Bradwell Marina for petrol, after which we had a marvellous sail to Stansgate, where we moored up after a quietly satisfying exploration of water rather than land for ten wonderful unforgettable days.

Eileen M. Clarke.

Cleaning G.R.P. Hulls

Many members whose yachts have plastic hulls will be distressed to find that their topsides, specially just above the waterline are becoming stained. Polishing has little effect, despite the maker's claims and some are resorting to painting.

These stains can however, be easily removed by painting with a solution of oxalic acid in water by brush. The drips which will inevitably run down on to the anti-fouling, do not appear to have any ill effect on the T.B.T. which was used in the case tested, although it is advisable to sponge off continually during application. The stain is removed like magic and after a good wash, it can be polished normally. The powdered oxalic acid can be bought from the chemist for 10 pence which is enough for several hulls.

NOTE It is poisonous and as well to use gloves when doing the job.

Eric Payne.

ENTERPRISE FLEET NEWS
(or Underwater Exploration part 31½)

The Regatta provided a good turnout for the Enterprises and again we were the largest fleet there, though only a few Marconi boats competed. We all seemed to enjoy the weekend, but next year I want to see more of you participating. You never know, if you sail enough this season and get in practice even YOU might win a prize next time.

Some people have been saying that this column is almost amusing and they look forward to hearing of my adventures afloat, as well as my adventures when actually in a boat. Yes, I did capsize at the regatta, twice, though I would like to believe that only one was really my fault. So for those of you who think this article is going to be funny too (especially young Weedons) here is an introductory discussion on Fluid Dynamics to help you understand the theory behind sailing.

In the 19th century a chap called Bernoulli investigated the phenomenon of fluid flow past an aerofoil section and proved that, within limits, the faster the fluid over the top surface moves the lower the pressure and hence the greater the lift force on the aerofoil. In a simple mathematical form, assuming partial (dv/dt)=0 Bernoulli derived the following 3rd dimensioral vectorial equation:-
curl v x v = grad (v²/2 + h + Q) where Q is a potential function, h is the enthalpy and grad is not a boat but a vector operator. By considering streamlines and using very simple maths, the equation can be written in its well known form of :-
intergral of ( dp/r + v²/2 + Q ) = C
where p=pressure, r = density, and C is salty (or a constant).

You all with me so far? No, well then I will talk about the next fleet party instead. The Cadet week we held immediately after the Regatta was very successful. Out of 23 Cadets taking the Elementary Day Boat Certificate 15 passed and will be presented with certificates pasted in each Cadets log book. What is more encouraging is the fact that each Cadet took their practical test in very severe weather. Force 5 winds, heavy seas and very cold. A true test indeed. Of the 15 Cadets, 4 were ladies, I would add that I was one of the men. We will be arranging a day at Stansgate probably a Saturday so that Cadets who have to take certain tests a second time can have a further opportunity.

I would like to take this opportunity to formally thank Colin Leveridge for his patient and persistent tuition and the time and trouble needed to secure success which was very evident.

If Colin and I can fit in the first of the Saturday tuition days in during June, I will ring everybody up in good time. I am sure everybody thoroughly enjoyed the Cadet week and hopefully we can repeat it again next year.

Rick Anstey, Cadet Captain.

The end of the season is approaching faster than any of us would wish and with it the Laying Up Supper. Members who feel they would like to find out more about the Cogmittee should not hesitate to discuss it with any officer or Committee member. Next month we shall be asking for final nominations but in the meantime why not give some consideration to standing for election yourself.
During the last year a sub-committee has been meeting to review the Club's Constitution and Rules which were in need of updating to bring them in line with custom and practise and the changed situation resulting from the purchase of the land and the opening of the new clubhouse. It was brought to the attention of the Editor that a long standing member of the Sailing Club, Tom Patterson, Senior Production engineer, Marconi, Basildon, was retiring on September 30th after 23 years with the company. To "celebrate" this event Bruce Long has magnificently illustrated our inside cover this month, and we received the following from John Taylor at Basildon.

I would be pleased if a mention of this laconic,cryptic, camera mad, boat "cat" mad otherwise agreeable Scot could be made in your September issue of Navigans. I don't know if this Scottish evolution business has anything to do with his leaving, but we have always maintained that had Hadrian's wall been another thirty feet higher Tom would not have suffered the ignominy of having his 'Supercat MK1 towed to a mud flat on Osea Island by a Mirror dinghy ably handled by Bruce Leggett and Eddie Groves who, loath to administer the 'kiss of life" brought Tom and Tony Essex back to life with a hot drink.

For a 'foreigner' say his associates he wasn't a bad 'un. I have very pleasant memories of his performance on a fiddle with Sweet Georgia Brown. His performance wasn't with Sweet Georgia - he played the tune at our annual Christmas Party and Dinner at the Masonic Hall Shenfield - his supporting cast, or backing being a bottle of CLAYVA or Drambuie.

We shall certainly miss Tom whose all round knowledge of Electronic engineering techniques, "stickos", "goos", araldites, resins etc was invaluable - especially when he was awake. MERSKA WEsK AND THe MARCONI SAILORS

At about 09.00hrs on Monday 9th August. 1976 about twelve people from Marconi Saili.
Club descended on Mersea Island. They took with them three Mirrors, one 420 followed by Frank Savill plus family plus Solo on Thursday and Friday. Not forgetting all the camping equipment. Apart from mud, mosquitoes and lack of wind at start times we all had an enjoyable week. The mud showed itself at low tide, (most days we launched at low tide), in the form of grey-black ooze, about a foot deep that spread everywhere. Feet sank in it, ropes trailed in it, sailing suits were covered in it, and launching trollies almost disappeared beneath it. By the time the race was over each day the tide was up and the mud was covered. The mud which had got into the boats was usually washed off during the race and disappeared through the self~bailers. The mosquitoes came out at dusk in their thousands. They must have been a special breed, they could sting even threwth thick clothing. Also they obviously enjoyed the finer things in life because they only seemed to bite the ladies. There were some very attractive ( and painful) pink and white mottled patterns on feminine legs the following
mornings. :
The wind wasabit late in getting up some mornin,s and on Thursday, Friday and Saturday the start line was out at the Nass Beacon, which meant paddling the boats for about a mile ( the blisters have almost healed now). Most days the wind did get up for start time and we had some good sailing.
On Saturday we launched extra early to allow plenty of time to get to the start, but the wind also came up early and we arrived at the start line about an hour early. Well one can't be right everytime, can one?
On the lighter side of the week, we had good weather, we won prizes, and had pleasant social gatherings in the evenings. One funny incident happened on Monday night, or was it the early hours of Tuesday morning, Pat? Pat was outside my tent calling, "Stan, something is wrong with my cooker".

THE MAMGU TROPHY

The MAMGU Trophy is a 12' to 1" model of Mamgu presented by Mr and Mrs A.M.Adams to the Marconi Sailing Club for two purposes:-
First, to commemorate the ship which for five vital years of the Club's growth served as our Clubhouse.
Second, to promote a wider interest in the sea and seamanship by encouraging members to go cruising and to share their experiences for the benifit of others.

The Trophy is to be awarded annually, and held by the winner for one year, for the best log and account of a cruise made in the preceding 12 months.

The cruise must be in a sailing or auxiliary yacht or dinghy, and should be generally of at least three day's duration, though a shorter passage of particular interest may be considered. Use of engine, if any, must be stated. The log may usefully include details of the yacht and any other interesting and relevant matter.

The author of the yacht must be a member or associate member of the Club; he/she must have taken an active part in sailing the yacht, but need not have been the owner, charterer or skipper.

A small panel shall be appointed by the Committee to judge the entries, the decision of the panel shall be final. The panel need not consist entirely of club members.

Logs are to be judged on their interest and value for others who may attempt similar cruises, and on the seamanship and enterprise implied by the whole undertaking. Thus riding out a gale or a passage in heavy weather, conducted in a safe and proper manner and described well enough to assist another mariner in a like situation, should score highly, whereas a colourful account of escapades arising out of gross ignorance or neglect of seamanlike prudence or out of sheer foolhardiness, may be placed lower than a cruise in which hazardous conditions were avoided by good planning. A copy of each log entered for the MAMGU shall be presented to the Club if the judges deem it worthy, to be kept for members to read, and to be published, if required in "Navigans".

The award of the MAMGU Trophy may be withheld in any year if the judges consider that no entries of sufficient merit have been received; but only after giving notice in "Navigans" at least two weeks before the closing date.

CRUISING PRIZES

Prizes will be awarded for member's first cruise, in the following categories:-
(a) For a cruise to a neighbouring estuary.
(b) For a week's cruise away from home waters.
(c) For a cruise abroad.

For (a) a cruise to a neighbouring estuary, it must be a complete out and return trip in one's own boat, sleeping on board, or camping, using only gear that has been carried in the boat. (The neighbouring estuary to the Blackwater does NOT include the Colne, i.e. the Blackwater and Colne are regarded as one estuary).

For (b), a week's cruise away from home waters, the extremities of the cruise must be 40 miles apart, on a sea voyage. A chartered boat may be used as long as the entrant has complete charge of it.

For (c), a cruise abroad, the boat can be one's own or a chartered one.

A brief written description will be required for all cruises, and these should be submitted to the Sailing Secretary.

It should be noted that anyone receiving outside assistance while sailing will not be eligible for a prize. All these rules are flexible and each cruise submitted will be judged on its own merits and with regard to the circumstances under which it was made.

SAILING NOTES

Sadly we have now reached the time of the year when the prospects for the next six months' Sundays are rather dull, for me anyway. However we can I am sure look back on a successful sailing season with the good weather playing a major part in our enjoyment.

A summary of the summer's racing results follows and comprehensive lists will soon be available from fleet captains or myself.

Mona Cup: 1st Ray and Katie Hampson(M), 2nd Roy and Richard Battye (M), 3rd Dave and Colin Harper (M). There were 25 entries altogether.

Pilot Cup: 1st Nigel and crew Peter James (E), 2nd Frank Savill (Solo). With only seven entries though.

The Marconi Cruiser Cup: which is open to members of other Blackwater clubs, attracted 27 entries which was more than we usually get. 1st Miss J. Pain from the Blackwater Sailing Club, 2nd J. H. Hedgley from the Maldon Yacht Club and 3rd P. Harlock from the Harlow Sailing Club. The highest placed Marconi boat was Ken Stevens' who was 7th.

The Marconi Dinghy Challenge Cup: also open to the other Blackwater Clubs , had 34 entries. 1st G. Palmer (Javelin) from Stone S.C., 2nd a 505 from Stone S.C., 3rd Julien and Ray Hampson from M. S. C.

The Helmsman of the Year Final: was ran as a two race event and the eight qualifiers borrowed Mirrors (and also crews in some cases). The wind was a lively force five, there were no capsizes but two people were seen to fall out of their unfamiliar boats.

CRUISER FLEET NEWS

Our October meeting saw further slides which were most entertaining. To those of us who have not yet cruised far afield it is very interesting to see the possibilities while also enabling those concerned to relive the occasion. Thank you, and also Vic for showing them.

Further changes to record; Vic has handed the moorings to Garden Pewter, whose works telephone is Baddow 538, and of course Brenda has handed over Navigans to Shirley. We all owe a lot to Brenda and Vic for a tremendous amount of hard work and midnight
oil - a very big Thank You to all the Tates from us all. I also hear that Robert
expects to be on his first ship by Christmas, best of luck.

The hoped for talk by the Coastguard will be in February, so I am trying to get a film for November, however I am sure members will not mind if the next meeting turns out to be informal.

Laying up is well under way now and I have been asked to point out that it is essential that NO MORE THAN 3 FSET SPACE is left between cruisers in the dinghy park otherwise we shall run out of suitable space.

We are very sorry to learn that George Charlton has passed away. He was always & very popular member of the club and has done a lot for uS, particularly helping at the bar, etc. We shall all miss him very much and our sympathies are with Bobby at this sad time.

A collection for Bobby will be made by John Smith of 16 [redacted]cent, Springfield, Chelmsford, Tel. Chelmsford [redacted].

Those who wish to be associated with this are invited to make contributions either direct to John or their Fleet Captains. It is hoped that sufficient monies will be raised to install a telephone in Bobby's cottage and thereby allow all her many friends to keep in contact with her during the years ahead.

Dear Editor,

It was a devastating trip. We were somewhere between Queenborough, Isle of Sheppy and Stansgate. The seas were enormous and I was shut - and bolted - below, as one less liability.

My body was stiff with terror as I lay on the floor to avoid having my limbs broken by the battering I was receiving. Feebly I struggled towards the bolted hatchway and

- 7 -

mustering all my strength I raised myself to peer with one eye through a crack. To my dismay I saw the tiller had been lashed and I appeared to be alone on our litte craft which had been home to us for every week-end during the season.

With a sob I sank again to the floor, my stomach heaving and my eyes full of tears. Suddenly there was a bang from above. He was there - not washed overboard as I had so firmly believed.

"Let me out," I shrieked, hanging on the hatchway. "Let me out".

I pushed but nothing happened.

"If we are going to die I want to be up there with you".

My voice was pleading, imploring, then howling as I realised he couldn't hear me above the roaring of the wind.

"I am sorry!" I shouted, "Oh I am sorry!" My voice broke as I remebered his face when I had informed him that there was going to be no more white bread in the house. Only home made nourishing whole wheat. I moaned aloud as I recalled the striken look in his eyes when told, "No more mountains of chips", and I wrung my hands despairingly remembering the weight falling from his body like melted lard.

Oh that I could have been so cruel to one I love so much.

"Oh God! please forgive me" I wailed.

I opened my eyes, and there was God.

"Thats funny! I though Jesus had blue eyes. This one had the most beautiful pair of soulful black eyes I had ever seen! My arms were outstretched towards him.

"Ha - you want to kiss and make up now, ha, but tell me, ' What were we fighting about?".

I said "Excuse me" and was seasick in a stainless steel bowl. The heart-throb moved away while I swayed up and down in my hospital bed, my eyes closed, thankful that the operation was all over.

I am at home now, recovering. My dream had such a profound affect on me, almost sacred really, that I would like to remain anonymous, but if my Cliff thinks he's going on eating the white bread, and the chips, which he did as soon as my back was turned, he's got another think coming.

Anonymous, (of course).

HOLLAND CRUISE 1976

The boat:- "Ace of Diamonds" 27' sloop the original wooden plug for the Halcyon 27's, owned by Tony Cherry and kindly lent to us for the trip.

The crew:- Vic and Brenda Tate, navigator and author respectively.
Son Robert aged 16 and acting skipper for this trip.
Daughter Mary aged 6½ and "flag officer".

- 8 -

The Plan:- To enjoy a 14 day "Holiday" Cruise to Holland crossing the North Sea via Harwich to Breskens on the outward journey and exploring the Veersmeer once on the other side. We were travelling in company with two other Marconi Sailing Club boats. Nick and Daphne Tovey and their children, Fennella and Peter on "Vanellus", and Brian and Jackie Bowsher with Nichola and Mark on "Natasha II".

We achieved all of our objectives, the boats behaved well, the weather eas changeable but never cold, any problem's were relatively minor and we enjoyed an extremely pleasant interesting and restful holiday.

This is the log of "Ace of Diamonds" from Friday 23rd July 1976 to Saturday 7th August, 1976.

Friday 23rd July 1976

06.33 Shipping Forecast. Dogger/Tyne, W3-4, veering NW. German Bight NW5 decreasing 3. Humber variable2-3. Thames/Dover variable 2-3 Tide H.W. Stansgate 10.30
10.00 Dropped mooring at Stansgate loaded to the gunwales with everything except the kitchen sink, which I missed for the whole trip. Wind WSW but almost non - existent. Skipper anxious to sail so all sails set. The full wardrobe was out to air, genoa and Nol jib boomed out, storm jib hang under the main.
11.00 Motor on and all sails down except the main.
11.30 Engine off, try again with main and genoa but only drifting past Bradwell.
12,00 Motor on again - motor sailing now.
12.40 Bench Head buoy abeam.
13.30 Half an hour's search to find the hand bearing compass, Vic had forgotten where it was.
NOTE Check's should be made before departue where all vital equipment is stowed on a borrowed or chartered boat. Vic had transferred the compass from our own boat onto "Ace" and secured it to a bracket screwed onto a length of wood that slotted into the boom crutch fitting. Robert and Vic now "swung the ship" to check and if necessay correct the compass for deviation. Robertsteered a constant course to 5 points i.e. Naze Tower, Walton Pier, Medusa and two ships to seaward of us. Vic checked these bearings with the hand compass on the foredeck away from any iron or steel. The error was never greater than 7°. This was done with and without the engine running and the electrical system on.
13.55 Shipping forecast. Humber/Thames/Dover/Wight/German Bight NW 3-4 Galloper W4, visibility 5 miles, pressure 1025 falling.
15.00 Walton Tower abeam. Weather now cloudy and overcast. Engine off and sailing reasonably well. Robert changing sails at every opportunity to catch as much of the wind as possible.
16.00 Off Harwich - few anxious moments caused by ferry departing from Harwich Pier but we were well clear of the channel marker buoys when she left.
17.30 Into Levington Marina with enough of the flood tide to get our 4'6" draft over the sill.
18.00 The Harbour Master had us changing berths and in the confussion I missed the Shipping Forecast much to my chagrin. We were charged £1.46p for a night's stay. The facilities are good with a telephone, loos, showers and ship's chandlers. It is worth noting that groceries can be delivered form the local store. Petrol and diesel can be brought. The Harbour Master was pleasant but not over friendly. There is a clubhouse but no invitation to enjoy its services was extended although I believe other club members have spent a pleasant evening there.
We enjoyed our evening meal and a quiet talk about what tomorrow might bring, on Vanellus.

To be continued.....

Are You Suffering From the "Itch"

There are, I understand, a number of people within the sailing club who have the "Itch". It is a condition which appears to affect members of all classes. The cause is hard to define, some of the afflicted claim that it is brought about by spending too much time in a trapeze belt, others claim that the conditions experienced in a small two person dinghy on a hot windless summer day are certain to bring on an attack. Then again, conversely, I hear that others sufferers claim a few hours spent each week strapped into a trapeze belt would solve their problem - and single handed sailors sometimes see a small two person boat as an instant panacea. So as you can see one persons salvation is another persons itch.

I do not believe there is an easy solution to the problem but there may be one gleam of hope - group therapy. Why not? It works for alcoholics, battered wives and compulsive flashers so why not for the poor old itch sufferer. A friend of mine

- 4 -

belongs to a therapy group - for nervous twitchers - they meet at a "therapy centre" called the Blue Lion. After an evening spent imbiding quantities of elixier and engaging in heart to heart talks my friend and his associates often find that their nerves are so steady that they can't move from their chairs let alone exhibit a nervous twitch, which demonstrates just how effective these groups are.

Anyway, I digress - back to the itch. Now this itch to change class - buy another boat - or even build one is a dilema facing a number of us. Should we change to a class already existing in the club? or should we start a new one?

I have made a few enquiries among the afflicted and after a bit of scratching around have come up with the qualities thought to be most desirable in a new class racing boat at the Marconi Sailing Club. She should be constructed from G.R.P. and be about 13' to 14' long, she must carry a spinnaker, be well represented locally and an established class nationally and should rate somewhere between 96 and 100. Cost and durability are also important. Now there must be lots of boats which would fall into that loose description - one of which must fulfill all our requirements.

This is where the "group therapy" comes in. I suggest that all we who are seeking a new boat should meet at one of the local health centres to see if the spirit moves us - who knows we may all end up as part owners of a quarter topper!

The incredibly fine sunner brought members to the club by the hundreds and I would venture that more members enjoyed more hours at their club than in any previous year.

Undoubtedly the major task of the year was the repair to the Hard last Christmas when many hundreds of hours of voluntary work were put in and with the generous help of friends of the Club, who provided machinery and plant, we were able to protect the launching facilities of the Club for the future. More recently we arranged for the repair of the road which provides our access to the site.

Our work last year to alter the drainage system was not so successful as we had hoped, due to the uncertain level of the water table on the site. To take advantage of the soak-away system we had installed, we were faced to introduce, during last spring an extra man hole and by purchasing a pump we have been able to pump over from the col- lection tank to the: dispersal system and in this way we have been able to cope with the continually increasing volume of largely fresh water waste created on the site. The pumping is normally carried out at times when there is little activity at the Club.

We have been fortunate again this year in having the continued services of Claud Emerson to look after our Clubhouse and its surrounds. He is often helped by his wife and between them they have done a magnificent job in keeping the Clubhouse in an almost continuous state of readiness for us. It would appear that the observations made last year on the general cleanliness of the Club did not go unheeded but we newer cease to be amazed by the amount of unclaimed lost property that accumulates and much of it not inexpensive clothing.

Financially we seem to be solvent still despite considerable expenses during the year and our Treasurer, Ted Barnes, has kept a close eye on our budgets, I am pleased to report that our contribution to the MASC for 1977 for the use of the site remains
_ unchanged.

During the year we experienced a break-in for the first time for 4 number of years but we were fortunate that our losses and cost of damage repairs was only £10. This does however highlight the need for constant vigilance and we are strongly of the opinion that our locked gate provides a major deterrent to the casual unwanted light fingered visitor and offers significant protection to both Club and personal property. While on the subject of g,to locks, many of you will have noticed the number of cars that accumulate outside our boundary and we are in discussion with the Tenant Farmer and the Owners of the adjacent sites on methods of discouraging the unauthorised usgof the approach road which is causing a4,:gravation to all the legitimate users.

Our sub-committee and volunteers have again worked extremely hard this year on all theactivities of the Club and many successes have been achieved.There is one area where a apecial mention is deserved and this is the Galley which has provided sustenance to many a cold and wet sailor throughout the year. Our thanks go to Jill Savill, who took this over when Margaret Cottam retired last year, and to her willing, cheerful and hard working band of ladies who have given a marvellous service which has been appreciated by 411 who use the Club, I am pleased to say she has volunteered to continue for another
year.

This year we say farewell to a few Main Committee members but I am pleased to say many others are offering themselves for re-election tonight. To those departing, Hric Royle our secretary for the last three years, Roger Durrant, Tony Cherry, Gerry Bamford

a

and Brenda Tate, Navigans Editor for the last three years, 1 would like to express my sincere thanks for the support they have given to me, to the Club and to past Officers during the time they have served the Club.

You may have noticed that one name has been left off the list. After 4 long and difficult search without much success among the members for a replacement Sailing Secretury John Weedon, who has already served four years and does not want to see the sailing activities decline in the Club, has offered to see us through another year. I am sure you will all want to thank him as I do for this act of generosity. I would add that in reaching this decision, I believe John was influenced by the willingness of a fairly new member to the Club Mike Vaughan, who accepted nomination for the main Committee with the express purpose of assisting John as Sailing Secretary, Thank you both for helping to solve what was becoming a very difficult situation. There are also a number of new names on the nominations list who will be readily welcomed together with the appointed Officers onto the Committees for the coming year.

During the year a lot of work has gone into bringing the Club rules up to date and later we have the formal proposition to adopt these revised rules. In parallel with the>, we have been redefining the function of the Club Officers and sub-committees. The need for both these activities arises out for the growth of the Club and its f,cilities and hence the work and it is being done so that more work can be carried out at Sub-committee level and thus the amount of detailed work done by the Main Committee can be reduced. The terms of reference are not finalised but the first drafts are available and the refined versions will evolve as experience is gained by using them. We are hopeful that these changes will do something to reduce the load on some of the Committee members by spreading it more evenly and that we may be able to shorten same of the meetings that can become bogged down in detail. Time will tell.

This report would be incomplete without mentioning our cadets, their skipper, Rick Anstey, and Colin Leveridge who together have achieved such success with their sailing, their tuition and their examinations for the RYA Elementary Day Boat Certificate. Con- gratulations to all who have been successful this year and good luck to all those going on into next year. Perhaps we should all remember that a strong and active cadet section today represents an insurance for the future of the Club and be thankful that this side of our membership is being revitalised.

In this report I have said very little about the sailing side of our activities as that will be covered by our Sailing Secretary in his report. I would however like to pay tribute to the hard working members of the Club who have provided the racing facilities by manning the Race box and Rescue launcles each weekend during the season and without whose help there would be no organised sailing.

A number of our social events have not been supported so well this year which is obviously a dissapointment to both our Social Secretary and your committee. A lot of hard work goes into the programme and without a feedback it is difficult to know what is required. We are always open to suggestions on the sort of thing wanted and extra help with the organisation is always welcome.

This year brought the tenth anniversary of our licenced bar at Stansgate.e. Hence your committees severe embarrassment when quite by chance it was discovered that our Club Registration had expired. Immediate action was taken to renew the Registration and I am pleased to report that there were no objections to it being renewed so we must have been thought to be keeping an orderly house and we can continue to drink with confidence for another ten years. SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT 1976

The year began with the Cadet Fleet captain, Rick Anstey, organising and Colin Leveridge instructing about 30 cadets and a few adults in the RYA Elementary Day Boat Certificate. Later on in the year 16 of these passed the examination, which included capsize drill. This winter has seen the start of further courses.

Before the start of the season a new lightweight race mast replaced the original one. Also an electronic clock was installed in the race box, which included an automatic five minute hooter.

As for the Club sailing , the mid-week races were very well supported and most of the class points series had higher entries that 1975, topped by the Mirror Summer points withan average of 13 boats. The cadet entry averaged nine and a half and the only decline was in the Ladies points and Barnacle points. A short handicap series was intreduced this year mainly during the summer holiday period when some fleets were expected to be depleted and although 56 boats entered only 11 raced on sufficient occasionsto qualify overall. The trophy events were keenly contested except perhaps the Pilot Cup which still fails to be popular. The Helmsman of the Year final was won for the 3rd year running by a helm form the Enterprise Fleet, on this occasion, Rob Swale. The crusiers enjoyed regular monthly social meetings and most members made good use of the hot weather, including curises in company to the Thames estuary and holidaying in Holland

The Club open events began with our traditional spring bank holiday Regatta which again provided plenty of facilities on and off the water for over 200 boats and supporters. The trend this year was for more single handed fleets. Our thanks to Gerry Bamford who was secretary, Robbie Sims as principal race officer and many others too numerous to name, who gave their assistance. This year we revived our team racing with Osea S.C. for which a splendid trophy "TheBoothby Cup" was already in existence. Sad to say however, we lost after being beaten home and away. The Hallam trophy, open meeting for Hornets was again scheduled in September but this year it was combined with a Mirror open event which seemed to work out reasonably well. Finally the Cruiser Cup with 27 entries, and Dinghy Challenge Cup with 34 entries were ran in mid-September the winners being Miss G. Pain (BSC) and Gordon Palmer (SSC) respectively. However one of our members (Dave Harper and Stephanie Gandy) sailing a Mirror won the corresponding Stone Dinghy event run later on the same day.

Away from the Club there were no outstanding sucesses except perhaps for the consistency of Roger Hance with Peter James, 6th in the Enterprise World Championships and equal first in the Nimbus series. Nearer to home the Club was well represented at the B and CD Championships winning the Mirror (Ray and Katie Hampson) and second in the 420

- 8 -

Class. Earlier in the year Mike Taylor and John Morrison in the 505 were going well in the M.B.Y.C. winter series. The Saltcote Open Cadet Cup was first won (13 years ago) by a member of this club (John Tillotson) and this year we regained it with Chris and Robert Weedon. The Club was also represented at many other local events including Ardleigh and the very enjoyable Mersea Week.

The duties (Officer of the Day, Race Officer and Rescue) were on the whole responsibly executed and we thank all the 'volunteers'. In addition I would like to thank all the members of the Sailing Sub-committee for their support throughout the year. One snag however has been the rescue boat's engine which proved more unreliable than it should be and a replacement must be considered.

Next year with the early summer bank holiday extending to the Tuesday we will run the Regatta over the Saturday, Sunday and Monday as usual with our Dinghy Challenge Cup and Stone's on the following day (Tuesday). A Hornet and Mirror weekend is again programmed for September. The Marconi Cruiser Cup scheduled for the first Sunday in September is being proceeded by a 'Blackwater' cruiser social evening at Stansgate. The remainder of the programme will be filled in over the next few weeks according to agreed suggestions from the fleets. Also I wish to bring your attention to the B and CD Championships to be held at Stone early in July as this will be a special anniversary event.

John Weedon, Sailing Secretary

Mona's Cup

I wonder how many of our present members know the origin of Mona's Cup? In the early fifties, when our headquarters were situated at Heybridge Basin, we made frequent visits to the Jolly Sailor whose proprietoress was Miss Mona Clarke, who inherited it from her parents.

As she was a very friendly soul, and took a special interest in our sailing activities, she kindly presented us with a fine challenge cup to be awarded to the winner of an annual all-in race, and this is still included in our programme.

On one occasion, Mona actually came aboard Mamgu and fired the gun starting this race. In later years, this has rather tended to be supported by dinghies from our present premises at Stansgate but in future, more cruisers should be encouraged to participate and it is suggested that Mona should be invited to be present for the occasion.

On one occasion when this race was sailed from Stansgate the first mark of the course was up river, and the Southey Spit Buoy had to be rounded but as the tide was falling some cruisers found there was insufficient water to make it!

Mona has now retired but still lives at Heybridge and The Jolly Sailor is now run by Eric Priestly, incidentally an ex Marconi man.

Incidentally, our first laying-up supper was held at The Jolly Sailor in October 1957; we hired the large inner room and ate our sausages and mince pies standing up, and went through to the bar for our drinks; there was no music to drown our exchanges of events during the past sailing season, and it was a thoroughly enjoyable evening.

Amongst our guests was Douglas Thompson, Commodore of the The Blackwater Sailing Club and Sam Poulton from The Maldon Little Ship Club. The price of the tickets was 4/- or 6/6 including the price of the coach which brought us.

- 4 -

Our first formal laying-up supper was held at the New Street canteen, which we were pleased to call The Palm Court, on Friday, November 1, 1958; most of the Commodore's of the clubs on the Blackwater were present as was Bill Hillman, Commodore of the B.B.C. Ariel Club, whoses premises are on the Thames at Teddington. The price of the tickets was 9/- including the band, but not the drinks!

We used to race against the Ariel Club at Teddington and in return, they came to Heybridge the following year, but eventually it was dropped largely because of the distance and absence of boats available. However, a trophy consisting of our respective burgees mounted on a plinth still exists, but as the Ariel S.C. were the last to win it, they are retaining it.

HOLLAND CRUISE

Saturday 24th July

06.33 Shipping Forecast. Tyne/Humber/Thames/Dover NW veering northerly 3-4.
Galloper N3, visibility 11 miles pressure 1023 steady

Vic bought two gallons of petrol as we had used more than anticipated yesterday. We now carried enough fuel for 19 hours motoring at full throttle. (Ace's consumption being 1 gallon per hour at full throttle.)

09-00 Slipped lines at Levington. Little wind but what there was came from the east, genoa and main set goose-winged down to Harwich but the engine went on to get us down river and off Harwich by 10.00. The sky was cloudy but plenty of sunshine.

G, 45 Clear of Harwich, off engine. Course set 115°C for Rough's Tower. Main and genoa sete

10.35 Engine on again 4s we are not making enough way for passage making. Genoa down as it was just flogging, log streamed.

11.40 Rough's Tower abeam, course altered to 100°C to allow for tidal set.
Plenty of Portuguese Man-of+War jelly fish and large clumps of weed around must be all the hot weather.
The wind began to freshen slightly and we could see rain approaching from the north west.

12.20 Rain arrived, Robert on the helm in oilskins.

12230 Lose sight of land, rain died away.

1235 Sunk Light vessel abeam.

17° 80 Engine off, sailing about 3kts. I went below to prepare a lunch of chicken sandwiches, cake, coffee and squash. It made me feel so bad I missed the Shipping Forecast again.

14.00 Engine on.

16.30 Galloper Light Ship abeam. Course altered to 110°C for North Hinder,
the really long leg of the trip. Wind beginning to freshen.

18.00 Vic asleep below, so was Robert, at the helm. I took the tiller while he got his head down, it was going to be a long night.

19.00 Unfortunately had to wake Vie and ask if the engine could be switched off. We were clipping along the time and a nasty quartering sea caused the gunwales to go under occasionally. Vic returned to his pit, Mary and I on helm.

21.00 Sighted North Hinder Light vessel.

22 200 North Hinder abeam, and in the very lust of the daylight we sorted out the bout for the night. Genoa down, No. 1 up, naviggtion lights on, all went gmoothly apart. frc Robert and Mary beiNé seasick but this they did with the

03.00 = 06.00 Robert on helm. Life jackets and life lines were always worn at night.

04.00 — 06.00 Vic asleep.

Our course for closing the Dutch coast north of Zeebrugge kept us out of the shipping lanes but we crossed over the Thornton and Raan Banks. This resulted in a very short, confussed, lumpy sea.
The next eight hours I recall very hazily as I felt decidedly "bad" and retired to my bunk. The wind had freshened and was blowing a fitful 4-5. I awoke about midnight and grabbed the washing up bowl quick. Once that was over I felt almost human again, but I had to perform one-handed gymnastics to get myself plus the bowl out into the cockpit avoiding Robert who was fast asleep on the floor cuddling the genoa. Outside in the fresh air things started to improve even more despite my husband's remarks about,"Do you wonder why you joined."
I sat down on the thwart and looked around. Over our stern were the con- stantly changing navigational lights of Vanellus and Natasha as they rode over the waves about two miles away. There was no moon to be seen but thousands of glittering stars above an inky black sea. Ace was tpamping on like a good'un through wave crests laced with tiny gleams of phosphorsce. There were ship's lights everywhere. Vic counted 14 on the edge of the bank. I returned to my bunk and dozed until around 03.00 when Vic awoke Robert to take his turn on the tiller.
Vic was relieved as although he had seem the loom er: Ostende and Zeebrugge and the lights of the ferries going into the harbour he was glad to get below, make a hot drink and check his chart calculations, which had been worked out about a week before we had set out to sea. Our E.T.A. for Breskens was 08.00, and we were about an hour ahead of schedule, which gave us the problem of having to punch a foul tide.
Between 03.00 and 04.00 everyone seemed to be scratching around even Mary
woke up and sat transfixed on the companion way steps gazing with eyes as hig as saucers.

04.00 All quiet again, Robert on the helm, Vic on the floor (his 3 star hotel he called it) and Mary and I on the leeward bunks. Wind blowing harder now.

06.30 Woke up, so I must have slept although it didn't feel like it. Breskens harbour entrance ahead. Log in, engine on, sails down, crept quietly alongside a large ketch moored on the visitors berth.

06.45 We were there.

Sunday 25th July

09 .00 The wind was blowing well now, Force 6, even behind the shelter of the marina wall. We breakfasted on fresh mackerel and decided that a passage across the Westerschelde would be very choppy and that it was worth staying the night and see how things were in the morning; because of this, the Harbour Master allocated us another berth to keep the visitors pontoons clear. Engine on, Robert on the helm, we moved away from the ketch out and across to the opposite line of pontoon. We found our place and Robert began to manoeuvre Ace in between two boats so that she would be lying bow onto the pontoon. I was standing by the pulpit on deck with a bow line ready. Vie shouted to Robert to throw the gear lever into reverse, but horror of horrors the cones did not disengage and Ace stayed ahead. She hit the pontoon with an almighty wallop, her bow rearing up out of the water and then sliding down again. As luck would have it the pontoon was a curved

- 7 -

wooden one, floating about a foot out of the water. We inspected the damage and found it was not as bad as we feared. The paint had been chipped away and the wood bruised in two places on the stem, well above the water line, but this would be repairable without too much difficulty. All we had was explain to Tony!! and handle the clutch with more care. Bresken's Marina is large accommodating approx. 700 boats. The pontoons are excellent with water stand pipes every 30 yards. Petrol and diesel are available. The only disappointing feature were the showers and loos housed in portable units at the top of the marina wall. The showers were a guilder a time. The Yatch Club is situated along the main road into Breskens about ¼ of a mile away. The town itself, with shops and supermarkets is about ½ mile from the marina.

In the early evening Vic and I strolled around the town and on the way back stopped to look at the Fishing fleet which was in the harbour. Vast nets were spread out to dry and hanging from derricks on the deck were huge "tickler" chains used for dragging the sea bed.

While cleaning my teeth in the lady's loos, I looked up and a vaguely familiar face said, "Hello". I suddenly realised that it was the lady who sometimes sails on Eric Young's boat Snedronning. It was lovely to have a chat, they were now on their way home having been up as far as Middelburg.

Monday 26th July

09.00 Up and away, destination Middleburg. As we had hoped the weather improved visibility was good, plenty of cloud but the sun was shinning. Fresh northerly wind. Genoa and mainsail set, once we were clear of the marina. Ace beat across the Westerschelde, we kept well down to avoid the large sand bank that lies to the east. We turned to starboard once near the northern shore and sailed up towards the lock entrance. Engine on and sails down, we didn't have to wait long dodging the ferries before we were in the lock. There were no difficulties with lines, we went along the wall. Brian brought Natasha alongside us. It wasn't very crowded. The lock at Flushing was the largest that we encountered during our cruise, as it is the enctrance to the canal system of Zeeland, it is used extensively by commercial traffic. The general procedure when entering any lock in Holland is to wait and listen for the Lock Master's instructions. He will have running bow and stern lines to the rings or bollards which are situated along it. These can then be adjusted as the water level alters, and can be quickly and easily slipped if required. Never, ever have fixed lines. I have seen the owner of a large, expensive motor launch hacking at his ropes with a carving knife as the water receded at least a foot away from his hull.

Once through the lock and into the canal system we made our way up to Middelburg. Brian made a quick dash into the Flushing Yatchhaven to see if twoother Marconi boats, Teal and Jestabel were in residence, without sucess No trouble with the three bridges that crossed the canal butan interesting incident while waiting to go through the last, the mainroad bridge by the railway station in Middelburg.

We were gilling around in company with half-a-dozen yachts and a couple of barges, Vic on the helm bent to adjust the throttle and the handle came off in his hand!! Vanellus took alongside while some fast repairs were carried out.

Under the bridge we passed with nostalgia the bus stop where the Marconi fleet had moored last year. Turning left off the main canal into the town system we had to wait about 5 minuites for a dainty white painted wrought iron road bridge to be raised. Once through we were delighted to find that this portion of the waterway had been piled and pontooned, there were even portaloo' and a rubbish truck on the quay side. In a few munutes we were safely tied up in our berth.

Middelburg, the county town of Walcheren, is charming, with many buildings

- 8 -

of historical and architectural interest, and on this occasion bursting to the seams with holiday makers.

We took the children on the pony bus to see the sights and then retreated back to our peaceful holiday haven. We spent a very pleasant evening, Vic and Robert in a local bar with a gentleman from a Maldon boat "Wigwam", I on Natasha with Brian and Jackie and their neighbours, a couple on "BarbareeII", out of Bradwell. It's a small world.

Shopping Trip To Maldon
By Linda Savill

Daddy and I planned to go to Maldon the following morning, Friday 23rd July and leave the club at 8.00 a.m. to go and get some crusty bread and newspapers. The next morning I was late in waking up. We left at approximately 8.30 a.m. Just beyond the hard was a cruiser, the man in it asked daddy something. We tacked and headed up to Maldon. The tide was due to change at 10.30 a.m. As we passed Osea Island we saw a bird diving. It was under water each time for about 30 seconds. As we came towards the entrance to Southey Creek the wind dropped and the tide turned. We did not hardly move. After a while some Curlews came over. We nearly turned back but we just about kept going. As we went over Northey Island road the tide had gone down a bit. I had to pull the centre board right up, and daddy jumped right out, and the road scrapped the hull. Daddy got back in and we were off again. As we were going between the cruisers I was looking for a place to land. The water was past the mud as we got close to the shore. I got ready to jump out. I half did and my foot got stuck in the mud and I nearly lost my shoe. I got my leg back in and then we landed in a bit better place. I got out and daddy gave me the anchor. Then he got out and we walked up the steps on to the prom. We went over to a girl and asked her the time. She said "Two minutes past twenty five past twelve". Of course we did not really beleive her so we went and asked a man. He said "Half past twelve". We ran through the park, daddy ran ahead I stopped,daddy was gone. I looked around daddy was gone. After about two minutes daddy came out of a bakers shop. We ran back to the boat, wrapped the bread and newspapers in my red oilskin top and started back. We did not go back the way we came because the tide was so that the road was showing quite clearly. We followed the main channel and got back to the shore at half past two. What an exciting 6 hours.

My brother Robert is in the Merchant Navy He is sailing away for 6 months on a tanker this Friday I hope to crew for Philip Cherry in his new mirror this Summer Mary Tate Age 7

WHY CHOOSE THE 420 DINGHY?

Further to the discussions held at a recent social meeting I would like to outline the reasons for promoting the 420 as a possible future fleet at Marconi.

When one considers the existing dinghy classes - Hornet, Enterprise, Mirror and
recently the GP14, these were all designed as hard chine, plywood skinned and thus suit— able for amateur construction. As many people are how likely to be attracted by the lower maintenance requirements of G.R.R., a boat designed solely for G.P.R. construction would be preferred (it is acknowledged however that the above classes, except the mirror are available in G.R.P. but these are not accepted as competitive ih all circles). The other requirements as far as I was concerned were to have a spinnaker, to be reasonably light and competively sailed locally without being too demanding physically. The 420 I believe fills these requirements. However the main snag encountered was the limited supply of suitable secondhand boats and as a consequence their cost.

Having acquired a 420 after overcoming the above problem I am pleased to report that the boat can be very satisfying to sail especially in a good breeze, being very stable but quick to accelerate in the gusts and comfortable to sail. Beating in light weather is probably one of its weak points but this can still be a challenge.

The foregoing is not intended to split the existing fleets but to encourage one or two mirror crews to graduate for which the 420 would be ideal or some of the handicap menagerie to change or even for those who are not yet boat owners to come to a satisfactory

THAT 'ITCH' AGAIN

Roy Battye, writing in the January Navigans, suggested that part of the first winter lecture would be concerned with the choice of dinghys, and that the discussion might help to resolve the issue of a new class within the club. Perhaps not surprisingly the meeting did not resolve this matter, and the discussion became the usual hard sell by individuals or groups wishing to promote their favourite class. In the end the clock terminated the discussion leaving the merits of some classes unsung.

I would like to take this opportunity to continue the discussion on a slightly different tack, but I must stress that this is a personal view and not a club view.

I want to consider the question - "Which dinghy classes should be adopted by the club?" But first let us look at the advantages afforded a class after it's adoption by the club. Class racing results are published, and in some cases class trophies provided for the various series sailed. The class is also represented directly on the sailing sub-committee, which obviously increases its influence on sailing matters. Also, the club looks favourably at requests for class open meetings and this in turn gives rise to increased interest in the class.

So, which classes should be adopted by the club? Surely the simple answer is that the club should adopt any class that can justify fleet status. By this I mean, any class large enough to support the race programme provided for it, and large enough to provie it's share of the effort required to run the race programme, namely Race officers and Rescue Crew. Classes no longer able to satisfy the required conditions must be relegated to the Handicap fleet, and the embryo classes must grow within this same fleet. After all it is still possible for the members of small classes to extract their own class results from the handicap results. Once established within the handicap fleet a fully grown class can apply for adoption by the club.

So mush for the club's choice of dinghy class; what about your choice? You must first decide whether to choose a two-man boat or a single-hander. If you have a regular working relationship with another person, a two-man boat will, ih my opinion, provide the greatest satisfaction. Of course, there are some of us who fail to cultivate that good working relationship. We have to be satisfied with a single sail, but don't misunderstand me it has the great advantage of independence, and with only myself to blame it is sometimes easier to analyse my mistakes.

The list of possible boats has now been reduced, and if your personal requirement can be met by an existing club class, your problem is solved. If you choose to sail single-handed there is no suitable club class a present. Even if you choose to sail with a crew there may be many good reasons why the existing club classes are not suitable to you. You are therefore about to join the handicap fleet.

What are the disadvantages of sailing with the handicap fleet? In any single race, even classes having the same handicap number will perform differently and winning is often amatter of luck. It can happen that even a long series of races over one course area will give an advantage to one type of boat due to the prevailing conditions. The handicap numbers will only be correct for a long series of races over all types of course on pond, river, estuary and sea conditions with fixed line and committee boat starts. Normal class racing tactics are irrelevant, and in general it is difficult, if not impossible, to improve your racing performance. Real improvement can only be achieved by racing against boats of the same class. One more of the same type will do, but the more there are the better the racing.

If you choose a boat class that will not give you the required competion at the club you will have to go elsewhere for your competition sailing. Indeed, if sailing

- 6 -

is more important to you than the club, it may be reasonable to move to a club with an adopted class to suit you. There are some advantages for both clubs and the class if this is done. An alternative solution is to choose a class sailed regularly by nearbye clubs, since this will at least enable you to attend their open meetings. It may help to look at the list of classes sailed at our own regatta.

Once you have decided to depart from the existing club classes the choice for you is quite wide because the actual type you bring to the club is not important. However, your choice will be affected by such factors as, do you wish to race, do you wish to improve your performance, are there plenty of local open meetings, price, second-hand market, the choice already made by others and whether your choice is likely to affect the choice of others. The last two factors are quite important since they affect the possible growth of a new class within the club.

Finally let me say that I will not be fully satisfied until I am able to sail in a club adopted class, and if , as might well happen, a Moth class is established due to the keeness of our cadet fleet, I might one day be persuaded to join. In the meantime I have made my choice and I am very satisfied with the sailing it gives me. Now it is up to you to make your choice and then go out and buy that SOLO or Moth or SOLO or 420 or SOLO or Express or SOLO or...

SUMMARY OF DINGHY HANDICAP RACING
AT THE CLUB IN 1976

As you may already know , all popular dinghy classes have allocated handicaps according to their known performance.

Each winter the R.Y.A. reviews these handicaps using completed questionaires received from many clubs including ours.

To find the handicap performance of any individual boat in a timed race, it's elapsed time is compared with the corrected time of the middle boat. This is a simplification but the full procedure is explained in the R.Y.A. booklet "Handicap Racing".

In our club in 1976 all the handicap events, except those with only a few starters or in very extreme weather conditions, were used to compile the following statistics:-

My observations over the last few years have indicated that some conditions will favour one class of dinghy more than others. The following list of characteristics is a summary of my conclusions:-

Dinghy Class - Favourable Conditions - Unfavourable Conditions
Hornet - Rough Water - Light winds
Laser - Smooth water and medium winds - Rough water
420 - Strong winds, reaching - Light winds, beating
Enterprise - Light winds, beating - Strong winds, and rough waters, dead runs
Express - Light winds - –
Int. Moth - Light winds, smooth water - Rough water
Graduate - Beating - –
Mirror - Strong winds (not single-handed) - –
The G.P.14 and the Solo showed no obvious trends.

In addition the slower classes are at a disadvantage when there is a large proportion of beating against a tide, particularly in light winds, but when the beat is with the tide they have the advantage. Things are further complicated when large mixed fleets are racing together causing disturbed air to affect relative speeds.

The R.Y.A. "averaging" system of producing class handicaps also means that it should be more difficult to succeedd using a boat whose average helm is of a high standard (e.g Laser) and V.V., because this will be reflected in its rating, but when the spread of performance in a class is large, then their better boats would be favoured.

All this goes to show that although you may have thought you sailed the best in a handicap event and then did not finish first when the results were calculated, other things have been loaded against you. Never-the-less your turn may come and anyhow over a series of races conditions should average out for a fairer overall result.

This coming season (1977) all handicaps will be increased by 20%, in addition to any other necessary amendments, by the R.Y.A. This general increase is said to be due to a larger number of fast classes appearing (and not as a result of inflation!)

TURNING OUT TIME

Would all of you who store your boats with Alf Cottam please get together with him for their removal on Sunday 27th March after 2.00p.m.

What's all this about a new dinghy class?

I attended a social meeting recently, at the M.A.S.C., held to obtain some tips from Roger Hance on the racing rules and I thought, to discuss the possibility of a new dinghy class for Marconi. Some of the comments made were sufficient to make any discerning class captain turn to sailing model boats and to make me write to Navigans! This is about the third season discussion has got around to a new dinghy class, however no-one has yet said exactly what is wrong with the present adopted classes. Well, I hope I can start your ink flowing by making these observations :-

It seems to me that as the Marconi Club is made up of people with different needs is sailing, such as:- those who are novices or have a young crew, those who require a cruising/racing dinghy, those who want a thoroughbred two sail racing dinghy, those who want an exiciting threesail racing machine, and finally those who want (or need) to sail single handed. In view of this, several complementary classes of dinghy are required to fulfil these varying needs, and I think the Mirror, G.P.14, Enterprise, Hornet and Solo or Lazer do just that. If there were two similar classes the effect woul be to waste potential of both classes. Therefore any new class would have to be completely different, or supersede one of these classes.

As an enthusiast who wants the challenge of a three sail racing machine, I believe the Hornet to be the best class on our river to fit the bill. I have written about its virtues before. It has after all been selected over the past 25years by many well known helmsmen, and has been used in Poland as an Olympic trainer. I don't intend to go into details about it's attractions, except to say that over the past ten years of sailing Hornets, I have had a lot of enjoyment from them, and made a lot of friends both at our club and around the country, and I would not wish (short of winning the pools) to sail any other dinghy. If you fancy the challenge of a three sail racing machine, why not try a Hornet? Anyone who wants to sail or maybe just crew,can contact Pete Clayton, out fleet captain who will make you very welcome, and may even buy you a beer at one of our Friday social meetings!

Mike Turner,
Hornet K 1937.

MIKE ALDERMAN
