Continuing THE LOG OF"ACE OF DIAMONDS" 1976

HOLLAND CRUISE

TUESDAY 27th July

09.30 We discovered that the wrought iron bridge was opened on the half hour, so after breakfast we left heading northwards for Veere. The wind was fresh northerly, cloudy sky. Approaching Veere we spotted a familiar boat flying the M.S.C. burgee, Davolas II. A quick tate-a-tate, or should it be tate-a-Tate, with John, who after a pleasant holiday was homeward bound. He told us that Tealand Jestabel were staying in Goes for a few days.
The Veere lock was very crowded, everyone jammed together like sardines in a tin. The Dutch coped in their usual efficent way, despite the help of an Irish gentleman, single-handed in a tiny but obviously well travelled boat. Locked out, into Veerse Meer turning to port and through the harbour entrance.

11.00 Tied up by the old town quay, occupying the same position as last year. Veere is beautiful, the town skyline dominated by the vast Groote Kirk and spire of the town hall, although like Middleburg, it was full of holiday makers.
The facilities at the Yacht Club, which is situated by the harbour entrance are excellent, meals are available, and their showers were the cheapest that I encountered (25c.). Petrol and diesel can be obtained from the Yacht haven near the entrance to the lock. The Post Office, shops and bank are literally across the road from the quay.
After lunch we set off for Goes. Vic had bought an excellent map of the area from the local chandler's, costing 95c. Studying this we decided to leave the boats behind and take to the Dutch public transport system. The Tovey's joined us, Brian and Jackie were waiting to meet some Dutch friends.

16.00 The bus journey from Veere to Goes via Middleburg was uneventful. We sat back, relaxed and enjoyed the countryside.

17.15 We arrived at Goes Yacht haven to discover it was my niece' Fiona's birthday so we joinedthe party and enjoyed a magnificent feast on Jestabel. The weather and setting were really superb, the wine flowed freely, and we very reluctantly took our leave just after 21.00
We caught the local train back to Middleburg only to discover that due to someone mis-reading the bus time-table (ME), we had missed the last bus home. It was a very weary party that bundled into taxi's to take us the last 7 kilometers into Veere, but it was all rather fun, I've never ridden in a Mercedes before.

WEDNESDAY 28th July

The wind had freshened and a good NNW Force 3-4 with the occasional stronger gust was blowing resulting in very choppy conditions in the Meer. Vanellus and Ace left mid-morning leaving Natasha who planned to travel further afield than us. Motored out of the harbour entrance, turned to the north set main and genoa, cut engine. Invigorating sail up to the North Sea dam, keeping a sharp look out for the marker buoys, there's no tide here and going aground here means a lot of trouble. Dropped the hook for lunch and then hitched a lift on Vanellus, who with her bilge keels could go alongside the jetty at the edge of the Meer.

We had a bracing walk along the top of the dam, the sea looked very unpleasant for sailing, but plenty of people were swimming. Ice creams by the rather murky waterside, interesting to note, plenty of portaloos and rubbish bins. Up anchor and sailed back down keeping to the north shore, still main and genoa.

17.00 Tied up in the Marina at Kamperland, which is on the far shore directly opposite to Veere. The Shipping Forecast was very bad that night with gales everywhere. Pity Teal and Jestabell, if they were now on their way home.

- 11 -

Thursday 29th July

The weather was certainly changable, although there was a good breeze the clouds soon cleared away and by mid-morning everyone including the mullet were basking in the sun. Kamperland is, as it's name suggests a large area for outdoor activities with campsites, bathing areas, marina and boat yard. The usual amenities are there, but I saw no evidence of any shops. Plenty of dinghy sailing especially Windsurfers. Robert was watching them with great longing, so Vic did a magnificent chatting up job with the Mama of a Dutch family off a large botteer moored at the end of our pontoon. She spent an hour showing Robert "the ropes" and then let him have ago. As our slides show, he was sometimes successful, sometimes not. After a very strenous bu throughly enjoyable morning in and out of the water, he came away saying it was twice as difficult as his own moth to sail.

A late coffee and away for our next port of call, Geerdijkse Haven an anchorage recommended by Ian Tate from Teal.

Turning to port after leaving Kamperland, we sailed down the Meer under jenny only passing between Haringvreter and the north bank and coming around the Goundplaat Spit. We had lunch under way.

Mid afternoon came into Geerijkse Haven recognisable by it's mimi-harbour and just managed to bring Ace alongside the jetty. We reckoned we had about 5' under us Ace drawing 4'6".

The sun was blazing down so we swam and lazed on the beach. After dinner, an evening stroll into the village for a drink at the local cafe-cum-bar-cum-garage. Coffee on Vanellus bought the evening to a pleasant conclusion.

Friday 30th July

Awoke to a rather miserable day, wind westerly good stiff breeze, cloudy and dull. After a lovely long lie in and a lazy breakfast we started the engine and headed eastwards for Kortgene and Delta Marina. As the journey was a short one we didn't bother to set any sail but we passed "Spanish Lady", a Brightlingsea based boat tramping up under full canvas. In the Marina tied up by mid-day. The weather now deteriorated and so after a quick walk around the town we settled down with books and playing cards for the rest of the day.

Delta Marina is about the same size as Breskens. The excellent facilities are housed in a new modern building which incorporates showers, loo's, washeteria, and ship's chandler's with a rather expensive looking restaurant above. The town of Kortgene is only a few minutes walk away and there are plenty of shops and supermarkets but the Post Office is at the far end of the town. There is also a Boat Yard with a crane.

COMMODORES NOTES

It is now two months since I contributed to Navigans and during this period I have felt very much akin to a boat in winter with polythene wraps over parts of the house and damp creeping in everywhere while alteration and rebuilding has been goingon. I am now pleased to say that with the advent of the brighter weather the work is complete and like most of you I am beginning to think about sailing again.

It is pleasing to note that even in these hard times our level of membership in renewal this year has dropped by no more than is normal in any year and may actually have dropped less than usual. It could be that people are inclined to see 1977 as a stay at home year and will be enjoying more of the excellent facilities they have on their own door steps.

As was reported last year the Stansgate farms were being offered for sale and we now know that the whole estate has been sold by Gonville and Caius College to a Dutchman who we understand has bought as an agricultural investment and is not aiming to build the projected marina in Ramsey Marshes. We have not as yet had any direct contact with the new owner or his agent but we hope to establish the same friendly relationship we had with Gonville and Cauis. We also understand that the farms will continue to be farmed by the existing tenant farmer.

Some of you may also have seen in the national and local Press suggestions that there might be a district refuse tip sited at Stansgate but I am pleased to advise you that common sence has prevailed and Maldon is going to keep its own rubbish and enlarge the existing tip.

With the Sailing season approaching the question of who is going to sail which class is again being asked. I have been following the discussion and correspondence with interest as it is a route we have been before. The main difference is that this time we already have four established classes (Enterprise, Mirror, Hornet and Handicap) and if we made the count a year or so ago five if we include the GP 14. Last time there were two classes (Enterprise and Handicap) and three if we included the then ailing Fleetwind Class. At this time we were, as now, considering what additional classes the Club should adopt. Many suggestions were made and many hobby horses mounted but in the end the new classes adopted, Hornet and GP 14 were determined by the endeavours of the protagonists of their classes overcoming the attempts of others to establish such classes as Snipe, Fireball and Flying Dutchman. This was achieved without destroying any of the existing classes. In a Club like ours, which is basically a family one open to any employee of the G.E.C. - Marconi Group of Companies, it is not our custom to make membership conditional on ownership of a particular class of dinghy or to stipulate that one must race a certain number of times a year. For these reasons the Committee cannot dictate the classes that will be sailed but can only recognise a trend and endeavour to steer people towards a particular class which when there is sufficient interest may be adopted. As I see it, and this is a personal view, there is a need to re-establish the GP 14 or to find a suitable alternative such as say the 420 so as to re-introduce the variety of choice of class for those wishing to graduate from Mirrors. There is also a very obvious need to look closely at the Singlehanded situation as, like most other clubs have at sometime or other, we are going through the phase where there is a demand for single handed class sailing. It is now probably too late to adopt a singlehanded Handicap Class within the Handicap Class and bears on the sucess of this make some recommendations for next year. In the final analysis however, the choice of classes must be arrived at by examining the track record of those offered. This means that a common and proved desire for a particular class must be demonstrated so if we really do need a new class or two some effective lobbying will be necessary to establish a class that meets the specification required by the majority seeking a charge. This I believe is now beginning to happen

but followers of our existing classes must not be complacent and will need to continue to canvas in order to maintain their existing strength as it is inevitable that in building up another class some converts will come from our already established classes and we could end up by weakening our competitve sailing and setting back the clock.

CRUISER FLEET NEWS

We have sold all available tickets for the Fleet supper evening but I would like to remind you all of the Club's Fitting out Party, also to be held at Stansgate on March 26th.

Fitting out must be well under way now and I hope that many of us have acquired new life jackets, learnt more about the use of distress flares, and have invested well in paint. But may I remind everyone of two essentials - firstly to carefully inspect rigging and replace any itme that is in any way doubtful and secondly , to examine mooring equipment for soundness before launching. It is too easy to assume things are O.K. because they were last year.

Many club members are interested in the traditional wooden boat and these people in particular will be sorry to learn that Reg Patten died a few weeks ago after a short illness. Reg spent many years with Dauntless while their business expanded in the early days after the war, and then about 1958 he set up Sea King in a little shed in Leigh High Street, He built sixty seven sailing Sea Kings and a few motor cruisers. It must be true that no two of these are identical as a policy of continuous improvement was adopted. Any customers ideas were built in and then often became the new standard. The first boats were 23ft and the range extends to just over 30ft, at which size there is no more room in the shed. Only one set of moulds is used, these fit the 23 footer and planking for the larger boats misses the moulds by the appropriate amount. A particularly remarkable process since not one plank in a clinker built boat is straight. When I asked Reg which bilge pump he recommended me to fit in Kalinka his reply was simply " You don't need one", Confidence indeed, but Kalinka has never taken in any water except rain since the moment of launching. Such expertise is getting rare these days but fortunately Keith Patten is continuing the business so you can still have a new craftsman built boat if you want one.

Continuing THE LOG OF "ACE OF DIAMONDS" 1976

HOLLAND CRUISE

Saturday 31st July

Up late, still raining. Vic and I spent the morning shopping and looking over a Sabre that we had noticed was for sale. Could this be our next boat? We certainly liked the look of her.

12.30 Left the marina heading up the Veerse Meer, main and genoa set, close hauled wind NNW Force 4. A fierce rain squall blew up after we had been out for 15 minutes and after a little arguing it was decided that the jenny was unsuitable in the adverse weather conditions and some what crowded waterways. We ran under main for a time and then set the No. 1.

All went well untill we reached the most southerly point near Aarberien Eiland, we now had to beat up towards Veer and this made conditions below somewhat unpleasant. We took down all sail and started the engine and motored on past Veere. We saw "Lady Ann", a boat owned at various times by several members of the Tate family and now kept in the canat at Heybridge, with Mirror tender anchored just north of the harbour entrance.

We carried on for another mile and went into Oostwatering. This is an enormous marina still uncompleted and we were the only English boats there.

We had a walk roun between rain squalls and then settled down for the night and listened to the wind howling in the shrouds.

Sunday 1st August

Clearer skies today, with the sun doing it's best to shine. I took advantage of the excellent facilities, shower's were a guilder and I washed, spun and tumble-dried a machine load of clothes for a £1. A bit expensive but well worth it. Robert visited the very luxurious chandlers (fitted carpets) and finished up repainting the bow damaged in Breskens. Vic cooked the lunch, we had salad!

In the afternoon we walked along the sea wall or rather Meer wall into Veere, which was more crowded than ever. Nick and Daphne treated us to some splendid ice creams at the quay side cafe, so we sat down in the sunshine watching the people and the boats come and go. We saw several yachts flying the Lawling Cruising Club burgee.

19.00 Left Oostwatering and in the evening sunshine motored back towards Veere and the lock. Vic demanded his camera every few minutes as the light was so fantastic. The lock was almost empty, 1 barge and 3 yachts including us.

21.00 Tied up in Berth 34 at Middleburg. Everyone went to the Yacht Club except me, they sneaked away while I was putting Mary to bed.

Monday 2nd August

The day was spent shopping in Middleburg and amongst other things large numbers of clogs were purchased. I had hoped to have a good look around the Town Hall, which is situated in the main Market Square, but a modern art exhibition was being held there with an exorbitant ehtrance fee, so I didn't bother.

The Bowsher's came in during the day and we all congregated on "Ace" for the evening I can't remember if that was the night I cooked a beans and sausage supper for everyone or not.

- 8 -

We were now heading for home so it was agreed that detailed reports of the 06.33 and 17.55 shipping forecasts would be kept. Our route home was to be via Ostende, this made the North Sea Passage a little shorter, and was the best port for picking up duty free.

17.55 Shipping Forecast. Gales in Finistere.
Fisher/German Bight W 4-5 veering NW 5-6
Humber/Thames W5, 6 later veering NW, decreasing 4-5
Showers, visibility good.

Tuesday 3rd August

06.33 Shipping forecast. Gales in Finisterre, ridge of high pressure filling in Shannon moving across Denmark Straits. Fisher/German Bight NNW 4-5 showers visibility good. Humber/Thames/Dover NW 4-5 decreasing 3, isolated showers, visibility good.

10.00 Vic and I took the kids to the local swimming pool and then had coffee, on the terrace, pleasant but chilly. We paid up our harbour dues which were 6 guilders per night (about £1.30).

15.30 Out of Middleburg and turned right down the main canal towards Flushing. On this occasion our timeing was bad as we came down to the Flushing road bridge and caught the full flood of the rush hour traffic, so we had to stooge around for about an hour. This was rather annoying, as the Yachthaven was almost a stone's throw away through the bridge tucked away on left going towards the lock.

17.30 Tied up in a cat's cradle of lines, with a lethal access to the pontoons.

17.55 Shipping Forecast. Gales Finisterre. High over Shannon moving westwards Fisher/German bight NW 6-7 in east, showers, visibility good. Humber/Thames/Dover West veering North West 3-4 showers, visibility good.

We enjoyed a drink in the clubhouse with some rather boisterous German gentlemen and then the Bowsher's joined us on Ace for coffee, crackers and cheese.

Wednesday 4th August

06.33 Shipping Forecast. High Shannon moving east to Fastnet. Low central Baltic moving east. Low Cape Farewell moving NW and crossing NW sea areas Fisher/German Bight NW 5-6 decreasing to 4 showers, visibility good.
Tide H.W. Flushing.

09.00 Departed Flushing Yachthaven destination Ostende. We shared a beer with Wigwam, who lay alongside us while locking out.

09.45 Out into the Westerschelde, blue skies but some rain clouds around. Wind NW but only 1-2, set mainsail and genoa, we ran down parallel to the coast keeping about a mile and a half off shore. Mary and I began to have attacks of the queasy tums again so Vic gave us something to do I went on the helm and Mary became flag officer taking down the Dutch and hoisting the Belgian colours and the yellow duster.

To be continued......

It is the time of year when a reminder concerning the subject of safety is appropriate. When sailing on one's own be especially cautious and at other times at the club the following notes are reproduced for guidance:-

1) Officer of the Day
a) Responsible in the vicinity of the Club.
b) Ensure that the Rescue crew have access to their equipment and are ferried to the boat(s).
c) Maintain radio contact with the boat. (This responsibility may be delegated to the Race Officer.

2) Race Officer
a) Check off the competitors at the start and as many times as is pracical during the race. Report any missing boats to the rescue crew.
b) Ensure that any boat not completing the course has returned to safety.

3) Rescue Crew
a) Check the boats sailing as often as is practical and if any are missing confirm their whereabouts.
b) When the racing has got under way take up station near the gybe mark in heavy weather or downtide in very light weather. In medium conditions a central position can be chosen.

4) Members
a) Ensure personal equipment and boat is adequate for the conditions. If the weather is such that you will not be able to cope do not venture out, ask if in doubt.
b) If, however you do require assistance on the water, stay with the boat and wave both arms up and down. Do not use more energy than can be helped and drop anchor if in danger of drifting away.
c) If racing sign off immediately afterwards, this is most important when retiring.

A letter to the editor.

Dear madam,

A long time ago I decided that my Blandford 12 footer had served me long enough and that it was time for a change. My considerations at that time and their outcome may be of interest in the current dinghy-class discussions.

You will say you have never heard of the Blandford 12 footer. Just so. It could not be raced against its peers, and as a handicap racer even with a P.H. of around 130 it was quite useless. So my first requirement was that the new boat had to be a recognised racing class on the Blackwater.

It had to be by a reputable designer, and to have some flair about it. Planing ability and a spinnaker were essential. At the same time it should not make excessively athletic demands upon a 36 year old helmsman.

Although I wanted to be able to sail single handed at times, a single handed boat

like a Solo did not appeal if only because it did not meet another of my requirements - that the chosen boat had to look right, to be pleasing to the eye. So the new boat had to be capable of being sailed singlehanded, (but not be a single hander) and, of course, be easy to right single handed after a capsize. Also it should not be so heavy as to preclude single handed trolleying.

I would not, however, be content with a pure racing machine for I wanted my family (1 adult and three children) to be able to share with me the pleaures of sunny summer day cruising, and so the boat would need to have practical accommodation for a few bodies additional to helm and crewman.

Looking ahead to longer excursions it ought to be large enough to accomodate two sleepers on camping cruises.

Finally of course cost (in the sense of value for money rather than mere cheapness) was a factor.

I tried to make a logical choice with all these points in mind but it seemed to me that the choice very quickly narrowed down to one. Nine years later in 1973 I disposed of my , by that time, much loved G.P.14 "Lady Clare" so I now have no particular axe to grind. I can say without exagerationthat, with the exception of the penultimate point (sleeping was rather a squeeze) she showed in very full measure that the G.P. 14 meet all the requirements set out above. At no time during my ownership did I regret my choice. Her purchase was one of the (few) right decisions I have made.

I still miss her!

Ken Beavins,

Maldon.

The following article has appeared in Navigans in previous years but a reminder at this time of year can be useful.

FALLING IN THE WATER

Compared with the high accident rate of road users, sdiling is 4 relatively safe pastime. However accidents do occur, and when they do are usually more serious as often rescue is either a long way away or more difficult to obtain.

It is therefore more important to take precautions and also to know what to do when an accident does occur.

Why do people die when they fall in the water? Other than a n attack by sharks or mechanical injury them are three main causes of death.

1. Hypothermia, i.e. lowering of body temperature due to the cold environment.
2. Drowning i.e. thexukwekxnfxwatar filling of the lungs with water,
and 3. Vaso - vagal shock, i.e. the shock of water entering the lower pharynx or
upper respiratory passages causing a nervous reflex which stops the heart.

To deal with these in turn, the first is by far the commonest cause of death due to immersion.

5 It has been shown that few people survive for more than seven hours in water at 59 F., muchhigher than British sea temperatures, and the survival time in water at 32°F. is only a few minutes.

As on land, the best way of keeping warm in the water is to wear warm clothing. Intom this category come ‘wet-suits' of whichthey should be best of all. If you can get out of the water and sit on your dinghy, so much the better as unless the wind is particularly cold your heat loss is slower. Contrary to what might be expected, movement in the water accelerates heat loss as the extra heat generated by muscular effort is more than offset by the removal of the warmer layer of water around, and heated by the
body.

Therefore unless it is to swim a short distance to a rescue boat or the shore it is much better to lie still as possible in the water supported by a life-jacket. As the time of immersion is obviously an important factor, one should stay as near as pos— sible to the point where rescue might by expected. This is usually near the boat.

There is no evidence to show that alcohol in normal quantities accelerates heat loss, which may be of comfort to those of us who indulge.

The quickest method of warming someone is a warm bath - tempera tue 97°F - 100°F,
but this is only of use if they can be bathed within 20 minutes and is seldom feasable. A warm atmosphere, hot water bottles, the close proximity of another human body and warm blankets after removal of the cold wet clothing are the usual methods.

So, if you cannot rescue yourself, wear warm clothing, keep still and make it as easy as possible for your rescuers by staying near the boat or where they expect you to
be.

To pass onto the last two headings, prevention is — wear a good life jacket and hold your breath as you go in.

Once a person has ceased to breath irreversible brain damage occurs with 3 -5 minutes so that any attempt to revive them must be made immediately. If drowning is complicated by hypothermia the chance of successful revival is very small.

Before considering how to revive a person let us consider briefly what happens when lungs fill with water. The water may be fresh or sea water. In the former case the osmatic pressure of the blood causes a rapid absoption of water from the lungs into the blood stream which so lowers the osmatic pressure of the blood that the red cells burst, releasing a large amount of potassium whcih the heart can not tolerate and it stops. This takes place very rapidly, as roughly speaking the minute sacs in the lungs if all were spread out would cover a tennis court and they are designed specially to absorb.

In the latter case the reverse occurs as the osmatic pressure of sea water is higher than that of the blood and this causes an outflow of fluid from theblood stream, flooding the lungs and preventing oxygen getting into the blood.. The heart can keep beating for a few minutes after this occurs, so the chances of successful revival are much higher.

The treatment of drowning and also of vaso - vagal shock is the same, namely - artificial respiration. I am sure that the simplest and most effective method is mouth to mouth respiration perhaps better known and the kiss of life.

As with all unconcious people, including unconciousness due to hypothermia, the first essential is to maintain a clear airway. This is done by hooking the forefingers of each hand behand the angle of the jaw of the rescued and lifting the jaw, and thereby the tonge, forward. If possible the lower teeth can be hooked over the upper teeth.

It is a waste of precious time attempting to empty water from the lungs of the rescued. It is much better to attempt to inflate that part of the lung which is not filled with water - usually a considerable proportion. If you kneel facing the feet it is possible to lift the jaw forward, hold the lips together in an airtight joint and breathe gently down the nose. In this position one can watch the chest to see it inflate. Remarkably little effort is required and adequate time should be allowed for the chest to deflate, about three times as long as the inflation period. If the airway is clear i.e. the tonge is not blocking the back of the throat, the movement of the chest should be gentle and easy.

I don't know how long one should continue this as it is mainly a moral question. If one considers that the brain is dead after five minutes and quadruples this time I think this is reasonable and is the criterion I have taken on the few occassions I have had to do it.

It is important to realise that if the rescued is breathing it is positively dangerous to give artificial respiration. This will only hinder theri own respiratory efforts and possibly inflate the stomach, blowing vomit into their air passages and killing them. It is only necessary to keep a clear airway and keep them warm.

One last point which I must mention is the question of vomiting. In a concious person they will get rid of their own vomit but in an unconscious person they may well inhale it with fatal results. Turn them on their side with the head lower than their waist and no fluid can possible enter the lungs.

This article has turned out to be much longer than I anticipated but even so is only an outline of what happens when one "falls in the water". Greater pens than mine have said "prevention is better than cure" and it is never more true than of sailing accidents.

A. Doctor.

Half way through May and we seem to have slipped from a wet winter to a wet winter to a wet spring without noticing the start of the Sailing Season and the improvement in the weather which we expect to accompany it. The club is however coming alive with the moorings filling up and the dinghy park sprouting masts of varying lengths as Members' winter deliberation turn into reality and the fresh boats arrive at the Club.

Continuing THE LOG OF THE ACE OF DIAMONDS 1976

HOLLAND CRUISE

Wednesday 4th August

13.00 Zeebrugge harbour entrance abeam, large dredger working about 2 miles off shore We had noticed a large cruising catermaran with a bright tri-coloured sail approaching from the south. As she closed in I bore away to give her plenty of room to windward, but she kept coming on an almost collision course. She passed about 20 yards to port and a weary looking helmsman shouted, "Which place is this?" We told him.

15.00 After a peacefulsail down, arrived off the Ostende pier heads. We followed a Dutch yacht in, but were surprised when on reaching the dog leg of the pier, he suddenly swung the helm and came out at full chat. So did we when we saw the Townsend Ferry coming straight for us. Tied up in Ostende without incident, 7 boats out on the middle trot. With a very spick and span, new Dutch boat next door, I cringed at the thought of the sand that would get onto the children's shoes and then be deposited on the deck.
A leisurely drink in the clubhouse, ordered duty free and changed our currency.

17.55 Shipping Forecast. Low Denmark straits moving NE. High 400 miles west off Land's End moving westerly. Gales: Bailey, Faeroes, SE Iceland. Fisher/German Bight NW 4-5, 6 later, showers, visibility good. Humber/Thames/Dover N 2-3, 4 later, showers then fair, visibility good.

We took an evening stroll to enjoy the sights and sounds with some frites and cream, and wandered along to the inner harbour. There to our surprise was a forlorn looking Jestabel, all tied up and nowhere to go. What had happened?

Thursday 5th August

As the forecast was reasonable, we decided to stay one more day and enjoy all the sunshine. We took it in turns to baby-sit so that the little ones could enjoy all day on the beach, while parents did mundane things like buying petrol, and spending the last of their currency.

17.55 Shipping Forecast. Gales: Bailey, SE Iceland. High southern Ireland. Low Denmark Straits moving NE. Dogger/Fisher/German Bight/Humber NNW 3-4, isolated showers, good visibility, Thames/Dover/wight Variable, northerly 2-3, fair, visibility misty and then good.

After hearing the forecast, we moved the boats backwards away from the main trot onto the outside pontoon, which would make life a lot easier when we slipped out in the early hours of the morning.

The rest of the evening we all spent on Vanellus celebrating Fenella's 17th birthday, with shrimps. prawns, camembert, cream cakes, wine and beer.

FRIDAY 6th August

0.2.00 Up and preparing to go to sea. Vic having Kittens, "Why are we waiting", Answer - Brian was having his breakfast, sausage and egg. We slipped out under engine quietly with no fuss hoping not to disturb anybody.

02.45 Clear of the pier heads, motoring on, course 306°C for West Hinder. spun log. No moon but visibility good, calm sea, no wind.
03.15 Robert and I returned to our bunks leaving Vic on the helm.

- 6 -

05.45 Woke as the dawn was coming up, took over the helm while Vic took photo's of Natasha. Plenty of shipping around.

06.10 West Hinder abeam, Natasher very close, Vanellus about ½ mile behind. Course 320°C set for Lond Sand Head.

06.33 Shipping Forecast. Dogger/Tyne/GermanBight Variable mostly westerly 3-4. Humber variable 2-3. Thames/Dover/wight/Portland/Plymouth North variable 2-3, locally 4. Galloper S2, visibility 11 miles, pressure 1023°, Varne Calm, visibility 11 miles, pressure 1023°. H.W. Harwich 11.00.

07.00 Refuelled.

07.30 Main and genoa up. Saw a white yacht about 1/4 mile away on ourport side, flying the German ensign and two black spheres from the cross trees, no sails set and no engine running and a motionless figure in the cockpit. As we didn't know what the signals meant we carried on but our ignorance left a nasty little question mark in our minds.

08.00 Robert up and about.

08.30 Engine faltered causing a few heart stopping moments.

09,00 Vic retired to his bunk to catch up oh some sleep.

10.40 Refuelled.

10.45 Galloper seemed to be getting too close, we should have been well down, the tide was setting us up, altered course to 300°C, sun now really hot, Vic down to just underpants.

12.20 Altered course to 290°C.

13.45 Long sand Head visible on the horizon, strong tide against us, no wind at all, only carrying main.

13.55 Shipping forecast. Tyne/Dogger/German Bight WNW 3-4. Humber/Thames/Dover variable NW3. Vic asleep, Robert on the helm, and navigating. We saw the Sunk Head Tower and in the far distance the Old Light House on the Gunfleet Sand. We reckoned that we were at the top of King's Channel and altered course to 270°C to take us doen towards the Sin Spitway, all sails down.

16.00 A few murky bumps on the horizon and then we could just make out the shape of the Naze Tower at Walton through the Haze.

16.05 Rassed Wallet No. 2 Nasty shock, wrong side of Gunfleet. On studying the the chart, we realised that the tide had been much stronger than anticipated and set us right across the top of the East Swin. Instead of travelling diagonally we had moved sideways. Woke Vic up and told him the glad tidings. Although the shore was hazy, it was not difficult to make our way down the Wallet to Colne Point and Brightlingsea.

16.45 Tied up along side John Roger's Macwester in Brightlingsea Harbour. Who should be on the same trot, "Wigwam". This time they gave us not beer, but a very welcome cup of tea.

No evidence of custom's officers around.

Saturday 7th August

H.W. Stansgate 11.08

08.45 A very weary officer returning from a spell of night duty at Colchester cleared us for customs.

13.00 The crew's of all three boats had an excellent lunch in the Jolly Sailor restaurant.

16.30 Left Brightlingsea, tide just beginning to flood, wind easterly. Motored out to the Colne but we had to give way to racing dinghies gybing around the channel marker buoy, which resulted in us just touching the mud. Luckily, we came off almost at once, Vic putting her hard astern.

18.30 Back to the mooring at Stansgate.

NORTH SEA PASSAGE

This is the story of the delivery of 'Victoria', a new 48ft. Motor Sailor from Maldon to Flushing in Holland, and the problems which were overcome during the North Sea Passage, on the lst of September 1976.

Some Sailing Club members may have seen the boat, either at Dan Webb & Feeseys Yard or at anchor off the Club (Sat/Sun 28th/29th August) the weekend before we left. She was moulded by Tylers and fitted out by Dan Webb and measured 48 ft LOA, 36ft. LWL, 13ft 5 Beam. 6ft 6 draft. Her power plant was a prototype heavy vehicle Volvo engine of 120 Horse Power. Her working sail area 1,100 sq. ft.

The crew were as follows:- Capt. & Owner - Jim, because it was easier to say but real name - Thage Bergrenn, from Sweden.
Navigator:- Bill Basson, the one armed ex bomber Pilot, Grand Prix Racer, come Deep Sea Sailor (Age 65+)
John Swinton of Dan Webb & Feeseys.
Jane John's 16 year old daughter.
Stan Campbell the writer
Jimmy Campbell his 14 year old son.

I think that it could be said that the crew were reasonably experienced sailors, though

- 8 -

not seasoned ones.

Navigational Gear

We had all the charts that were needed, hand bearing compass, radar, and radio direction finding equpment. We were,one could say, amply equipped for such a passage.

Time of Departure and Proposed Passage.

We were to leave Maldon at high water (6.20) p.m. On Wednesday lst September and our passage was to be made in roughly four tides (24 hr. approx.)

The route was to be via the Spitway Buoys off Brightlingsea, north up the East Swin to the Sunk Sand Towers and across to Longsand Head (off Harwich) thence via the Galloper Light Vessel between the North and South Hinder Light Vessels and then direct to Flushing, which was an overall journey of 120 odd miles.

The coastal Weather Forecast for 6.00 p.m. Thames and Humber was fairly good - Northerly 4 - 5 backing North Westerly later. Gales forecast from Heligoland, Dogger and area North, but a high was approaching from the South West.

Departure

This was made between 6.00 and 6.30 and before long we had settled down to what should have been a pleasant and straightforward trip. To our surprise we were showing 8 knots on the log although the Skipper had his doubts, chart checks confirmed this.

We agreed to have a hot cooked meal before we cleared the river, so Jane provided a meal of stew and dumplings (or were they golf balls?) followed by fruit and hot coffee. This ultimately proved to have been a very wise decision because our next meal was some sixteen hours later for reasons which will soon become obvious.

The first major problem came at nightfall when it was patently obvious that steering by compass was going to prove very difficult, if not almost impossible, as it was too small and mounted too far away from the wheelto be readable. All crew members tried with varying degrees of success, which did prove that it was not the crew members eyesight and that it had to be accepted and lived with.

However, the Benchhead and Knoll were passed, the Spitway Buoys negotiated and then North up the East Swin. At 00.30 we listened to the Shipping Forecast, which was as follows :- Thames, Humber N.W. 4 - 5 Gales in the area North still and a cold front moving South.

Jim (th Skipper) asked how long a front took to pass and I said that it could be days or hours, but at this time of the year it should not prove a problem, so we decided to press on. Galloper gave 4, but we thought it ought to be 5 and made a remark at the time. We were still in sight of Harwich and Felixstowe and Sunk Sand Tower Light. Not:- To sailors coming up the East Swin, remeber the light is on the north side of the Towers for the use of shipping out of Harwich. The Towers looked big and menacing in the dark and were passed quite a while before the light protecting them was left behind.

Continuing North Sea Passage

So far the weather had been warm and the sea slight, but a remark was made that whereas the wind had been steady it was now tending to gust to what one would call 5 plus. The boat was behaving well, Jimmy had locked the wheel and the ship steered itself for two hours apart from an occasional adjustment. Almost without warning (other than previously mentioned gusts) that eventually proved to be the cold front hit us. I will make no guess as to the strength of the wind for the next six or seven hours, but the sequence of events should give some idea of the weather conditions prevailing.

To begin with, it was the noise of the wind and rain that made conversation difficult, shouting being the order of the day. Steering by compass was now very difficult, indeed and and we needed to get sail off. We had the following sails on - Mainsail fully up with no reefs in, Genoa (heavy) fully up, but we could do something about that as it had furling gear worked through a drum and a series of lines form the cockpit, A jib with reefing gear was bent on and secured up forward ready to hoist to replace the Genoa. It was decided to furl the Genoa and hoist the Jib, which should have been quite simple at that point in time, but it was stuck and just wouldn't move. By now we were sailing on our ear and John went forward to try to release the furling gear without success. Later, whilst, John and I were trying to release the furling gear from the side of the cockpit, there was a most almighty crash and boat heaved over the other way. In the dark and confusion nobody knew immediately what had happened except that 'yours truly' was shot across the cockpit and unable to move. We had gybed! A torch brought from below shone on to me to show that when we gybed I was trapped by the Mainsheets, which by some freak of fate had entangled themselves in the snaphook attached to my harness at the chest end of my lifeline. Two and a half parts of the sheets had entangled and it took four or five minutes to free them ( the half had been cut into by the hook and a knife needed to free it). I was scared stiff that we would gybe again and I would repeat the performance perhaps with fatal results. I could feel no serious damage, which was a miracle considering that I had been flung violently across the cockpit completely without control, in the dark and with no warning. When I extracted from the Mainsheets, we had the Genoa aback and needed to gybe again to get on course. The quickest way was the most dangerous and put the mast under very severe strain in that we wanted to put the stern through the wind under engine to save going through a 360 degree or therabouts under the prevailing conditions.

This manouvre was executed successfully, but the Main still crashed over even though we want through the drill of pulling the sheets in and letting them go when the stern had gone through the wind.

Attempts were still being made to furl the Genoa when with no warning whatsoever there was a terrific crack and a shudder and the Genoa tack came adrift, the sheeets became detached and the Genoa shot up the forestay to within twenty feet of the masthead. We had an uncontrollable thirty feet or so of jumbled up sail flying out almost horizontslly from the Masthead and exerting goodness knows what strains at the point not designed for such. It was urgent now that the Main should be reduced to lessen the risk of losing the Mast, but we soon realised that it would have to come right down as the reefing gear was incomplete and therefore no reefing was possible. This was executed with some difficulty which I will explain later. for at this time a searchlight shone on us from two or three hundred yards astern, and a loud hailer blared out something which due to wind, rain and general conditions could not be decyphered. I did however wave and after three or four minutes the ship veered off and continued on its way.. In retrospect I consider this is what happed:- Our "Masthead Genoa" was in fact an indication of distress according to International Maritime Law, in that it constituted something conspicuous flying from the highest point of the ship. It was also lit up like a Belisha Beacon by the Masthead Tricolour Navigation Light. Some very alert lookout had seen it and true to tradition had closed us to see if we were in need of help. When close enough to see that a sail had carried away and that the man at the helm waved "casually" they assumed that we were capable of looking after ourselves and departed. It was

- 7 -

comforting feeling because it felt lonely out there at the time.

By now the sea was such that to look over ones shoulder could cause fear, for all that could be seen was the white curling tops of the next line of waves. Poor Jimmy had to look, for his Dad was at the wheel and looking ahead and he was looking for lights and timing them with a stop watch, for which he deserved a medal.

Things may not be in chronological order from now on nor may they ever, but lets get back to why we had trouble getting the mainsail down. Our lea rails were under the water at times and we had to get up iton the wind and withthe genoa gone, she didn't want to do it under sail alone. This meant starting the engine, which was as I said a heavy vehicle road one which had a shallow sump, and therefore heavily healed there would be no oil in the sump wot circulate. This risk had to be taken so the engine was started and the oil pressure monitored. We did get into the wind, the boat did come upright (and the sump) so we could get the main down and the engine running. How John and I did it I'll never know.

What to do next? The situation was as follows:- The Genoa was thrashing halfway up the Mast, but still acting as a steadying sail, the Main was down, but the engine was running, so we could 'relax', review the situation calmly and decide our next move. There was a unanimous decision to re-establish our position, which isn't surprising since for a couple of hours we had been at the mercy of wind and sea. It must be pointed out that we knew we had plenty of sea room to leeward so at no time had we been in danger of running ashore. That is why we were concerned out Mast, Rigging and Sails primarily. I think that the method of confirming our position is well worth bearing in mind for the Navigator never left his chart table. It might be worth noting here that conditions were such that all crew members had lifejackets or buoyancy aids on (lifejackets being blown up) and all were secured by some means or other to the boat. This was mainly because of the darkness and the atmosphere which noise. movement, spray, torrential rain and general uncertainty created. At times there was considerable confusion, but at no time was there panic.

Back to positioning ourselves, We knew that we were somewhere in the vicinity of the North and West Hinder so the helmsman (myself) steered as straight a course as possible, Jimmy had the stopwatch and the Navigator was at his chart table below. Most lights even if different colours, normally flash 'X' number of times in so many seconds. Jimmy's job was to look for lights, start the watch on the first flashof the next sequence, let it go through its sequence and stop the watch on the first flash of the next sequence. He then handed the watch down the hatch and said '4 reds every "that"' or '3 whites every "that"' - the "that" being the time that he couldn't see but the Navigator down below could. I added "fine on the port Bow" or "on the starboard beam" whichever was appropriate. Within twenty minutes we had a light and two light vessels looms to look at, but the waves were big enough and we were small enough to blank out whole sequences for quite long periods. We did however know that the two light vessels should have been the NOrth West Hinder which were about twenty miles off the Belgium coast, and about 8 to 10 miles from us. They were roughly were they should be but too distant to confirm without doubt. It was decided to close to what must be the West Hinder which we did, and within an hour could clearly count the light sequence. In fact we closed to within three or four hundred yards to get a good point of departure for the next buoy.

It was almost light by now and we were over the Hinder Shoals with the seas very big and confused which made steering even with a huge wheel quite difficult. They were by far the worst seas any of us had seen from a small boat, except maybe Bill, but he was below. It was suggested that it would be more prudent to make for Ostende as the 6.30 weather forecast was now quoting gales in our area for the next 12 hours, and we were still seven or eight hours from the Scheldt Estuary. We were very weary, very tired and those that had spent the night on deck, very wet (in spite of all the weather gear) and cold. It should be remembered that all this time the Genoa was flogging at the masthead, for even with lifelines it would have been too

Yet another amusing contribution from the amusing Rob Swale...

There were these two Flying Dutchman sailors who went out one day in their boat, and the weather was very rough.

Well, they capsized and both of them drowned, so being dinghy sailors they naturally went to heaven. When St. Peter found out they were just in time for the "Next World" Championships and that a brand new boat with all the latest goodies was waiting for them. So off they went in their perfectly rigged and tuned boat, and with it being held in heaven, naturally the wind was a steady Force 3-4, the tide was non-existent and the sun was shinning.

Well, the start was perfect with everyone at full speed and only one yard from the line when the gun went. Apart from one boat which was right at the coveted port end and was just 3 inches from the line as their was virtually no bias to the lineand the wind was steady, all the "perfect" boats arrived at the windward mark very close together, except this one boat which was just 10 yards ahead of the rest. At the next mark it was 20 yards ahead, at the third 30 yards until at the finish it was about 500 yards ahead of the nearest rival. After the race everyone went to the bar for a heavenly booze-up - there being no protests, of course - and the two newly arrived sailors, having done quite well, sought out St. Peter to thank him for such a perfect race.

"Fantastic, Peter" they said. "It was great, but who was helming that boat that won?"

"Oh" said St. Peter, "That was God - he thinks he's Rodney Pattison!"

Rob Swale.

(North Sea Passage)

dangerous to work right up forward in an effort to get it down, even if we could see how, whilst it was still dark. At about 8 O' clock after passing Middlekirk and Ostende Bank West Buoys, we could see the coast quite clearly, visually and on radar, from Neuport in South to Blankenburg in the north, with Ostende a welcome sight in between Perhaps readers have wondered why we couldn't pick up the lightships on the radar. The reason was as follows:- On very small ships with the aerial say only 25ft, above sea level, spray, sea clutter and heavy rain, all help to interfere with transmission and reception so much that the equipment ceases to function efficiently. The fact that the buildings ashore were much higher, more stable and had a greater reflective area did enable us to see the coast when we were fifteen miles offand yet not see the two lightships at three or four miles distant. The seas were now more pronounced in direction as we got clear of the Hinder and it was decided to try and get the Genoa down as we would have fouled everything had we tried to run up into the harbour.

COMMODORES NOTES

As is invariably the case following the Annual Regatta many views are expressed and at the first committee meeting a review of the event is undertaken and this year we had the added benefit of Tom Gaskell's observation which naturally stimulated lively discussion. At our meeting we analysed at length the various facilities required for an event of the nature of our Regatta and the following are brief summaries of the feelings of those directly responsible for the various crews of organisation.

Sailing - Well covered with good distribution of help. Minor problems with spotting due to inclement weather. Rescue facilities stretched but coped despite the Club being without a permaneant coxon at presetn.

Galley - Good preparation and supply of food etc., Some people spent more time in Galley than ideally we would like but this is ofter at individuals own insistance.

Bar - Good service given by Brewers. Generous support behind bar during peak periods but in general too much on one person outside peak periods. Some spells of duty particularly during Saturday evening party became stretched and mere advance com mitment required to spread load.

Clubhouse Facilities - This is the area in which we are most stretched to meet the demand. There are however problems with providing extra facilities but these are under consideration. Despite this shortcoming many people return each year knowing what to expect. This deficiency must therefore have its compensations.

No conclusions on the future of the Regatta were reached as the views expressed so far have been of an organisational nature and generally about people who have not in themselves taken such a pessimistic view.Before reaching any final decision the Committee also needs to hear the views of the Sailors on whether this sort of Open Competition is what they want during the Spring Bank Holiday where there is an opportunity to stage an event of at least two days duration. The question of Regattas is clearly an emotional one and unless some of these who enjoy it and want it continue say so the view will be one sided and it will surely die.

It should also be borne in mind that the problem of getting voluntary help to do things at the Club is not unique to the Regatta but is present throughout the year and is a older problem to which we have to find a solution if the Club Officiers and Committee are not to become disillusioned.

I would emphasise that the remainder of my notes reflect my own thoughts which are not necessarily shared by all the Committee. Tom's comments/observations published in last months Navigans are well intentioned and contain a considerable amount of fact but I question the conclusions he has drawn in a number of cases and I think we have to consider what the Regatta seeks to achieve. The main objectives as I see them are;
a) to provide good competitive sailing and an opportunity for ou members to sail against members of other clubs on our home waters. (1/6 of the total entry of 225 came from within the club and were represented in 9 fleets.)
b) to offer an opportunity to sail from our unique and much admired facilities to members of mainly local Clubs on the river and in Essex and thereby reciprocate the facilties available to our members at other Clubs.
c) to limit the disruption of Club life to a minimum of weekends in the year and to avoid openening the Club to all on too many weekends in a year. This was in defference to the wishes of the members who are not competitive dailors and who like to enjoy the privacy the Club can offer for the majority of the year.

I do not consider making a profit from the Regatta as a main objective, although naturally a successful one does make a substantial pfofit and if this were the prime motive I would not be prepared to spend the time supporting the event.

An analysis of the entries and those who were committed to helping with the event

- 3 -

shows that the majority of help came from the entrants and their families with additional support provided from the fleets on a rota.

The question of size and how to limit it and still offer open sailing is one to which there appears to be no easy solution but 12 years ago we were equally worried about size when we had 80 boats and since then we have held Regattas with more entries than this year's without the benefits of our present Clubjouse. Generally there has been a tendency over the years for the entries to level off. The main differences I think now really arise from our ability to accommodate more people under canvas than previously and not from the sailing organisation.

I cannot support Tom's view that the emphasis of the weekend should be on having a closed jamboree rather than an open sailing meeting. If sailing were not the prime purpose for holding the weekend with the social aspects being our means of entertaining our guests there would be little need for any special social activities at all during the weekend judging by the general low attendance of members at recent informal social events.

I am firmly of the opinion, and I am not alone in this, that to drastically curtail this as a sailing event is not in the interest or tradition of the Marconi Sailing Club and that it would be a receipe for disaster for the competitive sailing interest of the Club.

The suggestion of holding several open meetings during the year is an alternative but I am not convinced it is an answer as it still requires a great deal of organisation and commitment and it would be extremely difficult to interleave club racing with an open event as without rescue launch support from other Clubs our facilties would be inadequate for the number of boats on the water at any one time.

The idea of our cruiser members sailing in races with the dinghies is not a new one as it was one of the principles of the early Regattas and died very quickly. Our present experience shows the Barnacle races to be almost non existant, entries in the B.J.S.C. Cruiser races are very limited and we seem to be having difficulty in raising a Club team for the inter club cruiser team race. The idea is a non starter still I think.

I do not expect my personal view to be supported un animously by the Members or the Committee, but the Club consists of a lot of minority interests making up the whole and one of the jobs of the Committee is to try to cater for all these interests over a period of time and a balance has to be struck. If this sort of open cometition is still required then the Spring Bank Holiday is a very suitable time for it as it is still relatively early in the season and the large pottering section of the membership has not been brought out by the sun and warmer water temperature.

In conclusion I would say I have no regrets about the many hours spent on the Regattas since they first started and my reward is knowing our members and visitors are enjoying good sailing. I would not pretend that more help would not be welcome to spread the load in all areas but unlike Tom I belive it is there if it was realised it was needed. I am also strongly of the opinion that the Regatta has a very high reputation in the Sailing World and is something the CLUB should be proud of and should continue to strive to run.

John Witter, Commodore.

A number of incidents have recently occured at the Club which are of a petty but irritating nature to all concerned and place people under suspicion. Continuing North Sea Passage

The Skipper went right up into the bows when we found a point of steering which seemed to be most stable and after an inspection he called for the knife, John took this forward and when the necessary rope was cut, the sail dropped low enough to be got at and was eventually stowed. This is an over simplification for the job took almost an hour under the impossible conditions. No words can describe the boats movement, the noise of the wind and rain, the we cold hands which together with tiredness had to do what had to be done we could not have entered harbour.

I at the helm gave a hearty cheer, but even that was carried downwind and away. This then was our first bit of luck in a night of stbacks. With our large (pennant) down, which had acted in some ways as a steadying sail, we began to roll violently. Frightening noises below subsequently proved themselves to be tool boxes and provisions. A throrough inspection below showed that we had made water, but nothing serious. The clue was a very wet carpet up forward outside the toilet compartment. It was condirmed later that the water had spilled out several times when we were heeled ore were tossed about.

To prevent further noise and damage we decided to put the mizzen up as a steadying sail. One had to experience the change to appreciate the difference a very small sail can make. Note:- Whenever faced with a situation such as we were experiencing, always get some sail on, no matter how insignificant, for it can be the difference between acute discomfort and danger to body and limb, as opposed to a damped sideways movement which is far more bearable and much kinder to ship and crew. After an hour or so we had come inside the shoals off Ostende and we were comparatively sheltered. All hands came on deck and with great relief I am sure , watched as 'yours truly' (because he had been on the helm most of the time) was given the great privilige of taking 'Victoria' through Ostende breakwater to make her first landfall. That was one of the most satisfying moments of my life. Within an hour we were tied up and asleep.

- 9 -

On waking we inspected the boat and tidied up prior to going ashore for 'big eats'. The inspection showed the following:-
1) The Genoa was only slightly torn and damage marginal to one seam and the eyelet were the sheets were attached.
2) There were two deck leaks, one caused be the strain put on the handrail protecting the steering console and one round the forehatch.
3) A starboard side stanchion was bent as was the guardrail running from it. It's base screws had also gone and the angle plate strengthening damaged. It was where the end of my lifeline was attached wehen I was flung across the cockpit!!

Other than the above, no damage was found. On finding that we were still seaworthy and having had a sleep, we were ready for a night passage north to Holland. The coastguard however, informed us that the gales would continue for at least 48 hours so we decided to stay put. We walked out on the mole to the Harbour Entrance to see what the seas looked like and deceded that we did not want a repetition of the night before. The following morning we went to Zebrugge and took the Ferry home to Felixstowe in absolute comfort even if for the firsttwo hours we were in heavy seas. As we neared the English Coast the seas subsided and off Felixstowe we saw the familiar lights of Walton and Harwich.

In retrospect it is very difficult to know how some of the problems could have been avoided as it is easy hindsight to hold a post mortem. I would rather say that it added to our overall experience and showed that both young and old can co-operate as a team and face serious situations equally as well when the chips are down. Again in retrospect I feel that nor Maiden Voyage should have had such bad luck. However, it proved the boat for the Owner and proved the Crew to themselves.

The following advise could be given as guidance should somebody wish to make a similar passage.
1) Do a short night sail peior to the crossing to see that the compass is adequate.
2) At the same time familiarise the crew with working on deck in the dark for sail changing and any other necessary activities.
3) Have an alternative destination well planned should the original not prove feasible.
4) If there is a chance of seasickness take all the precautions for avoidance well in advance.
5) Remember that cold fronts invariably mean foul weather, so don't be afraind of them, but be prepared for a change of plans and some very uncomfortable sailing.
6) If it is ever intended to cook of even boil water on the passage, a fiddle rail and gimbals on the cooker are most essential even if only for safety.
7) Make sure that some of the crew have enough experience to take care of the boat under any conditions that might be experienced on passage.

I think apart from the compass, which was vital and the cooker which wasn't, Victoria's crew fulfilled all such requirements and a successful passage was made even if the original destination had to be changed.

Would I do it again tomorrow? - Of course I would -----

There was a vicar who was also involved in the running of the ocal marriage guidance council. One day he was asked to give a lecture on sex to some couples experiencing marital problems. He talked to his wife about the subject many times for advise and she encouraged hime to give the talk.

Several days later the vicar's wife bumped into a marriage guidance counsellor who had heard the vicar's talk and he told her how much he had enjoyed it.

"Yes", he said, "I didn't know he had only done it twice. Your husband said the first time he did it he was sick and the second time his hat blew off!!"

COMMODORES NOTES

September; the evenings drawing in, holidays over and one wonders where the summer has gone and with it all the enjoyable sailing in the longer days. With the comig of Autumn your Committee's thoughts turn to the events of the winter and the Club's future.

Now is the time to start actively thinking about the Laying-Up Supper which is only about 6 weeks away. There have been good turnouts for the sailing activities this year and we hope that you will all make a special effort to come to the Laying-Up Supper to put the seal on the season and to sample the cuisine at this year's venue - The Lion and Lamb - where we succeeded in getting a booking after a large body of opinion expressed a preference for a venue away from the M.A.S.C. We look forward to seeing you and any guests you may like to bring on November 4th. For those who find it difficult to meet the cost of tickets in one go, an "easy payment" scheme has been devised. To take advantage of this all you have to dois to purchase vouchers with your drinks over the bar in the Club or see one of the members of the Social Committee.

Following swiftly in the wake of the Laying-Up Supper is the Annual General Meeting at which the Committee for the ensueing year is elected. This year several of the existing Committee come to the end of the period they can serve an office and a number want to retire after giving many years of service to the Club. There will therefore be a number of officiers or positions on the General Committee to be filled and it would be good for the Club to have some new faces with new ideas grafted into the Committee. If you are interested in helping to run your Club please do not hesitate to have a word with any Committee Member to find out more about the job and if you agree they will make sure that you are nominated. Next month we will be detailing the Committees proposals and advising you who are willing to offer themselves for election, but in the meantime why not find out more about how you can help run your Club.

John Witter, Commodore.

HORNET FLEET NEWS

Six Hornets from the Club travelled to Cramond Boat Club for the European Championships. The club is situated on a small tributary to the Firth of Forth just outside Edinburgh invery picturesque surroundings.

We travelled up on the Friday, leaving early in the morning to arrive in time to pitch our tents. The practice race on the Saturday set the patten for the week by blowing force 5/6. Only two club boats were ready in time for this race. J. Tillotson and M. Turner who acheived their best position of 11th and E. Richmond and M. Strong. The wind increased for the first race and had to be abandoned after the first heat. We all managed to return to the club without serious mishap although Mike's store of spares was seriously eroded on Sunday evening. Monday's race had to also be postponed due to the strength of wind which was fortunate for those of us who needed to repair our boats. The rest of the week went well with one race on Tuesday, two on Wednesday and one on Thursday when the wind increased again to gale force.

Socially the week was very good which perhaps reflects our poor showing in the results. Mike and John did best with a 22nd overall.

We travelled back in time for the Hallam Trophy. For Saturday's racing it blew force 5 for a change, but at least it wasn't raining. Unfortunately the first race of the series had to be abandoned due to lack of water round F mark and other administrative problems but Saturday evening was enjoyed by all and Sunday dawned bright and sunny. Mike and John won the 2nd race easily in ideal conditions. The 3rd race was much harder work for them and they finished 2nd but this was enough for a win overall.

Don't forget the Fleet meeting this month.

Peter Clayton, Hornet Fleet Captain.

MIRROR OPEN MEETING

This event which was run over the weekend of September 10th and 11th of September attracted an entry of 31 boats, including 10 from the Marconi Sailing Club. Out of the total entry, 22 boats were crewed entirely by juniors (under 18 years old).

On the Saturday morning the practise race was held in force 4/5 westerly which gave fairly rough conditions on the first beat. Yankee Clipper (Phillip Brittain and R. Brittain, Maylandsea Bay Y.C.) established a lead at the windward mark and held it easily to take the winning gun. The first points race which was also held in a strong westerly saw Yankee Clipper away to a good start with some of the other boats being involved in colisions whilst beating inshore against the tide. The weather took its toll, causing over half of the fleet to retire but Yankee Clipper coping with the heavy weather conditions repeated their sucess in the practise race by again taking the gun after a 2 lap race, second was Skippy (Simon Kenworthy and Jane Kenworthy, M.S.C.) and third Mapacahepe (malcolm and Caron Stuart, M.S.C.).

COMMODORES NOTES

Next month these notes will come from the pen of your new Commodore to whom I wish every success. I hope he enjoys his period in Office as much as I have during the last three years. A club is an ever changing picture and each Commodore must have his own memories of his time in Office. When I look back, I see my term of Office as one during which there was change and experiment within the Club in aneffort to try to serve better theneeds and wishes of the Membership. Without doubt the highlight of my three years was that I was priviliged to be in Office when the new Clubhouse was completed and Commissioned and I feel that now we are firmly established in our new headquarters we should go forward with strength and I wish the Club every success in the future.

As with any Club when things are going well there is complacency and interest is not stimulated to the extent that members are prepared to let things continue as they are. One of the problems that your Committee is faced with is to find enough volunteers to fill all the positions which fall vacant at the AGM. In recent issues of Navigans we appealed for more volunteers to bring new blood to the Committee and despite this there are still some vacancies for either positions on the General Committee or to take up specific appointments. I am therefore making one further appeal for anyone who is interested in spending time in the service of his Club to contact any Committee Member who will be pleased to discuss your interests and tell you more about any of the activities.

At Our Laying-Up Supper this year we were pleased to hear John Dugdale-Bradley reminiscing about Stansgate in the 1950's. It was highly successful evening with all who attended having nothing but praise for it. Despite the high initial cost our numbers were up and it looks as if we may have at last achieved the right formula. It gave me great pleasure to be your Commodore on this occasion and I look forward to many more enjoyable Laying-Up Suppers as an ordinary member of the Club in years to come.

I look forward to seeing you at the AGM when you will have your opportunity to make suggestions and raise questions on the running of the club.

John Witter, Commodore.
