COMMODORES REPORT

During 1977 members have continued to enjoy the facilities of Stansgate with a wide variety of sailing activities and good social fellowship. Membership has stayed much the same as for the last few years and we seem to have settled down to a level which is about the maximum size that can be coped with on a mainly voluntary basis. This year we have not needed to call many working parties to assist with the general maintenance of the Club but the one held towards the end of October was very well supported and demonstrated a good spirit of co-operation and enthusiasm. If we can count on this sort of turn out when required we should be able to continue to operate with a minimum of paid help and thereby maintain our fees at a reasonable level.

As you will have seen from the agenda, there is no proposal to increase any of the fees this year which I am sure you will all welcome. Although financially all looks very healthy at present we did discuss the possibility of needing to raise fees by 4 small amount to keep pace with inflation. Your Committee decided, however,that if it was possible to delay this for a year we should try, as financially the year has been hard enough for everyone without adding to the burden.

Since last year's AGM no progress has been made with finding suitable alternative locks for the Clubhouse and gate but apart from the gate lock being rendered unservicable at the time of the break-in in May they have proved to be reliable. We shall continue to look for an alternative for when it is needed.

While on the subject of locks, one of the causes of serious concern to your Officers and Committee is the apparent lack of concern by Members for the security of the Clubhouse and site. During the year there have been many instances logged where the Clubhouse has beenfound to be insecure and the gate left open. We are also aware of many occasions that have not been logged. It would appear that we are not succeeding in getting the message over to Members that the Clubhouse must be locked when there is no OOD present even though you may be remaining on the site. In making it possible for all members to have access to the Clubhouse we rely on you, the Members, to protect your property by ensuring that you always secure the premises immediately after use. These instance have increased this year and we must remind you all that with Stansgate being so remotely situated it is not possible for a daily checking procedure to be established and I therefore appeal to you all to be extra careful to secure the Club after use.

The Committee, Sub-Comittees and volunteers have again worked hard in the service of the Club to provide Members with the facilities they have come to expect, including a galley, a bar, a well maintained Clubhouse, Dinghy Park & Moorings and busy Sailing & Social programmes. To all those who have helped to organise and provide these facilities may I say thank you on behalf of the Club and myself. It is perhaps an appropriate point to stress that these services are provided by voluntary help and that the same people cannot go on for ever and new helpers are always required and welcomed so as to spread the load during the year and across the years.

Claud Emerson has again served the the club exceedingly well during the past year and we must all be grateful to him fa the excellent state in which he maintains the Club and the Precincts.

This year there will be many changes on the Main Committee as a number of members have decided it is time to take a rest and let some new faces take a turn. At this point I would like to mention a few of the retiring members who I have been pleased to serve alongside and who will be taking a rest. These are Jill Savill, who after 2 years representing the ladies and running the Galley deserves a rest, Vic Tate who is stepping down to take a well earned rest from active office after championing the Cruiser's interests for many years. Ted Barnes, who has been keeper of the Coffers for the last 3 years, is recharging his calculator. Roy Battye, who after 3 years as Social Secretary, during which time not everything has gone his way, would now like to rest on his laurels after a highly successful Laying-Up-—Supper. The other retiring members Les Mendoza and Rob Swale have had less specific jobs but have nevertheless been valuable members of the Committee. The remainder of last year's Committee are offering themselves for re-election, To all of last year's Committee I express my grateful thanks for your support and service to the Club and to those carrying on "Good Luck".

Sailing highlights will be covered by our Sailing Secretary in his report but it would be remiss of me, as your Commodore, not to draw your attention to the contribution made by those members and friends in the race’ box and resuce boats who make the racing possible each week and express our gratitude. Also the cadets, who have sailed so enthusiastically again this year, and under the shippership of Rick Anstey and Colin Leveridge have worked on their Elementany and Intermediate Day Boat Certificatesto achieve a high level of sucess, are to be congratulated.

In making my report this year I must refer to the Annual Regatta of the Marconi Sailing Club. Many of you may not realise that I was Sailing and Regatta Secretary at the time the first one was put on some 12 years ago at the request of a number of the local Clubs who, because the date of the Bank Holiday was at that time fixed by the moon, and not the Government rarely had any water for sailing during the weekend. During my years in Office I have seen this event grow to what it is today; the most popular event on the Blackwater and probably in the East Coast Area.

It has always had its problems, even from the first year it was run, but a true test of its popularity is the fact that sailors return each year for this one event. I sincerely believe it is an event which the Club should be proud to present and should make every effort to improve for the benefit of all keen racing sailors as open competition on our own waters offers unique opportunities to our members. An analysis of the classes sailed during the weekend shows that we have our own members sailing in about 80% of the classes.

Since all the discussion in the summer, the Committee have considered the various shades of opinion and have concluded that there is a very strong body of opinion among the active racing members, whose families, incidently provide the majority .of the help, that the event should continue. We hear from neighbouring Clubs that there would be great disappointment if we did not offer our hospitality during this one weekend in the year and all those enquiring have been advised that the Committee believes there will be a Regatta in 1978.

During the year there has been a growing demand for Cruiser moorings and particularly for winter storage. Your committee recommended revised arrangements for this year, which will just about cope with the demand for 1977/78 winter, and have passed forward a recommendation to the new committee to review the situation for futue years during the early part of 1978.

- 7 -

Finally, as I retire from office I would like to say that I have been proud to be the Commodore of what must be classed as a very successful Club and to thank all with whom I have worked during my term of Office. I know you have spent many hours on the business of the Club during this time and we must all be grateful for this time voluntarily given to an activity which we all enjoy and in which we have a common interest. To you all I express my own and the Clubs appreciation.

After tonight you will have a new Commodore and I would ask you to give him your support and help so that he can undertake effectively the job for which he has volunteered to accept nomination, Ron you will certainly have my support and I wish you good luck and I hope you will enjoy your term of office as much as I have mine.

Thank you John Witter.

SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT 1977

At the beginning of the season the rescue boat was fitted out with a hew Mercury 40 h.p. engine to replace the four year old Crescent. The Mercury appears a better engine and the service back-up (by Shoreline) an enormous improvement.

Despite the colder weather this year Club events showed an overall increase in the number of boats sailing. In the Summer Points the Hornets averaged 5.4 boats (an increase of 1.1 over 1976), Enterprise 4.1 (a fall of 1.6), the Mirrors averaged 11.3, a slight fall of 1.6, still a very well supported class but the most significant change was the Handicap class which increased its turnout this year by 6.4 to an average of 14.3 boats. This was mainly due to a number of members changing to 420s and Solos and it seems likely that these two classes will earn fleet status next season.

The Cadets were again very active, particularly in the Mirror Class raceing, where cadet helms finished 1st, 3rd and 5th in the Summer Points and mostof the other boats were crewed by cadets. In fact the Mona Cup, one of the Club's best supported races was won by a cadet, with two more filling 2nd and 3rd places.

The new Club trophies introduced this year were the Jubilee Cup which was presented by the Commodore and attracted a record entry of 41 boats in one race and was won by a Cadet and a rather unique plaque made by Chris King in an effort to encourage the International Moth in the Club.

In Club open events, the Regatta entry seems to have established to just over 200 boats. The Dinghy Challenge Cup was not quite as well supported as last year but this was probably due to it having to be postponed to a Saturday and it was won once again by a member from Stone S.C. The Mirror and Hornetopen meeting lost some support from visitors in Hornets but gained popularity with the Mirrors.

As for open events outside the Club notable successes were obtained in the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships where the Hornet class was won by John Tillotson and Mike Turner who then went on to finish 2nd in the Cock of the River final. The Saltcote Open Cadet Cup was again won by the Marconi Sailing

- 8 -

Club (Colin Harper and Robert Weedon). The second boat was also from our club. Mersea Week was enjoyed by several of our members, with the Mirrors gaining the best results.

John Weedon

The estimated accounts for the present year show a very small current account less, but events since this was prepared indicate that it is more likely that we shall have a small surplus. The effects of inflation have continued to show themselves, and probably account for £300 - £400 of the increased expenditure relative to income. Committee

An experimental scheme of committee meetings was followed this year; with the Main Committee meeting every Second month and the Executive Committee meeting during the alternative months.

The intention of this scheme was to spread the load of running the Club more equally through-out the Sub-Committee's, by giving them more responsibility for longer periods. The Main Committee have monitored this procedure during the year and have concluded, that the sub-committees have welcomed more autonomy, but less frequent Main Committee meetings were not successful. This was due to the reduced forum for Communication between the sub-committees and their respective functions. Some committee members also felt that it was not as easy to become involved with the overall Club activities.

The committee do not therefore recommend this programme of meetings to their successors, although the sub-committees should retain the same level of autonomy.

CRUISER FLEET NEWS

Now that laying up is completed I would like to make a couple of observations which may help members next year:-

Firstly- The cleanest boats at the time of removing from the water were those that had the smoothest finish before application of antifouling. In fact one glass fibre boat with TBT antifoul looked ready for launching rather than laying-up. The owner said it had not be n touched up during the season. It is a recognised fact that if silt or mud deposits get on the boat then fouling grows on the deposit. If the surface is really smooth then the water flow will help prevent the silt deposits. Those with drying moorings may of course also get a bonus from wave action which those permanently afloat don't receive. However I shall certainly try to keep Kalinka's bottom as smooth as a baby's!

Secondly - ease of getting the boat onto the trolley. Those who can beach and then get a trolley under the keels are possibly the lucky ones. For the rest of us it is necessary to guide a floating heavy boat onto a submerged trolley, and too often this is attempted without sufficient preparation. The easiest boats to get out are often those which, due to their size are forced to have very strong trolleys. Because the owners of lighter boats can get away with a little less they sometimes run severe risk of damage to their boats and themselves. It is essential to have strong uprights on the trolley to guide the boat and resist its weight. The use of garden canes is crazy. It is also crazy to dabble feet, etc., to find out whether the boat is located. "Look Mum no teeth" may sound funny but it's not worth the risk of trapping a foot under a bilge keel. NOW while the boats are on their trolleys, is the time to put adequate guides and supports so that the boat will be well located and put on at least two really strong verticals I put mine on the upriver starboard side so that the rising tide holds the boat to the supports. Two warps from the scrubbing posts allow the boat to be eased into position before tying to the uprights with motor tyre fenders between. With planning and thought the job is simple, without, a lot of time is wasted by everyone.

Paint and anti-fouling will be available again at discount. I will start taking orders in January.

Merry Christmas to one and all,

Russell Fuller, Cruiser Fleet Captain.

A CAUTIONARY TALE

A few weeks ago there was a lot of news concerning small fishing boats which were lost in mist and fog off the East Coasts and stretched the services of rescue facilities. The following story relates to a works colleague of mine.

Having gone out for the day with a friend who keeps his boat in Walton Backwaters a day's fishing was completed somewhere near the Medusa Buoy off Walton. The boat carried a compass and torch but not a lot more. The return passage, under outboard power was commenced in conditions of slight mist. The owner knew the vacinity pretty well. Pye End Buoy came up through the mist, then No. 2 Buoy appeared. Stearing mainly by Compass due to the mist. At this point buoys are closely spaced - everything should be fine. Compass bearing O.K. - where is the next buoy? Time passes - open sea - more time passes - and more - fuel running low. Friend says we can't keep on like this - drop anchor. Kept warm in small cabin - 2 adults - 2 young boys. A shore rescue service noticed parked trailer and started searching.

Through mist my friend identifies Medusa buoy flashing. Darkness fall - good torch carried, several passing ships signalled - not seen. Eventually boat passed close - flash S.O.S. - its the lifeboat - rescue. Marvellous attention from the lifeboat crew, eventually everyone home safe and well.

Several days later small boy seen playing with magnets. Yes they were in his pocket that day. Do some tests, boy moves across cabin - compass swings about 120°.

Have your chidren got any magnets?

R. Fuller.

LIFEBOAT RESCUE AT STANSGATE - MAY 1977

The article below is reprinted from’ THE LIPTMBOAT journal. We happened to be at Stansgate that afternoon, finishing our fitting-out, and watched the whole affair, It was eerie, and perhaps a little sobering, to see red flares coming from Goldhanger Spit which is the sight of such innocent pursuits as our Mud Race. The rescued yachtsmen took advantage of our clubhouse for a ‘warm-up! and a cup of tea before going their own way, Perhaps this is a good reminder that any of us may need the R.N.L.I. no matter how modest our voyaging.

"Rradwell Coastguard Mobile was in the vicinity of Stansgate on the afternoon of Friday, May 20, keeping watch over a number of yachts off Osea Island, when, at 1723, a yacht was seen to be heading for the sand spit at the eastern end of the island and a red flare was sighted. Life- boat attendance was requested and the honorary secretary of West Mersea ILB station immediately gave authority for maroons to be fired. Meanwhile, it appeared that a second yacht was altering course to go to the aid of the first, she also ran aground on the spit, at the north-eastern edge.

The wind was north east, strong force 6 gusting to gale force 8, and, with a strong ebb tide, the seas were heavy and short. Predicted high water at Rradwell was 1548. The weather was fine with fair visibility.

At 1732 West Mersea Atlantic 21 ILB launched on service, Once clear of the West Mersea approaches she had to reduce speed in the heavy seas, but she reached the 23' sloop"Contessa", the second grounding, at 1752. Approach to the casualty was difficult in the shallow water as the two streams of ebb tide around Osea Island, reaching a rate of 3 knots, were meeting and causing very heavy confused seas of up to 6 feet against the gale force north-easterily wind, One crew member boarded "Contessa" and an anchor was run into deep water by the IIB.

Roth this yacht and the first casualty, the 25' sloop "Lionheart", were chartered from Maldon, The two men in "Contessa's" crew of four were loath to leave until told of the continuing bad forecast and an estimated re- floating time at 0100, All four of the crew were then taken aboard the ILB and landed at Marconi Yacht (sic) Club, Stansgate, where the Coastguard mobile awaited them,

The Atlantic 21 then went on to "Lionheart", reaching her at 1807, After the ILB had run an anchor away for them, the yacht's four crew members were taken off, the transfer, once again, requiring careful manoeuvring: the four people were landed at Stansgate at 1830.

Before returning to station the ILB continued westward to warn other yachts to remain west of Osea Island. The 6-mile passage back eastwards was again made at reduced speed with the ILB leaving the water frequently in the heavy seas. She was refuelled and ready for service at 1922,

For this service a letter of appreciation signed by Captain Nigel Dixon, RN, Director of the Institution, was sent to helmsman James Clarke, Letters of thanks signed by Commander Bruce Cairns, Chief of Operations, were sent to Crew Members Graham Knott and David Mills.”

Ray and Maureen Ball

SAFETY AFLOAT

It i. the time of your when a reminder concerning the subject of safety is appropriate. When sailing on one's own be especially cautious and at other times at the club the following notes are reproduced for guidance:-

1) Officer of the Day

a) Responsible in the vicinity of the Club.
b) Snsure that the Rescue team have to their equipment and
are ferried to the bout(s).
c) Maintain radio contact with the bout. (This responsibility
may ve delegated tu the Race Officer.

- 4 -

Safety Afloat cont.

2) Race Officer

a) Check off the competitors at the start and as many times as is practical during the race. Reprt any boats missing to the resuce crew.
b) Ensure that any boat not completing the course has returned to safety.

3) Rescue Crew

a) Check the boats sailing as often as is practical and if any are missing confirm their whereabouts.
b) When the racing has got under way take up station near the gybe mark in heavy weather or downtide in very light weather. In medium conditions a central position may be chosen.

4) Members

a) Ensure personal equipment and boat is adequate for the conditions. If the weather is such that you will not be able to cope do not venture out, ask if in doubt.
b) If, however you do require assistance on the water, stay with the boat and wave both arms up and down. Do not use more energy the n can be helped and drop anchor if in danger of drifting away.
c) If racing sign off immediately afterwards, this is most important when retiring.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

The Marconi Sailing Club Regatta is over for another year! All members who helped should feel proud that they contributed to its undoubted success.

For the first time in living memory the 'domestic' facilities survived the weekend and a large measure of credit for this must go to Cyril Drakeford our Clubhouse Secretary. Indicative of his efforts was the time on Sunday afternoon when he chose to sit on the sea wall for a few minutes well earned rest. No sooner had he settled himself comfortably when it started to rain! The strange thing was there were no clouds in the sky and he was the only person getting wet. You've guessed it, the water pipe to the Portaloos had developed a leak and was spraying a jet of water just where Cyril was sitting. Oh Well!, fetch the tool kit again.

Finally I hope that many of you will be on hand to welcome our friends from Rochester when they visit on Friday and Saturday 30 June/1 July.

Ron.

I had some doubts about accepting our Commodores invitation to write occasionally for Navigans. It seemed to me it would be all too easy to infuriate members by perpetually lecturing them about conduct at the club (you know - litter, dogs, kids and shut the gate) or by contrast by attempting to fan real or imaginary discontent with the way the club establishment runs our affairs to malign a very hardworking group of people. So I'll try to do neither - well, not much.

Have you noticed how the quality of the Stansgate Clubhouse bar staff varies from week to week? Sometimes it's quick service, agile mental arithmatic, smiling faces, nothing out of stock and all done with a smiling facility. Thats when Jack and Joyce Reeve doit. And sometimes the bitter and lager comes out all fizzy so it takes about half an hour to draw a pint, the barman doesn't know how many beans make five, his lager and lime takes about an hour because he keeps forgetting where he put the lime - and he dosen't even look as though he's enjoying it. That's when I do it!

I suppose the wide range of skill is inevitable when the "staff" as I called them are ordinary club members like you and me. I do wonder though how much longer we should go on without having some more formal arrangement which spreads this work more widely among membership.

RACING DICIPLINE

During the last few weeks there have been a number of collisions during racing. This is a situation that we do not wish to continue for everyones' sake so may I outline a few guidelines.

1) If a collision occures then one of the boats (the one who did not have the right of way) has an obligation to accept the penalty of retirement from the race or execute a 720° turn as soon as possible after the incident.

2) A third person who witnesses a collision can report this to the race officer and after a protest hearing both parties involved are likely to be disqualified if neither carried out their penalty as 1) above.

3) Beginners racing who do not understand all the rules are invited to discuss their situations as they occur and advice can be passed across the water at the time of any imminent incident.

4) The main reason for competing is for enjoyment (I hope) so we, and this includes myself, must not lose sight of this objective. This means to me observing the rules and not bashing a hole in anyones boat.

John Weedon, Rear Commodore.

MIRROR FLEET NEWS - PLEASE!

One day, I'm not sure when it was, but not too long ago,
Our Captain, old Stan Oaker, went and bought himself a boat.
His new craft, not a Mirror, but a flashy, fast, Solo,
Left all our Mirrors standing on the line, watching him go!

The sad farewells were over, and we Mirrorites got busy,
Our aim - a brand-new Captain - and it fairly made us dizzy!
We organised a meeting, to which not many came,
And we got a LADY Captain - Women's Lib. had struck again.

In times gone-by (in old Stan's reign) I'd pick up Navigans,
Look for the latest masterpiece, attributed to Stan.,
I'd read, I'd learn, and inwardly digest, as I should do,
But now,instead of M Fleet News I just see blanks - do you?

So come on Skipper, play the game - give us a piece to read!
Inform us, tell us what to do - but do it with all speed!
Next Navigans is coming up, don't leave us empty-handed!
We want our news and views - or do you want the fleet disbanded?

It's really not as bad as that, but come on, Skipper, please?
Just tell us what is happening, we beg you on our knees!
It's not male chauvinism, dear, that makes us thus complain -
We merely want our regular"M Fleet News" once again!

How about it?

Anon.

COXSWAINS REPORT

Since taking over as Coxswain at the beginning of the season the weather has been so fine that if a certain bearded member hadn't acquired a new Hornet I could have been made redundant!

Seriously though, we are lucky this year in having a few drivers available on a regualr basis and now the better weather is coming I am starting to accumulate volunteers for crews so hopefully more of you can be released for sailing.

We have bought a hook-over ladder so if you are unfortunate enough to have to be rescued from the water, getting into the Mariner should be easier.

Finally we are trying to tighten up our Radio Procedures. The Committee has backed the decision that the called station should be transmitted first and repeated for the first message of a group. i.e. If you are on Race Officer duty and wish tocall the Rescue Launch the conversation should start: "Marconi Rescue -- Marconi Rescue this is (or from) Marconi Base - Over", to which the launch will reply "Marconi Base from Marconi Rescue - Over".

420 FLEET NEWS

The 420's have the fastest growing fleet in the club. I have correlated boat names and crews so that we shall all know to whom we are offering advice to at the gybe mark.

Apart from a short hard blast a few weeks ago it has not been 420 weather The light conditions however have not bothered Paranoid crewed by Chris Weedon and Mark Savill. At the moment Paranoid is almost untouchable, often finishing minutes ahead of the remainder of the fleet. Perhaps Chris should adopt the flying W as his personal device. With Paranoid up front and out of the way the rest of us enjoy close interesting racing, minor errors on the part of a crew (collective) resulting in quite a few places being lost.

The Regatta series was won by Alf Lepper from the Osea Sailing Club, Paranoid and Wind-de-peg taking second and third places respectively for Marconi. The Sunday morning race was characterised by an almost total lack of wind, many of us made new acquaintances in the jamboree at the start line. The crew of Coquette decided to abandon their original intent to sail round the course and came home via a walk along the Osea beach followed by a short sail across the river followed by an even longer walk along the Mayland Creek beach - it was hell, I tell you! If it had not been for the vision of lovely cool galley ladies dishing out endless cups of tea and lumps of bread pudding I do not think that we would have made it.

The remaining races were much more enjoyable affairs and apart from a slight infringement of rule 37.2 in the gents showers the whole weekend passed off without one official protest being lodged.

Those of you who subscibe to the 420 Association will know that the shape and angle of dangle of our rudders has been resolved. The new shape allows the rudder to be carried more vertically. Plans of this highly desireable appendage are available from the R.Y.A., I shall obtain a copy on behalf of the fleet.

Owners who have purchased new sails will be pleased to know that arrangements are in hand to have a recognized 420 measurer in the club. I am not going to say who it is to be, except that Coquette will stand a very good chance of winning the summer points series as a result of this appointment.

Patrick Black, Fleet Captain.

'ACE OF DIAMONDS'

Summer Cruise 1977

Our Summer cruise started on Saturday 23rd July and we hoped to go as far as the River Deben. Not a long trip but long enogh with our crew, Wendy, Rachel(age 9) Philip (age 7) and Andrew (age 11 months). We had stowed most stores on board Friday evening so on arrival at Stansgate we had only to take ourselves, perishable stores and freshwater on board, deflate the dinghy and lash it on deck and prepare the Mirror for towing. Two painters and remember to block up the dagger board slot.

At 16.45 we let go the mooring and headed down river under No1 jib, with the tide, bound for Mersea for the night. The wind was from the south, force 4-5. On rounding the Nass Beacon the engine was started, but not used, and we continued to sail in. Off Cobmarsh Island the jib was lowered but as we were still making over the tide under bare poles we still did not use the engine until we tethered alongside Teal, which belongs to Ian Tate, my brother-in-law. Ian was preparing to go over to Holland with his family. We were in time to take advantage of an

- 10 -

offer to collect fish and chips for supper whilst land transport was available.

The forcast for Sunday was not promising but we turned in early in case.

Sunday 24th July

The forcast was as predicted S.W. 5-7 definetly not family cruising weather, neither was the morning rain. The day did brighten up later and some of the crew took exercise ashore in the afternoon and as the wind died down in the evening our two crews took the Mirror sailing for an hour or so.

The predicted forcast for Monday was better, N.W. force 4-5 so another early night in case.

Monday 25th July

Up early, Andrew is a perfect in-built alarm (offers for him from serious cruising crews will be considered). The 0.630 forcast was still N.W. force 4-5 and the ship was again ready for sea.

We left Mersea at 07.40 bound for the River Deben under engine and No1 jib, tide was beginning to ebb, out in the quarters the main was raised and the engine silenced. We goose-winged nearly to the Colne Bar buoy which we passed at 08.40. Teal was just ahead of us, having taken the inshore passage out of Mersea, bound for Flushing. Visibility was good and having crossed the Colne bar the seas were calm.

Clacton pier was abeam at 09.45 and Walton pier at 10.45. We arrived off the Deben at 12.15 a passage time of 4 hours 35 minutes with which we were pleased.

The big question to enter the Deben or not? One hour before low water, 'Ace draws 4' - 6" however several boats came out and they all indicated a depth of 6' - 0" over the bar so we decided to enter.

Down came the mainsail and on with the engine. Wendy does the first, Philipthe second. Rachel is looking after Andrew below, funny how bodies always want to get up at the wrong moment. Safely over the bar but in the entrance the engine began to run on one cylinder and we had to start to tack in under jib alone. A rain squall is apreaching fast and we hurriedly put on oilskins. Wind increased to force 6 for a short time accompanied by heavy rain. Still tacking in the entrance and making little headway over the tide. Rain stops and the wind dies down, Wendy raises the main and we continue to tack in making better progress finally rounding the Hoise Buoy and into the Deben proper.

The wind has now become light so Rachel and Philip take over the ship to continue tacking while I go below to look at the plugs on the engine, one is oiled up and when cleaned and replaced the engine functions well again.

There is another black cloud on the horizon so Rachel decided to go below to help Wendy feed Andrew. Philip and I replace our oilskins and sail on. The rain starts and windincreased. We are now luffing up 'Ace' a lot and being stoned by pea sized hailstones. The storm lasts for about ten minutes and then the weather clears again.

We finally drop anchor at the 'Rocks' at 15.20 after a mainly pleasant sail. Spent some of the evening ashore to allow the crew to stretch their legs.

.....cont/

BIRD SPOTTING ON THE BLACKWATER

Sitting on the Rescue Boat in all this fine weather has given me an ideal opportunity to spot our feathered friends on the River. You may recognise some yourself:

- 4 -

The Great Bearded Bates.

One of the Hornet family. Has great difficulty in flying back to the clubhouse without injury. Ususally flies up the opposite end of the River to the Rescue Boat. Has a mutual attraction to fishing lines and Hooks.

The King Moth Eater.

A wild untamed young bird. Spends more time in the water than it does in the air. Probably won't live to a great age.

The Orange Savill.

A solo bird with an unusual habit of standing up in the water. The female of the species spends all her time collecting food for all the other birds on the River.

The Curly Headed Windypeg.

This jovial bird is easily recognised - usually amongst a flock of female birds of another variety. It's speed across the river is mirrored in the deep red plumage of its female offspring. The latter looks after the older members of the flock - usually from the rear.

The Blackwater Grey Goose.

A difficult one to spot as it's a quiet type but through intelligent use of its enterprise (sorry!) has become the King Bird of the River.

Sailing Secretary Bird.

Not often seen on the River as it prefers to spend most of its time with is mate in the Clubhouse. Has a distinctive call of "It's a Rojer - It's a Rojer!".

The Black and Blue Bird.

The colourful female of the species is often seen wrestling with a flying spinnaker and heard cheerfully chirping under trying circumstances. The adult male stays well away but the male chick is a leading member of the fledglings whilst the young female sits gracefully around.

Continuing the log of 'Ace of Diamonds', Summer Cruise 1977

Tuesday 26th July.

Wind still N.W. Force 5 which is making the anchorage uncomfortable. Wendy took Rachel and Philip ashore whilst Andrew had his morning sleep. At the turn of the tide we motored up to Waldringfield where we found a mooring to pick up, with the advise of the "Fairways attendant", opposite the Waldringfield S.C. Jetty which has a freshwater tap at the top end.

The Mirror was rigged after lunch and we spent the afternoon sailing it around.

In the evening Rachel, Philip and I took the Avon behind the island at Waldringfield and put out our drift net. I had just been asked how we would know if we had caught anything when the floats begin Bobing up and down frantically, On hauling in the net we found we had caught five Mullet and one Jobe, all in about five minutes. This beats rod and line for productivity Fishing was stopped then as we had more than enough to eat.

Wednesday 27th July.

Went on shore to collect stores from the shop at Waldringfield, which is very well stocked, had some liquid sustenance from the Maytree and returned to the boat for a fish lunch, sailed in the Mirror with the children during the afternoon.

We debated whether to go up to Woodbridge on the evening tide but decided to do this tomorrow morning, at which point the owner of the mooring rowed by and said that he would like it back in a couple of hours. Decission reversed and we motored up to the marina at Woodbridge arriving about 21.00.

Thursday 28th July.

The day started with an unpleasant drizzle which persisted whilst we went into the town which we find fascinating.

The facilities at the Marina have been improved, since our last visit in 1975, with the addition of a toilet block with showers which we found were kept clean and had a good supply of hot water.

We met Peter Hammer, his wife and brother-in-law in the afternoon, they were over on holiday from Holland in the boat Knepie II which was a Deb 33. They were very enthusiastic about the quality of British boats and gear but were dismayed at the lack of stock held by chandlers as they were undble to buy several items they wanted.

Friday 29th July.

We all went to the swimming pool this morning it is an excellent pool and for those who don't know, issited just beyond the railway station. The weather is brighter now but the wind is still strong so we will stay a few days more. The children are making friends and I have been varnishing, fitting out has to be done when possible. The evening was spent on Knepie II.

- 8 -

Saturday 30th July.

Rachel and I took the Mirror out of the marina and sailed up to Wilford Bridge, this is something I have wanted to do for several years but haven't found time before.

We met Alan and Vera Jupp, from Mersea today. They had brought Pelican, Jack Bates last boat, up from Mersea for the first time and were enjoying their journey despite seasickness amongst the crew.

Knepie II left on the tide bound for Holland having obtained a reasonable forcast for the trip.

We spent the evening on board 'Ace' with Alan and Vera.

Sunday 31st July.

I finished some varnishing and the children were playing with Pelican's crew and Isobelle Deveedt from Palanis II, a Belgian boat belonging to her parents Ian and Hilda.

We took a walk in the afternoon along to the playing field behind Eversons boat yard and then onto a 'green lane' which led down to the river near Kyson quay and we returned along the sea wall.

In the evening we went aboard Palanis II. Ian is an architect and he also likes to paint and were shown some beautiful water colours of the Woodbridge river area.

Monday 1st August.

The weather had now improved and we left the marina at 12.45 with a gentle S.W. breeze to go back to the rocks where the children went swimming and looking for sharks teeth and were lucky enough to find half a dozen.

Pelican and Palanis II came down to join us and in the evening we had an enjoyable bar-b-que on the beach. We decided that tomorrow we would all go round to Woolverstone on the River Orwell.

"Last weekend the tides were right for bottom scrubbing. I was all for beaching near the club but wiser counsels prevailed. Betty's advice was good for although we were a long way down towards Stone the starting guns, public address commentary and other noise overspill from the open meetings in progress at our Club were clearly audible to an obtrusive degree. Anyone who has spent nights afloat on the Blackwater knows that it is often anything but quiet even in the small hours, and we all know how much din is created by speed boats, but I wonderered last weekend whether it was necessary or desirable for us as a responsible club to contribute so readily to the general noise.

By the time this appears the 4th Barnacle points/Marconi Cruiser Cup race will have been sailed and shall know whether all that back breaking bottom scrubbing did any good - I can guess! It was good to see many apparent cruiser entries for the Pilots Cup, an all-in race counting also as a Barnacle Points race. I say apparent because of a dearth of square burgees and because of the lassitude which seemed to overcome more than one boats crew (young enogh, may I say, to know better!) around lunch time in the vicinity of Bradwell.

All-in races are good for the Club because of their unifying influence."

CRUISER FLEET NEWS

Yet another sailing season, if not exactly over is at least getting well matured. The more experienced and hardier among us have made their trips to France and Hooland, braving some rather poor Summer weather. Some, like my family, have had another look pottering localy and up the East Coast. One advantage of sailing is that plans can be adjusted at the last moment to suit one's mood and the weather. We had every intention of sailing to London but it is said "Gentlemen do not sail to windward" so we didn't either. Walton Backwaters proved very hospitable at a time when it was rather blowy outside. We find that Stone Point for the children to play followed by an anchorage off Skippers' Island gives an excellent combination, with the odd dinghy trip to Walton for good measure. We made our first trip into the Deben, with "East Coast Rivers" as our pilot. No problems were encountered but I will endorse the comment that plenty of power is meeded to get out against a rising tide at neaps. This does give an easy passage over the bar however.

We very much liked the town of Woodbridge and enjoyed our stay in the tide mill marina - quite a change from swinging to the anchor which is usual for "Kalinka-on-Tour".

Enough of me however, how have you all been fairing? The best way to report is to bring all those holiday slides to "The Generals Arms" on the first Thursday in October. Don't Forget.

May I remind everyone as laying up time approaches to check over their trolleys. Good location makes things a lot easier while for keel boats some real strength is vital - there is still time to put things right - do it now!

At one time cruisers were always extremely steady and leaving or picking up a mooring was normally done under sail. Most of our fleet approach this situation and it is excellent that in suitable conditions we should practice handling under sail. However the modern design of cruiser racer is so skittish that it would be unwise to attempt this. At least one collision has already occurred to prove this - not with Kalinka this time I might say. In case of doubt therefore please use your motor until well clear of other boats - no one wants unneccessary wear and tear whether fair or otherwise.

See you all at the Generals Arms.

At our A.G.M. on November 22nd a very notable milestone will be reached in the history of our Club. For a number of years now our President, Sir Eric Eastwood has been suggesting that a successor be found and that he should be permitted to retire from office. Successive Committees have managed to persuade Sir Eric to continue whilst they have wrestled to no avail, with the problem of finding a worthy replacement - no mean task I am sure you will agree! CRUISER FLEET NEWS

Now that laying up has more or less finished and many of us have taken a look at or even taken up our moorings, there is a good opportunity to check over these vital items of equipment. A word of guidance might be useful regarding what is good practice for moorings.

A point often misunderstood with ground tackle is that electrolytic corrosion can be our worst enemy - far worse than abrasion and rust. The worst thing you can possibly do to a mooring chain is to put stainless steel wire onto your shackles. The combination of stainless steel and ordinary steel or iron produces an electrolytic cell which will rapidly destroy the shackle. Many an old hand has taken up his moring, found the shackle pins to be floating, held only by the wire and then said to others - "What a good thing I wired it or the pin would have fallen out". Poppycock!! If he hadn't made an electrolytic cell the pin and shackle would have been as sound as any other part of the chain. If you feel you must wire your shackles then the wire must be compatible with the chain and shackle. Galvanised iron wire does no harm but may not last very long. Monel will last forever but will cause just a little corrosion. I suppose belt and braces technique would be to put two shackles at every joint if the chain would accept them - I know which one would be in perfect condition at next inspection - the unwired one!

Finally on moorings - for anyone putting down new chain - the major cause of wear is movement between the links and the best investment is to put down the heaviest chain you can get. It will always move less and so wear less than a lighter chain, and when it has eventually worn a little will still be stronger and much heavier. However, movement causing abrasion is always more critical than simple rusting so it would be a waste of money to pay the extra for galvanised chain - the zinc coating will be removed in the first few weeks. The only exception is if you put a foot or so of chain on deck where you don't want rust marks.

When it comes to wire rigging the situation is completely different. One hopes the rigging is not immersed continuously in water and so the electrolytic business is not quite so important though must not be forgotten. On the other hand rigging shakes in the wind and I feel wiring is most important. Stainless rigging needs monel shackle wire. For galvanised rigging galvanised rigging in a mixture of boiled linseed oil and white spirit, then hang it up in the garage to dry. It should then last at least as long as stainless, which some people say can be brittle.

Finally, if you are still with me, an interesting observation on the above subject. If you have any assemblies of stainless steel, such as certain putley blocks for example, take a close look and see the rust forming at the junctions between two different samples of stainless steel'.

See you at the Generals Arms on the 1st Wednesday.

TUESDAY 2nd August

Up early, our baby alarm working to schedule, weather forcast was good and we were ready to leave as planned at 09.00. We beat down river with the last of the ebb and against the start of the flood to arrive out at the entrance about 2 hours after low water. We motored out of the Deben, Wendy throwing a well aimed line to Pelican, as she was having difficulty making over the tide, and we towed her out casting off after we had crossed the bar.

Sail was raised again and we had a most enjoyable sail into Harwich Harbour on into the River Orwell to Woolverstone where we found a berth in the marina along with Polaris 11 and Pelican.

We spent the evening in the Royal Harwich Y.C. who extended their usual pleasant welcome.

WEDNESDAY 3rd August

A large group set off this morning to walk along to Pin Mill and Chelmondiston for stores, then we went into the Butt and Oyster for lunch which we thought was good value for money. In the evening we followed a path along the river as far as Freston Tower then turned inland on footpaths which finally led back to Wolverston. The crew became quieter and quieter the further we went. I would do this more often if I was fit enough.

THURSDAY 4th August

We had decided to go to Walton backwaters today with Pelican, Polaris 11's crew wanted to stay another dayand then all meet again in Brightlingsea on Friday. Our intended 08.00 start was delayed due to fog until 10.00 which meant we missed the ebb. We motored out of the marina and across the river while Wendy was hoisting the sails and telling me how near the shore was. I thought I knew better and we went aground. Soon off as the tide was now flooding. It took us five hours to reach Stone Point which brought home the lesson about working the tides.

The S.W. wind was now increasihg raising doubts about our coastal passage tomorrow. Over a beer in the evening on 'Ace' with Alan and Vera we decided to listen to the 06.30 forecast tomorrow and decide then whether to go or not.

FRIDAY 5th August

06.30 forecast S.W. force 4-5 so we decided to go out and have a look. Weighed

- 6 -

anchor at 08.30. Sailed to Pye End buoy by 09.00 and were abeam of Stone Banks buoy by 09.35. The seas were rough and with the prospect of a beat down the coast in wind over tide conditions we decided to turn and go back to Pin Mill. Pelican could be seen ahead beating on. (We learnt later that they turned and went back to Walton) Just into Harwich Harbour we met Polaris 11 beating out and they turned around to join us. We picked up adjacent moorings at Pin Mill where we spent the rest of the day laying about. We decided to try again tomorrow.

SATURDAY 5th August.

06.30 forecast E to NE 4-5 occasional 6. As the wind was only about force 3 at present we decided to go as with luck we would be getting shelter from the shore further down the coast when we thought the wind would be strongest. Let go the mooring at 09.20 in company with Polaris 11. No.1 jib and main set. Left the Orwell at 10.10, worked the tides right this time! Once out of Harwich Harbour we realised the wind was stronger than anticipated, 'Ace's' handling made it apparent that we must reef. Wendy volunteered, she would rather be on deck than take the helm, I was unhappy about this as the waves were very steep about 6'-7' high, however in a joint effort we took down five rolls in the main and 'Ace' handled well again. The Naze Tower was abeam by 11.15 and as we were now running the jib was taken down to stop it flogging. Clacton pier was abeam at 12.35 and the seas and wind were moderating. Past the Bench Head buoy at 14.15 and picked up our mooring buoy at 15.30. Todays trip had been an experience for us as the seas were the worst we had been in and I was pleased with the performance of 'Ace' and her crew.

In conclusion we all felt our holiday cruise had been a pleasure, we hadn't covered a great distance but we had met some nice people, which is probably what a cruise is all about.

COMMODORE'S REPORT - 1978

It seems no time at all since we met here last year, but during that time many things have happened. Not the least some 300 races have been sailed, excluding our Regatta, and many successful cruisers have been made on waters near and far.

When you get wrapped up in the organisation and management of the Club it is easy to forget that we all joined to enjoy ourselves and if your Commodore and Officers always seem to be pleading for help it is because the Committee is trying very hard to provide you with the club it believes you want. They can only go so far, however, and if help is not sufficiently forthcoming some standards must decline.

I know from your very presence here tonight that those remarks do not apply to you. I certainly do not wish to imply that this year has not been anything other than successful or that the committee have in anyway been remiss. On the contrary they have all done sterling work and deserve the appreciation of us all.

I have however, detected a feeling that some of the enjoyment may have gone for that diminishing band of stalwarts who will always offer their services rather than see standards fall.

No! the ladies of the galley are not paid staff! Nor do any other helpers have any special privileges. I believe we must all take heed of this warning and share the work and responsibility willingly - it must be enjoyable for all! If you have any views on how we could improve our organisation please tell your committee as they do need your support.

After that cry from the heart I shall confine myself to the happenings of the year.

The lounge and exterior of the Clubhouse have been repainted. The lounge was decorated by our caretaker Claude Emerson who has again maintained the Club and its surroundings in a clean and tidy condition throughout the year. The lounge has been likened to an Art Gallery rather than a Sailing Club. They are nautical pictures after all but if anybody has any alternatives to offer lets 'have them'.

It is our intention that Claude will complete the decoration of the changing rooms and corridors, this winter.

Early in the year a severe storm damaged the sea wall and the site and the Clubhouse lower ground floor areas were flooded. Fortunately very little damage was caused, although the River Boards equipment made rather a mess of the dinghy park. It was however a reminder of the power of the sea and the fact that the sea wall is only just high enough! That is the reason why our newly aquired freezer cabinet is now standing in the lounge.

We have had several brushes with officialdom this year. Following the publishing of the River Blackwater Survey we were approached by the Maldon District Council with a request for a licence fee for siting our concrete hard and scrubbing parts on the foreshore. The sum of money involved was quite modest, but as a number of clubs had received similar requests and most were not satisfied with the terms and conditions of the licence the matter was referred to B.A.C.S.P.A. to investigate on everyones behalf. As a result of these investigations a new and more acceptable licence agreement is being drawn up.

Whilst on the subject of B.A.C.S.P.A. I must mention the able work done by Stan Allerton and Frank Savill who have only just relinquished their positions of Chairman and Secretary after 32 years of hardwork. Stan has agreed to continue on the B.A.C.S.P.A. Committee as our representative and Frank has agreed to rejoin our

- 4 -

Committee - a potential Flag Officer if ever I saw one!

In July we received another letter from the Council saying that Stansgate was situated in a zone on the South of the Blackwater where Camping and Caravaning amongst other things was forbidden without specific Planning Permission to do so. Application was immediately made and I am pleased to be able to report that we have been granted permission for the 28 days per year we requested, but only for a limited period until December 1981 when it will be necessary for us to re-apply. It therefore behoves us to be very circumspect in how we regulate and control our Camping if we wish to retain this permission in 1982. There were several legal objections to our applications. Our Camping marshal Jim Coy, ably assisted by Corrinne has laid the foundation for good camping behaviour but next year we will need to be very careful.

Our immediate neighbour has complained that members, particularly on busy camping weekends, trespass on her property. The Club has always enjoyed very good relations with its neighbours and I would ask you all to ensure that none of our members or visitors are allowed onto neighbouring land.

The River Blackwater has also become very popular as a potential Fishery for Oysters. The Committee have been watching developments very closely but so far nothing is planned which will prejudice our interests.

The Regatta is obviously the major event of the season. More races are sailed, more beer is drunk, more people visit the site than practically for all the rest of the year put together, and the exceptionally fine weather gave rise to a record attendance. The additional toilet facilities survived the onslaught.

The Barbecue however saw the other extreme and for the first time in many years the rain came and many people stayed away. This event requires almost as much physical effort from Club members as does the Regatta. The erection and removal next day of the Marquee, Bar, disco and barbecue scaffolding, equipment and covers is a mamouth task for a social evening. I am convinced we could well re-think the layout of this event and reduce the work load without detracting from the uniqueness of the occasion.

It was heartening to see the Cruiser Fleet and other social events taking place at Stansgate; it has always seemed a pity to me that we do not make greater use of our fine new Clubhouse on other than Sailing days.

The Sailing Programme will be reported on by our Sailing Secretary, but I should like to take this opportunity to thank him and all the Sailing team for organising such good sailing throughout the year.

The number of dinghy helms attending open meetings and winning glory for the Club has diminished considerably of late but support for the home series, particularly from our up and coming cadets has resulted in very vigorous and enthusiastic racing at the club. I chose those words carefully as I believe our knowledge of the racing rules and procedures is a little sketchy at the moment but this I am sure will improve with training and experience. It was certainly most gratifying to see the Cruiser Racing Series really beginning to take off.

Our collegues from Marconi Avionics at Rochester visited in force again and came very close to beating us.

A significant milestone in the history of the club was reached at the Laying Up Supper when Sir Eric Eastwood resigned from the Presidency of the Club. A small parting gift was made on your behalf as a memento to 25 years in office, and the last act of the retiring Committee was to bestow Honary Life Membership onto Sir Eric and Lady Eastwood and we hope to see both of them at Stansgate next summer.

ai She

Our new president eleci Jack Pateman has made the journey from Kent to be with us tonight and I hope you will make him welcome.

Security has continued to be of increasing concern. The Clubhouse doors and windows, and the gateway are frequently left open. Several items of members property have been stolen. We must all take more pride in our Club and make sure that everything is secure before the site is left unattended — security must become a ritual. The gatelock was broken open mid-season and the code key stolen. In view of this and the increasing number of cards lost or not returned, the committee have decided to change the security codes and issue new card keys to all members as they renew next season. ‘The locks will be changed on March lst 1979.

As outlined in Nuvigans the Committee consider that it is now necessary to increase our subscriptions. The subs have remained unchan,:ed for the last 3 seasons and it is intended that the increases proposed will see us through a further 3 years.

The major item of expenditure will be the repair and resurfacing of the road. for the past few years we have done the absolute minimum amount of work on the road in case the Marina Project came into being. Whilst this may yet still happen the prospect becomes more and more unlikely as time goes by. The road can be left no longer without running the risk of rapid and serious, ieterioration and astronomical expense.

To patch and shingle only the bad areas will cost around £1,500 and to tar and shingle most of the road in about 2 years time will cost a further £2,000 and we have been advised that it would be prudent to consider resurfacing every 5 years or so to retain a waterproof layer on the surface. We must therefore be putting aside some £60 per year just for road maintenance. Whilst we have a reserve capable of funding the initial stages of this work, we believe that we must maintain a reserve of around £2,000 in order to preserve our independence and cope with those unexpected expenses which pop up from time to time. ‘The immediate provision of new radio equipment plus the prospect of an increased rental contribution to the M.A.S.C. make it necessary for us to raise an additional £1,200 per annum over the next 3 years. This is roughly equivalent to £3 per membership — still very good value I believe.

I cannot finish without making a special reference to our lady members. Can you imagine the Club without Jill, Margaret and the galley team, without Shirley or Navigans, without Joyce and Pat in the bar, without lady Race Officers, without our Wives and girlfriends to feed us when we return from sailing or load the stores if we are going cruising? I hopenot all of us take you too much for granted.

Finally I would like to offer my personal thanks to the retiring committee and to the many members who have helped make my year of office so enjoyable and inparticular to David Lawson and the social committee for the Laying Up Supper
arrangements.

SOLO '78

With the 1978 season over for all but the most hardy I feel this is the right time to look back and see how the SOLO faired during its first season as a club class.

The average turnout in races prior to our Regatta, was less than 4, and I did begin to think that the fleet might not justify the status granted to it by the Club. However, apart from one early race when both Pete Rouson and I were at the Maylandsea Open Meeting, their have been sufficient entries for all class races in both the Spring and Summer series. By the end of the season the club had 12 Solos registered and 10 of us managed to get together for one of the Summer Points races. The fleet has seen some very keen close racing with an equal first in one race and an equal second in another.

One thing that is certain is that Solo (single handed) sailing with a una rig is different. This was perhaps best demonstrated during the Helmsman of the Year final when the participating helms each sailed 4 races using different boats. The Solo was voted the most difficult boat to sail on the day and I may have lost some potential fleet members. I thing I can counter the anti Solo feeling by saying that most if not all of the regular helms quickly find it a reasonable boat to sail. Norman Richards will tell you that it is more forgiving on the run than his previous boat, an Enterprise. I have also been pleased to see how well son Mark can cope and Colin Harper sailed particularly well in the final scratch race.

Performance can only be improved by competitive sailing, but not everyone wants to spend all the summer travelling. I personally find the number of available local Open Meetings a reasonable compromise. This year I managed to get to open meetings at Maylandsea, Harlow, King George and Dabchicks as well as the Nationals at Southend. We also had 15 boats at our Regatta and a separate class at the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships. I am sure my performance is improved by this competition. One of our local helms, Ian Shaw of Maylandsea, sailed into second place at the Nationals but my own placing of 24th was the next best th t the Blackwater could offer. Blackwater Clubs entered a total of 14 boats at the Nationals.

SARLCIFA 4

What of next year. I hope that our numbers will increase further. There are a number of rumours of new bouts, re-built boats and new helms. We will have to wait and see. One fact is that Eleanor Witter has joined the fleet having recently purchased a wooden boat from the south coast.

If as a club we have as many boats out next year as we have this year, I for one will enjoy sailing SOLO in '79.

THE NAUTICAL MILE

The length of a nautical mile in relation to navigation

When I was young, I looked out of the club windows across the marshes into the far distance and it seemed to me that the earth was flat. When I went to my first school, I told my teacher that the earth was flat. "No" she said, "That is not so} it is a sphere." "What does that mean?"”. "It means that it is round like a ball" I wrote that the earth was a sphere and they thought me so clever th t they sent me to Grammar school. I told the geography master that I knew that the earth was a sphere. "No" he said, "It is a spheroid". Wet does that mean?" "It means that it is slightly flattened at the Poles". I wrote down that the earth was a spheroid, and they thought me so clever that they put me in the sixth form. I told the Senior Geography master that I knew that the earth was a spheroid. "No" he said, "That is not se; it is an oblate spheroid! "What does that mean?" "It means that one Pole is flattened a bit more then the other". I wrote that the earth was an oblate spheroid and they thought me so clever that they sent me to University. I told my Tutor that I knew that the earth was an oblate spheroid. "No," s aid he, "That is not so; it is a geoid". "What does that mean?". "It means, earth shaped," He replied:

(Note:- Greek, Geios means "To do with the earth")

How does all this affect our navigation?

Although there are 360 degrees in a circle, because of the flattening of the earth at the poles, they are not all of the same length. At the equator their
length is 1842 metres, while at the poles, they are 1861 metres. However, the
Admiratly issued a notice to MarinersNo: 1518 in 1970 announcing that the
International nautical mile was precisely 1852 meters, which is, in fact, the length of a sea mile in latitude 45 degrees. When we wish to measure distance on our charts, we place our dividers along the (vertical) latitude and@le which caters for the variation in length at different latitudes and are therefore quite safe in taking one minute as being the length of a sea-mile for that
particular chart. In other words, we have no need to worry - all this has
been thoughtfully provided for on t e charts which we use.

Eric Payne.

1978 Sailing Report

The 1978 season saw two new fleets in the club, the 420 and Solo. These fleets to date are totalling 14 & 17 respectively, with additions to both certain before the commencement of the 79 season.

The dinghy series last season saw average entries for the Spring Series ranging from 3 for the Enterprise to 7.5 for the 420 & the Summer Series averaging between 3.5 for the Enterprise to 7.6 for the 420. The most popular races which were scheduled during the season was the Wednesday Evening Races, these attracted a total number of 156 boats, averaging at 13 per race.

The Cruiser Barnacle Series has received anincreased interest last year, with four races scheduled. There was a total of 12 cruisers entered during the series with 6 competing in 3 out of 4 races to qualify. It is planned that with increased interest this series will be extended to 6 races for the 1979 season.

The Mona Cup, Pilots Cup & Mud Race received entries of 29, 17 & 25 respectively the former two racesencompassing part of the Barnacle Series.

The two Open Trophy races attracted entries of 35 for the Dinghy Challenge Cup & 24 for the Cruiser Cup. The Dinghy Challenge Cup unfortunately a victimof the English Summeron the scheduled date with the race on the reserved date suffering from entries.

The Hornet/Mirror Open meetinghad an entry of 30 Hornets and 24 Mirrors. The Hornet entry attracted one of the largest entries to date. It has been planned to arrange additionally a Solo Open Event in 1979.

The rescue boat organisation during the past season has seen a great improvement under the auspicies of Norman Kerridge. The number of drivers for this duty was kept small by design & this system has enabled rescue facilities to be manned regularly. Our thanks must goto Norman Kerridge & his team of drivers from all club members, with the knowledge that they are there if required during racing.

The race officer manning unfortunately has hot been in the same position. There has been the regular group of experienced members who covered this duty but more experienced members are required and to hold Race Officer instruction during one of the forthcoming Winter Meetings with follow up work at Stansgate next spring. Anyone interested will be welcome.

Finally thanks to all the Fleet Captains and members of the Sailing Committee for the help during the past year.

M.J. Vaughn.

SPRING SAILING

The calender on my kitchen wall is trying to tell me that Spring isn't far away, while the appearance of paint and anti-fouling colourcharts and the smell of varnish emanating from the lounge shout out the fact that the fitting out has begun. In a few weeks time, amongst a melée of daffodils, Easter eggs, why haven't I washed the sails yet, and where oh where are all the East Coast charts, the sailing season will have begun again.

With this in mind, I thought members might welcome a couple of suggestions for trips at the beginning of the cruising season. During April and May, the weather can be a bit nippy and unreliable and a short sail with somewhere to go at the end of it is more appreciated by the family than roaring off to the Bench Head and back, when everyone except Dad gets cold, wet and miserable and it all takes too long.

So, where to go, first there's Bradwell. A quick sail down river to the power station, turn right and you're there. A couple of points to mention, the channel is very tortuous and should be negotiated with care. Follow the witheys and buoys, it is very easy to run aground on the mud banks. Excellent practise for making a passage using the echo-sounder, a useful job for a junior crew member calling out the depth. Moorings are available in the creek and there is usually someone around to ask it it's O.K. to pick one up.

There is also the marina, convenient for taking on water and fuel, but it is expensive. For a warm welcome ashore you don't have to go far, just walk up the slipway and stop at the first building on the right, The Bradwell Quay Sailing Club. Here, the majority of members are cruiser owners and although they have a comprehensive, keen racing fleet, there are plenty of potters to exchange gossip with over a pint or two.

We called here during the autumn last year, and met Bill Basson, one of the founder members, who due to an injury received in the war, looks like a benevolent Captain Hook when he gives you a wave. We were invited to a "Pirate's Evening" and for a £1 a head, no charge for children, we had an excellent cold supper, and there was draft Abbott and a band as well. All very informal and pleasant. If you like walking, it's very pleasant to stroll round the village and if you really like walking you can go to St. Peter's on the Wall, the first church in England.

Another easily reached port of call is Heybridge Basin. Just leave the moorings and head up River towards Maldon and stop at the "Jolly Sailor". Here, one can lock into Heybridge Canal, although a few moorings are available on the river. The lock is small, but good practise with fenders and warps, if you are thinking of being adventerous and going foreign later in the season. It is good manners to let the lock-keeper, George Clarke, know you are coming if a few boats intend to go together.

Once safely moored up in the canal, and if you can get Dad out of the pub, put the outboard onto the stern of the tender and potter up the canal to Beeleigh. It's well worth the effort. The factories and cottages built by Bentalls at the turn of the century are reminders that Heybridge was then a thriving industrial community and not the rather sleepy backwater we know today. You pass around the back of Maldon alongside the golf course and then up to the first lock at Beeleigh. Here you can wander around the outskirts of the Abbey grounds or along the tiny country lanes edged with oak and horse chestnut trees in the meadows, beds of wild watercress grow, dark and green.

This trip is more fun in company, and ideal for children, big or small, when you can play dogems with one another or race someone along the tow path. You can even stop off at the shops and buy the odd Mars bar.

As I said previously, the idea of these two "excursions" is an hour or two's

sailing for Dad, combined with an outing for the family. For all the information proper required, you should beg, borrow or buy a copy of Jack Coote's "East Coast Rivers". Bradwell Sailing Club produce a very useful chart showing the creek and it's entrance with all the relevant marks in full, which is well worth acquiring.

This article was written with new cruiser owners also in mind, who are about to discover the delights of sailing the Blackwater. May I wish everyone good sailing in 1979.

Brenda Tate.

SAFETY

Just a timely reminder to all members whilst the water conditions are cold and the weather unpredictable. The following notes are recommendations for all time at the club.

1) Officer of the Day:
a) Responsible for safety in the vicinity of the Club.
b) Ensure that the Rescue crew have access to their equipment and the boat(s). Club events should be postponed if the available facilities cannot cope with the prevailing conditions.
Maintain radio contact with the rescue boat. (This responsibility may be delegated to the Race Officer).

2) Race Officer:
a) Check off the competitors at the start and as may times as is practical during the race. Report any missing boats to the rescue crew.
b) Ensure that any boat not completing the course has returned safely.

3) Rescue Crew:
a) Check the boats sailing as often as is practical and if any are missing confirm their whereabouts.
b) When the racing has got underway take up station near the gybe mark in heavy weather or downtide in very light weather. In medium conditions a central position can be chosen.

4) Members:
a) Ensure personal equipment and boat is adequate for the conditions. If the weather is such that you will not be able to cope do not venture out, ask if in doubt.
b) If, however you do require assistance on the water, stay with the boat and wave arms up and down. Do not use more energy than can be helped and drop anchor if in danger of drifting away.
c) If racing sign off immediately afterwards, this is most important when retiring.

John Weedon,
Rear Commodore.

1979 GILTONIAN WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP FOR 18FT SKIFFS

-

SYDNEY HARBOUR

Just before Christmas I received an invitation from the New South Wales 18 footers Sailing Club in Sydney, to participate in the forthcoming Giltonian World 18 foot Skiff Championship, to be sailed in the Harbour.

With snow lying thick on the ground I decided that, in spite of a very pregnant wife, and an imminent house move, this was an offer I couldn't refuse. Travelling expenses were to be met by British Airways, who had also chartered the Australian "Overseas Containers Limited" boat for the event - all I had to do was get in it and sail it. Unfortunately my crew once again were to be left behind. Sailing an Eighteen is very much coordinated teamwork by 3 specialists, all jobs are equi-important and a scratch Australian crew, however good, would not substitute for the 4 years that Bob Fawkes, David Elphinstone and myself have sailed together.

After the snow and 24 hours sitting in a 747, stepping into the Sydney sunshine was like stepping into Paradise. All the British team had arrived at least one week previously and had quite established suntans, made me feel like a maggot by comparison! After the initial Board of Control meeting - the Board governs the affairs of the "Titles" and is comprised of the member clubs throughout the World, I went to see "British Airways". The boat was beautifully turned out sporting the British Airways logo lettering up the side in red and blue, and 8ft diameter smiling cartoon Jumbo's, B A's latest advertising gimmick, on the mainsails. The boat was of very light wooden construction - about 160 lbs with rope and fittings, excellently built using Cedar and Gaboon ply. A glance around the dinghy park however, showed that in the past year tremendous advancements have been made, particularly with plastics and foam on paper honeycomb cores. At Plymouth, all the Australian contingent with the exception of "Color 7" were wooden, now all the top twelve boats are plastic reinforced with aluminium "space" frames to take the stress points. Mechanical rig tensioning gear, has in many cases been dropped, in favour of hydraulic mast jacks. "Color 7" still retains a mechanical system at 64:1 on each shroud, but has boxed the whole tension system in along the hog in case one of the muscle boxes 'explodes' damaging someone's foot.

Masts are now moving aft, and so correspondingly are rudders, which are being slung from sponsors about 9" to 1' behind the transom, and of course, they're still getting lighter - or so any true Australian Eighteen sailor would have you believe.

Ingenuity is the watchword. Simple ideas such as sprinkling sugar on to wet varnish or resin to create a nonslip finish, the sugar simply disolves away, leaving a rough finish, but no messy sand for fitting out next time round. "Clam Cleats" are extensively used (metal version), however the Australians streamline them by filing away unwanted metal and drilling lightening holes in them. Just a few grams saved, but the top racing is very, very close and no gear lightening is too much trouble.

Incentives to win are high, an Australian 18ft Champion is ranked among the leading sportsmen, and will undoubtedly be featured sometime on Television and in the papers. He also has to consider the new boat for the coming season, which may cost over $35,000 (approx £18,700) for one year, poor results will mean the sponsor will either pull out, or look for more promising materials - only the winners get publicity.

5

Innovation in the Eighteens, for many years was slow in coming. Like so many classes the crews were not prepared to look around for inspiration from other dinghy sailors and failed to take stock of the changing techniques.

Bruce Farr arrived on the scene in 1970 and developed a line of light weight, wooden, functional thoroughbreds for 3 handed sailing, 70 lbs lighter than anything designed before. Furthermore, the bouyancy incorporated into the hull shape of each design was geared to fit the crew weight expected to sail in the boat, along with the exact requirements and details for the sailplan and the rig change and wind speed.

Farr's designs reigned supreme for 5 World Championships until 18 year old Main Murray appeared with a radical, 10ft beamed boat, sponsored by Color 7 T V. The Murray/Color 7 combination have now won 3 World Titles in succession, and Murray has led the Eighteens from "night" into "day", by revolutionising construction methods and making the glass fibre/paper honeycomb core construction work. His designs are faster than Farr's and carry incredible amounts of sail - almost as much as the old 4 handers. He is a crack 12 footer sailor (much harder to sail than an 18 footer), and bared his ideas on the radical Twelves. He incorporated high freeboard, hitherto frowned on because of the extra weight of higher sides, wide aft chines and a very 'U' shaped forward entry for improving "nose-dive" characteristics. Perhaps this progress is the good side of sport sponsorship, development has now reached fever pitch and the money is there to see new ideas succeed or fail, anyway, new ideas have now come along to benefit all dinghy sailors - if they care to look that is, and progress makes development in the 470 and Flying Dutchman look Mediæval.

I won't bore you with details of my efforts in Sydney, fact is we weren't so hot, but certainly one of the biggest problems for all competitors were the washes set up by the spectator craft. Hundreds of people turn out in craft of all shapes and sizes to watch the Eighteens. The water's natural wave pattern soon gets broken up into large confused seas. On the fourth race British Airways was doing about 18 knots with the biggest Spinnaker set, and the crew all trapezeing ("three stringing under the biggy" - Australian slang), when we happened upon two large converging washes. I had no option but to steer for the centre of the subsequent eruption, only to find as we careered over the crest there was no water beyond, just a large trough. With nothing under the keel of course we just nosedived and that was that.

The following race we found ourselves on the wind with "ITEL Computers" just above us. Gear failure aboard "ITEL" caused her to capsize slowly, but as she did so her mast head picked up my trapeze wire. The next second I was hoisted 15ft in the air as the wire was pulled by British Airways across ITEL's mast head. I must have hit a shroud on the way up, as my face felt as if it would fall in two. With no one at the helm, and my Aussie crew, Phil and Les looking extremely worried, British Airways never faltered, and sailed straight and true. The next second I was back in the drink and swinging back to my position on the side. Undamaged, I might add! However, while British Airways fuddled about, the real battle was between "Color 7", "Steelstocks" and "KB". The racing was filmed by the "Color 7" Helicopter and Launches, and we were able to view the smooth operations of the leaders on TV in the evening sport's bulletins.

I'm afraid to say that we in British Airways did not do so well, finishing 3rd out of the 4 British Skippers and 29th out of 34 overall, a result which will take a lot of living down. Entries were received from America, Italy, France, New Zealand, Australia and of course Great Britain, and the Eighteen now appears international if only in small quantities.

Bruce Long
